CALL FOR PAPERS DEADLINE  April 4, 2005


Abstract Submission:


ISTFA 2005 will consider abstracts in English only (two-page minimum) including representative images, figures  and references.  It is highly advisable to include sufficient detail to allow for fair evaluation of the work discussed.  Also, include the following information for all authors, presenting author listed first: complete name, title, affiliation  with complete mailing address, telephone and fax numbers, and email address.  This information must be  included with the abstract or it will not be considered for evaluation.  Please go to www.edfas.org/istfa to  submit your abstract.  The deadline for final submission is April 4, 2005.


Manuscript & Presentation Submissions:


All authors accepted into the ISTFA 2005 Symposium are required to submit a full manuscript and presentation in  electronic format.  Pre-approval to present your work at ISTFA 2005 is highly recommended to ensure ontime submission.  All costs associated with your participation will be at your expense (travel, housing, registration, etc.).


For inquiries or information on ISTFA 2005, you may contact:  ISTFA Conference Administrator, ASM


International, Materials Park, Ohio 44073-0002 440.338.5151, www.edfas.org/istfa

Microscopy at the Nanoscale


William E. Vanderlinde and Vincent W. Ballarotto


Laboratory for Physical Sciences, College Park, Maryland, USA


Introduction


One of the greatest challenges of working with nano-scale


devices is imaging and characterizing features on such a small  scale. Although there are a number of microscopy tools with  nanometer or near-nanometer resolution, each tool has  specific limitations. This paper compares the use of different  microscopy tools for characterizing several types of nanodevices. We show that the most information can be obtained  by using several complementary tools to analyze each device.  This paper also provides a survey of the more common nanoscale devices such as carbon nano-tubes, fluorescent nanoparticles, and molecular conductors. These devices can  currently only be fabricated as prototypes but they represent  the future of microelectronics as Moore’s law drives device  size below the scaling limit of traditional transistors.


Techniques


Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was performed using a  LEO 1550 FE SEM with a nominal spot size of 1 nm at 20  keV. Two non-standard techniques were used in the SEM: scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM-in-SEM) and forward scattered electron imaging (FSEI). In both cases, the non-standard SEM techniques were implemented by using  special sample holders.


STEM-in-SEM


A typical “STEM-in-SEM” holder is shown in schematic in  Fig. 1 and in an optical photo in Fig. 2. [1] A thin film sample  is mounted on top of a graphite block. After passing through  the thin film, the electron beam travels down a narrow hole  drilled in the graphite block. By absorbing the most highly  scattered electrons, the graphite block collimates the beam  which improves the image resolution. After passing through  the collimator, the electrons strike a pair of gold reflectors that  create secondary electrons which are collected by the ordinary  in-chamber secondary electron detector. Alternately, one can  invest in a dedicated STEM-in-SEM detector which can be  added to some SEM models. The STEM-in-SEM allows one  to achieve very high resolution in the SEM, see Fig. 3. STEMin-SEM is a useful alternative to STEM or TEM because (1) it


# Microscopy at the Nanoscale


is much less expensive and more widely available, (2) the  sample size is not limited to 3 mm, and (3) it can be used for  high resolution x-ray mapping which is not available in many  TEMs.


Figure 1: Design for a “STEM-in-SEM” sample holder. The  overall height is 2.5 cm.


Figure 2: Optical photo of the STEM-in-SEM sample holder  mounted to the SEM stage. The pole piece of the objective lens  is visible above the sample holder.

Figure 3: STEM-in-SEM image of an aluminum line  connected to a tungsten plug contact. The barrier layer and  the plug liner are visible.


FSEI


Forward scattered electron imaging (FSEI) also uses a special  sample holder in a SEM, but unlike STEM-in-SEM it does not  require any special sample preparation. [2] When a high  energy electron beam enters a sample at a very shallow tilt  angle, a significant fraction of the incident electrons will be  forward scattered from the sample surface. The forward  scattered electrons that undergo the smallest amount of  deflection will carry very high spatial resolution and surface  sensitive image information. The FSEI holder is designed to  collect the forward scattered electrons with the smallest  angular deflection.  The FSEI holder places the sample at high  tilt angle to the beam. The forward scattered high-energy  electrons will strike a gold reflector and create secondary  electrons that are collected by the SEM’s regular secondary  electron detector. The holder is designed with the sample  surface pointed away from the secondary detector so that only  the forward scattered electrons contribute to the image.


FSEI is significantly different from secondary electron  imaging (SEI) since in FSEI the image is formed by scattered  electrons from the incident beam, not secondary electrons  from the sample. Although backscattered electron (BSE) images are also formed by electrons from the incident beam, backscattered electrons generally penetrate deep into the  sample and the resulting images are not surface sensitive and  often lack high spatial resolution. FSEI is most similar to  scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) since in  both cases the image contrast is produced by scattering of the  incident electron beam in the sample. FSEI might almost be

It has been found that FSEI images have very high spatial  resolution, good surface sensitivity, and are largely immune to  charging, even when using high beam voltage on insulators  like photoresist, see Fig. 6.

PEEM


The photoelectron emission microscope (PEEM) is a novel  microscope that has several features such as good spatial  resolution, real-time imaging, and unique contrast mechanisms  that may be useful for failure analysis.  [3] The novelty of the  microscope is due to the fact that the imaging electrons are  photoelectrons generated by absorption of UV light in the  specimen.  The spatial distribution of emitted photoelectrons  is used to form an image of the sample surface in real-time  with no rastering.  In the typical experimental arrangement, the sample is grounded while the first imaging element is held  at 10 kV.  As a consequence, the excited photoelectrons are  accelerated toward the imaging column of the microscope, see  Fig. 7.  The electrons then pass through an additional series of  electrostatic lens that magnify the image.  Finally, the image is  projected onto a phosphor screen after the intensity is  amplified with a multi-channel plate and is recorded for  analysis.


Experiments were conducted with a commercial-built PEEM (Staib 350) mounted in an ultra-high vacuum stainless steel  chamber in which imaging is done in a vacuum of  approximately 5 x 10-9 Torr.  It has a nominal spatial  resolution of 80 nm with a 200 micron field of view that  allows video rate analysis.  Samples were mounted  approximately 4 mm away from the aperture lens on a 5-axis  positioning stage that allowed adjustment of the sample  normal to within 1º.  The light source is a 100 W mercury  short-arc lamp that produces a continuous broad-band  spectrum up to approximately 5.2 eV.  A chevron-type multichannel plate is used to intensify the image.  The final images  were recorded with a CCD camera.


Figure 7: Block diagram of photo emission electron  microscopy system.


AFM


Atomic force microscopy (AFM) was performed in a Digital  Instruments Dimension 3100 in tapping mode. AFM works by  measuring the deflection of a small tip that is scanned in close  proximity to a sample surface The silicon cantilever tip has a  radius of curvature of about 12.5 nm. AFM can provide very  accurate vertical height and horizontal distance measurements, but the curved tip limits the capability to correctly image high  aspect ratio features as shown in Fig. 8.


Figure 8: AFM tip with radius of curvature R scanning across  a high aspect ratio sample.


Nanodevices


Fluorescent nano-particles


Metal particles below approximately 50 nm diameter display  unusual fluorescent properties that depend on the diameter and  shape of the particle rather than the electron transitions in the  band structure. The fluorescence emission wavelength can be  finely tailored by adjusting the particle diameter, and  nanoparticles coated by dielectric can be used to enhance the  natural fluorescence of biological materials such as DNA. Fluorescent nano-particles have found applications in  biological sensing and labeling, and as unique tags, and are  being investigated for data storage applications.  [4]


In developing a method to fabricate metal nano-particles, it is  necessary to measure the height, shape, diameter, and density  of nano-particles. Fig. 9a shows a scanning electron  microscope (SEM) image of fluorescent silver nano-particles  deposited on a silicon substrate by electron beam evaporation. Particle size, density, and shape are easily observed, however  the height of the particles is difficult to determine.


Fig. 9b shows an atomic force microscope (AFM) image. The  AFM data provides a very precise measurement of the height  of the particles. However, the particle size and shape are  distorted due to a tip-convolution effect. Since the particles  are approximately the same size as the AFM tip, one sees a  convolution of the tip shape with the nano-particle shape  rather than the true nano-particle shape. The result is that the  particles appear to be roughly 25 nm larger in diameter in the  AFM image and somewhat more rounded as compared to the


SEM image. The SEM image also shows larger gaps between  the particles and a lower surface coverage of metal.


100nm

Figs. 9a and 9b: Identical magnification SEM and AFM  images of fluorescent silver nanoparticles ~ 50 to 100 nm in  diameter.


More extreme distortion is seen in Fig. 10 where the particles  are smaller than the AFM tip. SEM images show that the  nano-particles are about 5 to 10 nm in diameter while the tip is  about 25 nm in diameter. Consequently, a convolution of the  particle and tip shapes causes the particles to all appear  circular and about 25 nm in diameter in the AFM image. Because the AFM tip is larger than the particles the AFM  image gives no useful information about the particle size or  shape, although it does still give a good height measurement. Thus the SEM and AFM images are complementary and both  are necessary to provide the best characterization of the nanoparticles.

Carbon Nanotubes


Carbon nanotubes are one of the most promising  nanostructures for device electronics. A carbon nanotube is a


cylindrical network of carbon atoms which can range from  one nm to several nm in diameter and up to several microns


1um


long, see Fig. 13. They can be thought of as a sheet of  graphite rolled into a tube, with half a buckyball on either end. Depending on the orientation of the lattice with respect to the  tube axis, a tube will be metallic or semiconducting. Carbon  nanotubes have extraordinary mechanical, thermal, and  electron properties. They are incredibly stiff and tough  mechanically and are the strongest known fibers.  Carbon  nanotubes conduct heat as well as diamond at room  temperature.  Carbon nanotubes are very sharp, and thus can  be used as probe tips for scanning-probe microscopes, and


5


field-emission electron sources for lamps and displays.  The  mobility of semiconducting nanotubes is higher than 100,000  cm2/V-s at room temperature, higher than any other known  semiconductor. Simple electronic switches and memory  devices have been demonstrated. [5]


Figure 13: Diagram of a carbon nanotube, not to scale. The  diameter may be 1 to 5 nm but the length is up to several


3HL#E000ASignalA=MPSEDate:28 Apr 2004


thousand times longer than the diameter.


Because of their very small diameter, carbon nanotubes are  difficult to image with ordinary microscopes. Individual  nanotubes are invisible in optical microscopes, and in the  SEM they are only show good contrast when using a passive  voltage contrast technique. Unfortunately, when using passive  voltage contrast the nanotubes appear to be hundreds of nm  wide and their true diameter is not apparent, see Fig. 14. AFM  measurements can determine the tube diameter but this is a  tedious process that takes about 100 times longer than  imaging with a SEM. Nanotube diameter is a critical  parameter and it would be very useful to be able to measure  many tube diameters rapidly.

However, the PEEM image is very useful for  locating grains of iron catalyst that is used to initiate the  nanotube growth. The iron particles show up as very bright  spots in the PEEM image.

Pentacene Films


Pentacene is an organic molecule which acts as a  semiconductor and can be fabricated into nano-scale  transistors. [6] The pentacene grain size and surface  morphology are critical, especially where the material is


FOV~89μm


deposited over a metal-insulator interface. Several different  SEM techniques were used to image the pentacene surface  including low voltage SEM, intermediate voltage SEM on a  sputter coated sample, and forward scattered scanning electron  imaging. The 1 kV SEM image (Fig. 17) provides an excellent  sense of the surface texture but the image looks somewhat  fuzzy due to the limited source brightness and large spot size  of the SEM at low voltage. The 5 kV image (Fig. 18) is very  poor due to the large beam penetration and poor surface  sensitivity of the image. Sputter coating the sample (Fig. 19) improves the image somewhat, but some surface detail is  obscured and sputter grain artifacts are introduced. The  forward scattered image (Fig. 20) is extremely sharp and  surface sensitive but the sense of surface texture is not quite as  good as the low voltage image. For this material, a  combination of low voltage (1 kV) SEM and forward  scattered (30 kV) imaging provides the most information.

Break-junctions are used to characterize nano-devices and  materials such as single-molecule conductors, see Fig. 21. [7,8] A basic test structure is defined by photo-lithography  and fabricated in aluminum metal, such that separate electrical


connections are made to a number of large (~ 2 micron) gaps, see Fig. 22. The large gaps are bridged by individual 50 nm  wide gold wires, fabricated by direct write electron beam  lithography and metal lift-off. A current is applied to each line  and the voltage is increased until electromigration forms a  small gap, resulting in a sudden increase in resistance. In  many cases the final gap resistance is on the order of 1 G Ω, typical for tunneling across the gap, which indicated a gap  distance of a few nm or less. The result is a set of test probes  with gaps on the order of a few nm, see Fig. 23. Materials  such as organic conductors can then be applied across the

Conclusion


Imaging at the nanoscale presents challenges that may require  the use of several different microscopy techniques to obtain  the most information. Scanned probe techniques such as AFM  and STM have very high resolution but suffer from low scan  rates and tip convolution effects. Low voltage SEM is very  surface sensitive but has limited resolution since SEMs have  large spot size at low voltage. SEM resolution is improved at  higher beam voltage but may require sputter coating which  obscures the surface and introduces sputter grain artifacts. A  new technique called forward scattered scanning electron  microscopy permits the use of high beam voltage (30 kV) to  be used while retaining a surface sensitive image, so it appears  to be ideal for many nano-technology applications.

# Polarization Difference Probing: A New Phase Detection Scheme for Laser Voltage Probing


Polarization Difference Probing: A New Phase Detection Scheme for Laser Voltage Probing


William Lo, Nagamani Nataraj, Nina Boiadjieva, Praveen Vedegarbha, and Kenneth Wilsher


Credence Systems, DCG, 150 Baytech Drive, San Jose, CA, 95134-2302, USA


Abstract


A novel laser based technique for waveform probing of integrated circuits is presented. This new technique exploits polarization-dependent opto-electronic effects in silicon integrated circuits to give phase sensitivity via a simple common-path interferometer design. The system utilizes a 10-ps pulse-width mode-locked laser  to generate equivalent-time sampling pulses. A custom wavelength-tunable and spectrally matched external-cavity laser diode source is used for noise cancellation. A 20-GHz intrinsic system bandwidth with a 2x lower noise-floor, in comparison to current laser voltage probing technology, is shown.

Internal signal probing in CMOS circuits is a critical capability for efficiently ramping from prototypes to volume production of advanced integrated circuits. The first probing tools, mainly mechanical and electron-beam probers, required direct access to metal lines in order to make a measurement.


However, with the advent of flip-chip packaging and the increasing number of interconnect layers, signal lines are no longer easily accessible. As a result, alternative probing technologies were developed.


The first commercially available optical backside probing tool was introduced in 1997, driven mainly by the introduction of flip-chip packaging in the mainstream microprocessor market.


This system, known popularly as the Laser Voltage Probe(LVP), used a non-contact, through-silicon technique for measuring the electrical activity inside an integrated circuit(IC). It has been used successfully to probe CMOS logic ICs,even in geometries as small as 90 nm.


More recently, time-resolved emission (TRE) has become a very popular and useful tool for internal signal probing. Based on significant advances in lens and infrared photon detection technology, TRE has surpassed LVP as the tool-of-choice for most debug labs. Its main advantages are high reliability, easeof-use, completely non-invasive operation, and SOI


compatibility. However, the bandwidth of practical TRE technology is limited to about 8-GHz. Bandwidths of 10-GHz may be possible, but represent significant technological challenges.


We are investigating a new measurement technique that can achieve a bandwidth of 20-GHz. The technique is similar to LVP but uses a fundamentally new acquisition scheme based on polarization-dependent opto-electronic effects in silicon. It incorporates a new phase-detection mode that is less optomechanically complex, has better noise immunity, and is far easier to set up and use than the Phase Interferometric Detection (PID) mode used in the last generation of LVP systems. The improved noise immunity, together with the use of a custom laser-diode source, gives the new technique significantly better signal sensitivity. In the lab, we have demonstrated a noise floor 2x lower than the best LVP system. The higher signal sensitivity and the use of an ~10-ps pulse-width mode-locked laser source makes a 20-GHz intrinsic bandwidth feasible. The new features of the technique are described and preliminary data taken using an engineering test-bed is presented in this paper.


Laser voltage probing


In LVP, the electrical activity of an IC is predominantly encoded in the phase of the 1064-nm laser beam reflected from the active regions of the IC. To detect this phase information, a Michelson interferometer is used in the current PID mode (Figure 1).[1] One arm of the Michelson interferometer contains the DUT while the other arm contains a reference mirror. Interference (or ‘mixing’) of the reflected beams from both arms converts relative phase modulations between the beams into intensity modulations. To maximize stability, the interferometer is positioned as closely to the DUT as possible and is incorporated into the laser scanning microscope (LSM) used to deliver the laser beam to the DUT. In the diagram of the PID optics shown in Figure 1, the laser beam is incident from the upper-left. To monitor laser power fluctuations, a 5% beam splitter (5% BS) is used to ‘pick-off’


1


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa009


a small portion of the beam. The polarizing beam splitter(PBS) cube is oriented to reflect the remainder to the 10%beam splitter (10% BS) where 90% of the beam is directed into the DUT arm and 10% is directed into the reference arm of the Michelson interferometer. The beams retro-reflected from the DUT and reference-arm mirror are spatially recombined at the 10% BS. They are then transmitted through the PBS and interfere to form the reflected signal. [Doublepass through the quarter-wave plate (λ/4) in each arm rotates the polarization state of the pulses by 90 degrees.]


The reference arm mirror is mounted on a piezo-electric actuator for fine adjustments of the relative phase (i.e., path length) difference between the two interferometer arms.


Coarse path-length differences (due, for example, to differences in die thickness, or the use of a diamond heat spreaders) can be compensated for by adjustment of the finepitch screw.

Figure 1. Diagram of the original LVP phase-detection scheme (PID-mode). BS: Beam Splitter, PBS: Polarizing Beam Splitter, λ/4: Quarter-Wave Plate, p/o: pick-off. A Michelson interferometer (consisting of the DUT and Reference arms) is used to convert phase modulations into amplitude modulations. The dotted arrows above the 10% BS indicate the portion of the retro-reflected DUT and Reference arm beams that is lost.


While PID mode can give a significant improvement in waveform signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compared to the original amplitude-sensitive LVP mode, it requires careful and time consuming set up of the phase conversion parameters by the user.[1] These parameters include DUT/reference-arm power matching, path-length matching, and phase-offset value(a small, deliberately introduced, path-length difference between the DUT and reference arms). The PID system is also optically and mechanically complicated due to the space constraints inside the LSM, which can adversely affect system reliability.


The LVP phase signal is extracted with the help of sophisticated noise reduction techniques that includes active feedback control of the reference arm path length and a duallaser, equivalent-time-sampling scheme.[2] Without these noise reduction techniques, extracting the ∼1000-ppm LVP signal modulations buried in the 100,000-ppm to 200,000-ppm reflected beam modulations caused by vibrational noise would be impractical.


In the dual-laser noise reduction scheme, illustrated in Figure 2, paired measurements are made during each repetition of the DUT signal using sampling pulses from two lasers. The ∼35-ps wide sampling pulses from a mode-locked laser (MLL) are swept in time through the signal of interest, in the manner of equivalent-time sampling, to measure the electrical DUT activity. The ∼150-ns sampling pulses generated by externally chopping the output of a continuous-wave laser (CWL), on the other hand, are held stationary in time with respect to the signal. The CWL pulses are thus made to be insensitive to DUT signal variations. Any low frequency DUT vibrations,however, affect both MLL and CWL pulses. Referencing the MLL measurements against the CWL measurements for each pass of the signal, therefore, removes the common-mode noise


0-0-0-1


caused by DUT vibrations.

Figure 2. Dual-laser noise reduction scheme. Three repetitions of the DUT signal to be measured are shown. For each pass of the signal, paired measurements are made using the pulses from a mode-locked laser (MLL) and from an externally modulated continuous-wave laser (CWL). Taking the ratio of the MLL to CWL measurements for each pass reduces the effects of common-mode noise, such as that due to mechanical DUT vibrations.


As will be shown, the effectiveness of the dual-laser scheme depends crucially on how well the MLL and CWL pulses are matched with respect to their interactions with both the DUT and the system optics. Important parameters are wavelength,coherence length/spectral width, and peak-power.


Polarization Difference Probing


Polarization sensitivity of LVP signal


The new Polarization Difference Probing (PDP) mode takes advantage of the natural polarization dependence of the LVP signal. This polarization dependence is thought to originate from the intrinsic asymmetry of CMOS transistors (Figure 3)and has been detected in CMOS ICs fabricated in 0.35-µm to 65-nm processes using a test bench/prototype PDP system.


For maximum Franz-Keldysh Effect (electro-absorption/


↑


refraction), the laser beam’s polarization state should be aligned parallel to the direction of the strong modulating fields in the gate/drain regions of the transistor, i.e., along the gate length direction (along Ex in Figure 3).[3] On the other hand,the Plasma-Optical Effect requires the laser beam to drive the


charge carriers induced under the gate. Since the charge carriers are less constrained in the gate width direction, a laser


山


beam polarized along Ey should be most sensitive to this effect. (See [4] and references within for an overview of the possible modulation mechanisms in LVP.) In practice, the laser beam is found to be most strongly modulated when its polarization vector is aligned along Ey .

Optical path


PDP mode utilizes a common-path interferometer design for phase detection (unlike the split-path Michelson interferometer design that is used in PID mode). The PDP optical path is shown in Figure 4. Two orthogonal, linearly polarized 1064-nm laser beams, generated from the same laser, are incident on the same point in the DUT. The polarization directions of the beams are aligned with the transistor gate width and length directions in the DUT. The


3


beam modulation due to DUT interaction is unequal for the two beams because of the polarization dependence of the LVP signal. The two beams are made to interfere after their DUT interactions. A ‘differential’ detection scheme is employed to increase signal modulation.

The incident beam path for PDP mode is shown at the top of Figure 4. Incident laser power is monitored using the incident pick-off (incident p/o) signal generated at the first PBS cube(PBS1). The next PBS cube (PBS2) is oriented to transmit the remaining vertically polarized beam. The beam’s polarization state is rotated 45 degrees from the vertical by the action of the Faraday rotator (FR); the third PBS cube (PBS3) is oriented to transmit this beam. An equivalent description of the beam at this point is that it is the superposition of a vertically polarized beam and a horizontally polarized beam,both beams equal in amplitude and in phase with each other.


The fast and slow axes of the variable-retarder (VR) are aligned along these two polarization directions. Thus, after passage through VR, the beam incident on the DUT consists of two spatially coincident, equal-amplitude, orthogonally polarized beams that are phase-shifted (retarded) with respect to each other by a small amount (nominally, 4π ). The DUT is oriented such that the polarization directions of these two beams are aligned with the length and width directions of the


transistor gates. Interaction with the DUT phase modulates one of the beams relative to the other by a small amount.


After retro-reflection by the DUT (Figure 4, bottom) the two linearly polarized beams retrace their path to VR. Passing through VR introduces an addition phase-shift between the two return beams (now nominally phase-shifted by 2π ). At PBS3, half of each beam is reflected and half is transmitted.


The transmitted halves are deflected out of the beam path via the action of FR and PBS2. The reflected halves interfere,since they are now in the same polarization state, and generate the reflected-A signal. The transmitted halves also interfere for the same reason, generating the reflected-B signal.


Figure 5 is a photograph of the prototype PDP optics. As with the original LVP system, an inverted confocal LSM is used for imaging and beam delivery. The LSM is mounted to an x,y, z stage for DUT navigation and focusing. A polarizationmaintaining fiber optic cable is used to deliver the incident laser pulses (generated by lasers located on a separate laser platform) to the PDP optics shown. The incident pick-off and the reflected -A and -B beams are delivered to remotely located photodetectors and their associated signal acquisition electronics via multi-mode fiber optic cables.

Dual-laser noise rejection


Background


The original dual-laser scheme uses the short pulses from a MLL to measure the electrical activity inside the DUT while the pulses generated by externally chopping the output of a diode-pumped, solid-state (DPSS) CWL is used to measure the DUT noise (from mechanical vibrations). Noise common to both CWL and MLL pulses can then be eliminated from the


MLL measurements by referencing them against the CWL measurements.[2] For this scheme to work as effectively as possible, MLL and CWL pulses must ‘sense’ the DUT vibrational noise as identically as possible. In addition, the pulses from both lasers must traverse the system’s optical path without experiencing non-common-mode intensity variations(such as those caused by inadvertent interference effects, or by non-linear optical effects). To meet these requirements, laser pulse wavelength, spectral width, and power density should all be matched as closely as possible.


Peak power can only be matched if a second MLL is used in place of the CWL. This option has the additional advantage of providing close coherence length and wavelength matching.


Unfortunately, using a second MLL is impractical because of potential invasive effects, the high costs involved, and the increased complexity of the system. An attempt was made to overcome these limitations using a time-differential probing(TDP) scheme, but the TDP scheme itself suffers from several limitations.[5] These include: ‘waveforms’ that consists of positive- and negative- going pulses instead of logic levels, a bandwidth versus signal strength trade-off, and a limited data acquisition time-window.


The PDP mode still relies on the dual-laser scheme to reduce

the effects of vibrational noise. However, a wavelengthtunable, external-cavity laser diode (ECLD) source is being developed to replace the original DPSS-CWL. Though peakpower matching to the MLL pulses is not possible, a 2x improvement in noise rejection can still be achieved by

Spectral matching


The short pulse-width of the MLL output makes it less sensitive to inadvertent interference effects in the system optics (LSM, fiber optic cables, objective lens, etc.). The coherence length of the individual ~10-ps MLL pulses is ~3-mm in air (the spatial extent of the pulse along the beam direction). In the DUT, the coherence length is reduced ~3.5 times due to the silicon index-of-refraction. Therefore, MLL pulse reflections from optical surfaces spaced further than half of this distance can not interfere.


A DPSS-CWL, on the other hand, can have a coherence length of many meters, or more. Reflections of the DPSSCWL pulse from the ends of the fiber optic cables can still interfere, causing non-common-mode differences between the DPSS-CWL and MLL signals. These differences degrade the dual-laser noise rejection scheme’s performance. A source with wide spectral width is required to reduce the coherence length of the CWL pulses. In addition, the wavelengths of the CWL and MLL must be matched so that any residual interference effects that modulate the MLL pulses (reflections from the front or back surfaces of a thinned die, and the final lens element in the objective lens, for example) similarly modulate the CWL pulses.


Figure 9 compares the spectra of the new ~10-ps pulsewidth MLL and the DPSS-CWL used in the original LVP system.


Also shown is the spectrum from the custom ECLD-CWL source (discussed in more detail below). It is evident that the output of this particular DPSS-CWL is not well matched to the output of the MLL. In general, the spectrum of the DPSSCWL sources used in the original LVP system has been found to vary from unit to unit and can even vary over time for individual units. The output of the ECLD-CWL, on the other hand, offers a much closer match, both in center wavelength,and in spectral width.

External cavity laser diode source


Figure 10 is a photograph of a prototype ECLD-CWL. The laser diode (LD) itself is housed in a thermal-electric cooler(TEC) to control its temperature and is not visible in the figure. The front facet of the LD is anti-reflection coated while the rear facet is mirror coated to form one end of the laser cavity. A Bragg reflector (BR) is used as the output coupler for the external laser cavity. The Bragg reflector provides optical feedback into the LD only over a narrow wavelength band, stimulating the diode to emit over the same narrow band. The Bragg reflector is ‘chirped’ along its length to allow wavelength tuning via translation of the mirror across the laser beam (Figure 11). The Faraday isolator is used to reduce unwanted optical feedback caused by reflections off the ends of the polarization-maintaining, beam-delivery fiber(PMF).


The drive electronics (DE) allows the LD to be operated in either continuous wave (CW) or in pulsed modes. CW mode is used for LSM imaging. Directly pulsing the laser diode eliminates the need to externally chop its output using electooptic modulators. This capability greatly simplifies the laser platform design and reduces optical losses. Optical losses are further reduced by time-multiplexing the MLL and ECLDCWL beams to spatially combine them, instead of using a fixed ratio beam combiner. Minimizing optical losses is important because the power output of the ECLD-CWL is only a few mW, much less that the 500-mW DPSS-CWL used previously.

Several prototype ECLD-CWL sources have been built. They exhibit similar spectral width and wavelength tuning behavior,but have not all been tested in a PDP system yet. In addition,they exhibit ‘mode-hopping’ behavior during wavelength tuning so their wavelengths can not be continuously adjusted.


Work is underway to try to resolve this issue. Long term spectral stability studies of these prototypes are also underway. Preliminary results are encouraging. A sealed,


temperature controlled ECLD-CWL source is being developed, which is expected to further improve stability.


Noise rejection performance


Performance of the dual-laser scheme using a ECLD-CWL was evaluated using a vibration test fixture. This fixture consists of a DUT mounted onto a piezo driven z-stage. The zstage is driven by a function generator, which allows a controlled amount of DUT vibration to be introduced. The function generator is synchronized to the timebase electronics of the prototype PDP system and is set-up so that the piezo zstage is driven by a single cycle of a sine wave during each sweep of the timebase. The resulting DUT vibration causes the reflected signal to vary, as shown in Figure 12. In this case, the reflected signal is modulated by 13% using the piezo.


This level of modulation is not uncommon during LVP signal acquisitions and must be significantly reduced by the LVP dual-laser noise cancellation scheme to enable waveform probing.  A 100x oil immersion objective lens was used for waveform acquisitions.[6]

of reflected beam modulations reduced to ~13,000-ppm of PDP waveform noise). The other waveforms have larger noise amplitudes and/or are distorted (i.e., they do not have the shape of a sine-wave). The distorted waveforms are a strong indication that some inadvertent interference effects are present (caused by the DUT/Oil/Objective lens interfaces, for example). Since these interference effects can change across the die or vary with temperature, the noise cancellation performance can vary greatly if the LDS is operated at the wavelengths where these effects are prominent.

Perfect noise rejection would yield a flat trace. The deviation from this ideal gives a quantitative measure of the effectiveness of the dual-laser scheme. Noise rejection performance of the dual-laser scheme also depends significantly on the power level of the MLL, as shown in Figure 14. The ECLD-CWL was adjusted for best wavelength matching. The MLL power was attenuated externally. The origin of this MLL power dependence is thought to be non-linear effects in silicon.[7] The peak power of the new ~10-ps pulse-width MLL is over 100,000 times higher than that for the ECLD-CWL, for equivalent pulse energies.  Another possibility being investigated is non-linear effects in the acquisition electronics, including the InGaAs photodiodes used to detect the laser pulses.

Summary and Conclusions


A new laser probing technique that exploits the polarization dependence of the LVP signal has been presented. This polarization difference probing (PDP) scheme utilizes a common-path interferometer design that is more immune to DUT vibrational noise than the Michelson interferometer used in the current LVP system. Besides better noise immunity, the common-path design eliminates the need for path-length and power matching between the two interferometer arms.


Intrinsic system bandwidth has been improved through the use of a shorter pulse mode-locked laser source. Using an ~10-ps pulse-width source in place of the original ~35-ps source has increased system bandwidth up to ~20-GHz. The new laser source uses passive-mode-locking technology that was not available when the original LVP system was developed.


Besides the shorter pulse-widths, passive mode-locking provides additional benefits, including the elimination of manual cavity length adjustments, mode-locker temperature cycling, and quasi-q-switching behavior during normal operation.


Finally, the measurement sensitivity of the system has been significantly improved, compared to LVP. This improvement was achieved through the use of a custom, wavelength tunable, diode laser source. Wavelength and spectralwidth/coherence-length matching between the diode and mode-locked lasers has decreased the system’s noise floor by at least 2x. This improvement helps maintain measurement SNR in the face of shrinking transistor geometries and decreasing operating voltages.


The prototype PDP system is currently undergoing extensive evaluations. PDP-mode and the new passively mode-locked laser source have greatly improved the ease-of-use of laser probing technology, while the tunable diode laser source has significantly increased the measurement sensitivity of the system. Acquired waveforms such as those shown in Figures 16 and 17 demonstrate the high signal-to-noise ratios possible using the new system. We plan to investigate this technique on new technologies as they emerge. Testing of PDP with a solid immersion lens is also planned.

Spray Cooling for Time Resolved Emission Measurements of ICs


Rama R. Goruganthu, David Bethke, and Shawn McBride   Advanced Micro Devices, Austin, TX


Tom Crawford, Jonathan Frank, and Dan Cotton


Credence Systems, Mountain View, CA

Isothermal Systems Research, Liberty Lake, WA


Spray cooling is implemented on an engineering tool for Time


Resolved Emission measurements using a silicon solid  immersion lens to achieve high spatial resolution and for  probing high heat flux devices.  Thermal performance is  characterized using a thermal test vehicle consisting of a 4x3  array of cells each with a heater element and a thermal diode  to monitor the temperature within the cell.  The flip-chip  packaged TTV is operated to achieve uniform heat flux across  the die.  The temperature distribution across the die is  measured on the 4x3 grid of the die for various heat loads up  to 180 W with corresponding heat flux of 204 W/cm2.  Using  water as coolant the maximum temperature differential across  the die was about 30 °C while keeping the maximum junction  temperature below 95 °C and at a heat flux of 200 W/cm2.  Details of the thermal performance of spray cooling system as  a function of flow rate, coolant temperature, and probing  position on the die are reported.


The current trends in ULSI technology include ever shrinking  device geometry, higher transistor density and count, lower  operating voltage, and increasing device heat dissipation and  correspondingly high heat flux.  Driving these trends are high  pin count microprocessor and graphics processing chips  whose roadmaps show dramatic increases in heat flux.  Due to  the large number of power, ground, and I/O connections on  these products, flip-chip bonding technology is typically  implemented.  Design of a thermal solution for high-power  devices in systems now requires implementation of cooling  technologies beyond conventionally used forced convection  air-cooled heat sinks.


Fault isolation on flip chip devices employs common optical  based techniques such as LIVA, TIVA, SDL, Laser Voltage  Probing and Time Resolved Photon Emission.  All such  techniques require optical access to the entire die surface from


# Spray Cooling for Time Resolved Emission Measurements of ICs


the backside and often require sample preparation.  This will  include removal of any existing package lid, thinning of  silicon to improve photon transmission through the silicon die  and if appropriate, applying an antireflective (AR) coating.  Essentially, fault isolation and failure analysis techniques on  these products require a thermal solution to control the  temperature of the chip while gaining optical access over the  whole backside die surface.


In this article, thermal management of high heat flux devices  for debug and fault isolation using a Time Resolved Emission (TRE) microscope is explored.  The higher circuit density and  smaller line widths require higher imaging resolution and  greater efficiency for collecting the emitted photons.  A  thermal solution based on a transparent diamond heat spreader  has been reported by Eiles et al. [1] to address the needs for  optical based techniques including TRE.  They reported this  solution capable of removing 25 W/cm2 from a test die with a  maximum across die temperature differential of 34 °C.  They  achieved a maximum temperature on the thermal die of 4 °C  using chilled air at –130 °C and showed power handling  capability of 100 W holding junction temperature below 95 °C.  This indirect cooling of the die addresses many goals for  thermal solution for optical based FA techniques.


Eiles and Pardy [2] have reported a liquid immersion lens (LIL), which makes use of the diamond cold plate thermal  solution but increases the image resolution by increased  numerical aperture (NA) of 1.1 for the objective.  This NA has  to be contrasted with the 100 X dry lens of 0.85.  The new  device technologies using 90 nm and beyond would require  higher image resolution and better localization of the emission  spot by further increasing the NA.


The Solid Immersion Lens (SIL) technology using a silicon  lens in contact with the silicon die has been pioneered by  Credence (formerly Optonics, Inc.) for TRE.  A high-heat flux  thermal solution compatible with SIL technology has been  identified as a spray cooling solution.  Ansari et al. [3] have  reported the thermal performance of a spray cooling solution  using a dielectric coolant PF5050 implemented on TRE


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa018


microscope with SIL.  The cooling system showed heat flux  levels of up to 82 W/cm2 while keeping the die below 60 °C  and the temperature differential across the die was 31°C  similar to that obtainable with the diamond cold plate.


Ansari et al. [3] have also investigated if there was any effect  of vibrations caused by coolant droplets impinging on the die  for imaging and on the timing waveform.  They have  concluded that these effects are negligible.


In this paper we report on the thermal performance of a spray  cooling solution implemented on a fully functional TRE  microscope with silicon SIL objective (NA = 2.45) using  water as coolant.  This engineering evaluation system uses the  same TRE detection system as the EmiScope®-II [4].  Isothermal Systems Research has provided the spray nozzle  assembly.  It is shown in this paper that the thermal solution is  capable of handling heat flux in excess of 200 W/cm2 while  keeping the junction temperature below 95 °C.  The  temperature gradients across the die have been found to be  similar to those reported using diamond film heat spreader  thermal solution.


Spray Cooling with SIL


In this section implementation of a spray cooling module on a  time resolved emission microscope with a silicon solid  immersion lens is discussed.  A brief overview of spray  cooling technology is also presented.


Silicon solid immersion lens provides for achieving high  numerical aperture (NA) for the objective.  The immersion  lens makes contact with the die surface in a small area of the  die.  Because of the high refractive index of silicon, an NA  value of 2.45 with a magnification of 350 X has been  achieved on this prototype system.  Corle and Kino [5] present  a good description of the use of solid immersion lenses.  The  SIL is a chromatically corrected design for wavelengths  between approximately 1-1.5 µm with a resolution of 0.25 µm.


Figure 1: Comparison of heat transfer coefficients realized for  various cooling techniques


Thermal management schemes for die cooling often use a heat  spreader in contact with the die and are referred to as indirect


cooling schemes.  On the other hand, direct cooling of the die  without use of a heat spreader requires cooling technologies  that provide a large heat transfer coefficient, as heat flux from  the die is not spread out.  Only direct cooling schemes are  compatible with the silicon solid immersion lens because the  SIL has to directly contact the die surface.  One direct cooling  scheme is the use of air-jets directed at the die surface.  In  Figure 1, heat transfer coefficients reported for various  cooling technologies have been summarized from the data  collected from Ref [6].  For high heat flux devices, a cooling  technology with a high value for heat transfer coefficient such  as spray cooling or boiling of fluoro-chemical liquids is  required.


In spray cooling a fluid is sprayed on to the hot surface.  The  coolant droplets impact the surface at low velocity and form a  thin layer of liquid film on the surface.  This fluid film is  heated up to its saturation temperature until the fluid film  boils.  This two-phase heat transfer gives very high value for  the heat transfer coefficient because of the latent heat of  evaporation.  The vapor and the heated fluid are pumped to a  heat exchanger to remotely dump the heat and to condition the  fluid for pumping back to the sprayer.  A schematic of the  flow loop implemented on the system is shown in Figure 2.  Depending on the system pressure (which drives the coolant  boiling point) and the die heat flux, the heat transfer may be a  combination of single and two-phase cooling.

Figure 3 shows a picture of the spray chamber with spray  heads together with the silicon SIL objective.  Two arrays of  spray nozzles are utilized that are fixed relative to the SIL  objective in a chamber for cooling the die.  The chamber, together with the load plate in which the device is mounted  keeps the coolant contained.  The SIL objective and the  associated spray heads and chamber can be positioned  anywhere on the die surface.  The whole chamber with sealing  ring slides on the load plate surface to laterally position the  lens on the die.  The SIL objective can be brought into  position vertically to contact the die surface for imaging and  for TRE measurements.  The SIL objective does obstruct the  spray from reaching the entire die surface.  De-ionized water  is used as a coolant in this study and the spray chamber  pressure is maintained at ~1 atmosphere.  The system also has  a low magnification microscope objective for coarse  navigation on the die.

Experimental


The thermal performance of the spray cooling technique is  evaluated with a thermal test vehicle (TTV) consisting of a  4x3 array of resistive heaters.  Each array element has a diode  thermal sensor to monitor the temperature.  The TTV chip is  flip-chip bonded to a 754 micro-PGA package.  The silicon  thickness of the TTV die is nominally 100 µm, which is  compatible with the SIL lens for time resolved emission work.  The micro-PGA package is plugged into a printed circuit  board for powering and measuring voltages across the heating  elements, and for accessing the thermal diode sensors.


The TTV is biased so that a uniform heat flux across the die  surface is obtained using a constant current power supply.  The TTV effective heated surface area is 0.88 cm2.  The  power to the heaters in the die is measured by measuring  current and voltage across the heating elements.  The diode  thermal sensors are calibrated first by placing the device and  the printed circuit board in an oven held at three different  known temperatures, approximately at 30, 60, and 90 °C and  measuring each of the diode voltages while sourcing 1 mA of  current to the diode.  The diodes are forward biased for  temperature measurement.  The diode equation,

Figure 4: TTV die relative to the atomizer arrays.  The heater  array elements of the TTV are numbered and are referred to  in the results section.  The atomizer arrays are fixed relative  to the SIL lens that is in contact with the die.  The sprayed  area is much larger than the die size so that the die is covered  with coolant for all probing locations on the die


Thermal performance is characterized as a function of fluid  temperature, fluid flow rate, and position of the lens array on  the die by sourcing different heat fluxes and measuring the  temperature across the die at each of the twelve array  elements.  Figure 4 shows the numbering of heater elements in  the TTV and die orientation relative to the spray nozzles.  In  the present study, fluid supply pressure, which is directly  proportional to the volumetric flow rate through the nozzles, is  measured.


Results


A. Thermal performance as a function of flow rate


In Figure 5, the temperature at each of the heating elements on  the TTV is shown for a given lens position, supply pressure (40 psid and 60 psid) and DUT heat loads.  Note that the  supply pressure is directly proportional to flow rate and is the  differential pressure between the inlet manifold pressure and  the chamber pressure, which is 1 atmosphere.  The maximum  across chip differential temperature (dT) is also indicated in  centigrade.  The heat load was increased until the maximum  diode temperature was 95 °C or below.


Increasing the flow supply pressure from 40 psid to 60 psid  has the effect of decreasing the across die temperature  gradient by 8 °C at ~ 120 W/cm2.  In general a higher supply  pressure, and hence flow rate is found to increase the  temperature uniformity across the die.

B. Effect of coolant temperature:


The fluid temperature is varied from 15 °C to 25 °C in an  effort to find the effect of coolant temperature on the thermal  performance.  Figure 6 shows the temperature measured on  the die at different heat loads for a given lens position and for  a fixed flow supply pressure of 40 psid.


The effect of changing coolant temperature on the temperature  gradients across the die surface is minimal.  Figure 6 shows a  change of 9 °C in average die temp for a 10 °C change in  coolant temp.  The sensitivity to coolant temp is almost linear, which is somewhat significant.  The temperature at any point  on the die varies uniformly with the change in coolant  temperature.   This fact perhaps can be utilized to run a device


at a given average die temperature by adjusting the coolant  temperature without affecting temperature gradients across the  die within some range of coolant temperatures.


C. Effect of lens position:


In the present configuration of the spray module, the spray  nozzles are fixed relative to the SIL lens.  So it is expected  that the coolant flow to different parts of the die will be  different depending on the probing location or SIL position.  The sensitivity of the temperature gradients to probing  position for different heat fluxes, fluid temperature, and  supply pressure has been evaluated.  Data obtained with a  supply pressure of 60 psid and at a coolant temperature of 18 °C for three different lens positions are presented in Figure 7.

At ~100W of heat load, or 120 W/cm2 of heat flux, moving  the lens diagonally from corner to corner on the die resulted in  a change of ~ 9 °C at a given location.  This is within the  temperature differential across the die.


Discussion


Thermal characterization using a TTV has provided key


performance data on the spray-cooling module.  The data


presented in Fig. 7 clearly show that this technology can  maintain the die at a junction temperature below 95 °C while  handling over 180 W or a heat flux of 204 W/cm2.  There is  the possibility of handling even higher heat fluxes by lowering  the coolant temperature.


Thermal characterization work by Ansari et al. [3] reported  spray cooling using PF5050 at a maximum heat flux handling  capacity of 82 W/cm2 while keeping the die below 60 °C.  Water as coolant showed much better thermal performance.


The temperature gradients across the die with spray cooling at  over 200 W/cm2 are similar to those achieved with transparent  diamond heat spreader or diamond cold plate at 25 W/cm2.  However, note that the temperature gradients using a diamond  cold plate remain the same irrespective of the probing location  on the die, while with the spray cooling module in  combination with the SIL shows varying temperature  gradients depending on probing or lens position.  This can be  expected as the SIL objective intersects the spray jets so that


different parts of the die are sprayed on at different rates  depending on its position on the die.

Figure 8: Heat transfer coefficient calculated from the data  obtained on TTV for spray cooling using water as coolant.


A measure of thermal performance for different cooling  schemes is the observed value of the heat transfer coefficient, h.  The heat transfer coefficient obtained on the present spraycooling module from measurements is shown in Figure 8 for  three different supply pressures ranging from 30 psid to  60psid.  The heat transfer coefficients obtained for the current  implementation are in the range 2.2 – 3 W/cm2 -°C.  These  results are in the range of h-values for boiling heat transfer for  water given as 0.7 – 100 W/cm2 -°C by Mudawar [7].


Conclusions


Spray cooling using water as a coolant showed excellent  thermal performance for time-resolved-emission  measurements of high-power devices.  The spray cooling  solution is compatible with the silicon solid immersion lens  objective, which has very high magnification and numerical  aperture.  The cooling system is capable of handling over 200  W/cm2 of heat flux from the device and a heat load of over  180 W.  The temperature gradients across the die are  dependent on the probing location.  These temperature  gradients are comparable to those achieved with diamond cold  plate, which is not compatible with the silicon SIL objective.

For low sensitivity and high spatial resolution, we have  shown that GMR is the right solution. In principle, the high  sensitivity of SQUID could allow high spatial resolution  thanks to its very high sensitivity and high SNR. This ability  is proven with via test structure but it is not always possible. Experiments were carried out on multi-turn inductors to  validate this but spatial resolution is not sufficient in this  case (figure 9). The main reason is the interaction between  different turns at long working distance. It smoothes the  resulting magnetic field and does not allow the expected  spatial resolution.


Figure 9.  SQUID analysis on multi-turn inductor.


SQUID is the right solution when very high sensitivity is  required. It is the case for low current and long working  distance. It was proven on SIP packages. On the other hand, GMR is the best solution for high spatial resolution.


MTJ sensor offers a balance between spatial resolution and  high sensitivity. In our case studies we underlined the best  choice (GMR or SQUID) according to sensitivity or space  resolution requirement and MTJ was not mentioned but MTJ  has a higher sensitivity than GMR and quite a good spatial  resolution as demonstrated in figure 10 that shows SIP  image with MTJ sensor.


Figure 10: MTJ analysis on SIP (200 µA current)


In summary, magnetic techniques are quite new. Available  commercial equipments are continuously evolving: SQUID


spatial resolution is improved by the addition of a magnetic  fiber and the spatial resolution and the sensitivity of MTJ  are constantly improving.


Magnetic Field analysis techniques can measure current  flow in IC even through multiple metal layers and metal  planes. We demonstrated this technique is highly suitable  not only for die level fault isolation but also on packaged  device. It opens a new range of application when No  Destructive Analysis is required. The high sensitivity of  SQUID allows very high working distance even with low  leakage currents.  Each kind of detector offers specific  performances. Commercial availability of these tools  triggers a wide range of applications. Our purpose is mostly  to give a feedback of an user point of view and to underline  the interest of these techniques in different case studies in  order to select what is the best magnetic detector choice or  if it is worth to use them compare to other techniques.

Discrete electrical characterization of sub 30nm gatelength

Besides involving feature sizes below optical light resolution

Additionally, the 20nm  silicon layer thickness and the

Atomic Force Probe (AFP) techniques are therefore


particularly suited for electrical characterization of sub-65nm


node SOI devices with multiple metal interconnect levels and


low-k back end of line (BEOL) interlevel dielectric films.


AFP electrical measurements of sub-30nm gatelength SOI


MOSFET devices will be described.

AFP Probing of 30nm Gate length SOI  MOSFET Devices


At the 65nm node and below, scaling trends in thinner silicon  layer thickness, thinner gate dielectric films combined with  SOI   wafer substrate materials underscores the desirability of  AFP in electrical characterization


This technology node typically employs BEOL low-k  dielectric interconnect films combined with optically  irresolvable copper via interconnects. Clearly, alternatives to  conventional tungsten wire probing of the copper  interconnects are required to avoid damaging the underlying  low modulus BEOL dielectric films [19].


AFP avoids the risks attendant with highly energetic incident  SEM electron beams or FIB gallium ion beams that could  rupture the thin gate films or induce charging effects on the  thin silicon layer.


Moreover, gallium ion implantation during FIB deposition of  tungsten pads for electrical contact probing pose real issues of  ion induced shifts in threshold voltage characteristics of SOI  MOSFET devices.  [20,21].

AFP Sample Preparation Procedures


As with any atomic force instrument (scanning capacitance


microscopy [SCM], scanning probe microscopy [SPM], or


scanning sheet resistance microscopy [SSRM]), sample


surface preparation is all-important for any successful


outcome.


For discrete MOSFET device electrical characterization, the  region of interest must be planar and deprocessed to slightly  expose the tungsten interconnects level. For optimum AFP


scanning, imaging, the dielectric layer surrounding the


tungsten interconnection must be recessed below the height of  the tungsten via. This is accomplished by brief buffered


hydrofluoric wet etch. The objective is to recess the dielectric  layer surrounding the tungsten via to a depth of approximately  20 to 60 angstroms. Wet etching is usually accompanied by an  ethanol or isopropyl rinse to remove any residuals and a


nitrogen gas aerosol blast.


It is recommended to immediately begin AFP probing of the  sample. If this is not the case, the sample should be stored in a  nitrogen purge atmosphere cabinet to minimize surface


oxidation of the tungsten interconnect.


BEOL via interconnect deprocessing is dependent on the type  of BEOL build such as via metal type (copper or aluminumcopper), interlevel dielectric type (low-k dielectric,


conventional oxide deposited film, or FTEOS).


Surface preparation is not only essential for electrical contact  but also for satisfactory AFP scanning. /imaging of the


specific site under investigation. A surface with a topology


roughness of greater than 10 RMS is not optimum for


scanning / imaging and can, like any other AFM technique,


damage the tips.

AFP Characterization of Ion Beam Damage in  90nm SRAM Array


As device geometries shrink and gate dielectric film thick


nesses are reduced below 2nm, the susceptibility of MOSFET  devices (particularly SOI MOSFET devices) to charge induced  damage becomes pronounced.


In dense, minimum spacing array regions like SRAM CACHE  arrays, incident energetic SEM electron beams (above 5 kEV)


or Focused Ion gallium beams become especially vulnerable


to charge induced device damage [21,22].


AFP electrical probing was performed in an area adjacent to a  FIB deposited oxide pad in preparation for FIB deposited


tungsten probe pads. In this experiment, the incident FIB beam  was 7kEV acceleration voltage whereas in another region, the  acceleration voltage was 50kEV.


In areas adjacent to the FIB deposited oxide pads, AFP was


performed on exposed tungsten via interconnects. AFP


electrical results disclosed leaky gates adjacent to these FIB


deposited oxide pad regions. Other areas, remote from the FIB  deposited pad areas showed normal electrical characteristics.


Figure 6: SRAM array with FIB deposited tungsten pads for


contact electrical probing. Note adjacent region characterized  by AFP


Figure 7: Family of curves obtained by AFP probing SRAM  device in region adjacent to FIB tungsten deposited pads. Note  leaky gate characteristics.


The applicability of AFP (atomic force probing) for electrical  characterization of sub 30nm gate length SOI MOSFET  devices and beyond has been described. AFP is particularly  suitable for electrical characterization of 65nm node BEOL  structures where the copper interconnects is no longer  optically resolvable with conventional light optics


AFP probing 65nm technology node and below where BEOL  build involves low k, low modulus dielectric films is  especially applicable.


Requisite sample preparation steps required for AFP probing  have been discussed. Both AFP probe tip life, AFP image  quality as well as the AFP electrical outcome are all dependent  on planar surface topology and necessary recessing of the  dielectric surrounding the metal interconnect to be AFM  imaged and contacted.


The extendibility of AFP to multi gate, non-planar MOSFET  devices (FinFETs) is currently under investigation with  satisfactory results to date [20]

Combination of SCM/SSRM analysis and Nanoprobing technique   for soft single bit failure analysis


Larry Liu, Yuguo Wang, Hal Edwards,  David Sekel, Dan Corum,


Texas Instruments Inc. Dallas, TX


Traditionally, many semiconductor companies have used  SRAM memory to develop their process technologies. The job  of the failure analyst is  often to physically deprocess the  sample and hope to find the defect with only the bit map  location to guide them. The success rate has been better in the  past when the size of these SRAM cell were bigger. With the  technology shrinking every 2 years, the chance of finding  physical defects has become less and less. Besides the  shrinking SRAM cell geometries, the electrical failure signature  for many of the failures is  marginal (soft failure), presenting  difficult challenges for failure analysis  (FA). Physical analysis   of these soft SRAM failures at the sub-100nm technologies is   often non-visual without detailed isolation and electrical  characterization. Therefore, additional techniques are needed  to improve the successful FA on newer technologies. In this   discussion, we will present the uses  of both SCM/SSRM (scanning capacitance microscopy / scanning spreading  resistance microscopy) analysis  and nanoprobing technique  for fail site isolation.


In the past, ATE bit map data was usually sufficient for fail site  isolation when dealing with DRAM or SRAM memory cell  failures. These memory cell failures can be categorized as row, column, multiple bit, double bit or single bit signatures. The  failure analyst can go to the failing bit(s) as long as the row  and column  mapping is correct. The traditional physical  characterization method is to remove the layers of metal and  dielectric from the failing location and inspect with Scanning  Electron Microscope (SEM). This  method is still sufficient for  some hard failures caused by particles, missing contact or  gross patterning defects. However, SEM inspection alone has  had very low success rate to resolve soft failures.


A single bit failure is  categorized as soft failure when it fails  intermittently or only marginally. A good memory tester is   capable to determine how a bit failure behaves. It can check the  voltage and frequency range. It can find out whether it has  write or read sensitivity. It can also verify if it has data  retention or disturb issues. The more electrical data that can be  collected, the better the hypothesis  can help target a  successful FA. However, an educated guess at the fail


# Combination of SCM/SSRM analysis and Nanoprobing technique for soft single bit failure analysis


scenario followed by "blindly" looking around very seldom  resolves these failures.


Based on SRAM cell layout, the most of essential component  that would cause single bit soft  failure is  at contact level and  below. A typical 6 transistors  SRAM cell arrangement is  with 2  loads, 2 driver and 2 pass gate transistors  (see figure 1). When  one of the transistors  is  not functioning, the electrical test will  identify it as a single bit failure. A single bit failure can be  classified as a hard or soft bit failure. A soft bit failure typically  only fails  at certain voltages or frequencies. The soft failure  signatures are most common when the new technology  process is  still maturing and transistor performance is below  design targets. A common soft failure can be attributed to  imbalance or asymmetrical problem inside a single SRAM cell. The conventional techniques of SEM passive voltage contrast  and top down SEM inspection are extremely limited to identify  transistor related problems . When the top down SEM analysis   fails  to identify a fail mechanism, one has to try other  techniques which target a portion of the failing cell such as  TEM or backside silicon etching. These techniques are not  always successful to identify the failure mechanism since the  fail site has not been isolated to a particular node of the bit cell. This  paper will demonstrate the successful use of SCM/SSRM  and internal nanoprobing of soft bit failures which enabled the  failure analyst to understand the electrical behavior of the  transistors  and pin-pointing the failing location prior to  attempting physical failure analysis  (PFA).

# A Novel Technique for Detecting High Resistance Fault Using Electroplating


A Novel Technique for Detecting High Resistance Fault Using  Electroplating


H. S. Wang, J. H. Chou, H. C. Hung, H. H. Lui, W. H. Yang, L. C. Sun and C. J. Lin


Yield Enhancement Service Department, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Ltd.  1, Nan-Ke N, Rd., Tainan Science Park Tainan , Taiwan 741-44, R. O. C.


This paper will demonstrate a new copper (Cu) electroplating technique [1] for accurately isolating high  resistance fault locations with resistance below K-order  ohms. This phenomenon is achieved by having different  electric field intensity leading to different copper deposition  rate on the sample surface. From experiments, the interface  between the thicker electroplated and thinner electroplated  copper layer on the sample surface accurately indicates the  high resistance fault location. Also, Optical Microscope (OM) and Focused Ion Beam (FIB) are used to inspect the  localized fault site of the electroplated sample. Furthermore, this technique, Electro-Plating Localization Method (EPLM), can process several samples or the entire wafer at the same  time. In addition, this technique can be applied in the fully  open cases of test vehicles with logical circuit as voltage  contrast localization method.

task in the Failure Analysis (FA) field. If high resistance


faults are the main failure mode in the semiconductor


process, failure analysts will need to spend an increased


amount of time on localizing the failure site. Furthermore, 23


21

the failure analysts may often experience difficulties in


performing failure analysis. Several techniques for


localizing the high resistance defects including, Infrared


Optical Beam Induced Resistance Change (IR-OBIRCH) [2],


Thermally Induced Voltage Alteration (TIVA) [3], Light


Induced Voltage Alteration (LIVA) [4], Resistive Contrast


Imaging (RCI) [5] and Passive Voltage Contrast (PVC) [6],


have been published in the past. These techniques, however,


require complicated and expensive equipments. In addition,


IR-OBIRCH, TIVA, LIVA or RCI are inaccurate at


pinpointing the defect sites on the chip with long and 星H-VOLTAGE7repeating structures. Also, passive voltage contrast has very LO limited performance in the sub-mega ohm resistance region.
