The novel electroplating technique introduced in this paper AFSEAMPSRNECOARSE uses simple equipments and can not only pin-point the defect F


GND+


site with resistance below 1K ohms but also observe the  failure site under the optical microscope.


Principle and Experiment


This experiment mainly employs simple principle of copper  electroplating. This technique utilizes the reduction principle  of copper. If copper ions gain electrons, the copper ions will  reduce themselves and form solid copper which are then  deposited onto the metal islands. Besides, the different  electric field intensity between the cathode and the anode  lead to the different copper deposition rate on the metal  islands.


In this experiment, via chain structures of process monitor  vehicle shown in Figure 1 were the focus of this experiment.


Figure 1: The simplified diagrams show the via chain  structure used in this experiment. The upper diagram is the  cross-sectional view and the lower is the plane-view.


In this experiment, a beaker, copper sulphide, copper strip, and power supply are the necessary elements for this  experiment and the whole experimental framework is shown  in Figure 2.


Figure 2: This picture shows the whole experimental  framework.


via


metal


Experiment and Principle of Fully Open Cases


In the first phase of this experiment, via chain structures of  the process monitor vehicle, with fully open defects, were  used to test and verify if the electroplating technique can  correctly and effectively localize the fully open defects. This  is done using the reduction characteristics of copper. Copper  ions can only gain electrons to reduce themselves to form  solid copper on the ground side and not on the floating side. In the experiment, the passivation layer has to be removed by  High Density Plasma (HDP) before electroplating the  samples. After the passivation layer is removed, one end of a  wire is bonded to a conventional Aluminium strip that is  glued to the sample. The other end of the wire is bonded to  the contact pad of via chain. The next step is to connect the  Aluminium strip to the cathode and the copper strip to the  anode. Then, the sample and the copper strip are soaked in  the copper sulphide solution for a given length of time to  make a well defined boundary.


Experiment and Principle of High Resistance Cases


In the second phase of this experiment, the objective is to  localize high resistance fault in the high resistance via chain  structures. In high resistance cases, the passivation layer has  to be removed and then two conductive wires are bonded  separately on two sides of contact pads of the via chain  structure. The free ends of the two wires are then bonded  onto two separate Aluminium strips that are glued to the  sample. An additional power supply is needed to provide a  voltage across the via chain structure so there will be a  greater voltage drop across the failure via with the high  resistance compared to the normal via chain during the  electroplating process. This phenomenon will lead to  different electric field intensities on the two sides of the high  resistance via opposite to the copper strip. Subsequently, the  sample and the copper strip are soaked in the copper  sulphide solution for a given length of time to make a well  defined boundary.


Experiment and Principle of Test Vehicle with Logical  Circuit Case


In the third phase of this experiment, this technique was  applied to test vehicle in actual logical circuit cases. In this  application, the aluminium strip glued to the backside of the  chip was connected to the cathode. Then, the sample was  soaked into the copper electrolyte solution to be  electroplated for a given length of time during Physical  Failure Analysis procedure. If the suspected path localized  by the Photo Emission Microscopy (EMMI) hot spots is a  floating path in the chip, the copper will not deposit on the  top end of the suspected path, because the copper ions can  not gain electrons to reduce itself from the top end of the  floating path.


Results and Discussion


Experimental Result and Discussion of Fully Open Case


After electroplating the sample, one side of the via chain  with the open-fault will be electroplated with copper and the  other side will not. Because copper ions are reduced on the  cathode end of the via chain and the ions are not reduced on  the floating end of the via chain, this will form a boundary  from the reduced copper. In the experiment, the grain size of  the deposited copper is an important factor because the  spacing between any two metal islands in the via chain  structure is becoming narrower. As a result, if the grain size  of the deposited copper is too big, it will bridge the floating  end to the end connected to the cathode. Furthermore, the  deposited copper will extend to cover all the metal islands  and the location of the fault site will become difficult to  judge. This phenomenon is shown in Figure 3.


Figure 3: The grain size of the deposited copper is too big, so all the metal islands are bridged together through the  deposited copper. Furthermore, the deposited copper covers  all the metal islands. The fault site becomes difficult to be  observed using electroplating method.


After decreasing the concentration of the electrolyte  solution, the supplied power, and the soaking time, the grain  size of the deposited copper was small enough for localizing  the defect site in 0.13um process, and even 90nm process. The size of the copper grain is shown in Figure 4. The  fine-tuned concentration of the CuSO4 electrolyte solution  we used was 1.5g CuSO4(s)/100g H2O(l) and the applied  voltage was 0.5 Volt.


Figure 4: After adjusting the electroplating condition, the  grain size was small enough to avoid bridging caused by the  deposited copper between adjacent metal islands. The  deposited coppers can be observed in the box.


After adjusting the condition for electroplating, the success  rate for localizing the failure sites was approximately  80%-90%. The failure rate of this technique is contributed  by human errors. After electroplating the open via chain, we  can observe the open fault location by judging whether  copper was deposited on the surface or not under the optical  microscope. The result is shown in Figure 5. The border  between the two areas, covered or not covered by copper, indicates the fault site. Figure 6 is the Scanning Electron  Microscope (SEM) cross-section view according to the fault  site shown in Figure 5. In addition, this technique can be  used on a whole wafer setting. Several dies of a wafer can be  electroplated at the same time.


Figure 5: This optical microscope shows the border formed  by the deposited copper. The border in the box pinpoints the  fault site.


23


Figure 6: This SEM image is the cross-section view  according to the fault site localized by electroplating method  in Figure 5. It shows a metal open-fault in the box.


Experimental Results and Discussion of High Resistance  Cases


In the second phase of the experiment, the fine-tuned  condition of the copper electrolyte solution is still used. The  experimental results of three cases with high resistance  faults are shown below. In the first case, the interface formed


by the thicker and thinner deposited copper layers indicates  the high resistance fault site having resistance below 100K  ohm accurately in Figure 7. This phenomenon is formed by  the different deposition rate on the two sides of the high  resistance fault. The different deposition rate is caused by  distinct potential differences between the two sides of the  failure site in the via chain opposite to the copper strip  during electroplating. The cross-section view of this  localized high resistance fault site is shown in Figure 8.


Figure 7: This via chain is judged to be high resistance with  the failed via having a resistance below 100KΩ according to  HP 4156B measurements. This image is the optical  microscope image of the failure site, which is circled in the  box.


Figure 8: This TEM image is a cross-section view of the  localized high resistance fault site. It indicates the abnormal  metal.


In the second case, the experimental results are shown in the  Figure 9 and 10. The resistance of the localized fault site is  determined to be about 29K ohms according to the  measuring data of SPM.


Figure 9: The failed via is determined to be about 29KΩ  according to SPM measurement. This image is the optical  microscope image of the failure site, which is circled in the  box.


Figure 10: This TEM image is a cross-section view of the  localized high resistance fault site in Figure 9. This image  indicates the abnormal vias.


In the third case, it is difficult to determine whether the via  chain is failed or not by using the HP4156B analyser but this  novel technique still can localized sub-K ohm resistance  fault site and find the tiny defect in this via chain. The result  was shown in Figure 11 and 12.


Experimental Result and Discussion of Test Vehicle with  Logical Circuit Case


During PFA procedure, top of the via of the suspected path  according to the EMMI emission spots was not  deposited  with the copper but all the other via tops were deposited with  the copper. The path of via top without deposited copper was  suspected to be floating. As a result, every node of the  suspected path was checked by the FIB. The result was a  line-end open of metal was found. The suspected path is  floating, so the copper ions can not gain electrons from via  top of the floating path to reduce themselves to deposit on  via top. The experimental results were shown in Figure 13  and 14.

This technique employs simple equipments and the whole  FA procedure for the via chain structures of process vehicle  can be performed in a relatively short time. The root cause of  low yield wafers can be identified quickly and yield  improvements can be carried out efficiently. Furthermore, high resistance cases with K-order ohm defects that voltage  contrast localization method can’t resolve can be resolved  easily in a short time. In addition, this technique can be  applied in the test vehicles with logical circuit as the voltage  contrast localization method to check if the suspected path  has open fault.

# Magnetic Current Imaging Techniques : Comparative Case Studies


Olivier Crépel, Philippe Descamps, Patrick Poirier


LaMIP- 2 rue de la Girafe - 14079 Caen Cedex 5 – France


Romain Desplats, Philippe Perdu


CNES 18 avenue Edouard BELIN - 31401 Toulouse Cedex 9 – France


Abdelhatif Firiti


ST Microelectronics Rousset


Magnetic field based techniques have shown great  capabilities for investigation of current flows in integrated  circuits (ICs). After reviewing the performances of SQUID, GMR (hard disk head technologies) and MTJ existing  sensors, we will present results obtained on various case  studies. This comparison will show the benefit of each  approach according to each case study (packaged devices, flip-chip circuits, …). Finally we will discuss on the  obtained results to classify current techniques, optimal  domain of applications and advantages.


Diagnostic of integrated devices can be conducted with  several contact-less techniques. From the front side of the  device, voltage contrast can measure dynamically signals  flowing through the two highest metal levels. With multi  metal layer IC technologies, other techniques are necessary  to gather information below these two metal layers. Thermal  laser stimulation techniques (TIVA/OBIRCH) are  successfully used to pass through the first three metal layers  through the silicon backside or through the last three from  the front side.


With future technologies of 9 metal layers, the challenge is  the investigation of signals flowing through the three middle  layers. Magnetic techniques offer the potential to measure  such current flowing through a device. The advantage of  magnetic field based approaches is their relative immunity  shielding effects by metal planes.


Current systems based on SQUID or magneto-resistive  sensors have demonstrated astonishing results in ultra low  current sensitivity through packaged devices and sub 100 nm  resolution. Unfortunately, physics laws do not allow both  performances simultaneously, current sensitivity from a  distance and spatial resolution: are these states of art  techniques really bringing a compulsory value to IC failure  analysis?


From a wide case studies spectrum, we have conducted  comparative evaluation of magnetic field techniques, mainly with SQUID for high current sensitivity, GMR  sensors for high spatial resolution and MTJ sensors, which  offer a compromise. In some cases we also compare  obtained results with other techniques such as OBIRCH.


After a brief review of magnetic techniques for contact-less  measurement of current flows, we will present each case  study and the obtained results. We will finish the document  by a first classification showing the benefit brought by each  technique.


Magnetic techniques for current measurement


Basically, the current flowing in a line dL creates a  magnetic field B. The detected magnetic field equation is:

4 3 0


π

where r is the distance between the line and the detector. In  the case of an infinite electric line, the magnetic field  intensity B is a function of the current intensity I, and B  decreases with the distance r. This last dependency shows  the importance of the working distance for magnetic  techniques.


For the specific case of integrated circuits, additional  constraints must be taken into account: the low current  range, often less than one mA, and the submicron lateral  resolution which is mostly driven by detector size and  working distance. Signal to Noise Ratio (SNR) and detector  sensitivity are also key parameters. They play a role in  spatial resolution. Among the different approaches for IC  investigation, we will focus on low frequency or static  current flow, putting aside magnetic loop antennas, Electrical Forced Microscopy or other RF techniques. Three approaches remain and they are SQUID, GMR and  MTJ.


SQUID (Superconducting Quantum Interference Device) is  the existing most sensitive sensor. This system uses  Josephson effect phenomena to measure extremely small  variations in magnetic flux. Its magnetic sensitivity is about  few pT. Advertised current resolution is as little as hundreds  of nA flowing in a conductor and advertised spatial  resolution is 3µm [1, 2].


Giant Magneto Resistive (GMR) sensors consist of a  multilayer material, which includes ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic layers (Fe-Cu-Fe). GMR is a phenomenon  based on exchange coupling in sandwiches of ultra thin  magnetic and nonmagnetic layers [3]. GMR sensors can  detect few tens of µA with a 50nm spatial resolution.


MTJ (Magnetic Tunnel Junctions) devices contain a pinned  layer and a free layer separated by a very thin insulating  layer. The tunneling resistance is modulated by magnetic  field [4-6]. 10µA current resolution can be obtained with  these sensors with 1µm spatial resolution.


Case studies


System In Package (SIP)


SIP allows the integration of heterogeneous technologies in  the same package (ie logic, sensor, power, RF …). In our  first case, the issue is to localize a polysilicon resistive line  on a die hidden by another die stacked on the top of it. Figure 1 shows the SIP assembly. The HVQFN package  contains two flip chip stacked dies. The polysilicon line is at  the bottom of the package therefore it could have been  possible to access directly to this polysilicon line by package  micromachining or chemical decapsulation. On the other  hand this sample preparation destroys the integrity of the  device and cannot be considered as a non destructive  analysis. In addition, according to the small size of the  package and the fine pitch of the pins, this sample  preparation is very challenging.

Figure 1: PHILIPS System in package schematic. The  minimum distance between the analyzed area and the  SQUID sensor is 700µm.


To assess the right behavior of this polysilicon line we  power the device at 2V. The current flowing inside the line  is 18 µA. The first trial was to scan the backside of the  package with a SQUID detector. For other devices, the  current could be as low as 0.5 µA. In these cases we


obviously need a very high current sensitivity and we use a  SQUID detector. The result is shown figure 2.


Figure 2: SQUID results with 0.5µA current through  400µm backside. Magnetic field (left) and current density  right)


But the most interesting advantage is the ability of this kind  of detector to work with very long working distance. It is  possible to localize the polysilicon line from the front side  of the package. It allows one to work on devices already  assembled on a PCB as shown in figure 3.


Figure 3: Double flip chip SQUID results for a 700µm  distance and an 18µA current in a 600ohms resistive  element. Area scan: 5000*5000µm with 20µm step size in  20 minutes.


Multi-turns integrated inductor in an open CLCC84  package


This kind of integrated passive component is very useful for  mobile application (Figure 4). The principal modules of a  RF circuit including integrated inductors are the Low Noise  Amplifier (LNA), the Voltage Controlled Oscillator (VCO) and the filtering circuits. Such inductors have high values  and may generate important coupling. So frequency  instability may occur which is unconceivable for a VCO for  example. So one of the critical questions is to evaluate  coupling effects between these integrated inductors and the  other parts of the device. Distance between inductors or any  inductor and IC core are few hundred micrometers and  strongly depend on the application itself. A closer choice  induces a smaller device but more interferences, therefore it  is very important to evaluate coupling effect by accurate  Magnetic field

magnetic field measurements. Magnetic field emission of  such structure may alter the operation of nearby components. Magnetic characterization is useful to place these  components properly.

Figure 4: PHILIPS Integrated inductor optical image used  in mobile phone circuits.


Another question is about defects that could cause an open (no current so no magnetic field) or a short between two  turns of the inductor. In this second case, it is necessary to  get a spatial resolution in the order of the distance between  two turns.


The static or low frequency current inside the inductor is  from 100µA to few mA. In both cases (coupling evaluation  and failure analysis), the critical parameter is the spatial  resolution and not in this case the sensitivity. GMR can be  used because it offers a high spatial resolution related to its  size and to the allowed low working distance.

Via chain test structure in an open SDIP56 package


In this last case, the device is a test structure that contains a  huge via chain (A defect was detected: its electrical  behavior is a current leakage of a few µA. See figure 7).


Figure 7: ST Via chains test structure. The goal is to  evaluate both current sensitivity and spatial resolution to  solve the difficult problem of resistive via localization.


This kind of defect (conductive short can be localized by  Thermal Laser Stimulation (TLS) such as OBIRCH or  TIVA [7], the TLS sensitivity strongly depends on the  relative resistance of the short and current value. These  limitations can be overcome by high sensitivity magnetic  cartography. In this case SQUID is required. Submicron  spatial resolution is obtained although a working distance is  greater than 30 µm and the detector size (figure 8). As  working distance increases, magnetic field is getting  weaker. On the other hand, TLS is not working distance  dependant. The choice between SQUID and TLS in this  case is between very high sensitivity and very long working  distance.

Nanoprobing technique


Since SCM/SSRM is non-destructive, an analyst can proceed  with additional analysis. A SEM based probing system was  used in this  analysis  [4] (see Fig. 4). We were able to navigate  four probe tips and land them on a source, drain, gate, and well  contacts. A family of I/V curves were collected on the good  and failing transistors. After reviewing the IV curves and  comparison with the reference good bit, we confirmed a 50  kOhm short  between source and drain of the suspect transistor (see Figure 5). This  result was consistent with SCM finding of  source to drain short  at the right side driver transistor. With  the failing transistor isolated, additional physical analysis  was  targeted at this  component to understand the root cause.


Figure 4. This  figure shows four probe tips touch down on the  source, drain, gate, and the well of a single transistor.

Figure 5. Nanoprobing of a single NCH transistor shows 50k  ohm resistance between the source and drain contact.


Once SCM/SSRM and nanoprobing have isolated the failure to  a particular transistor, the analysts  can plan a deterministic  physical analysis  approach. In this  particular case, a TEM  cross section was performed at the failing transistor. The result  showed that the source-drain leakage was due to a small  silicon dislocation in the channel (see figure 6) [5]. This  defect  was previously non-visual by top down SEM and other FA  methods since silicon stains are too aggressive for such small  surface dislocations and small geometries.


Figure 6. TEM cross section finds a dislocation at the edge of  the transistor channel.


Additional Case Studies


The above sample A demonstrated the successful usage of  both SCM/SSRM analysis  and nanoprobing technique to  identify the failure site which was previously non-visual by  blind inspection. With additional samples and case studies , we  recommend having both techniques available for fail site  isolation since one of the techniques might not yield useful  data, such as the case for the second case study (sample B).


Sample B


In the case of sample B, the problem was a Vmin sensitive  single bit SRAM failure. Top down SEM analysis  was not  successful to identify the root cause. Unlike sample A, SCM  analysis  was also unable to identify any problems  or isolate a  bad transistor. Nanoprobing at contact level was required for  successful fail site isolation. Based on the electrical data  collected from nanoprobing, the left driver transistor was noted  to exhibit with excessive resistance in one direction (asymmetrical Ion behavior). Once the failing transistor was  identified, a TEM sample was prepared to understand the  asymmetrical behavior. The result of TEM revealed a small  poly notch at the bottom of the gate electrode. This poly notch  created the asymmetrical behavior and subsequent imbalance  between the left and right side driver transistors. In this  case, the defect was not “visible” with SEM nor SCM/SSRM  analysis  but easily explained by the nanoprobing data which  lead to conclusive TEM cross section (see Figure 7 and 8).


Figure 7. TEM cross section of a failing transistor shows a  poly notch at the left bottom corner.


Figure 8. Probe data and TEM result correlated with observed  asymmetrical behavior. The poly notch causes  weak inversion  or even in depletion under low gate voltages.


Sample C


In the case of sample C, several top down SEM inspections  were performed on a voltage sensitive single bit failure but all  results were non-visual. SCM/SSRM was performed on the  failing bit and a leakage path was identified from gate to the  source/drain (see Figure 9). Nanoprobing was performed at the  contact level to validate the SCM/SSRM findings. The  nanoprobe result confirmed that there was a resistive short   from gate to source/drain of the PMOS transistor (see Figure  10). In this  case, both SCM/SSRM and nanoprobing identified  the same failing transistor.


This  failure mechanism was attributed to a gate oxide integrity  issue. Physical characterization of the ultra-thin gate oxides by  top down or backside deprocessing is very challenging due to  selectivity issues  with current FA methods using choline  based etchants.


Figure 9. SCM/SSRM image shows gate contact (box) has the  same leakage behavior as the source and drain of a p-channel  transistor when Vtip=-1.2V.

In this  presentation, we have demonstrated the successful use  of both SCM/SSRM analysis  and internal nanoprobing  technique for fail site isolation. We have also shown that  without one or the other, the FA result might not be very  conclusive. With the combination of both, we have found  small silicon dislocations, gate profile defects, gate oxide  integrity issues  and other defects which were previously nonvisual during standard PFA inspections. Our experience has  suggested that these softer mechanisms  and non-visual  defects are becoming more and more common at sub-100nm  technologies.

# Current Image Atomic Force Microscopy (CI-AFM) combined with Atomic Force Probing (AFP) for location and characterization of advanced technology node.


Current Image Atomic Force Microscopy (CI-AFM) combined with Atomic Force  Probing (AFP) for location and characterization of advanced technology node.


Tom X Tong*


Intel Corporation, Hillsboro, OR., tom.tong@intel.com


A N Erickson**


Multiprobe, Inc. Santa Barbara, CA., andy@multiprobe.com


Many of the standard techniques of Failure Analysis (FA) are breaking down or becoming less useful as feature  sizes drop below 100nm.  The tenth micron milestone appears  to be a fundamental limitation to many common techniques. Use of Current Image-Atomic Force Microscopy (CI-AFM) combined with Atomic Force Probing (AFP) brings about a  combination of technologies, which allow for extension of FA  below the nano-scale.


Nano-scale Failure Analysis


Integrated circuit complexity and density have


increased to the point that 90nm devices are now in wide scale


production and the 65nm process node is under intense


development among top tier semiconductor suppliers.


Devices and structures below 100nm long are defined as


nanoscale.1  Therefore semiconductor FA is now really nanoscale FA.  Nano-scale fault isolation and failure analysis is


made extremely difficult, as conventional techniques are not


compatible at sub 100nm length scales.  Staples of failure


analysis such as optical microscopes have become useless


when required to image these structures.


Further complicating the analysis is the incredibly


thin and leaky gate oxides.  Electrical failure analysis (EFA)


must take into account even pico-coulombs of beam current


when a nano-scale device is subjected to a charged ion beam.2


It was found that such devices when subjected to far less than


1pC suffered significant device degradation.  Another staple


of FA community is passive voltage contrast (PVC) carried


out with both SEM and FIB tools.  This technique suffers Dfrom both the charge damage issue as well as a lack of


sensitivity to failure modes common to advanced nano-scale


processes. As technology scaling progresses, the problems SGwith PVC become critical.  The leakier gate oxide requires


larger ion beam current to charge the gate in order to show


any contrast, also the thinner interlayer dielectric (ILD) for the W65nm node does not leave much room for repeated scans


before the area of interest is totally damaged.


One paper from ISTFA found a mere 30% hit rate on


fault isolation for PVC.3  More specifically, because the


technique is already suffering from a lack of signal, it is


typically only capable of finding shorts and opens.  The leaky


gate oxides do not give a sufficient signal to noise on good  versus bad unless the problem is a gross failure.  Resistive  contact vias are now beyond the range for PVC to identify.


One of the most useful tools available as a probing  technique is the focused ion beam (FIB).  The FIB is typically  used in construction of micro-probing pads after fault isolation  localizes failures to individual transistors of small circuit  blocks such as SRAM cells.4  Floating gate irradiation with a  charged beam and charge deposition on interlayer dielectrics  ILD can shift device parametrics and shield actual failures  lowering confidence in results obtained.  Analysis at first level  metal (M1) is also often used partially due to the larger  separation geometries and also to allow for protection of the  inverter gates.  Fault isolation at M1 requires some modeling  of results and identification of failure mode signatures in order  to localize to a particular transistor or via.5


SRAM transistor probing in the nano-scale is  particularly difficult.  FIB deposited pads may be used to  contact source, drain, gate, and well/substrate of the  transistors. For 90nm and 65nm nodes, the geometry of the  pads effectively limits probing to one or two transistors in one  cell.   As shown in Fig. 1 below, the micro probing pads cover  large adjacent areas of the array, completely obscuring nearby  cells.  Furthermore, sample preparation time may require ~1-2  days if urgent and yield rate for functional samples 50% or  less.6  This technology may not work as transistor technology  shrinks below the tenth micron critical dimension.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa042


Figure 1.  Focused Ion Beam deposited micro pads on 130nm  SRAM array.


Atomic Force Microscopy


Atomic Force Microscopy has been used for many  years in characterization of electronic materials.  The most  useful of the techniques for the failure analyst, made possible  by the AFM are the electronic measurements such as  conductive AFM (C-AFM), scanning capacitance microscopy  SCM, and nano-spreading resistance microscopy n-SRM.  These measurements are extremely effective in characterizing  material properties such as nanoscale doping, conductivity, or  resistance.7 8  For instance SCM9 and n-SRM10 have become  standard tools for characterizing failures associated with  implant profiles, missing implants, and other non-visible  defects.11 12


Figure 2.  CI-AFM measures the current flow between a  biased tip and ground return via the IC sample.  The AFM  permits force feedback and scanning to allow the probe to  ride over the surface mapping the current.


CI-AFM Measurements


Recently, a 90% success rate in identifying root cause failures  in samples delayered to contact level has been achieved  through the use of CI-AFM.13  A schematic view of this  promising technique is shown in Figure 2.  Its application can  be considered as being roughly equivalent to Passive Voltage  Contrast achieved in the SEM or FIB.  However, because the  contrast mechanism is current flow, the sensitivity is very  greatly enhanced.  The higher sensitivity results in a three  times higher hit rate compared to PVC.  Furthermore, as  opposed to PVC, the current data is quantitative in nature.  The sample analysis time is minimal and a further capability  to take a local sweep and measure the IV spectra for a given  contact is critical in determining the electrical characteristic of  the failure thus further increases the value of the technique.


In order to generate the CI-AFM images, the author  applies 0.5-2 Volts for the sample and the C-AFM sensor


measures the current.  The IV spectra show diode turn on  voltages of 0.7 to 2 Volts.  The high bias value is required to  overcome the probe and contact resistance inherent in  traditional AFM probes.


Figure 3 shows Pico-CurrentTM images of a 65nm  advanced SRAM technology polished to contact level.  The  probes used for the analysis were made from solid tungsten  wire and provide a lower contact resistance and more  consistent image quality relative to AFM probes made from  coated silicon or diamond.  The contact resistance of the wire  probes is estimated from the IV results in the following data  sets as being a few tens of ohms.  The lower contact resistance  provides far higher sensitivity and higher current at lower  bias.  The images are forward and reverse bias images with  using positive and negative 10mV applied to the probe.  Therefore in the forward bias image on the left current flows  out of the probe into the P-type contacts and the reverse  contrast on the right.  At higher biases, the floating transfer  gates become visible and it is possible to distinguish between  gate leakages in the pA level.


Pico Current Sensor


Photo Detector


Biased Conductive Probe


0.cop申


Figure 3.  Pico-Current CI-AFM image contrast for a 65nm


Sample and Chuck


Current Image


process technology node.  The left image is with the probe  forward biased at pos10mV and the right reverse biased at  neg10mV.


Results from the advanced technology node using the  more conductive probes showed a great deal of contrast in the  contacts including several suspected failed sites.  One Vss  contact is highlighted in Fig 4 below and was found even  though no corresponding bit cell failure was registered.  An  IV sweep of the contact was recorded and compared with a  neighboring normal contact and the results are shown in Fig 5.  Although the contact does leak in the forward bias condition, it does not affect the operation of the memory cell because it  is the Vss contact in this case. However, if the contact leakage  was on a different contact in a cell, e.g., one of the contacts to  nodes, then the cell would fail. Known failure mode for leaky  contacts from physical FA could be due to multiple sources. One example is contact punch through the P/N junction from  over etch. Therefore, this technique does demonstrate the  capability of detecting contact leakage, which could cause cell  failures depending on the location of the contacts in the  memory cell.

Atomic Force Probing at 65nm


The technique of Atomic Force Probing (AFP) is being  adopted as a tool to overcome both the single probe  limitations in AFM and the limitations to traditional electrical  probing under an optical microscope and using FIB deposited  micro-pads.14 15  The AFP has many inherent advantages  relative to other probing methods such as the FIB pads method  or in chamber probing in either SEM or FIB or dual beam  system.  The primary benefit is that the probes being attached  to a scanned probe microscope (SPM) with force feedback  and piezo actuators.  The force feedback permits repeated  contacts and scanning (imaging) without bending the probe  tip.  The primary disadvantage is in alignment of probes onto  a given device since the AFP system lacks an overview image  of the probes as is available in an in chamber prober.


The AFP has advantages and disadvantages relative  to traditional AFM.  Though the system has superior  positioning accuracy with closed loop scanner positioning in  all three axis, the configuration has a higher noise floor than  AFM tools designed strictly for imaging.  The advantages are  that the system uses probe tips made from solid tungsten for  excellent contact stability and low resistance however; the size  of the probe wire will be generally higher that conventional  etched silicon probe tips.  Collectively, these features allow  the AFP to gain durability and ohmic contact at the expense of  imaging resolution.


The trade off is partially offset by the ability to  perform CI-AFM imaging in-situ while locating the feature (cell) of interest and aligning the probes.  The current images  are of excellent resolution and contrast and contain valuable  information for fault isolation as discussed above.


The trade-offs between microscopy performance and  probing capability is not only mandated by the probe and  scanner configurations.  The AFP allows multiple probes in  very close proximity to permit probing of multiple terminals  of nanoscale devices.  For the ultra-high density SRAM arrays  measured below, 3 of 4 probes must be contacting in >1/50th µm2!


It is also non-destructive to allow further FA done on  the failure sites located. Examples of 65nm transistor ID-Vds & Vgs curves are show in figures 6 and 7.  The contact  resistance is estimated to be a few tens of ohms and therefore, real device operating parametrics can be extracted from the  data.  The AFP combined with CI-AFM capability provides a  natural progression for nano-scale FA allowing combination  of FI and root cause in a single tool platform.

Challenges for nanoscale FA are not currently being met by  existing toolsets.  Due to sensitivity to both dimension size  and charged beam sensitivity, current FI and FA techniques of  passive voltage contrast and FIB deposited micro-pad probing  are suffering when faced with sub 100nm devices.   The clear  advantage of the AFP is the ability to carry out all of the  functions of CI-AFM and analytical probing on such  nanoscale devices.  Combining multiple probes to accomplish  parametric data extraction as part of the same analysis allows  for fault isolation and root cause identification while using the  same tool.  Adoption of the scanned probe microscope as a  probing tool will further increase the importance of this  technology.

Towards High Accuracy Fault Diagnosis of Digital Circuits


Camelia Hora


Philips Research, Eindhoven, NL


Stefan Eichenberger


Philips Semiconductors, Nijmegen, NL


Due to the development of smaller and denser manufacturing  processes most of the hardware localization techniques cannot  keep up satisfactorily with the technology trend. There is an  increased need in precise and accurate software based  diagnosis tools to help identify the fault location. This paper  describes the software based fault diagnosis method used  within Philips, focusing on the features developed to increase  its accuracy.


Failure analysis and diagnosis are becoming key activities in


today’s IC manufacturing processes. Successful silicon debug,


yield improvement and reliability enhancement heavily rely on


the ability to quickly and precisely identify the root cause of


the defects. Once the defect is detected and characterized,


correction measures can be taken to avoid its appearance in


the future.


A traditional failure analysis process consists of three        steps: fault localization, deprocessing and defect


characterization/visualization. Smaller feature sizes, higher


integration densities, new materials and new defect


mechanisms introduced at each new technology node,


challenge the traditional physical fault localization methods.


Below are some of these challenges as they are mentioned in


the ITRS [1]: “it becomes more and more difficult to probe a


defective transistor for defect behavior characterization and


localization without altering its functionality, to penetrate 6 or


more metal layers with a laser beam (e.q. OBIRCH) to


activate the defect in order to locate it; and to use front side


and backside waveform acquisition techniques (e.q. PICA)


because transitions emit less light”. Therefore, precise and


accurate software-based fault diagnosis methods are needed to


supplement and/or substitute some of the physical localization


methods.


Traditional software based diagnosis methods imply two


elements: a fault model and a matching/comparison algorithm.


It is common to speak of locating faults when in fact the target


is the physical defect. Physical defects do not allow an easy


# Towards High Accuracy Fault Diagnosis of Digital Circuits


mathematical representation for test pattern generation and  diagnosis, therefore logical representations of the effect of the  defects on the functionality of the circuit, called fault models, were developed. Two main directions for improving the fault  diagnosis capabilities can be recognized in the papers  published in the last years. On one side more complex faults  models such as resistive bridging, resistive opens, path delay, fault tuples [2] are being used for diagnosis purposes to try to  cover all the defect behavior for better localization, at the cost  of increasing the simulation time. On the other side, the use of  composite signatures and/or more complex matching  algorithms [3,4] try to overcome the disadvantages related  with a simple fault model to achieve the same goal. Adding  the layout information, the electrical characteristic of the  neighborhood of the suspect fault location [5] has become a  must if a good spatial resolution is desired.


Until recently, software based diagnosis was mainly used in  single die analysis. Only the last years it started to play an  important role in yield improvement [6-8].  Being software  tools, they run automatically and consume only CPU, so any  effort spent in perfecting them will have as a consequence an  increase of the physical analysis success rate and also an  important decrease of the time needed to perform the physical  analysis. All this actually translates in faster process  improvement, better quality and high yield.


Regardless of its application field, an ideal software based  diagnosis callout has to contain only one suspect (the correct  one) and the physical search area should be very small (ideally  the spatial resolution to be limited to a single transistor or a  metal line not longer than 10 µm [1]). These requests are not  so easy to fulfill and the rest of the paper will describe our  efforts to make the software-based diagnosis method an  indispensable instrument for the failure analyst and the yield  engineer.


The rest of the paper is organized as follows: the first section  will describe our approach for fault diagnosis, followed by  some directions to improve the diagnosis accuracy. Next the  application of fault diagnosis for yield improvement will be  briefly discussed and finally, conclusions and some directions  for future work will be described.

Fault diagnosis approach description


The generic flow of our software based diagnosis tool is  shown in Fig.1.


Fig.1. Generic diagnosis flow


The inputs are the failing vectors as stored by the tester and  design related information (test patterns, netlist, layout) and  the result is a callout which contains an ordered list of suspect  locations: the signal/gates suspected to have a defect, the type  of the fault and the X/Y coordinates of the suspects.


Our fault diagnosis method is based on the stuck-at fault  simulation results, which are combined towards more complex  fault models and a ranking procedure to increase the precision. It consists of two major steps: identification of the faulty nets  and mapping with a fault model. We call a faulty net a signal  whose functionality is affected by the presence of a defect. The procedure of identification of the faulty nets starts with  back coning from the failing flip-flops to determine all the  signals and gates located in their logic clouds. All the stuck-at  faults associated with these signals and gates are simulated  and the results are stored. Based on these simulation results, the second step of the fault diagnosis procedure is applied. Fault signatures are built for the following type of fault  models: stuck-at, bridging, and open. A ranking algorithm  composed from two ranking counts is applied to determine the  top signal/gate and the fault model that best explains the  behavior seen on the tester. If none of the fault models is  better, then the suspect will remain as a faulty net.  The fault  diagnosis algorithm is able to locate with good precision up to  3 defects present simultaneously in a bad die. A more detailed  description of the diagnosis algorithm is done in [9].


Increasing the accuracy of fault diagnosis


As already mentioned in the previous subsection, software  based diagnosis algorithms pinpoint to a fault, whilst our  target are the physical defects. Examples of defects are


contaminants, extra or missing material, misalignment of the  equipment relative to the wafer being processed, etc.  Knowing the area of the suspect fault is becoming a must  since it is desired to have short analysis times. Also knowing  the type of defect helps the FA engineer to choose the right  physical procedure to further localize and characterize the  defect, increasing the success rate.


It is commonly known that several different defect types can  be mapped to the same fault type [10] and the other way  around. Therefore, we divided the defect types in two main  categories: defects located inside the library cells (contact, poly, active level) -front-end defects; and defects at  interconnect level -backend defects. In the last category there  are two main defect types: shorts (extra material which creates  a connection between two conducting structures) and opens

Using the bridge fault model we were able to localize not only  shorts between two metal segments but also open vias (the  signal which had the open via became “weak” and was  dominated by a stronger signal situated in the neighborhood). To improve the diagnosis accuracy, the layout information is  very important. In the case of bridges, the diagnosis algorithm  only takes into consideration realistic shorts as extracted from  the layout. For open faults, after the diagnosis algorithm  calculates the signature of the possible failing branches, a  topologically justification procedure is applied to determine if  it is possible that an open on a metal segment or via can  disconnect all suspect branches from the driver without  affecting the other branches (if they exist). In case the  branches are topologically justified the effort required for FA  can be reduced to cross-section of the suspected via and/or  metal segment. The previous step of identifying the open  location using a physical method (e.g. voltage contrast) can be  eliminated or limited to a very small area. If the branches are  not topologically justified, the defect can be located anywhere  on the signal or inside the signal’s driver.


Fig. 4. Topologically justification of open faults


The topologically justification procedure works as follows: Let’s consider that the diagnosis algorithm identified branches  N1 and N2 of net N (Fig. 4a) as faulty. It then will pinpoint as  the main suspect an open fault on net N. The topologically  justification procedure will determine the routing of the signal  N starting from the driver (gate A) to the gate B and C where  the failing branches are connected. If there is a metal segment  or a via  common to these two branches which does not belong  to other braches then the open fault is considered topologically  justified (Fig 4b).


We applied the topologically justification procedure described  above to several dies that were suspected to have an open  defect and the success rate was very high. Fig. 5 and 6 present  the results obtained for one of the samples. In Fig. 5 the  routing of the suspect signal is shown, the top right box marks  the location of the driver and the left ones the gates where the  failing branches are connected. The suspected open fault is  topologically justified, the possible locations are the metal  segment and the via marked with a think line. The photo in  Fig. 6 is the SEM picture of the defect which was an open on  the marked via.

One other source of very useful information in determining the  type of the defect is the shmoo plot. Shmoo plots are widely  used as a characterization tool for the performance of the IC in  relation with the changes in the environment such as  temperature, timing and power supply voltage. They are  created by plotting the pass/fail information obtained during  the IC test when multiple parameters (e.g. power supply, timing, temperature) are varied.


One of the most common types of a shmoo plot used is the  power supply versus clock speed. In Fig. 7 a) and b) the  shmoo plots of a good device and one where a short or an  open defect respectively is present are shown. The lines are  marking the boundaries between the fail and pass regions, the  black line for the good device, the gray line for a bad device. The shapes of the shmoo plot for the two bad devices are quite  different, the shmoo plot for a short shows dependence in  voltage while the one for an open shows dependence in  timing. Knowing upfront if the defect is an open or a short will  help the analyst to choose the method (TEM, FIB) and axis to  perform the cross-section to successfully visualize the defect. Also, in [11], we have shown that timing related faults can be  better handled with targeted fault diagnosis algorithms.

Fault diagnosis for yield improvement


The severe competition on the semiconductor market  decreases the process and product windows. Hence rapid yield  learning and reliable yield monitoring systems are becoming a  must. Data, which in principle is available for yield learning  but hasn’t been widely explored so far, is the electrical wafer  test data from running products. This data, translated into  useful information by software based fault diagnosis methods, is a reliable instrument in monitoring and quickly detecting  yield loss causes.


The research in this field is just beginning. In [6] and [7] complex diagnosis systems are described, which rely on  statistical post-processing of callouts and also correlate them   with in-line inspection data; in [8] we described an special  diagnosis algorithm able to analyze a small amount of fail data  without losing localization precision.


Just to mention some of the benefits resulting from using fault  diagnosis for yield improvement:


- by using the test data from products one is able to


detect design or/and process issues specific to logic


blocks, which are difficult to catch with general test


structures or memories;


- can be used to distinguish between nuisance and real


defects detected by the in-line inspection tools;


- highlight systematic defects which are not detected


Bad i0


by the in-line inspection tools;


- can speed up considerably the time needed to solve a


yield loss incident.

The following case study will illustrate the advantages of


mimd


using fault diagnosis as yield monitor. In one of our fabs, a  sudden yield loss was noticed on several products. Their wafer  map signatures were similar (see Fig.8).


Fig. 9. The suspect fault location (a) and the picture of  the defect  (b).


The result of equipment commonality analysis pinpointed to a  scrubber (for via4) but more info was needed to correct it. One  of the products was monitored with our statistical diagnosis  tool and 21 identical fault locations, as shown is Fig. 9a, were  found on 3 wafers. These locations were not present on other  wafers.  A cross-section on the suspect via 4 revealed a via  recess (Fig. 9 b). The time needed to find the root cause of this  yield loss incident was reduced from couple of weeks to  couple of days.


Conclusions and future work


The importance of software based diagnosis techniques  increases not only in their traditional application field, single  die analysis, but also in yield improvement activities. More  accurate and precise  methods are needed to suplement and/or  replace some of the physical locatization tecniques. This paper  presents the fault diagnosis tool used in Philips, focusing on  the new features developed to increase its accuracy: topologically justification of open faults. Also, some results  obtained by applying the tool for single die analyis and  yield  improvement are presented.


Until now, the software based fault diagnosis methods are  more focused on localizing defects which affect the  interconnect (backend) level of the device [2-5]. Currently, work is in progress to increase the localization capabilities  inside the gates (front-end). Also, especially for yield  improvement activities, we are working to replace the logic  information from the diagnosis callout (suspect signal and/or  gate) with layer information (suspect metal layer, via).

Broken Scan Chain Diagnostics based on


Time-Integrated and Time-Dependent Emission Measurements


Franco Stellari a, Peilin Song a, Tian Xia b and Alan J. Weger a   a IBM T.J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, NY, USA b ELE Dept., University of Vermont, Burlington, VT, USA


Light Emission due to Off-State Leakage Current (LEOSLC)


is used in combination with the Picosecond Imaging Circuit  Analysis (PICA) method to effectively diagnose and localize  defects in a broken scan chain. As usual, the emission base  method shows to be very effective in debugging the problem; the defect is successfully identified by the optical technique  and confirmed by Physical Failure Analysis (PFA).


Scan chain diagnostics is becoming progressively more  important since new VLSI designs are getting much more  complex, and more scan latches/flip-flops are used in the latest  designs. However, if the scan chain is not working or is  defective, scan chain diagnostic must be performed. Several  approaches to tackle this problem have been proposed in the  past: reconfiguration of scan chains [1], adding set/reset  capabilities to the latches [2], bidirectional designs [3], fault  simulation and matching algorithms [4], etc. In general, all  those approaches require design overhead and do not  guarantee 100% fault isolation. Emission-based methods have  been developed in recent years. Most of them are based on  optical access from the backside of the chip because the dense  back-end-of-line structures and flip-chip packaging obstruct  signal lines and active devices, making front-end analytical  testing techniques impractical. In this paper, we show that  time-integrated and time-dependent measurement of Light  Emission due to Off-State Leakage Current (LEOSLC) [5,6] can be used to effectively diagnose and localize defects in a  broken scan chain (i.e. a scan chain with a stuck-at-fault).


Scan chain design and diagnostics


The scan-based design is one of the fundamental Design-ForTest (DFT) features that are widely used in modern VLSI  designs because it simplifies the test patterns generation and  reduces the chip debug time. As shown in Fig. 1, sequential  circuits are converted into combinational circuits via  scannable latches or flip-flops during test [7]. Therefore the  controllability and observability of circuits are greatly  enhanced and, as a result, the circuits are structural testable.


# Broken Scan Chain Diagnostics based on Time-Integrated and Time-Dependent Emission Measurements


Moreover, the cost of scan-based test is also lower than  functional test, especially for submicron designs.


For all these reasons, more and more latches/flip-flops are  added to new designs: for example, the IBM G6 S/390  microprocessor has about 76,000 scannable latches [8] and the  IBM zSeries 900 microprocessor has more than 110,000  scannable latches [9], leading to an overall chip area penalty  slightly less than 10% [10]. However, in some other cases, scan chains can occupy as much as 30% of chip area [11]. As  a result, on average from 10% to 30% of random defects of a  chip affect the scan chain, making it fail. Therefore, rapidly  identifying defects inside the scan chain can significantly  improve the overall manufacturing yield and ramp-up time.


Several methods have been proposed in the past decade to  tackle scan chain fails. In [12], a reconfiguration of the scan  chain was introduced to identify stuck-at-fault by capturing  them in a partner shift register. Of course, this works only if  both shift register and its associated partner shift register are  not defective at the same time. In [13], XOR gates are inserted  between scannable flops/latches. During diagnostics, the scan  chain can be reconfigured with the XOR gates to achieve  single and double stuck-at-fault diagnostics. In [2], the  existing scannable flop is modified with adding set/reset  capability. Therefore, broken scan chain can be easily  diagnosed. Similarly, in [14], some overhead is added to the  scan flops in order to flip or set/reset the scan flip-flops. A  bidirectional scan chain design is proposed in [8] where the

DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa052


scan fault can be diagnosed by performing both forward and  backward scan tests.


Software-based approaches also demonstrated to be very  effective, although they rely on extensive fault simulation and  huge data collection. Sequential Automatic Test Pattern  Generation (ATPG) technique is used [11], along with fault  simulation and matching algorithm [4]. In [15], the ATPG  patterns are applied at first to identify a range of suspect  latches/flops and fault simulations are subsequently used to  narrow down the failing latch.


All the above diagnostic techniques have some (different) limitations that make them not generally applicable. In  particular, they all have problem in tacking multiple  concurrent faults, as well as faults in the clock tree feeding the  scan chain. Although a suitable combination of different  methods guarantees in general a high coverage, compromises  on circuit overheads and chip area limit the fault coverage  below 100%. Therefore, novel emission-based diagnostic  methods were developed in the past years to attack some of  the most resistant problems. In particular, the Picosecond  Imaging Circuit Analysis (PICA) technique [16,17] has been  shown to be an invaluable method for detecting timing-related  faults by accurately measuring propagation delays, clock  skews, pulse widths and slopes [18,19]. Here we discuss an  extension of the technique, based on the detection of Light  Emission due to Off-State Leakage Current (LEOSLC) [5,20].


Light Emission from Off-State Leakage Current


Off-state leakage current is an undesired current flowing from  drain to source of modern CMOS transistors when the gate is  off. Due to transistor shrinking and threshold reduction, this  leakage current is becoming larger and larger, thus creating  significant problems for power consumption and chip cooling. On the other hand, associated with such a current there is a  faint near infrared (NIR) emission, which can be effectively  utilized for testing and debugging VLSI chips [5,6]. The NIR  light emitted by sub-micron transistors can be measured by  means of NIR photodetector such as Charge Coupled Device


(CCD) cameras, Photo Multiplier Tubes (PMTs) [21] or single  point detectors such as the Superconducting Single-Photon  Dtector (SSPD) [19,22] and the InGaAs Avalanche  Photo-Diode (APD) [23].


Although the exact physical mechanisms of the emission are  still under investigation, LEOSLC has been observed since the  very first introduction of the PICA technique [16,17]. However, with the advent of very short-channel CMOS  transistors, it has become an intense source of light, comparable with the hot-carrier emission, thus making it a  powerful method for testing chips [5,20].

As shown in Table I, the intensity of LEOSLC is strictly  correlated with the state of the gates in the circuit under test. For example, considering an inverter gate, the n-FET is  emitting light every time the output is logic high, while the  p-FET is emitting in the opposite state. This light is additional  to the hot-carrier luminescence emitted during a switching  transition and extensively used in the conventional PICA  measurements. Fig. 2 shows the time-dependent light emission  acquired from both the n- and p-FET of an inverter gate. The  initial state of the input is logic “0”; as a result, LEOSLC is  coming from the n-FET, while the p-FET is dim. In the  specific example, at time 3 ns the input switches to logic “1” (Vin=VDD) as shown in Fig. 2: a switching transition (emission  peak) is visible in the n-FET waveform of Fig. 2. A small  pulse is also visible in the p-FET emission due to the  temporary cross conduction during the non-instantaneous  switching transition. While the input is steady logic “1” the  LEOSLC of the n-FET drops down while the emission from  the p-FET increases significantly. After another 5 ns, the  electrical pulse ends and the initial state is restored with  another switching transition indicated by the optical pulse in  the p-FET waveform. Summarizing, in the case of an inverter  gate, the LEOSLC of the n-FET replicates the shape of the  output voltage signal (aside from peaks during the switching  transitions), while the LEOSLC of the p-FET has the same  behavior of the input voltage signal.

Fig. 3 shows an example of emission pattern that one can  measure with a CCD from a signal buffer composed by two  inverters. When the input to the buffer is logic “0”, the n-FET  of the first inverter (1) and the p-FET of the second inverter


(2) are leaking and emitting light (see Fig. 3(a)). On the  contrary, when the buffer input level is logic “1”, the situation  is opposite with the p-FET of the first inverter and the n-FET  of the second inverter causing LEOSLC (see Fig. 3(b)).


Based on the above analysis, the logic state of a gate can be  detected in both static (time-integrated) and dynamic (time-dependent) fashion [5,6,20,24], if the locations of the  transistors are known. Furthermore, if there is a defect in the  gate causing a logic fault, its light emission will be different  thus making it easy to pin-point the failure location by a direct  comparison of the NIR images of passing and failing circuits  or to a layout. Any emission difference can be used to locate a  defect in association with layout overlay [25]. If no abnormal  emission (high or low) is observable in a given area, the  detection of the logic state of the gates can be adopted in a  binary search approach along the failing path in order to locate  the first gate that has the wrong state or is unable to flip state.


Electrical diagnostic


111


In this paper we discuss the diagnostic procedure aimed to  locate the root cause of a broken scan chain in a test chip  fabricated in a 90 nm SOI technology. Although the failing  scan chain is only one of the many available on the IC, its  debug is of particular importance since that chain controls the  operation of the chip during most of the tests.


The scan chain fail was first observed and verified on the  tester using standard flush-scan test: a stuck-at “1” condition  was observed. Subsequently, a power-on scan test approach  was adopted to narrow down the range of failing latches. Every time the chip is powered on, the scan chain fills up with  a random distributed sequence of “0”s and “1”s. By scanning  out such sequence, one can retrieve the random bits until a  constant series of “0”s or “1”s is observed due to the fault. By  repeating the procedure (power on → scan out → power off) many times, one can locate the rough position of the stuck-at


fault in the chain. For the chip under test, the previous method  leads to the identification of four possible candidates: latches  from #1 to #4 as shown in Fig. 4. Based in this finding, Physical Failure Analysis (PFA) was immediately performed  at the coordinates of those latches without being able to  indentify any defect.

Optical testing


Due to the failure of the previous tester-based approaches, optical methods based on the LEOSLC detection were used. In  order to test the circuit using light emission, a Laser Scanning  Microscope (LSM) with multiple detectors (see schematic in  Fig. 5) is used to take both time-integrated (static) and  time-dependent (dynamic) measurements of the emission. The  static images, obtained by means of a high-sensitivity Charge  Coupled Device (CCD), are used to localize the light  emission; a single-element Superconducting Single-Photon  Detector (SSPD) with elevate NIR sensitivity [22] is used to  acquire the optical waveforms. The circuit under test is  prepared for backside measurements: the package is open and  the silicon substrate is thinned down to about 100 µm in order  to avoid excessive attenuation of the emission due to  absorption by doped silicon. An IMS tester is used during the  optical acquisitions to scan-in different patterns.

Time-integrated measurements of the scan chain


At first, a series of time-integrated images of the LEOSLC


coming for the buffers in between the suspicious latches are


acquired and a binary search approach is used to precisely


locate the failing gate in the scan chain. There are some


advantages in using a CCD camera for the test:


1) it has a good sensitivity and allows short acquisition times;


2) it allows the test of multiple latches in the same field of


view during a single acquisition;


3) it does not require dynamic patterns for the chip (ideally a


tester is not necessary during the measurements).


In fact, during these measurements, steady “0”s or “1”s are


scanned-in the chain and a CCD image is acquired for each


case. Then the two images are compared for each latch under


test. If the two images do not show variations similar to the


ones in Fig. 3, the latch is not switching and therefore the fault


is presumably on that latch or a previous one in the chain.


As an example, Fig. 6 compares the images from the buffer


following a working latch (i.e. #1 in Fig. 4) when “0”s and


“1”s are scanned-in: a difference in the emission pattern of the


latch is observed. In particular Fig. 6(a) shows that the n-FET


of the first stage of the latch is especially bright (leaking)


while in Fig. 6(b) the p-FET of stage one and the n-FET of


stage two are emitting LEOSLC. Note that the second stage of DDDthe buffer is significantly larger than the first stage. Therefore,


the leaking first stage p-FET is not clearly visible in Fig. 6(b). -DDD


All the latches in the range #1-#4 were carefully analyzed in


the same fashion until a different behavior was observed after


latch #4, as depicted in Fig. 7. In this case, emission is not


significantly changed by varying the scan-in pattern: the


second stage n-FET is always the bright emission source. This


behavior is consistent with the stuck-at fault fail, thus  suggesting that it could be the defective latch in the chain. Nevertheless, previous Physical Failure Analysis (PFA) investigations on this latch did not show any visible defect. Consequently, the associated clock tree was examined as a  possible suspect.


Time-integrated measurements of the scan clock tree


Figure 3. Physical Model of a probe card.


In order to study the impact of probe resistance, five simulation  models were constructed. Four of the five models used a uniform Rp value for all 21 VDD connections. The Rp values chosen for each of the four models were 1 Ω., 1 mΩ, 8.77 Ω and 30 Ω. These models will henceforth be referred to as S1, S2, S3  and S4 respectively. The 8.77 Ω model was chosen because the  parallel combination of 21 8.77 Ω resistors yields the same  equivalent resistance as that obtained by the parallel combination of the inserted probe resistances on the CUT. Similarly, the  30 Ω model was chosen because it represents the mean of all  the probe resistances on the CUT. The fifth simulation model  was constructed to reflect the actual “non-uniform” probe  resistances present in the CUT. This model will henceforth be  referred to as S5.


A set of 1260 simulations were run on each of these simulation  models by placing current sources at each of the (x,y) locations  corresponding to the positions of the test circuits on the CUT  shown in Figure 1. Twenty one of these locations represent the  positions of the calibration circuits. For every location, the  branch currents were measured at the 21 supply ports and normalized by dividing by 1mA, the value used for the current  source in the simulations. The sequence of all 21 normalized  supply port currents (IVdd0 IVdd1...IVdd20) for a given (x,y) location represents an ordered list and is referred to as Current  Profile Vector (CPV) for that location. Equation 1 shows the


definition of a CPV. The CPV for every location was stored in a  database for use in the calibration and Look-Up Table based  localization procedure described below.


Calibration Procedure


As mentioned previously, the contact resistances of the probe  card will vary not only from touch-down to touch-down but  also from pad to pad. The probe card contact resistance variation will distort the natural current distribution determined by  the power grid alone. In order to reduce (ideally eliminate) the  impact of probe resistance on the current distribution profile, it  is necessary to calibrate the measured currents. In this section, we illustrate the basic principles of the calibration procedure  using the simple two-port network shown in Figure 4.


The circuit in Figure 4(a) represents the test case and the circuit  in Figure 4(b) represents the simulation case. The test case has  probe resistances Rp1 and Rp2 while the simulation case has a  uniform probe resistance of Rp. First the calibration circuit (C1) at location X is turned on in the test case. The currents through  V1 (I1CXT) and V2 (I2CXT) are measured2. Similarly, currents

In the absence of grid variations and grid modelling inaccuracies, the transformation is exact. To demonstrate this, we  applied the calibration procedure to the data obtained from the  S1 and S5 simulation models. Recall that S1 had uniform 1 Ω  Rps and S5 had a highly skewed Rp distribution that is representative of the actual CUT resistances. In this case, simulation  data from the S1 model was used to calibrate the data from the  S5 model.


Figure 5 shows three CPV curves, an Uncalibrated S5-CPV, an S1-CPV and a Calibrated S5-CPV, computed from simulation data obtained when the test circuit at location (2325,7396) (indicated by ‘X’ in Figure 1) was activated. The y-axis in Figure 5 shows the fraction of the total current drawn from each of  the 21 supply ports identified on the x-axis. The S1-CPV and  Calibrated S5-CPV curves are identical, confirming the claim  that the transformation is exact. These curves also illustrate the  usefulness of the transformation. For example, the large value  for VDD15 in the Uncalibrated S5-CPV curve incorrectly suggests that the current source is in the vicinity of VDD15. In contrast, the Calibrated S5-CPV portrays the expected current  distribution in which the largest current is through VDD0, the  VDD closest to the source at location (2325,7396).


Hardware Experiments


The total current and branch currents were measured using  Keithley 2400 sourcemeters on a set of 9 chips as each of the  test circuits on each chip was individually activated. The  branch currents were measured using a custom board that  allowed automated switching across the 21 VDD ports. The  total leakage and branch leakage currents were also measured  in each chip. In this case, no test circuits were enabled. The  leakage currents were subtracted from the currents measured  with the test circuits enabled.


Figure 6 shows the normalized hardware current profile for  VDD0 as each test circuit in one of the CUTs was enabled. The  x and y axis in Figure 6 represent the location of the enabled  test circuit and the z-axis represents the normalized current  drawn from VDD0. It is evident from this plot that test circuits  in the vicinity of VDD0 draw a higher fraction of current from  VDD0 than test sites that are situated farther away.

Time-dependent measurements


The location of the fault is also confirmed by time-dependent  measurements with the SSPD. The active region of the  detector consists of a 10 nm-thick, 200 nm-wide stripe of  superconducting NbN on a sapphire substrate [22]. The stripe  is fabricated into a serpentine pattern occupying a region of  10 µm × 10 µm. A closed-cycle, liquid-helium cryocooler  cools the SSPD to <3 K, well below the ~10.5 K  superconducting transition temperature of the NbN film. During operation, a voltage-limited current source is used to  bias the stripe just its critical current (~10% below). When the  NbN stripe absorbs a photon, a hot-electron is generated that  collides with and breaks apart Cooper pairs in the


superconducting stripe. This process cascades rapidly, resulting in the formation of a small resistive hot-spot that, by  itself, is not large enough to span the entire width of the NbN  stripe. As a result, the superconducting current is shunted  around the hot-spot, causing current crowding in the  remaining superconducting regions. As a result, the critical  current density is exceeded and the superconductivity in the  stripe breaks down making it resistive in few 10’s of ps. The  resulting transverse resistive segment creates a voltage pulse  across the ends of the stripe that can be detected by a high  bandwidth amplifier followed by comparator, used to trigger  the timing electronics.

The use of Light Emission due to Off-State Leakage Current (LEOSLC) combined with the Picosecond Imaging Circuit  Analysis (PICA) technique demonstrated to be very effective  in quickly locating the failure even when it is very far away  from the initially suspected location on the scan chain latches. Fig. 11 shows a Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM) image  of the defect that was identified by PFA on the clock buffer #2  in Fig. 8 at the location indicated by the emission-based  method. A short between the poly-silicon gate of the n-FET of  the second stage and a metal line causes the abnormal  emission observed with the CCD.

# Hardware Results Demonstrating Defect Localization Using Power Supply Signal Measurements


Hardware Results Demonstrating Defect Localization Using Power Supply Signal  Measurements


Dhruva Acharyya and Jim Plusquellic


Department of CSEE, University of Maryland, Baltimore County adhruva1, plusquel@cs.umbc.edu


The power supply transient/quiescent signal (IDDT/IDDQ) methods that we propose for defect localization analyze  regional signal variations introduced by defects at a set of  power supply ports on the chip under test (CUT). The methods  are based on the comparison of the CUT with a golden reference chip, either simulated or determined to be defect-free, with the objective of distinguishing anomalous signal behavior  introduced by a defect from that introduced by process variations. However, variations in contact resistance between the  probe card and the CUT introduces anomalies in the measured  power supply signals that complicates the task of comparing  data between chips. This paper presents hardware results that  demonstrate the effectiveness of a previously developed calibration technique designed to eliminate these types of signal  anomalies introduced by the testing environment. The CUT  hardware data presented in this work is calibrated using simulations of the CUT’s power grid and special on-chip sources of  stimuli called ‘calibration circuits’. Several novel Look-Up  Table based defect localization techniques are proposed that  analyze the calibrated power supplies signals. The results of  predicting the locations of emulated defects in nine copies of a  test chip demonstrate the effectiveness of the techniques.


The Test and Test Equipment section of the 2003 edition of the  International Technology Roadmap for Semiconductors (ITRS) indicates that traditional Physical Failure Analysis (PFA) is facing significant challenges [1]. The objective of  PFA is to determine the root cause of failure in an IC. The major steps in PFA include fault localization, deprocessing and  physical characterization of the defect. However, as CMOS  technology migrates to smaller feature sizes, more complex  devices and additional metallization layers, PFA is becoming  slower and more difficult to be performed routinely. ITRS indicates that the role of PFA is likely to shift to a “verification” process as software-based localization methods continue to  improve.


The localization method proposed in this work can be classified as “a non-destructive software-based method” because it


is based on the analysis of electrical signals measured under  normal testing conditions. Unlike other logic based fault localization techniques, the method proposed here analyzes power  supply currents (IDDT/IDDQ). Unfortunately, any method based  on the analysis of analog signals is challenged by the “analog  baggage” that naturally accompanies such techniques. For  example, IDDT (and IDDQ) methods require a well defined  threshold between good and bad chips that does not erroneously degrade yield or quality. Factors that contribute to the  difficulty of defining this threshold include process variations  and variations in the testing environment itself.


Since our proposed method for defect localization analyzes  power supply currents through multiple supply pads on the  chip, the impact of variations due to the testing environment  are more pronounced than they are for traditional approaches  such as techniques that analyze a single global IDDQ or IDDT  measurement [9][11]. More specifically, variations in probe  card contact resistance have a significant impact on the distribution of currents through each of the supply ports, which  adversely affects the resolution of our defect localization  method. In previous work, we developed a calibration method  to eliminate probe card variations (and performance variations) using simulation experiments [4]. The hardware chips analyzed  in this work verify the effectiveness of the calibration method  described in [4].


Once the variations due to the testing environment are calibrated for, it then becomes possible to develop reliable detection and localization methods using the multiple supply pad  signal measurements. In this work, we develop Look-Up based  defect localization techniques that exploit multiple supply pad  measurements. Experiments conducted on nine hardware chips  show that it is possible to predict the location of emulated  defects with reasonable accuracy in the presence of extreme  probe card contact resistance variations.
