# A Novel Approach to Identifying and Validating Electrical Leakage in Printed Circuit Boards through Magnetic Current Imaging


A Novel Approach to Identifying and Validating Electrical Leakage in Printed  Circuit Boards through Magnetic Current Imaging


Craig Hillman


CALCE EPSC, University of Maryland, College Park, MD, USA  chillman@umd.edu, 301-405-5316


While failures due to electrical opens can require innovative  techniques to determine their root-cause, it is relatively  unproblematic to locate the failure site through a series of  electrical measurements. Electrical shorts are much more  problematic. In addition to being more difficult to pinpoint  because they can be located over a much wider area, their  intermittent behavior can result in halting progress.


Superconducting Quantium Interferance Device (SQUID) microscopy is a radically new technique that uses detection of  magnetic fields to image current paths within electronic  devices. This technique has been successful in nondestructively identifying the location of low leakage currents, even when the failure site was between a power and ground  plane (roughly equivalent to finding a needle in a haystack). The use of low voltage and low current is vastly superior to  thermal imaging, which often results in irreparable  damage to  the failure site and masking of the true root cause of failure.


In this case study, the customer was experiencing ignition of a  20-layer printed circuit board after approximately 1000 to  4000 operating hours in an indoor-controlled environment. High currents on the board resulted in extensive damage, effectively preventing initial identification of the failure site, failure mechanism, or root-cause.


Failure Mechanism Identification


All field failures originally occurred in fully-populated  assemblies. While this implied that the original failure site  could have been at the component level, temperature/humidity/bias (THB) accelerated tests1 on bare  boards demonstrated shorting between power and ground. Assuming that the accelerated tests were triggering the same  failure mechanisms seen in the field, the results suggested that  the root-cause that was internal to the board and was not a  function of component failure. Time dependent reduction in  the bulk insulation resistance of printed boards after exposure  to temperature, humidity, and voltage bias mimics the classic  failure behavior of conductive filament formation (CFF)


Conductive Filament Formation (CFF)


1 85oC/85%RH/48VDC


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa082


Multi-layer organic laminates used in printed wiring boards  can develop an electrical short between two biased conductors  due to the growth of conductive filaments. This phenomenon, called Conductive Filament Formation (CFF), is an  electrochemical process that involves the transport, usually  ionically, of a metal through or across a nonmetallic medium  under the influence of an applied electric field. The growth of  metallic filaments is a function of temperature, humidity, voltage, laminate materials, manufacturing processes, and the  geometry and spacing of the conductors.


CFF usually involves higher electrical fields than Define  ECM… Electrochemical Migration?? ECM and does not  involve metal redeposition at the cathode. There are two  traditional paths for CFF: Delamination along the epoxy  resin/glass fiber interface and Hollow Fibers. Delamination at  the resin/fiber interface can be the result of defects in the  manufacturing process , extensive temperature changes during  operation, such as thermal cycling or thermal shock, humidity  cycling or high humidity environments. Hollow fibers are  caused by impurities in the glass melt. Hollow glass fibers  increase the opportunity for failure between close conductors  because the capillary provides a convenient path for the  formation of conductive filaments. CFF can also be  accelerated due to copper wicking. Aggressive drilling can  lead to excessive damage and delamination, allowing copper  plating solutions to wick into the interior of the printed board. This can reduce the spacing between conductors and hence the  time necessary for CFF failure.


Accelerated testing on bare boards resulted in drops in  insulation resistance from tens of gigaohms to less than ten  ohms over a period of 48 hours. While insulation drops after  THB mimic the classic behavior of CFF, the time scale was  far shorter than expected. The CALCE model [1] predicts a  failure time of approximately 7500 hours for 5 mil PTH  spacing at 50C/85%RH and 7.5 volts. When testing boards  fabricated with Matshuita laminate, an automotive supplier  did not measure insulation resistance in the megaohms until  after 2000 hours at 85C/85%RH at 10 volts. Sun  Microsystems did not experience insulation resistance in the  megaohms until after 500 hours at 65C/85%RH at 100 volts


[2].


CFF consists of path formation, dissolution and migration. Path formation tends to be the rate-limiting step. The rapid  time to failure for the bare boards during accelerated testing  suggested that path formation had already occurred.


Based upon a methodical review of potential failure  mechanisms, construction analysis, and accelerated testing, traditional failure mechanisms and root-causes did not seem to  provide adequate explanation for the observed failure  behavior.


Failure Analysis


Resolution required actual physical identification of a failure  site. Unfortunately, this was hindered by the large area  covered by the power and ground planes, which made  identification of the failure site using functional or parametric  testing virtually impossible. Visual inspection was also  difficult due to the absence of a controlled burn area. The high  glass transition temperature (Tg) of the dielectric material, 180oC, made it relatively resistant to high temperatures. The  temperatures necessary to ignite the material were so high as  to result in thermal runaway. The effect was binary: failed  boards had either no visible charring or had large areas of the  board severely burned, with any evidence of root-cause  destroyed. Either case tended to hide the physical object  causing the electrical short.


This behavior also prevented use of thermal imaging, because  the energy required to dissipate sufficient heat also tended to  result in damage to the failure site. The initial solution was to  modify a procedure used to identify very small voids that  bridge multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) and cause  current leakage. The resistance between a power and ground  pin were monitored as the board was sectioned. Using a  binary approach, the potential failure site was narrowed to a  relatively small area. This area was very slowly ground and  polished until a change in resistance was observed. At this  point, large angular particles were observed in the crosssection.


There were two problems with this initial approach. First, considering the size of the board and the corresponding  internal power and ground planes, the time required to find the  short was time consuming. In addition, visual observation  could not conclusively determine if these particles were the  cause of the conductive path between power and ground, especially given the absence of a detectable conductive  filament. More rapid and conclusive identification of the  shorting path required the use of SQUID microscopy.


SQUID Microscopy


A Scanning SQUID Microscope is a sensitive near-field  magnetic imaging system.  This microscope can image buried  current-carrying wires by measuring the magnetic fields  produced by the currents, or it can be used to image fields  produced by magnetic materials.  By mapping the current in  an integrated circuit or a package, short circuits can be  localized and designs can be verified to ensure that charge is


flowing where expected. The SQUID microscope used, Neocera MAGMA-C10, uses a high temperature SQUID with  a sensitivity of 20 picotesla or two million times smaller than  the Earth’s magnetic field.  The microscope has been designed  to keep a high temperature SQUID cooled below 80K and in  vacuum while the device under test (DUT) is at room  temperature and in air.  The unique design of MAGMA-C10  also enables the SQUID to be positioned as close as 50 µm  from the area of interest.  Even though the SQUID is not in a  magnetically shielded environment, the sensitivity is high  enough to image currents as small as 600 nA at a 100 mm  working distance with 30 ms averaging.


The magnetic field produced by a sample can be imaged by  rastering the sample in close proximity to the SQUID. If the  sample contains a permanent magnetic field, as in many land  grid arrays and lead frames, the microscope will map out this  constant or “DC” magnetic field.  In addition, electric currents  in the device produce magnetic fields.  The presence of a short  circuit in an electrical part typically appears as a very strong  concentration of magnetic field strength, with the field in  opposite directions to either side of the short.


During non-contact imaging of room temperature samples in  air, the system achieves a raw, unprocessed spatial resolution  equal to the distance separating the sensor from the current, or  the effective size of the sensor (~30 microns for a standard  SQUID tip), whichever is larger.  To best locate a short in a  buried layer, however, a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) backevolution technique can be used to transform the magnetic  field image into an equivalent map of the current in an  integrated circuit or printed circuit board.  The resulting  current map can then be compared to a circuit diagram to  determine the fault location.  With this post-processing of a  magnetic image and the low noise present in SQUID images, it is possible to enhance the spatial resolution by factors of 5  or more over the near-field limited magnetic image.  This  enhanced resolution describes how well a scanning SQUID  microscope can resolve current paths in a sample.  The  system’s output is displayed as a false-color image of  magnetic field strength or current density (after processing) versus position on the sample.


The results from performing SQUID microscopy on a shorted  board are displayed in Figure 1. The bright yellow area on the  current map corresponds to the area of highest current density. This is representative of necking down of the conductor path, which is often a strong indication of an electrical short. Crosssectioning of the board was performed at this location based  upon the SQUID image.


Figure 1: Current map (left) and corresponding photograph (right) of an electrically shorted printed circuit board.


Figure 2 (500x): Particle identified between internal power  and ground planes in the approximate area of electrical  leakage.


The SQUID images are shown in Figure 3. The results clearly  demonstrate that current is flowing through the particle, therefore verifying that the identified particle is the location of  the short. However, bridging alone can not explain the  electrical failure. This is because the angular nature of the  particle suggests that it is electrically insulative. An additional  mechanism, known as Electrochemical Migration (ECM), was  most likely required.


Figure 3: Current map (left) and corresponding optical image (right) of the board cross-section shown in Figure 2. The red  arrow identifies the particle sandwiched between layers 10  and 11.


Electrochemical Migration (ECM), also known as Metal  Electromigration (MEM), Dendritic Growth, Conducting  Filament Formation (CFF), and Conductive Anodic Filament (CAF) growth, is the redistribution of metal resulting from  directed electrochemistry.  Electrochemical migration on or in  printed wiring boards (PWB’s) can result in electrical shorts  that cause the conductive path to fail. Traditional  electrochemical migration involves four steps, path formation, electrodissolution, ion migration, and electrodeposition, along  with these three requirements: ions (usually halides), moisture, and bias.


For this failure mechanism, two path formations were  speculated. The first possibility was the cracking of the  particles, possibly during laminate manufacturing or board  stackup. If such a crack were to occur, it would most likely  run perpendicular to the pressing direction, providing an open  path for filament migration to occur between layers 10 and 11. The second possibility was that the interfacial strength  between particle and the epoxy matrix was poor, resulting in  partial delamination during reflow, temperature cycling, or  humidity cycling.


The minimum requirements for electrodissolution to occur are  an electric field and a polar liquid such as water [3]. The  magnitude of the electric field must be such that the anodic  electromagnetic force (EMF) exceeds the standard electrode  potential of the outermost anode material, which is 0.34 Volts  for copper.


In the presence of moisture, the following electrochemical  reaction will occur in water adjacent to the anode:


2H20 → O2↑ + 4H + + 4e -


The increased concentration of H+ will reduce the pH of the  water below 7.0, making the anode material susceptible to  electrodissolution. In the case of copper, this can transpire as  either


Layer 10 (power)


Layer 11 (ground)


Cu → Cu + + e - or


Cu → Cu ++ + 2e –


If the electrolyte consists of water alone, Cu++ will be the  predominant metallic ion.  If the chloride ion Cl-, is present, the formation of the CuCl- ion will cause Cu+ to be the  predominant metallic ion. Therefore, the presence of halides is  not required to induce electrodissolution of copper.


Ion Migration


The electric field drives ionic migration. This causes the  positive ions to travel along the field lines from the anode to  the cathode through the ion transport path provided by the  aqueous medium. The electrons to travel from the anode to the  cathode through the ion transport path provided by the wiring  to and through the biasing supply.


Electrodeposition


Once the ions reach the cathode, the following  electrochemical reactions occur:


4H20 + 4e - → 2H2↑ + 4OH -


Cu + + e - → Cu or


Cu ++ + 2e - → Cu


Because cathodic electrodeposition is largely diffusion  controlled, its rate depends on the metal ion concentration in  the aqueous medium.  The production of hydroxyl ions (OH-) at the cathode can reduce the rate of electrodeposition by  combining metal ions with hydroxyl ions to form hydroxides.  These hydroxides remove metal ions from the aqueous  medium through partial precipitation.


Thus the ECM rate is correlated with the solubility product of  the metal ion hydroxide.  Ionic contaminates, such as Cl -, can  further change the ECM rate by forming alternate reaction  paths and by forming additional ionic species, such as CuClin the case of copper and Cl-.


Halides (Theory)


Previous research has shown the presence of copper chloride  salts during examination of suspected conductive filament  formation (CFF) failures.  X-ray dispersion studies on CFF  performed by AT&T always showed copper affiliated with the  conductive filaments and sometimes the presence of either  sulfur or chlorine [4].  When investigating a potential CFF  incident, IBM performed Laser Mass Spectroscopy (LMS) on  an area around a hollow glass fiber in FR-4 epoxy resin [5].  LMS detected positive sodium and copper ions and negative  bromo-chlorinated copper ions. After performing a plasma  etch to remove several molecular layers of material, LMS  identified positive potassium and copper ions and negative  chlorine and copper chloride ions.


Measurements using Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (EDS) on suspected conductive filaments revealed that the material  was primarily copper with either chlorine or bromine  identified as an additional major constituent. Electron  diffraction studies performed on similar conductive filaments


showed a microstructure comparable to 2CuCl2-5Cu(OH)2-H2O [6]


As previously discussed, the presence of halides is not  required for any of the steps involved in electrochemical  migration (ECM).  A classic example of this is Migrated Gold  Resistive Shorts (MGRS). Research  has found that the  presence of chlorides led to the formation of dendritic  filaments, while decreases in the insulation resistance still  occurred when halides were absent. Halides can decrease the  moisture threshold limit necessary for ECM to occur. This can  lead to environments where ECM occurs only in the presence  of halides, such as printed boards in controlled office  conditions.


If halides are present, they allow for a parallel chemical  reaction to occur, which can accelerate the rate of ECM and  therefore decrease the time to failure. Additional studies have  shown that the presence of non-halide materials, such as  glycol, can also greatly accelerate the occurrence of ECM; however, like halides, glycol is primarily an accelerant and is  not required for ECM to occur.


Halides (Sources)


Chloride can be present in small amounts in the glass fiber  used to reinforce the epoxy matrix of the PCB. This is, because chloride is a common byproduct of the glass  production method.  The most common source of chlorides in  PCBs is the etching process.  Prevalent chemistries used in the  etching process include alkaline ammonia, cupric chloride, peroxide-sulfuric acid, persulfates, and ferric chloride.  Three  of these, alkaline ammonia (ammonium chloride), cupric  chloride, and ferric chloride, contain chloride ions, which can  become absorbed or trapped in the printed circuit board.  Persulfates are sometimes formulated with mercuric chloride, while peroxide-sulfuric acids are chloride-free.


Other sources for chloride in the board fabrication processes  include the cleaning and degreasing of laminates with  hydrochloric acid and chlorinated solvents2, methylene  chloride as a solvent in the liquid photoresist stripping  process, hydrochloric acid as a neutralizer in the etch and  resist process, sodium chlorite in the oxide bath, sodium  hypochlorite in the potassium permanganate (electroless  copper), palladium chlorides as a catalyst (electroless copper), salts from human contact, and cleaning with non-deionized  water.  Fluxes with chloride as an activator can also be a  source.  Most of the sources for bromide, including solder  masks, marking inks, and fluxes that have a bromide as an  activator material, are surface processes. The epoxy matrix  can also be a source for bromides from the flame retardant  chemistry. Process specifications such as IPC-TR-476A [7]  state that bromide in epoxy resin can diffuse to the surface, most likely during a high temperature process such as  soldering.


2 Rare due to concerns about chlorinated hydrocarbons (CHCs) effect on the ozone layer.


Halides (Measurements)


While halides are not critical for ECM or CFF based failure  mechanisms to initiate, the presence of halides will greatly  accelerate the process and would be expected considering the  rapid speed in which the failures occurred.


There are currently two specifications for measuring halide  content in printed wiring boards. The draft document, “IPC  White Paper on Halogen-Free Materials Used for Printed  Circuit Boards and Assemblies [8],” refers to ASTM-D-1847


[9] as a test method to measure total halide content in epoxy  resins. This test method was not used because the total  concentration would include halides that were tightly bound to  the epoxy matix. These immobile ions would not be expected  to react with copper, forming the copper salts that lead to  conductive filament formation. Instead, the extractable ion  content was measured based upon test guidelines defined in  MIL-STD-883, Method 5011 [10].


The first step is to ensure extreme cleanliness of the  experimental setup. Extraction flasks were prepared by  pouring 20 ml of nitric acid and an equal amount of deionized  water, and agitating the solution. After agitation, the solution  was allowed to stand for 15 minutes before the flasks were  rinsed with deionized water ten times. The flasks were then  fitted with condensers and refluxed for approximately 24  hours. The boiled water was discarded and the flasks were  filled with fresh deionized water. The water was boiled for a  few hours or until 2/3 of the water evaporates. Flasks were  then allowed to air dry upside down.


Before extraction, samples are prepared by cutting in 3 grams  of measured dimensions to use in volume calculations. The  length, height and thickness measured samples were added to  250 ml extraction flasks subjected to the cleaning process  described above. 150 g ± 0.01 g of deionized water with a  resistance of at least 18 megaohms was added to each flask. The prepared flask was refluxed for 60.0 hours ±1 hour. After  allowing the solution to cool to room temperature, the extracts  were analyzed by taking the extract solution and injecting it  into the Dionex600 Ion Chromatograph injector port. The  chromatograph was calibrated with 0.5 ppm, 1.0 ppm and 1.5  ppm chloride and bromide standard solutions.


Three boards and two laminates were subjected to ion  chromatography. One of the boards was used as a reference  sample. Specimens of similar volume were cut from each  board. Special care was taken to ensure the saw was clean and  was cooled and lubricated in deionized water. Powder-free  gloves were used to handle the specimen. Solder mask was  removed by grinding. Solder mask removal was necessary, because surface sources of contamination, such as from the  solder mask, were not considered in this report. The prepared  samples were then washed in 18 megaohm water, again to  prevent any surface contamination in the extraction flasks. For  the three printed board samples, extract solutions were  analyzed twice. For the bare laminates, extract solutions were  analyzed once.


The results for printed board samples are shown in Table 4. The ion concentrations in the extract can be converted to the  extractable concentrations by multiplying by the deionized  water volume at the end of refluxing (W) and dividing by the  volume of the solid (V).


Solid concentration = extract concentration  x  (W/V)


As an example, the calculated volume for the sample cut from  one board is 718 mm3. The measured concentration of  chloride in the extract solution was 0.335 ppm. The volume of  the extract solution was 108 ml. Therefore, the concentration  of extractable chloride in this board is calculated as


cCl = 0.335ppm × (0.108 liters ÷ 0.000718 liters) = 50.3 ppm  The extractable chloride and bromide ion concentrations were  calculated according to the above formula and are displayed in  Table 1.


Table 1: Extractable chloride and bromide concentrations


|Type |Identifier |Chloride Concentration |Bromide Concentration |
|---|---|---|---|

|Board |1 |50.3 ppm |222.1 ppm |

|Board |2 |17.2 ppm |163.4 ppm |

|Board |Referenc e |10.9 ppm |17.1 ppm |

|Laminate ||||

|Laminate |1 |0.6 ppm |0.0 ppm |

|Laminate |2 |0.0 ppm |0.0 ppm |

Epoxy resins can be shown to contain measurable levels of  chlorine, such as sapponofiable, hydrolyzable and fixed  chlorides. Additional halogens are added to laminates through  glass sizes, wetting agents, curing agents and resin  accelerators. The results from ion chromatography showed  that there was very little extractable halide content in the base  laminate. Instead, the source of halides found in printed  boards was more likely from the board fabrication and  assembly processes. Sources for chlorides in the board  fabrication process were discussed previously.


There are currently no specifications regarding the total  amount of halides in printed boards and the total amount of  extractable halides. With regard to environmental issues, both  the United States and Japan are considering proposals that  would limit chloride levels to 1200ppm and bromide levels to  900ppm. In regards to extractable levels, the only equivalent  would be the experience of epoxy molding compounds (EMCs) in the electronic packaging industry. Before  extractable chloride levels were linked to long-term  performance, EMCs had extractable chloride levels of  approximately 40 to 170ppm. Due to improvements in raw  material selection and manufacturing process, current levels  have dropped to 0.1 to 10 ppm. Thus, based on experience  with EMCs, if a path is available and sufficient moisture is


present, the amount of chloride in the laminates would be  adequate to accelerate ECM-based processes.


Moisture


Studies by Augis [4] indicated a voltage-dependent moisture  threshold, below which no CFF should occur.  For office  conditions, this voltage exceeds 60 volts3.  This finding was  later validated by Rudra [1]. However, these studies assumed  a traditional CFF path, which is delamination between the  epoxy resin and the glass fiber.


Corrosion


There is some evidence that the observed particles were  reactive even without the presence of a voltage bias. During  visual examination of the printed wiring boards, small  discolorations were observed on the surface (see Figure 4). Cross-sections determined that the presence of particles  corresponded to these discolorations. The particles seemed to  attack the oxide bond, leading to localized delamination. The  most likely corrosive element that led to oxide debonding is  hydrochloric acid (HCl). The presence of extractable chlorides  and moisture condensation can often lead to the formation of  HCl.


Figure 4: Optical image of discolorations observed in the  printed board


In conclusion, based on a review of potential failure  mechanisms, measurement of relevant parameters, and the  results of SQUID microscopy, the process of electrochemical  migration around or through the particles was determined to  be the most likely root-cause of electrical shorting between  power and ground. Actual evidence of a conductive path was  not observed. This is not surprising. A calculation of the  conductor thickness, assuming that the conductor is a copper  slab and that the particle is about 2 mils on a side, shows that  the conductor is probably 2 to 5 nanometers thick. This  calculation explains why the conductor was not seen optically. 3 Augis et. al. considered only absolute voltage, not strength  of the electric field.


Even if the resistance prediction, similar to copper, was overly  generous, an increase in resistance by three orders of  magnitude would still only result in a conductor with a  thickness of 2 to 5 microns.

Extracting Acoustic signatures of  Solder Bump Defects using Wavelet Power Spectra and their  Proceedings from the 30h International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis,


Classification using Normalized Cross- Correlation.


Ramanujachar. K.


Texas Instruments,12203 South West Freeway, Stafford ,Texas


In  a  previous contribution  we highlighted the  potential use  of  spectral analysis of acoustic signals reflected from solder  bumps as a means to identify anomalies  in the bump. With  numerous interfaces in contemporary solder bump geometries, time domain interpretation of acoustic signals is not  straightforward. Frequency domain analysis is hence another  route to utilizing information contained about defects in  acoustic signals emanating from suspect bumps. In this  contribution we highlight the use of Wavelet transforms and  power spectra in analyzing acoustic signals and demonstrate  with a few examples how the transform may be used to obtain  unique finger prints of anomalies. We also discuss how cross  correlation technqiues may be used  to classify a fingerprint   once a comprehensive library of finger prints is empirically  constructed.


Solder bumps in contemporary flip chip packages are  multilayered structures wih numerous interfaces.  Anomalies  at one or more interfaces in the solder bump frequently cause  continuity failures in the flip chip package. Scanning acoustic  microscopy  can be used to visualize the locations of   anomalies in a flip chip package, but the images acquired  often in themselves do not help to classify defects.  In the  course of this contribution we shall explore how A scan  acoustic signals acquired from solder bumps may be analyzed  in order to identify and classify solder bump defects.  The  central thread running through this paper is the use of  frequency analysis of  A scan acoustic signals using Wavelet  techniques. Traditionally fequency  analysis has been carried  out using Fourier transforms. We shall briefly discuss   limitations of Fourier analysis  and the how Wavelet   transforms can help mitigate some of these limitations. In  particular we shall discuss the flexibility afforded by Wavelet  transforms both in the choice of the basis function chosen to  match the charctersistics of the signal being analyzed  and   multiresolution capability which enables concurrent time and  frequency domain resolution. The paper is organized along the  following lines.  We shall first highlight the potential of  frequency domain analysis through transfer matrix


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa088


simulations. This data has been previously presented[1]. Next   we discuss the limitations of Fourier based frequency analysis. We discuss the Wavelet transform and in particular how  Wavelet transforms can be used to address some of the  limitations of the Fourier Transform already highlighted. We  show how the Wavelet Power Spectrum is a useful tool for  identifying solder bump defects.  Finally  we describe how a  library of empirically constructed fingerprints can be used to   classify  solder bump defects using normalized crosscorrelation.


Frequency Domain Analysis Using Transfer  Matrix Simulations.


We have already alluded to the fact that solder bumps in  ceramic flip chip packages are multi-layered structures  constituted by materials with varying thickness and density. The tin lead solder bump in a ceramic flip chip package  contacts the ceramic substrate through a multi-layer metal film  and the die through an under bump metallization scheme  which is also a multi-layered metal stack. When an acoustic  wave is directed at this stack it suffers reflection at each  interface which separates materials with differing density. The  time domain reflected acoustic signal is constituted by a  number of such reflected waves which are mutually interfering  with one another.  It is this wave interference that makes time  domain analysis of the A scan signal difficult.  On the contrary  frequency domain interpretation of the acoustic signals can be  used to glean information about defects in solder bumps. In  Fig 1(a) and (b) we exhibit the results of transfer matrix  simulations[1] which enable a calculation of the frequency  content of an acoustic wave reflected from model structures in  which defects have been computationally introduced. The  model structure replicates the thickness and material  characteristics of contemporary solder bump geometries. In  Fig  1(a) the defect ( an air interface) has been introduced at  the solder bump die interface and in Fig  1(b) a similar defect  has been introduced at the solder bump substrate interface.  As  is clearly evident the frequency response peaks shift with the  peaks moving to higher frequency as the defect recedes deeper  into the solder structure.  These simulations show that  frequency domain analysis of acoustic signals may yield  valuable information about anomalies.

Limitations of Fourier Transform Analysis


Traditionally frequency analysis of signals has been conducted  using Fourier Transforms. The Fourier Transform method is  however not without its limitations. In particular Fourier  analysis uses sine and cosine functions to reconstruct signals. The sine and cosine functions are periodic and extend  infinitely in time. They are not appropriate basis functions to  be used for those signals that change abruptly in the time  domain. The second limitation of the Fourier transform has to


do with windowing.  Fourier Analysis assumes that the signal  being analyzed extends infinitely in time and is perfectly  periodic. When we are dealing with finite duration signals the  Fourier transform is computed after windowing the signal with  an appropriate function which tapers to zero at its extremities. As a result of convolution effects that accompany windowing  the Fourier transform cannot simultaneously achieve good  resolution in both the time and frequency domain.  Convolution effects mentioned previously also results in  spectral leakage that affects the power spectrum. As we will  see the power spectrum carries valuable information about  solder bump anomalies and windowing introduces artifacts in  its calculation.  A third drawback of the Fourier transform has  to do with the fact that when the transformation is carried out  all time information is lost. That is we know the frequency  content of the signal but we do not now what section of the  original time domain signal possessed particular frequencies. This drawback may be addressed with the short time Fourier  Transform, in which the original signal is segmented and the  transformation of each segment is carried out. However  segmentation requires a fixed windowing function with

concomitant limitations mentioned above.

Wavelet Power Spectra


The Wavelet transformation computed as explained in the  previous section can be converted into a power spectrum.  When the squared similarity coefficients calculated in Fig 5  are averaged over all scales we obtain the Wavelet Power


spectrum of the original acoustic signal. In a previous  contribution we speculated that the Wavelet Power spectrum  would contain information related to solder bump  anomalies[1].  Subsequent analysis of many acoustic signals  has revealed that the difference between the wavelet power  spectrum of a suspect bump and a good solder bump tends to  highlight bump anomalies. We have also found that the  difference power spectrum serves as a unique finger print for a  solder bump anomaly.


The mechanics of computing the difference power spectrum  are as follows. The A scan acoustic signal is captured several  times from a suspect bump.  Alternatively if it is suspected  that a number of solder bumps have similar anomalies an A  scan acoustic signal can be captured once from a number of  these bumps. The wavelet power spectrum of each of the  signals is then calculated. A mean power spectrum and  variance at each scale can then be computed.  A similar  process can be followed for known good solder bumps. The  difference power spectrum obtained by subtracting the mean  power spectrum of the good bump from the anomalous bump  scaled by the variance of the measurements has been found to  offer  an unique fingerprint of  the anomaly in the suspect  bump. A Morlet basis function was used for all  transformations. All transformations were carried out over  scales ranging from 1 to 64. Fig 6 shows three solder bump  anomalies and the corresponding difference spectra.  The three  different anomalies present in the solder bump are a diffused  copper stud, a dissolved copper stud and finally an open  interface. In the diffused copper stud case the difference  power spectrum shows a side lobe to the right of the main  peak at a higher scale, while there is no discernable side lobe  in the case of the dissolved copper stud. In the case of the  open interface there is a side lobe this time to left of the main  peak at a lower scale. This example serves to illustrate how it  is possible to distinguish the three defects from one another  based on the difference power spectrum.


Normalized Cross Correlation.


The fact that difference power spectra are unique to a  particular defect type can be used in the identification of   defects. However in order to achieve this identification it is  necessary to be able to find which signal in a library of  previously collected difference power spectrum signals bears  the closest resemblance to the signal at hand.  This is a  template matching problem and one approach to its solution is  with a technique called normalized cross correlation[3]. Normalized cross correlation consists of computing the  similarity  between a portion of one  signal and a time shifted  portion of another   ‘template’ signal. In practice it is most  conveniently computed in the Fourier transform domain by  multiplying the transform of one signal with the conjugate of  the transform of the template signal. Fig 7 shows how  normalized cross- correlation can be used to find the one  power spectrum difference signal that bears the closest


resemblance to a test difference power spectrum signal. In this  case the test signal has been chosen to be signal 3 in the  library. As the table below exhibits the test signal is perfectly  correlated to signal 3 of the library and hence a positive  identification is obtained.


The question that remains however is the adequacy of the  library or expressed differently how comprehensive is the  library and consequently how reliable is the match obtained by  cross- correlation? This is a question that can be addressed by  a technique referred to as principal component analysis (PCA). A short synopsis of principal component analysis is as  follows. Since all the difference spectra are computed over the  same range of wavelet scales, a covariance matrix of all  spectra in the library can be calculated. A matrix of the  eigenvectors of the co-variance  matrix ordered according to  the values of the corresponding  eigenvalues can be  constructed. A projection of the test signal on this eigenvector matrix can be used to calculate the contribution of  individual eigen-vectors  in reconstituting the original test  signal. Using this projection a reconstructed signal can be  obtained and compared ( subtracted) with the original signal.  Good reconstruction implies a good library and reliable crosscorrelation measures. In a test conducted with the same test  signal 3 and the library used in Fig 7, test signal 3 could be  reconstituted well enough that the difference between the  original signal and the reconstituted signal was smaller than


10-15.


Summary


We have discussed the utility of  frequency domain analysis of  acoustic signals in the identification and classification of  solder bump defects. In particular we have demonstrated that  difference Wavelet Spectra are sensitive finger prints of solder  bump defects.  The use of normalized cross- correlation as a  template matching tool for classifying defect types has also  been demonstrated.

# A Novel X-ray Microtomography System with High Resolution and Throughput For Non-Destructive 3D Imaging of Advanced Packages


A Novel X-ray Microtomography System with High Resolution and Throughput For Non-Destructive 3D Imaging of Advanced Packages


David Scott,


Fred Duewer, Shashi Kamath, Alan Lyon,David Trapp, Steve Wang, Wenbing Yun


Xradia, Inc., Concord, CA


dscott@xradia.com


X-ray microscopy has the potential to solve many failure analysis problems associated with advanced package technologies because of its ability to non-destructively inspect advanced multi-layer package designs.  In addition, x-ray imaging has the potential to perform fault isolation in 3D using well-established tomographic reconstruction methods.


The ability to perform high-resolution, artifact free tomographic reconstructions will be critical to the Advanced Packaging Failure Analysis community.


In this paper we discuss the requirements for a highresolution, three-dimensional tomographic imaging microscope.  We explain why conventional projection based microscopes are not well suited to high-resolution tomographic imaging.  Finally, we discuss the results from the Micro-XCT an x-ray tomographic imaging microscope designed by Xradia, Inc. to overcome the problems associated with conventional designs.


Requirements for High Resolution X-ray Imaging


To understand the problems associated with high-resolution tomography in a projection based x-ray microscope we need to understand the resolution considerations of such a system.


The resolution of an x-ray projection microscope is commonly thought to be driven by the x-ray source spot size.  Figure 1 illustrates the geometric configuration of a projection type xray microscope.  High resolution is achieved by magnifying the object onto the detector.  Notice, that as the distance between the source and the object gets smaller the magnification increases.  However, so does the blur induced by the size of the source spot S.  This blurring is given by


rS = Sba


Eq 1


where S is the size of the x-ray spot, a and b are the source to object distance and object to detector distances respectively.


To scale the resolution back to the object plane we divide by M the geometric magnification given by


M =a + b a


Eq 2


The blurring caused by the size of the x-ray source is commonly referred to as geometric unsharpness or penumbra.


In reality, the system resolution is a combination of the source spot size and the resolution of the detector. Therefore, the resolution of a projection based microscope system can be approximated by a convolution of the detector resolution and the source spot size scaled by the geometric magnification


rtotal =rD2+ rS2M


Eq 3


where rD  is the resolution of the detector system, and rS  is the blurring due to the geometric unsharpness,


For conventional x-ray projection based microscopes the resolution of the detector system is typically about 120um.


This means that in order to achieve 1um system resolution,the object must be placed very close to the source so that its projection is magnified to a point where the detector resolution is negligible.  Consequently, the x-ray source spot must be very small to minimize the geometric unsharpness.

Requirements For Artifact Free Tomographic


Reconstruction


In this section we will discuss some of the basic principles of tomography to gain an understanding for the requirements of a projection type x-ray microscope.


Figure 3 illustrates the case of a projection type x-ray microscope with an x-ray source, a simple object and a detector.  X-rays are emitted from the source, pass through the object and are measured by the detector.  As x-rays pass through the object they are attenuated according to the BeerLambert Law.


The Beer-Lambert Law states that the linear x-ray absorption through an object for a monochromatic x-ray source is given by the following equation:


I = I0el


Eq 4


where I  is the measured intensity after passing through a distance l  of an object with an absorption coefficient of


and an incident intensity of I0 .


If we measure the attenuation  along many parallel ray paths we generate a projection of the object as illustrated in Figure


3.  The Radon Transform models this forward projection process through an object as a line integral of the form [1]


P (t) =

Eq 5


Where P (t)  is the set of projected line integrals through the object represented by its absorption coefficient x,y( )  as shown in Figure.


Figure3 The process of acquiring x-ray projection images for tomographic reconstruction.


P (t)  is commonly referred to as a projection and can be


obtained by capturing x-rays that pass through an object using a line or area detector [1,2,3].  By rotating the sample through


one can acquire projections from many different angles of the object.  In the case of a projection based x-ray microscope for IC package inspection the required projections can be obtained by using a CCD or image intensifier to simultaneously capture a set of line integrals to form the projection from a single x-ray image.  The sample is then rotated to the next angle and the next projection is acquired.


This process is repeated until all the necessary projections have been acquired. Notice that with an area detector like a CCD or Image Intensifier, not only are the projections for a single slice acquired in a single exposure, but many slices are acquired simultaneously as well.


To understand how the projections can be used to recover the absorption coefficient information of the object we must understand the Fourier Slice Theorem.


The Fourier Slice Theorem states that the one-dimensional Fourier transform of P (t)  is equivalent to a line or “slice”


within the two-dimensional Fourier transform of the object taken at the same angle .  This concept is more easily


understood graphically.  Notice in Figure 4 we have taken a projection through the object at an angle  relative to the object.  We will call this projection P (t) .  The Fourier Slice


Theorem states that a slice at angle  through the twodimensional object transform gives the same values as the one-dimensional Fourier transform of P (t) .


Notice that as we acquire projections at various angles of


by rotating the object we start to fill in the frequency space of the object.  To completely fill the frequency space we must acquire projections over at least 180 degrees.  With a complete measurement of the frequency space through the x-ray projection process we can generate enough information to fully recover the absorption information of the object x,y( ) .


The reconstruction can be done by either direct Fourier inversion or by backprojection methods which reverse the forward process of the Radon Transform.  By creating a reconstruction for every row in the area detector we can stack the resulting reconstructions into a 3D cube of data representing the full object. The resulting reconstruction represents a 3D map of the absorption properties of the sample.  Since a typical IC sample is primarily made of relatively absorbing copper and lead structures surrounded by relatively non-absorbing FR4 we get a three-dimensional structurally accurate representation of the sample nondestructively.


Notice however, that if we do not collect data over 180 degrees we will insufficiently measure the frequency space and we will be unable to properly recover the object properties.


This is commonly referred to as the limited angle tomography problem and is discussed in more detail below.


The Limited Angle Problem


It is clear from the Fourier Slice Theorem that to completely fill the frequency space of the two-dimensional Fourier transform of the object using forward projections we must collect data over at least 180 degrees of the object or greater.


If we acquire data over less than 180 degrees then we will not completely fill the frequency space of the object and we will be unable to recover some of the object information as desired.


Figure 5 illustrates the problem encountered when not acquiring enough information to fully fill the two-dimensional frequency space of the object. In this example projection data has been acquired over a large angular range of the object filling most of the frequency space.  The black areas represent the regions where projections are missing. This results in a missing wedge of data in the frequency space.  The result in the reconstruction is that all frequency information is lost over


P(θ)

projection at angle θ


The impact on IC package inspection is that defects that lie parallel to the missing wedge of data will be very difficult if not impossible to detect due to the severe reconstruction artifacts.  These defects include interlayer-cracks, via delaminations, solder bump delaminations and small voids.


Achieving High Resolution Tomography in a Projection


Based X-ray Microscope


The question is   how   do  these  requirements  for   high   resolution imaging,   specifically   the  requirement   to    place   the    sample   in near     contact      w ith   the     x-ray     source,     impact     the      ability     to perform   high  resolution  tomography  ?


For an advanced package structure that is typically 12mm x 12mm x 2mm up to 60mm x 60mm x 2mm it is clear that it will be difficult to satisfy both the requirement from a resolution standpoint of placing the sample in near contact with the x-ray source and simultaneously satisfy the requirement for tomographic data collection where it is necessary to acquire at least 180 degrees of data around the object.  This is because in a conventional projection based xray microscope it will be impossible to rotate the sample without interfering with the x-ray source housing.  One can move the sample further away from the x-ray source, however,the result will be a severe penalty in system resolution as shown in Figure 2.

Thus, there are two options: 1)  move the sample away from the source and suffer the penalty of reduced system resolution or 2)  acquire less than the full 180 degrees of angular data and suffer the penalty of reduced Z resolution and reconstruction artifacts.


We have developed a system that overcomes both of these problems.   The system delivers high resolution tomographic imaging that is capable of acquiring high resolution images while simultaneously acquiring the required 180 degrees of projection information.


To demonstrate the capabilities of the MicroXCT system for advanced package inspection we have selected a flip-chip micro-processor package. This sample was selected for its multi-layer complexity containing copper vias, plated throughholes and C4 connections to the silicon die.


The data was collected using the Xradia MicroXCT x-ray tomographic imaging system.  721 projection images were collected over an angular range of 180 degrees.  The total data collection time was approximately 2 hrs.  The images were reconstructed using Xradia’s Tomographic Reconstruction Engine software.


Figure 6 illustrates the “virtual” cross-sections through the 3D tomographic reconstruction of the flip-chip package.  Notice that there are no blurring artifacts since the required 180 degrees of data was collected on this sample while simultaneously maintaining high resolution.


Figure 7 shows a “virtual” cross-section through the 3D reconstruction with 1um resolution.  Again, notice that there are no inter-layer blurring artifacts common to systems that acquire limited angle data.


Figure 6 "Virtual" cross-sections through the XZ plane (A) and YZ plane (B) of the 3D reconstruction of a flip-chip package. The C4 layer is at the top and the pin connections to the socket can be seen at the bottom of the image.  The plated through holes and copper inter-connects in the package are clearly visible.   Resolution is approximately 5um.


Figure 7 "Virtual" cross-section through reconstructed 3D volume of flip-chip package showing the C4 solder bump connections.


Resolution is approximately 1um (A).  “Virtual cross-section through failed C4 solder bump (B).


Figure 8 Volume rendering of reconstructed 3D flip-chip package.


We have shown that high-resolution, artifact-free tomographic imaging poses a problem for conventional projection based xray microscopes.  Acquiring the required projection data requires full rotation of the package sample.  This requirement results in a loss of resolution since the magnification must be decreased to achieve the required rotations.  The MicroXCT xray tomographic imaging system designed by Xradia has been developed to overcome these problems.  Its unique design allows for the required 180 degrees of sample rotation while simultaneously maintaining resolutions as high as 1um.  This capability enables non-destructive, high-resolution, artifact-free tomographic imaging which will prove to be vital in the failure analysis of complex three- dimensional advanced package structures.

Bridging faults are a common failure mechanism in integrated


circuits and scan-based diagnosis does a good job of isolating


these defects. Diagnosis, however, can sometimes result in


large search areas. Typically, these areas are caused by long


repeater nets. When this happens, physical failure analysis


will become difficult or impossible. This paper concerns itself *with using a bridging fault analysis as a means of reducing


these large search areas.


Bridging Faults


A common defect found in CMOS integrated circuits is the  bridging fault.  A bridging fault is a short between two or  more nets resulting in contention when the nets are in different  logic states [1].  To describe the behavior of bridging faults, several fault models have been put forth. These fault models  are: 1) wired-AND 2) wired-OR and 3) dominant [2].  Figure  1 depicts a bridging fault between the outputs of two buffers. The wired-AND model predicts that the ‘0’ logic state will  prevail when one of the nets is at ‘0’. Under this model both  OUT1 and OUT2 are ‘1’. The wired-OR model predicts that  the logic ‘1’ state will prevail when one of the nets is ‘1’. Under this model both OUT1 and OUT2 will be ‘0’. The  dominant model states that one gate will dominate over the  other gate. If gate G1 is the dominant gate both OUT1 and  OUT2 will be logic state ‘0’.


A feedback bridging fault occurs when a net is shorted to a net  in its combinational logic [3]. Depending on the resulting  logic configuration, this could result in oscillation or a  memory element being created [4]. The Byzantine Generals  Problem is another phenomenon in dealing with bridging  faults. It occurs when the bridging fault’s contention is  interpreted differently by two different logic gates [5].


The bridging fault analysis flow described in this paper uses  the dominant bridging fault model. This model is used  because failing vectors, caused by bridging faults, will yield  high correlation numbers for adjacent shorted nets. This can  lead to successful isolation of bridging faults. This model is  also used for passing vectors. Lower correlation is expected  for passing vectors. The reason is that under the dominant  fault model the shorted nets are supposed to be in the same  logic state. This is not always the case. Based on the results  shown in this paper, using the dominant model for both  passing and failing vectors has proved itself adequate in the  isolation of bridging faults.

Bridging Fault Analysis


Bridging Fault Analysis Flow


Figure 2 shows a block diagram of the bridging fault analysis  flow. It starts with a diagnosis of failing scan vectors. This  diagnosis produces a list of suspect nets. These suspect nets  are then located in a layout database and their adjacent nets  extracted. These adjacent nets are paired with their  corresponding suspect nets and simulated. A correlation on  the logic states of the pair is performed. Finally the unit is  submitted for physical failure analysis.


The first step in the bridging fault analysis is to diagnosis the  failure. This can be done using commercial software and a  tester data log of failing flops. The results from this step will  be a list of suspect nets (SN) to be looked at during failure  analysis. The assumption is made that a single defect is  responsible for the device failure. Also included in this  diagnosis is a look at whether the data supports the possibility  of a bridging fault. One such check is to see if the diagnosis  shows vectors exhibiting both stuck at 1 and stuck at 0  behaviors on the same net. Another check is to look at the  cone of  logic of a failing flop. If the cone’s logic state is the  same for both a passing and failing vector, this is a bridging  fault signature. In practice however, a sub-cone can be used. If  either technique shows evidence of bridging, the assumption  is made that the defect is a bridging fault.

Figure 2: Bridging Fault Analysis Flow


Adjacent Nets


The task of finding adjacent nets (AN) begins after the  diagnosis is complete. The first step is to locate all the suspect  nets in a layout database and extract the adjacent nets.  Adjacent nets are signals that appear immediately to the right  and left of the suspect net. They are selected only if they are  within a predetermined distance. This distance is chosen to be  large enough to catch most bridging faults. A distance of 3  times the minimum pitch for the layer is a good value to use. Only adjacent nets on the same layer are extracted. The  reasons for this are as follows. Same layer shorts occur more  frequently than inter-level shorts and the extraction process is  currently being done manually. To extract inter-level nets  would require more time and increase the number of nets to  analyze by a factor of 5x or more. This is due to the common  routing practice of alternating between vertical and horizontal  tracks as metal layers are increased.


Simulation


Once all the adjacent and suspect nets have been determined a  logic simulation must be preformed. The logic states of the  nets right before flop capture clock [6] must be determined. These logic states will be used in the next step for correlation  purposes.


Correlation


Correlation begins with the assumption that adjacent nets  dominate over suspect nets. For failing vectors, a pair (AN,SN) of nets correlate positively (FV+) if they have  opposite logic states. They correlate negatively (FV-) if they  have the same logic states. Of course this assumes that a  sensitized path [7] exists from this net pair to the capture flop. If a sensitized path does not exist, the correlation is negative  since this could not be the cause of the flop failure. For  passing vectors, a pair (AN,SN) of nets correlates positively (PV+) if they have the same logic state. They correlate  negatively (PV-) if they have opposite logic states. Once again


this assumes that a sensitized path exists from this pair to the  capture flop. If a sensitized path does not exist the correlation  is positive since this fault is not propagated to the capture flop. The following 2 equations are used for judging how well the  pair of nets correlate with the passing and failing vectors. They are respectively called Failing Vector Correlation (FVC) and Passing Vector Correlation (PVC). FVC is the better  predictor of bridging faults. PVC is a cruder measure of  correlation and is mainly used to validate the FVC, and as  shown later in this paper, PVC can be as low a 60% and still  locate a bridging fault.


FVC =  # of failing vectors with positive correlation   X 100%


# of failing vectors


PVC =  # of passing vectors with positive correlation  X 100%


# of passing vectors


Once correlation has been completed it is time to digest the  results. If the correlation is good adjacent net pairs are located  in the layout and the unit is submitted for failure analysis.


Unit 1


Unit 1 was from a group of 4 units, which had identical failure  signatures. Diagnosis narrowed the location of the defect to 4  possible nets shown in Figure 3. Three of the nets were small  but the one coming from the buffer was 8000um long. A total  of 59 adjacent nets were extracted from layout. Simulation  and correlation were performed and the top 15 net pairs are  shown in Table 1. Nets were numbered in the table to improve  readability. Net pairs with 100% FVC and greater than 60% PFC were located in the layout and the unit was sent for  failure analysis. The reduction in search area was from  9000um to approximately 700um. Failure analysis found a  defect on net pair #2. A photo of the defect is shown in Figure

Unit 4


Diagnosis of unit 4 resulted in a single suspect node with a  length of 3000um. Layout extraction resulted in 40 adjacent  nets of which one was VSS. Most of the time power nets do  not correlate well and are not considered when extracting  adjacent nets. This unit is an exception. It correlates well with  VSS and is included in Table 4 as net 0. Overall correlation on  this unit is extremely good. There are 9 pairs of nets with  100% FVC and greater than 93% PVC. This high correlation  is most likely the result of the low number of failing vectors. Only 16 out of 3400 total vectors used in testing failed. The  search area reduction was only 15%, due in part by the VSS  net which was adjacent to the suspect net in several places. Despite the best correlation numbers of all 4 case studies, this  unit was not submitted to failure analysis and is being held  awaiting further reduction of the search area.


Bridging Fault Analysis has proved useful in reducing the  length of nets, which must be searched for defects. Of the 4  units examined, two resulted in defects being found, one was  unresolved, and the last unit being kept for further area  reduction. Further analysis is needed to set guidelines for  good PVC and FVC. For now 100% FVC and 60% PVC are  the current lower limits which have proved successful. This  analysis is non-destructive and worthy of consideration if time  is available (approximately 3-5 days). Once the flow is totally  automated, the time factor should be reduced to less than a  day per analysis. Automation will also allow the search for  inter-level bridging faults without the associated time penalty.

# Cavity Up and Stack Die Backside Failure Analysis for Thin Die and High Pin Count Devices


Cavity Up and Stack Die Backside Failure Analysis for Thin Die and High Pin  Count Devices


Dat Nguyen, Thao To, Ray Harrison, Cuong Phan, John Drummond


Dallas Device Analysis Operation, Texas Instruments, Inc., Dallas, Texas,  dat@ti.com, t-to1@ti.com, cphan@ti.com


High pin count devices which may contain hundreds or  thousands of inputs/outputs (I/O), are commonplace in the  semiconductor industry and have posed challenges to failure  analysis (FA) for some time. For flip chip and high pin count  Ball Grid Array (BGA) packages, substrate routing and/or  package solder balls cover much of the front or backside of the  die. Furthermore, traditional front side analysis has been  limited due to multilevel metallization (>5 layers), dummy  metal layers, and dense metal coverage, which cover much of  the active circuitry. For these types of devices, FA is limited to  the backside of the die.


Another important aspect of high pin count devices is that in  order to pack more functionality into a die, they are fabricated  using the more advanced process technologies, such as


0.25µm channel length and below. These advanced  technologies utilize the chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) process. Since die planarity is important in the patterning  process of dense circuitry, dummy metallization is introduced  to ensure adequate metal density to maintain planarity across  the die and the wafer.


Moreover, effective backside failure analysis requires thinned  die [1] as leakage has fallen in the nano and micro Ampere  region along with migration to smaller geometric  technologies.


When a device is packaged, the bond out can be classified as  cavity up or cavity down. Cavity up means that solder balls  reside on the backside of the package; and cavity down means  that solder balls reside on the front side (Figure 1).


For cavity down packaging, the backside can be exposed  without compromising chip functionality; therefore FA can be  done readily from the backside. However, for cavity up  packaging exposing the backside of the die requires the  removal of package material, interconnect, and solder balls.


Figure 1: This is a simplified illustration of cavity up and  cavity down packaging.


Recently, the use of stacked die packaging configurations has  become more common. (Figure 2) By adopting this packaging  methodology, system integration schemes are optimized by  packing more functionality into smaller packages and  increasing operational speeds due to reduced-interconnect  impedance between die. However, stacked die configurations  pose even greater challenges to failure analysis since many  popular backside techniques require not only electrical and  physical isolation on the die but also pre-thinning of the die to  increase the chances of fault localization [1].


Figure 2: This is an example of a cross-section of a type of  stack die packaging. The top and middle die are cavity up, while the bottom die is a cavity down flip chip.


Due to the configuration of cavity up and stacked die  packaging and the requirements of backside analysis, both  packaging types require similar sample preparation steps. This

In general, the process includes testing and isolation of the  failing die, die re-packaging with cavity down, electrical  failure analysis (EFA), and physical failure analysis (PFA).


Figure 9: (a) (b) The P-V TEM image at weak-bit site. The  images showed substrate dislocation under node contact and  word line pass gate.


In this study, substrate dislocation may be caused by  insufficient stress release during the shallow trench isolation (STI) etching process, and can be eliminated by either high  temperature anneal or extra buffer layer adding at STI related  processes. Nevertheless, high temperature anneal or STI buffer  layer adding may influence the front-end doping and STI  oxide deposition, respectively. How to optimize these  parameters to get a dislocation free and high performance  device are also a great task for in-line engineers, but it’s not  the key point we discussed in this paper. The test results show  such process issue has been fixed and the yield has been  improved successfully as expected.


Bit line failure caused by one weak-bit is difficult to analyze, especially for substrate dislocation. With the assistance of  suitable test patterns, it’s possible to approach the leakage site.  Using FIB PVC and P-V TEM, solid failure mechanism and  suspected failure cause can also be dug out. Finally, FIB pad  deposition and electrical micro probing give us clear evidence  of contact or junction leakage caused by substrate dislocation.

Overcoming Environmentally Induced   Probe Drift for Sub-300nm Fault Isolation


Clint A. Waggoner


The Micromanipulator Co., Inc.


cwaggoner@micromanipulator.com, 775-882-2400


This paper defines environmentally induced probe drift and


elaborates on the problems and challenges associated with it  as they relate to physical sub-micron fault isolation systems . Vibration, acoustical, and thermal disturbances are discussed. Probing hardware that can be affected by environmental  conditions will be summarized. A comparison of the different  approaches is presented with the “pros” and “cons” of each  approach summarized. Optimal methods of managing probe  drift are presented to give the reader a complete understanding  of how environmentally induced probe drift may impact their  own physical sub-micron fault isolation. Examples, images, and  device data are presented when appropriate.


The pursuit of Moore’s Law is challenging semiconductor  companies in many ways. 90nm processes are pushing the  limits of technology, and announcements for 65nm and even  smaller process developments are common. Inspection and  deprocessing tools are pacing these developments with


# Overcoming Environmentally Induced Probe Drift for Sub-300nm Fault Isolation


moderate levels of success, but fault isolation, and particularly  physical fault isolation at these levels represents perhaps the  most daunting of challenges facing today’s semiconductor  industry.


Physical fault isolation remains an important step, but today’s  smaller devices are simply too small for traditional light optic  based probe stations. As a result, various approaches to  physical probing of sub-300nm devices have been developed.  Irregardless of the approach taken, the challenges of submicron probing are universally applicable. A difficult challenge  is environmentally induced probe drift that causes probes to  move off probing targets like those shown in Fig. 1. This type  of movement can prohibit multiple probe measurements and  can damage probes and/or samples.


Environmentally induced probe drift is defined as  uncontrollable multi-dimensional probe movement resulting  from ambient temperature variations, acoustical disturbances, or vibration induced disturbance of probing hardware [1]. This  type of uncontrollable probe movement can result in the  following:


Figure 2: NANO-100™ probe station with SEM optics.


Figure 1: SEM Image of 250nm probing targets with  contact probes.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa115


1. Inability to maintain contact for a period long enough  to make electrical measurements


2. “Noisy” measurement data


3. Damage to devices under test


Acoustical and vibration disturbances are often the result of  today’s lab environments. However, ambient acoustical and  vibration excitations can be magnified or sourced by  equipment design or inadequate implementation. Changes in  temperature can result from more than simple ambient room  temperature changes and may also be induced by probing  hardware itself. Individually or in combination, these problems   may directly impact the productivity and outcome of submicron probing operations. In severe cases, their impact can  render probing sessions and the data produced useless.


Engineers must consider an approach to maintain contact for a  period long enough to make electrical measurements with  multiple probes, without damaging devices, losing  functionality, or altering measurement data.


Affected Probing Hardware


Any sub-micron probing system has the following common  elements that can be affected by environmentally induced  probe drift.


• Sample holder


• Sample holder support mechanism


• Probe point positioners


• Probe point positioner support mechanism


• Probe holders


• Probe points


• General probing environment


Individually, or in combination, the items shown in Fig. 3 affect  probe stability at the DUT surface. The design of the  components shown in Fig. 3 is  key to achieving probe stability. Implementation of these elements must be made as a system  and be robust enough to mitigate the effects of ambient  vibration and acoustical disturbances, while not introducing  resonant excitations of their own.


Problems and Challenges


The problems and challenges for sub-300nm fault isolation  systems are:


1. Vibration disturbances


2. Acoustical disturbances


3. Thermal variation


Vibration Disturbances


Vibration isolation has long been a cornerstone of maintaining  probe stability. Light based probe stations have successfully  used passive, as well as active, isolation devices to prevent


floor and other vibration sources from transmitting to probing  samples and probe points. These basic vibration isolation


techniques provide a baseline for sub-micron probing systems, but more is required to meet the vibration isolation  requirements of sub-300nm probing systems.


Today’s light based probe station designs are usually not  adequate for sub-micron probing applications. Sensitivity to  floor and other vibration sources must be substantially  reduced to address sub-micron probing requirements. The  design of vibration isolation components must effectively  isolate a broad band (1Hz to 2kHz) frequency range.


Vibration can be multi-directional and will result in noisy data  and device damage [1]. The potential for damage increases  with Al and Cu probing targets and is complicated when  probing serpentine and similar layouts. Damage can short  devices or result in migration. Figure 4 shows an example of  vibration on a probe point and sample. Figure 5 shows noisy  SubVT data that was induced by an environmental vibration  disturbance.


Acoustical Disturbances


Acoustical disturbances are typically induced by acoustically  noisy lab environments. These types of disturbances can  result in minor air pressure changes that can excite probing  hardware. Typically insignificant to human senses, pressure


Figure 4: SEM Image showing vibration induced  disturbance.


Figure 3: Probing hardware that can be affected by


environmental factors.


changes can impact sub-300nm probing equipment, especially  if the probing hardware is not resistive to acoustical  excitations.


Many assume acoustical disturbances can be managed by  simply adding an external enclosure or enclosed probing  chamber. While this is generally true, more is required. Enclosures must be resistive to a wide range of both audible  and sub-audible excitations. And enclosures must maintain  their internal pressure and stop external pressure changes from  transmitting physical excitations to sensitive hardware.


Some companies design special rooms for sub-300nm probing  equipment installation. While it is true that certain lab  environments are simply not conducive to sub-300nm probing, proper equipment design can enhance installation site  possibilities while reducing ownership costs.


Thermal Variation


The thermal problems and challenges faced by today’s submicron probing systems include:


1. Variations in room temperature


2. Probing hardware temperature variations


Air conditioning and heating systems do a reasonably good  job of maintaining temperature for human comforts. But they  can not maintain temperature sufficiently well for sub-300nm  probing. Minor variations in temperature can translate into


substantial probe movement over a very short period of time. A mere 1°F change will result in linear expansion of 150nm (0.15um) per inch of steel [2]. Simply providing a “thermally  stable” room or enclosure will not provide the level of


temperature control required for sub-micron probing. Effective  probing hardware design and implementation must be able to  resist ambient room temperature variations that can be as large  as 10°F. The linear relationship of room temperature and steel  expansion is shown in Fig. 6.


Sub-300nm Probing System Comparison


Today’s FA Managers have several sub-300nm probing  approaches to choose from:


1. Addition of AFM (Atomic Force Microscope) based  probing technology to standard light based probing  systems.


2. Adding probing hardware to existing SEM (Scanning  Electron Microscope) or FIB (Focused Ion Beam) systems.


3. The NANO-100™ probe station with SEM optics.


Each choice approaches the management of environmentally  induced probe drift differently. The “pro’s and con’s” of each  are discussed below.


AFM on Standard Probe Stations


AFM’s have been used successfully for many years as an  imaging and topology tool. Recently, AFM imaging  technology has been married to existing probe stations for  physical sub-300nm probing.


With AFM technology, vibration isolation is provided through  the capabilities of the equipment intended for the standard  probe station used. A traditional light optic based probe  station is shown in Fig. 7. The rigidity and rejection band of  the standard vibration isolation hardware is designed for use in  light based probing operations. The station must be equipped  with a sub-micron stability platen (for holding positioners) and  microscope bridge and must rest on a high stability vibration  isolation table. This approach can be sensitive to and even  magnify acoustical excitation.


AFM based probe systems operate in atmosphere and  therefore require room thermal stability or a thermally stable  enclosure. For AFM’s to be useful, temperature variations
