must be less than 0.1°F. Enclosures can be added around AFM  based probing systems  to control thermal variations. In order  for these enclosures to be useful, they require time to reach a  point of thermal equilibrium that is good enough for submicron probing. These enclosures must also compensate for  changes in room temperature, which becomes increasingly  difficult as difference between internal enclosure temperature  and room temperature increases. Complicating matters, enclosures are constantly opened and closed to facilitate  sample loading and tip replacement. Enclosure opening and  closing may prohibit the enclosure environment and probing  hardware from reaching temperature equilibrium.


Pro


1. Uses standard “off the shelf” vibration isolation  hardware.


2. Potential to produce high resolution images.


Con


1. Can be sensitive to environmental exc itations.


2. Non-systems  approach to managing probe drift .


3. Light based probe stations are not specifically  designed for sub-micron probing.


Adding probing hardware to existing SEM’s and FIB’s


Another approach to sub-300nm probing is to add probing  hardware to existing SEM’s or FIB’s.


Generally, vibration isolation is required for the SEM or the FIB  system itself. However, it is important to remember that SEMs  and FIBs are designed with consideration of the relationship  between the imaging column and the sample itself only, and  not with concern for separately mounted positioners. It is  possible to couple vibrations of the column and sample to  obtain good imaging. However this will not allow stability of  the sample for probing. So the SEM or FIB system used in a  probing application must have active vibration isolation   elimination. And any hardware added cannot introduce any  resonances that may introduce additional excitations.


These systems are typically designed for easy removal from  SEM/FIB vacuum chambers. They are removed from the  vacuum chamber to accommodate probe tip and sample  replacement. Repeated removal of these probing systems from  the vacuum chamber causes them to see temperature changes  as they move from the vacuum chamber to atmospheric room  temperature. These temperature fluctuations may prohibit the  systems from achieving a state of thermal equilibrium, which  can translate to poor long-term probe contact. Furthermore, these types of probe stations are added to systems as an “addon” component. Therefore, the entire probing system (imaging  system and probing hardware) are not designed as a system to  manage the effects of environmentally induced probe drift.


1. Inexpensive solution if SEM or FIB is already  available.


2. Probing hardware may be used with a variety of SEM  and FIB systems.


1. Systems must be removed from the vacuum chamber  to facilitate sample and probe tip replacement.


Removal from the vacuum chamber causes   temperature differences between the vacuum chamber  and room.


2. The entire probing system, including imaging and  probing hardware, are not specifically designed for  sub-micron probing and therefore do not compensate  for probe drift in a system fashion.


NANO-100™ probe station with SEM optics


The NANO-100 is a sub-300nm probing system with SEM  optics and probing hardware.


The Nano-100 system incorporates custom vibration isolation  of the entire vacuum chamber and probing hardware. The  mounting of the probing hardware and SEM are designed as a  system to ensure stability, robustness, and in-phase motion of  probing hardware and SEM image. The vibration hardware is  designed to minimize susceptibility to acoustical and other  potential excitation sources.


To achieve long-term probe contact that is not affected by  thermal probe drift, the NANO-100™ incorporates a  thermally  stable design. From the manipulators to the control electronics, each component design considers the effects of temperature  on long-term probe contact. NANO-100™ probing hardware is  permanently affixed to the inside of the vacuum chamber. The  NANO-100™ also incorporates active temperature control  hardware that allows for adjustment to compensate for varying  lab environments.


1. Systems approach to managing environmental  disturbances.


2. Adjustable active temperature control hardware.


1. SEM is dedicated to and optimized for probing  operations.


2. FIB capability is not available.


This paper has discussed how environmentally induced probe  drift can effect physical fault isolation of sub-300nm  technologies. The paper has explained how the different  approaches to physical sub-micron fault isolation are impacted  by and manage environmentally induced probe drift. Comparisons were presented for the different approaches  available to address the real need to probe sub-300nm devices. Readers will be able to use this information in deciding how  best to approach their sub-micron probing needs.


Key Words:


Fault isolation, sub-micron analytical probing, transistor  characterization, and failure analysis .

Gunnar Zimmermann and Philipp Riess

The introduction of p+ implanted areas at the drain side of  source-drain-gate salicide-blocked electro-static discharge (ESD) protection diodes resulted in a better ESD robustness, however at the expense of increased leakage currents in up to  40% of the 90nm technology test structures. Leaky devices are  found to be randomly distributed across a wafer. The leakage  current exhibits only weak temperature dependence and is  linearly increasing with the p-implanted area. Photoemission  microscopy revealed spots located exclusively in the p+ implanted areas. TEM imaging visualized, that the leakage  path is caused by dislocations, reaching from the silicon  surface through the p+n junction zone into the substrate. Based  on these results and the implant conditions, a theory of  dislocation formation was postulated and countermeasures had  been defined.


ESD robustness is one of the fundamental parameters for  reliable integrated circuits. However, the design of ESD  protection circuits has to take into account and balance also  other - sometimes contradictory - key aspects, like area  consumption, technology compatibility and feasibility. During  the joint development of a 90nm technology platform between  United Microelectronics Corporation and Infineon  Technologies, different ESD concepts had been analyzed with  respect to a best fulfillment of these basic requirements.


In this article we will report on salicide-blocked ESD devices  with an additional drain-side p-implant. Salicide-blocking of  NFET diodes is widely used to increase the ESD robustness  by increasing the gate resistance and thus providing a higher  ballast loading of the protection circuit [1]. An additional  boron implant at the drain side of such devices (PESD  implant) was proposed by Tang et al [2] to further improve the  voltage clamping behavior. Due to this implant the drain side  parasitic npn bipolar transistor is effectively by-passed under  ESD stress conditions by an early triggering of the Zener


# Dislocation induced leakage of p+-implanted ESD test macros in 90nm technology


breakdown mechanism. This concept has the advantage of not  sacrificing area consumption, although it is increasing process  complexity by the addition of an extra mask for PESD  implantation.


This article is organized in three parts: a detailed description  of the investigated devices and the employed test and failure  analysis equipments and methods is presented in the  Experimental section. The Electrical results section then  highlights some of the obstacles, which were encountered  when introducing this ESD concept into the 90nm technology  platform. Emission microscopy and TEM results are  summarized in the Failure localization section. Finally the fail  root cause is discussed and possible countermeasures are  proposed.


The used ESD device is based on an IO NFET with a GOX  thickness tox of 52 A and a gate length Lgate of 0.23 µm, manufactured using a 90nm CMOS process on p-type  substrate (5e17 cm-3). P-well implantation consisted of three  boron (B) implants at 400, 250 and 140keV, respectively, followed by LDD and halo implants. The whole area was nimplanted for source and drain formation. Several annealing  steps with temperatures around or exceeding 1000 deg C were  applied after implantation for re-crystallization and dopant  activation purposes.


The p-ESD implant (B 50keV@5e13cm-2) was applied only to  the 2.5V IO devices. Salicide-blocking over the source, gate  and drain region is used in combination with PESD  implantation on the drain side of the 2.5V IO NFET (figure 1) to increase ESD robustness and voltage clamping behaviour. The area of PESD implant was varied for different devices  and did not necessarily include the drain contact row. Single  and multi finger test structures were tested. Devices were  analyzed either on fully processed wafers or on short loop  wafers, pulled after metal-2 completion and covered with the  final aluminium and passivation layers. Both wafer types  showed similar ESD characteristics.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa120


Failing samples were submitted for failure analysis, involving  emission microscopy localization with a Hamamatsu Phemos  1000 equipped with an HP4156 electrical analyzer and sample  holders for front- and back-side analysis. For metal-2 wafers a  front-side emission setup could be used, because only the  contact rows of the ESD diodes were then covered by metal. Samples from fully processed wafers required back-side  sample preparation [3,4] including wafer thinning to about  300 µm and mirror-polishing.


Figure 1: Schematic description of the ESD device. IO NFET  with salicide blocking on source, drain and gate (dotted area) and drain side PESD implantation (dashed outline box).


TEM samples were prepared both manually and with focused  ion beam for plan-view and cross-sectional inspection using a  JEOL 4000EX, operating at 400kV and allowing a  transmission of up to 4 µm of silicon or a Philips CM200 – LaB6 for conventional imaging of thin samples at 200kV.


Electrical results


The electrical effect of the PESD implant is illustrated in  figure 2, showing the IDVD characteristic of gate, source and  substrate grounded IO NFET devices with and without PESD  implantation. The drain side breakdown voltage of the n+ diffusion to substrate junction is decreased. This is lowering  the trigger voltage of the parasitic bipolar device of the NFET  and is effectively clamping the voltage at below 6V.


The drawback of this extra implant is the appearance of a  randomly distributed parasitic leakage between n+ diffusion  and substrate. The defects are randomly distributed over the  wafer. About 40% of the dies showed an increased leakage in  the range of (1e10 - 1e08) A/µm, which was up to 3 orders of  magnitude higher than the expected currents.


The number of leaking dies per wafer and the average  amplitude of the leakage current decreases as the area of  PESD implant is reduced. Figure 3 shows a linear dependency  between the average leakage current and the PESD area. No  significant difference in the fail mechanism was detected for  single or multi finger test structures.

The temperature dependence of this leakage current does not  show the activation of a classical pn junction. It is only  slightly temperature dependent (see figure 5). This indicates, that the leakage path could be a point defect which area is  limiting the current flow.


Failure localization


Emission microscopy revealed emission spots in the voltage  range between 2.5 and 5.3V. The application of higher  voltages resulted in the onset of the pn junction breakdown  mechanism, and the associated strong emission of the junction  area was inhibiting other observations. Failing devices  typically showed one or two spots, while “pass” devices


revealed no emission below the junction breakdown. All  emission spots were located inside the respective PESD  implant area of the defective device. Leakage current and  emission image were very stable even for voltages just below  the junction breakdown and integration times of more than 30  minutes.


A representative front-side emission microscopy image of a  multi finger fail device is shown in figure 6 for a voltage of


5.1V and a leakage current of 5.4µA, viewed through a 100x  lens at 30s integration. In both cases the emission is inside the  PESD implant area near the drain contact row.


Figure 6: Front-side emission microscopy image of a failing  multi finger test structure (5.1V, 5.4µA, 100x lens, 30s  integration) showing two emission spots in the PESD  implanted area near the drain contact rows.


Although the spot localization was not always sufficient for  TEM sample preparation, dislocations were found in the  vicinity of the emission sites for a significant number of  samples. For the sample shown in figure 6, a plan-view TEM (figure 7) was prepared to exactly localize the dislocation. Then a cross-sectional cut was done for the identical location  to visualize the origin of the leakage current (figure 8).


Figure 7: TEM plan-view of the emission area (circle) showing several long oblique dislocation dipoles (A-C). Specimen thickness is 3µm.


Figure 7 exhibits several long oblique dislocation dipoles (AC) between the gate and the drain contact row, out of which  dislocation B lies within the emission area (circle). Figure 8a  is a cross-sectional TEM view of the same sample, while  figure 8b shows details of the dislocation in the zoomed area  of fig. 8a (dashed lines). The cross-sectional specimen  thickness is estimated by the two lines in figure 7.


Several defect zones are visible in figure 8, which can be  attributed to different implants. The long oblique dislocation  dipole B in fig. 8a is reaching from the sample surface about


1.6µm deep into the substrate. Additional large dislocation  loops are visible at a depth of 0.8µm and 0.9µm below the  surface. Both types of dislocation are related to the high  energetic triple p-well implants (compare table 1 in the  discussion section).


A bifurcation of the dislocation B is present in a depth of  about 0.5µm, penetrating a defect-rich plane with {111} dislocation loops at 85nm below the sample surface. These  loops correspond to the n-implants. The bifurcation of one  long oblique dislocation dipole near the surface was observed  for all emission spots but not at random sites.


FA Process Flow for Cavity up and Stack Die


In the case of high pin counts and complex functionality, testing for FA is performed on automated test equipment (ATE). Consequently, fault isolation must be completed on  ATE as well. The FA process flow includes testing  to  determine the nature of the failure, failure correlation to chip  and/or internal circuitry, die preparation for repackaging, die  repackaging in a cavity down configuration, ATE testing to  verify the integrity of the pre-packaging failure mode, backside thinning, global fault isolation, backside  reconstruction, and defect identification by front side  deprocessing. See Figure 3.


Figure 3: FA process flow for cavity up and stack die for thin  die and high pin count devices.


Failure ID on ATE


EFA for high pin count devices frequently involves the use of  ATE and the implementation of an appropriate fault isolation  strategy during the design phase. High pin count device testing  may be performed on various testers, with the major  difference major difference between high pin count and low  pin count device testing residing in the availability of complex  pin resources. Moreover, special analysis modes are frequently  required in the test program. With this special analysis, the  user can run I/V curve traces and perform special tests outside  the normal production test program. These special analysis  modes provide a valuable tool for the user to debug the failure. The analytical mode is more critical for high pin count  devices, but it can also be applied to low pin count devices. In  either case, the basic strategies for testing and fault isolation  are similar. Devices are thoroughly tested to narrow down  candidates for the failing circuitry. This may involve  modification of the test program or the use of specific  diagnostic vector sets. For continuity failures, a simple curve  trace on the bench can confirm opens and shorts. With stack


die, the failure may be associated with a specific function of a  particular die. In this scenario, once the failure has been  identified, it can be traced through the pins and onto the die  within the stack. An example of a stack configuration could be  an ASIC with two (2) flash memory devices (Figure 4). If the  failure was functional, then FA should be done on the ASIC, and if the failure was in the memory then one of the flash die  would be isolated for FA. If the failure cannot be traced to a  single die in the stack, the FA process will be much more  complex and may require extensive simulations to be  completed by the designer. In either case, the failing die needs  to be repackaged in a cavity down configuration to gain die  access from the backside for global FA techniques.


Backside Access for Cavity up and Stack Die


For a high pin count single die in a cavity down configuration  such as flip chip devices, a simple decapsulation or heat sink  removal, can expose the backside of the die for EFA (Figure  1). However, for cavity up devices, only the front side is  exposed after decapsulation. With dummy metal layers and  dense metal buses blocking photons and dissipating heat  during photon emission and thermal transition analyses, traditional front side FA is limited (Figure 5). Moreover, cavity up packaging often covers the backside with substrate  routings and solders balls (Figures 1 and 5).


Similar issues arise for stack die with two (2) or more dies  stacked together into the same package (Figures 2 and 4). Depending on the location of the failing die in the stack, access to the backside of a die with full electrical functionality  requires repackaging in a cavity down configuration [2].


Backside access for FA of cavity up and stack die devices  involves removal of the die from the original package, repackaging as cavity down, failure re-verification, and backside  thinning.

Repackaging, Verification & Backside Thinning


Repackaging starts with the investigation of whether a  repackaged device can be successfully integrated back into the  ATE test board/socket. This involves working with the  designer, test engineer and repackaging vendors to provide a  transposer, which is specifically designed to translate the new  package footprint back to the original footprint. Since each  type of device has a unique footprint, a different transposer  will be needed for each one. See Figure 7. If a transposer  solution is not available, re-design of the test board and test  program is necessary to reflect the new packaging. It should  be noted that if a stacked die configuration is used, the design  team should plan to have separate cavity down packages  available that will be compatible for each unique die in the  stack. [4].


Once a suitable solution has been identified, the dierepackaging process can begin by preparing the original  package. The top and the bottom package materials of the  original device can be polished away. The re-bond process  requires exposed bond wires, however, in some cases, exposed  bond balls may be needed to provide a larger contact area than  the bond wire diameter.  The sample needs to be polished to  the bond wire or to the bond balls depending on the situation  for re-bonding. After exposing the bond wire, a cavity down  package is selected and wire bond to wire bonding is  performed [4]. See Figure 6. The new cavity down package is  then re-adapted back to the test board through the use of a  transposer (Figure 7). The new package is re-tested on the  ATE for verification of the original failure, and the backside is  then thinned by parallel lapping.


Figure 6: Repackaging of a cavity up or stack die package  into cavity down packaging. The cavity up package is first  front side polished to expose the bond wires; second, it is  mounted inside a cavity down package; third, the exposed  bond wire is bonded to the new cavity down package; fourth, it must be encapsulated with clear epoxy; and finally, the  backside solder balls must be polished away and the backside  of the die thinned.


Figure 7: This is a cross section of how a cavity up foot print  package is being transposed from a cavity down package back  into the original footprint.


Global Fault Isolation on ATE


High pin count and thin devices are typically associated with  complex and multitudinous functionalities, and are coupled  with advanced process technology. Due to the complexity of  the circuitry, failure verification and fault isolation must be  completed using ATE. In addition, FA from the backside by

probing with a Laser Voltage Probe system is typically time  consuming and tedious. From the time and cost point of view, backside FA on these high pin count and stack die devices  must rely on the existing global FA techniques.


Once the conversion from cavity up and stack die packaging  to cavity down packaging is completed, electrical fault  isolation of the failure can be accomplished through the  normal backside FA process. However, as mentioned above, the complexity of testing makes it difficult, if not impossible, for bench setup to duplicate the ATE failure. EFA is often  facilitated on the ATE, with modification of the test program  to isolate the failure. While the device is being tested on the  ATE, global fault isolation techniques, such as photon  emission microscopy (PEM), thermal transition analysis, thermal imaging, and Scanning Optical Microscopy (SOM) like TIVA and LIVA, are utilized. Localization of the defect  from the backside can be identified using LASER and IR to  look through silicon. Furthermore, because the global fault  isolation techniques mentioned above involve voltage/current  defects, for functional failures, test software modification is  needed to lock the failure in a loop. Testing for FA include  halting on or looping on failed vector. This allows the repeated  exercise of the failing circuit so that photon emission or other  abnormalities can be observed. As always, comparison  between the behavior of a good or passing die and a bad or  failing die must be made before PFA.


Backside Reconstruction and Front Side  Deprocessing


Most often a stack die is a thin die (below 200µm). However, depending on the failure, die thinning below 50µm may be  needed if leakage is in the nano-ampere level. For the case of  extremely thin die (<100µm), PFA is done after backside  reinforcement [3]. The thinned backside is reconstructed using  a layer of heavy-duty epoxy sandwiched with a piece of  silicon or Kovar metal plate. The product requires curing for 3  hours and then trimming with a diamond saw. After the  reconstruction, the front side package materials can be  polished away [3]. HF is then used to remove the remaining  epoxy materials. The remaining deprocessing steps now can  now be completed using traditional methods, i.e. polishing, plasma etches, or chemical etches. However, for CMP process  devices, the preferred method of front side deprocessing is  parallel lapping or polishing. Front side deprocessing is also  preferred over backside deprocessing because it allows the  viewing of all the active circuitry.


Case History


The following images represent successful repackaging efforts  of cavity up packages. The reader should understand that the  procedure is the same for stack die packaging.


In this example, a cavity up device with dense upper  metallization, as seen on the right hand side image in Figure 4, had an Iddq failure after an Electrical Static Discharge (ESD)


test on the power supply pin. The package was polished on the  front and back sides to expose the existing bond wires. See  Figure 8. It was then placed inside a cavity down package, rebonded, and then encapsulated with clear epoxy. See Figures  9-10.


The converted package was then adapted back into the original  ATE fixture through a transposer, which mapped the new  package solder balls into the ATE test board for testing. The  backside of the die was then thinned below 100µm for  backside global FA.


The new package device was next tested on the ATE, which  put the device under proper power up and failure conditions. While the device was in the failed mode, photon emission  analysis was performed using Infrared Emission Microscopy (IREM). An anomalous emission was observed under the  power pad, which was the subject of ESD test. Subsequently, backside reconstruction was done (Figure 11) to allow front  side deprocessing, which revealed the ESD damage. See  Figures 12 and 13.

In another case of cavity up repackaging, the failure was Iccq  after an ESD test. The same repackaging process was followed  and the die backside was thinned to less than 100µm. Backside IREM was performed on the ATE. Furthermore, because of the leakage at the pin, backside liquid crystal  analysis was also performed using the Vcc power pin as an  electrical stimulus. An 1153nm LASER was used to reveal the  underlying active circuitry. PEM and LC data were taken  together to determine the actual failure site. See Figure 14.

An example of a stack die repackaging effort consists of a  wireless device stacked with two flash memory die. The stack  die packaging is as shown in Figure 4. In this case, an Iddq  failure was submitted for analysis. The failure is related to the  wireless device, and the original package was then polished to  remove the flash die and to reveal the bond balls (Figure 15). The wireless device was then repackaged as a cavity down

device and backside thinned. The device was then subjected to  retesting on the ATE to confirm the original failure.


IREM backside analysis was then performed while the ATE  was halted on the Iddq failure. A strong emission site in the  RAM block is shown in Figure 16. Front side deprocessing  indicated metal 2 to metal 2 shorting, possible due to CMP  micro scratching (Figure 17).

Summaries and Conclusions


While there are challenges working with modern circuits  housed in cavity up and stack die packaging, FA can be done  by repackaging the failing die into a cavity down package. Since FA can only be performed on one die at a time, a stack  die package needs to be converted to a single die cavity down  package. For cavity down packaging, the backside can be  exposed without compromising chip functionality; therefore, FA can be done readily from the backside. However, for  cavity up packaging exposing the backside of the die requires  the removal of package material, interconnect, and solder  balls. In all cases, re-verification of the original failure mode  must be completed after repackaging is completed. Finally, a  transposer is used to translate the footprint of the new package  back to that of the original packaging. Once the conversion  process is finished, FA can be successfully accomplished  through traditional backside FA processes. However, because  of the complexities of testing involved, backside FA for high  pin count devices must usually be done on the ATE. ATE FA  can often be performed using special analysis modes and the  modification of the test software to put tester in a halt or a  loop during fault isolation.  When this is completed, global FA  techniques can be used.

Investigation of Substrate Dislocation Induced Bit Line Soft Failure


Jian-Chang Lin, Yung-Tsai Hsu, Chih-Kuo Huang, Wu-Chin Tsai, Yung-Hua Chou


United Microelectronics Corporation, Hsin-Chu, Taiwan, ROC


In modern integrated circuits (IC) using sub-micron or deep  sub-micron process rules, substrate dislocation is a common  failure mechanism in SRAM or embedded SRAM products. Depending on the position of substrate dislocation in the  SRAM cell, it may result in problems including junction or  contact leakage, gate oxide early breakdown, low threshold  voltage, and poor data retention. In this paper, we’ll focus on  the test methodology and physical failure analysis to dig out  the failure mechanism, substrate dislocation under SRAM pass  gate and node contact. In addition, we will measure the  electrical behavior of such substrate dislocation. Several FA  techniques, such as Passive Voltage Contrast (PVC) [1] pad  deposition by Focus Ion Beam (FIB), and electrical micro  probing [2] will be used during leakage verification and  measurement.


It’s a very important job to localize the exact failure site or  address during SRAM function failure analysis. Incomplete  test data or error scramble will increase the uncertainty and  difficulty of failure analysis. In SRAM common failure modes  such as single bit, twin bits, and multi-bits failure, they are  easier to debug since the failure area has been narrowed down  to one, two, or several bits only. By using Scanning Electron  Microscope (SEM), FIB, and Transmission Electron  Microscope (TEM) at the failure sites, most of failure  mechanisms can be dug out. But for some SRAM failure  modes such as bit line (BL), word line, I/O, Block, and etc., if  no hot spots by liquid crystal detection (LCD) or no emission  spots by emission microscope (EMMI) can be found, PlaneView (P-V) layer-by-layer check or Cross-Sectional (X-S) inspection at memory cell or decoder circuit is unavoidable  but probably with a quite low success rate.


For bit line failure caused by slightly leakage at bit line  contact, it’s a troublesome job to localize the failure site  during electrical and physical failure analysis. FIB PVC  technique is a nice tool for leakage contact inspection, but it


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa109


# Investigation of Substrate Dislocation Induced Bit Line Soft Failure


will be restricted by small leakage current and large failure  area.


In this paper, a test skill will be introduced in a FA case to  successfully approach the failure bit line to a single weak-bit  within failure bit line. By narrowing the failure area down, it’s  possible to localize a substrate dislocation under bit line  contact and measure the leakage current.


Test approaching and fault localization


The microelectronic failure analysis process consists of five  main steps, namely: failure validation, fault localization, sample preparation and defect tracing, defect characterization, and root cause determination. [3] Among these items, how to  localize physical failure site is a key job and it strongly  decides the success of failure analysis. In this section, an  effective test procedure will be introduced and adopted to  approach the physical failure address. Base on test result, failure analysis cycle time will be greatly shrunk and  successful rate will also be increased.


Prior to starting formal failure analysis, several key  observations were made by product engineering: (1) the  failures could be induced with Scan Checkerboard or March  pattern, (2) the failure bit counts increased as Vcc decreased, i.e. the lower Vcc, the worse of the failure, (3) failing devices  could pass with Scan all “1” or “0” pattern. As Figure 1 shows, one partial bit line failure can be localized by Scan  Checkerboard or March pattern and it became a full bit line  failure as Vcc decreased. But when we test the failure die by  using the Scan all “1” or “0” pattern, the failure bit line  disappeared and passed even the Vcc lower than 1.0V. The  normal Vcc voltage is 1.2V in this product. This is a typical so  called soft failure which suffered Vcc minimum and pattern  sensitivity issues.


Figure 1:


(a) Partial bit line can be localized by Scan Checkerboard or  March pattern.


(b) The failure mode became full bit line fail as Vcc decreased.


(c) The failure bit line disappeared and became passed by  Scan all “1” or “0” pattern.


By using special test methodology (As the chip pass the Scan  all "1" or "0" pattern, then we intentionally write an inverted  data "0" or "1" to any bit within this bit line and read the bit  line by high Vcc), a weak-bit within this bit line can be dug  out successfully. Actually, the state of this weak-bit has been  flipped by leakage path during writing an inverted data to the  other bit within this bit line and it also caused the whole bit  line failure when read at low Vcc. As Figure 2 shows, when  we test the failure die by such test methodology, the failure bit  map showed only one bit fail instead of one bit line fail. Thus, we can focus on this weak-bit for further failure analysis to  find out the failure root cause.


Figure 2:  Single bit fail instead of bit line fail was dug out by  test methodology.


Failure mechanism and analysis algorithm


The detail analysis algorithm and failure mechanism is  showed as Figure 3. Owing to the signal in BL (or /BL, bit line  bar) becomes Hi (or Lo) and Lo (or Hi) alternately during  Scan Checkerboard and March pattern. In Figure 3(a), it was  suspected that a weak cell suffers pass gate leakage which  should cause a leaking path from /BL to SRAM cell while  other bits from this BL are read. Thus, the partial bit line fail  should happen due to a leaking signal from /BL. And, it  became a full bit line failure at low Vcc operation because the  lower Vcc should decay the sense capability of sensing  amplifier (S.A.) and the reduced delta V between BL and /BL  are worsen the failure. In Figure 3(b), it's very clearly that  there is not any leakage path for Scan all "0" pattern. So, it can  pass the test pattern even Vcc lower than 1.0V. Then, we  intentionally write of an inverted data "1" to any bit within this  bit line (ex. write data "1" to address Row 0, failure column) showed as Figure 3(c). The data of weak-bit would be flipped  to "1" by pass gate leaking to /BL during this intentionally  write an inverted data into other bit. And, the leakage path  between this weak bit and /BL would be formed. The signal of /BL should always leak to "0" and BL should rise to "1"


during read operation. Thus, the bit line failure should happen  when we read "0" to whole chip. Actually, the data is flipped  only happen in this weak-bit. So, by high Vcc to enhance the  sense capability of S.A. and increase the delta V between BL  and /BL is very helpful to improve the read performance and  avoid such read error. In Figure 3(d), the real weak-bit which  data was flipped can be readout easily by higher Vcc (ex. 1.5V  or above). Thus, the failure address of single weak-bit within  failure bit line can be accessed successfully by such effective  test methodology.

Focus ion beam passive voltage contrast  technique


According to test results, FA will focus on this weak-bit. Since  bit line is at metal-3 layer in this eight-transistor (8-T) embedded SRAM product and single bit cell is below metal-1  layer, it was reasonably suspected the existence of a leakage  between weak-bit and failure bit line through bit line stack-via (or bit line contact). Bit line contact is a stack-via structure for  inter-connection between bit line and drain (or source) region  of word line pass gate MOS through Via-2, metal-2, Via-1, metal-1, and contact. For leakage tracing, two kinds of FA  methods will be adopted. One is a qualitative analysis by FIB  PVC technique, and the other is a quantitative analysis  including current measurements by micro probing at both  good and bad sites.


FIB voltage contrast is a familiar but useful method during  failure analysis. By different level of secondary electron  collection due to different potential voltage at sample surface, we can easily distinguish the floating, leaking, or wellconnected circuits, except too small difference between good  and bad circuits. Before PVC inspection at bit line stack-via, it’s necessary to remove metal-3 layer because stack-via  belong to the same bit line are tied together by metal-3 layer. Here, metal-3 layer is removed by using Chemical Mechanical  Polish (CMP) method and FEI 800 FIB single beam system  will be used for PVC inspection. The bright PVC image at  Via-2 layer in Figure 4 indicated bit line contact leakage and  the location was just close neighbor to the weak-bit identified  by tester. The result indicates the existence of leakage path


between failure bit line and substrate, possibly through a  defective gate.


Figure 4: Passive VC image at Via-2 layer. The bright PVC  image indicated leakage at bit line stack-via site.


By SRAM layout examination in Figure 5, bit line contact was  connected to N+ junction and P-well, and was surrounded by  two word line pass gates in poly layer. In other words, the  bright PVC image may be caused by leakage between bit line  and word line or between bit line and substrate layer. Since no  abnormality could be observed at any layers above the  substrate by using P-V SEM and X-S FIB, N+ junction or Pwell failure in substrate layer would be suspected in this study.


Figure 5:


(a) The poly and active area structure in SRAM cell.


(b) X-S FIB picture of bit line stack-via structure in Xdirection.


(c) X-S FIB picture of bit line stack-via and word line pass  gate structure in Y-direction.


Pad deposition by focus ion beam and I-V


characteristic curve measurement by electrical  micro probing


Electrical micro probing at SRAM block is a helpful but  difficult job for cell leakage measurement. By suitable micro  probing at 8-T SRAM MOS terminals at contact layer, we can  measure the leakage current quantitatively. To achieve this  purpose, at least four-pin probe is necessary to provide proper  bias condition for leakage MOS (pass gate MOS in this case) at source, drain, gate, and P-well region. Due to small cell size  in this product, it’s not easy to do pad deposition with high  success rate to measure the I-V characteristic curve. To  simplify the job and increase success rate, it was suggested to  have a comparison for junction leakage current between good  dies and bad dies (or between good and bad sites in one failure  die) instead of completely measure the characteristic curve of  leakage MOS. By this way, electrical micro probing can be  executed at Via-2 layer and not at contact layer. In other  words, two-pin probe at bit line stack-via and P-well is enough. Besides, an extra benefit can also be gained since wider layout  spacing at Via-2 layer than that at contact layer will greatly  increase the success rate of pad deposition.


As we know by layout examination, bit line stack-via and Vss (GND) at Via-2 layer will be stacked from active layer  through contact, metal-1, Via-1, and metal-2 layers. Furthermore, bit line contact and Vss were connected to the  N+ junction and P-well region, respectively. When we try to  re-wire bit line contact and Vss sites by Via-2 layer, it’s  possible to measure junction leakage between N+ junction and  P-well by electrical micro probing technique. Before FIB pad


deposition, one thin oxide film will be deposited on sample  surface to prevent shortage between different Via-2s during  Platinum (Pt) film deposition. Figure 6 shows the top down  view of the deposited pads and Figure 7 and 8 show the I-V  characteristic curves by micro probing. Two L-shape lines are  Pt film deposited by FIB for micro probing, and two short  damage lines are FIB marks for failure site marking. As data  showed in Figure 7 and 8, the breakdown voltage with 1uA  leakage current was about 2.3 and 4.3 volts at failure bits and  pass bits, respectively. That is to say, the N+ junction to P-well  showed smaller breakdown voltage in bad sites than in good  sites.


Figure 6: Pad deposition result at bit line stack-via and Vss  sites.


Figure 7: The I-V characteristic curve at failure site by  electrical micro probing. The curve showed about 1uA  leakage current at Vcc=2.3V.


Figure 8: The I-V characteristic curve at normal site by  electrical micro probing. The curve showed about 1uA  leakage current at Vcc=4.3V.


Failure mechanism study by P-V TEM


After electrical measurement by the above technique, an  evident leakage current exists at N+ junction or P-well region. To exactly clarify failure mechanism and failure cause to  make a suitable and effective action item, a substrate quality  check is executed by P-V TEM to make sure if there is any  substrate defect at the weak-bit. After that, it was found that  there is obvious and serious substrate dislocation under word  line pass gate and node contact at the weak-bit site. Furthermore, no similar substrate dislocation can be observed  at good sites as shown in Figure 9. This kind of dislocation  under poly gate and close neighbor to diffusion contact may  cause gate oxide leakage, diffusion contact or junction leakage, or poor device characteristic.


Therefore, it was postulated that the dislocation under the  word line pass gate and close neighbor to bit line contact  would induce the risk of pass gate leakage, N+ junction  leakage or bit line contact leakage, and result in bright PVC  image at bit line contact nearby the weak-bit. Since the N+ junction is surrounded by P-well (GND), this leakage current  would induce bit line failure through bit line stack-via at the  failure site.


Figure 8: figure 8a shows a TEM cross-section of the area  between the indicated positions in figure 7. Figure 8b shows a  detail of the dislocation dipole near the surface.


Figure 9: TEM cross-section of the region near the surface on  a different sample. Additional defect zones are visible.


A zoom into the region near the surface (figure 9) is revealing  additional dislocation loops on {111} planes in a depth of  about 30nm. Additional defects, like loops and micro-twins  are visible directly under the surface. These can most likely be  attributed to the LDD and PESD implants.


Based on the TEM images it is obvious, that long oblique  dislocation dipoles, reaching from the sample surface through  the pn junction are randomly affecting the leakage current  performance of the IO NFET protection diodes. The dangling  bonds at the dislocation cores lead to conductivity as well as  possibly to dopant diffusion along the dislocation line (“pipe  diffusion”, see e.g. Kranzer et al. [5]).

To further discuss the impact especially of the B implants on  the dislocation generation, the critical point defect density in  as-implanted state (not taking into account the influence of  annealing) was calculated for the different B implant  conditions according to Hobler et al. [6].


Obviously the p-well implants at 250 and 400keV generate the  highest point defect density well below the surface (figure  11a). During the annealing steps these point defects form the  dislocation loops observed in a depth between 0.8 and 1.0µm  together with the long oblique dislocation dipoles. Deep well  implants may lead to clear separation of vacancy and  interstitial profiles which generate vacancy and interstitial  dipoles after annealing. It is assumed that the long oblique  dislocation dipoles are of vacancy type though this has not yet  been verified by TEM contrast methods.


The p-ESD implant close to the surface shows a comparable  point defect density peak as the two deepest p-well implants (figure 11b). Though the implants are carried out at different  process stages with several anneals between them, it is  tempting to argue that the point defects originating from the pESD implant agglomerate at the tip of some long oblique  dislocation dipoles and elongate them to the surface during  annealing. These dislocations finally cause the leakage.


Another finding reported in the literature corroborates our  view: Schreutelkamp et al. [7] showed by RBS and TEM  observations, that dislocations are produced by a B  implantation and a following vacuum-furnace anneal at 900  deg C, when a critical number Nc of 1.5e16cm-2 displaced Si  atoms per layer is exceeded. The total number of displaced Si  atoms is obtained from the point defect density profiles by  integration (see the listing in table 1).

Both the 250keV well-implant and the p-ESD implant yield a  number of displaced atoms per layer that is higher than the  critical number given by Schreutelkamp. They  generate a  high point defect density from close to the surface down to a  depth of about 2 µm, which is able to generate dislocations  upon annealing.


Large oblique dislocation dipoles, reaching from the sample  surface through the pn junction zone into the substrate, have  been identified by TEM to cause increased leakage currents of  salicide blocked NFET ESD protection diodes, which are  PESD implanted on the drain side to improve the voltage  clamping. The increased conductivity is most likely caused by

dangling bonds at the dislocation cores in combination with  dopant diffusion along the dislocation line.


A defect density calculation for different boron implants  revealed, that especially the PESD implant causes a high  defect density near the sample surface, able to prolong the  dislocation dipoles up to the sample surface. This observation  fits to the observed dependency of average leakage current on  PESD implanted area, as well as to the fact, that emission sites  are always located within the PESD-implanted area.


Possible countermeasures include a reduction of PESD area, a  reduction of the p-ESD dose below the critical point defect  density, a change in the implant energy to shift the defect  layer, a change in the integration scheme and an increase in  annealing time to reduce the generation of long oblique  dislocation dipoles.

# A Purpose-Driven Decision-Based Methodology for Debug and Failure Analysis


A Purpose-Driven Decision-Based Methodology for Debug and Failure Analysis


Steven P. Maher


Oklahoma Christian University, Oklahoma City, OK, USA  Steve.maher@oc.edu


3) Design: translate specifications to a set of engineering  deliverables (e.g. Computer Aided Design (CAD) file) that are used to produce an actual product.


There are many different discussions and perspectives on  processes for product debug and failure analysis (FA) of  integrated circuits [1][2][3][4], with some even minimizing  the aspect of process for FA. Most attempts to-date at a  process for FA have been either task-oriented or capabilityoriented.


4) Prototype/1st Article: produce first physical


implementation of product (e.g. First Silicon) from design  deliverables (engineering, manufacturing, or lab).


5) Debug/Validation: identify and fix any problems in


functionality; test all features and specifications of


product to validate design.


In this paper, a high-level purpose-driven decision-based  methodology is proposed, with goals of:


6) Qualification/Certification: test and stress in statistically  meaningful ways to ensure quality, reliability, and


manufacturability (often including testing to meet


industry or government standards).


1) Establishing a high-level discussion of Debug process;


2) Initiating a high-level discussion of FA process;


3) Encouraging a broader "world view" in the context of the  product life cycle;


7) Ramp Production: build first capability to mass-produce; add capability/capacity as product engages market; tweak  design or production equipment if problems emerge and  to optimize production variables.


4) Emphasizing clarity of purpose (of Debug or FA actions)


- "why do we (the analysts) do what we are doing?”


5) Establishing context for synergy between Debug and FA.


8) Volume Production: disengage product engineering; product ownership fully assumed by manufacturing  organization (until production end of life).


9) End of Life: in order: dismantle manufacturing as market  demand declines; discontinue active service and support; dispose/replace product as it becomes obsolete.


Versions of the purpose-driven decision-based approach have  been successfully applied to debug and FA of high-end  microprocessors [2], as well as to other digital products.  This  paper explores this methodology by presenting (1) an  overview of each process for Debug and FA; (2) a definition  for each step of the process, with examples of how each step  applies to various situations; (3) perspectives on how to set up  and optimize the process; (4) a holistic approach for  establishing and maintaining the process, tools and  capabilities; and (5) implications to lab funding, corporate  training, and college/university (higher) education.

The product development life cycle (Fig. 1) provides a highly  appropriate context for the exploration of this methodology.  Integrated circuit products (and, in fact, most products) undergo an equivalent process.  For some products, this life  cycle is years long (e.g. military and space products); for  others, it is substantially shorter (e.g. personal computer  chipsets).  And of course, as in all development processes, the  earlier problems are caught the better (and cheaper).


Figure 1: Model of the Product Life Cycle


Product Development Life Cycle


Throughout the product life cycle, a fair amount of overlap  exists between the purposes and capabilities for Debug, FA, and even low-yield analysis (LYA).  A product tends to  require Debug capabilities first (for example, for “First  Silicon”); then FA (for certification and process troubleshooting); then LYA as the product ramps into production.  A  high-level purpose-driven approach to defining each of these  component processes reveals these similarities and overlap.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa126


For the purposes of this discussion, the process steps for  product development are defined as:


1) Definition: identify, specify, and document the


requirements for the product based upon customer


requirements and requests.


2) Planning: determine and document resources needed


(type and amount), project timeline, and costs/ROI.


By taking a synergistic approach to these three areas, a  product development group can look for optimizations and  leveraging of capabilities.


Overview of Debug Process


Debug, typically the first FA process application in the  product life cycle, will be reviewed first.  The overall  purpose-driven, decision-based process for Debug is  summarized in Fig. 2.


Detect a Fault


(Test, Fault Detection)


Internally Isolate the Fault


(Fault Isolation)


Determine Design Flaw


(Bug Identification or Root Cause)


Fix the Bug


(Engineering Change Order)


Verify the Fix


(Design Verification)


Characterize the Fault (Fault Characterization)


Figure 2: Overall purpose-driven, decision-based process for  Debug


Key to this approach is keeping the debug process as simple  as possible, and staying focused on the overall purpose of  each step.  Detecting a fault or failure initiates the process.  Once a fault is detected, the single overall objective is to find  the root cause of the bug, fix it, and fix it as rapidly as  possible.  To this end, it is useful to break the process down  into a few fundamental steps that are critical in achieving this  end.


Each of the six steps identified in Fig. 2 flows from one to the  next, but each is also fundamentally different in purpose, methodology, results, and the tools used to complete it.  Although some commonality of equipment and tools applies  to multiple steps (for example, testers and test software), the  application for each step is different.  Therefore, the tools are  optimized differently for each particular step.


Another aspect of this approach is that each step can employ  multiple avenues to achieve the purposes for that step.  This  means that parallel paths and different combinations of tools  can be used to complete the step depending upon the  particular bug or problem.  This, in turn, opens up many ideas  and possibilities for parallel analysis paths, risk mitigation, debug process optimization, speeding up debug, and teamoriented approaches to debug.


Debug Process Steps


As noted earlier, fault detection is the (obvious) starting point  for Debug.  This step may sound trivial, but its significance  should not be underestimated - in debugging First Silicon of a


product, it is critical to detect all faults as soon as possible.  In  practice, the goal of fault detection should be to detect 100% of the design faults with as few false failures (faults that are  not design bugs; e.g. testing glitches, pattern errors, or setup  problems) as possible.  A good test approach will optimize test  coverage while also providing ways to quickly eliminate false  test failures.  Once a test failure occurs, the analysis process  should either 1) quickly identify it as a test or setup error, or  2) confirm that it is a true failure and insert it into the next  step as quickly and efficiently as possible.


Once a failure is confirmed, the second step is to characterize  the fault.  In this step, the purpose is to find out as much as  possible about the failure without physically breaking into (de-constructing) the part.  This is a “black-box” approach  where the device is tested in various ways and the test results  analyzed in detail, with an end goal of comparing exactly what  the part is actually doing to what it should be doing (plus  providing a high-quality hypothesis for root cause of the bug).  Examples include observing which test sequences fail, which  outputs fail, scan results, data dependencies, parametric  dependencies (such as voltage or temperature), and results  from various functional test patterns.  Scan-based and self-test  methodologies are very useful for this step.  A good designfor-debug (DFD) and characterization methodology will yield  fault isolation to a very small portion of the die very quickly.   Why do so much work here?  First, it is critical to obtain as  much information as practicable from the device under  analysis (DUA) before any steps are taken that may destroy  the part or alter its behavior.  Next, many times the passing  behavior is as important (in terms of determining final root  cause) as the failing behavior.  Finally, quality work here will  minimize time required for the subsequent steps.


Many designers operate under the misconception that 100% fault isolation success can be achieved at this step.  Although  some bugs can indeed be isolated during this step, other  analyses will be close but not quite sufficient to determine  root cause of the bug.  For example, several gates or multiple  hypotheses could explain an observed failing behavior.


The third step is to internally isolate the failure.  The purpose  of this step is to determine exactly where the bug is on the  design schematic and layout.  Often, the best way to confirm  this is to probe the device to identify exactly where the device  function breaks down (e.g., input is passing and behaves as  expected, but output is failing and not behaving as expected).  This can be performed with micro-probers, e-beam probers, laser probers, or optical probers depending upon the device, process technology, and particular bug behavior.  Many  design groups underestimate the power of this step.  Often, by  doing a precise job of isolating the failure, the root cause of a  bug becomes obvious.  The best analysis identifies the “smoking gun;” that is, the specific transistor or design  module that exactly explains the externally observed behavior.   Many groups overly depend on Step 2 to isolate bugs, and end  up with flawed analyses and flawed design fixes (or take  much too long to isolate the bugs).  On the other hand, groups


that overly depend upon probing can fall into doing a sloppy  job in Step 2.  This causes them to probe many more points  than necessary while they hunt for the exact location of the  fault, costing both time and money.  A better approach is to  optimize Steps 2 and 3 together to develop a process that  quickly and efficiently enables test results to inform probing  guidance.  This probing activity, in turn, yields internal signal  behavior that precisely explains the external test results.


Once the fault is isolated, Step 4 follows to determine the  design flaw.  The goal of this step is to describe exactly what  is wrong with the design.  As stated earlier, the root cause of  the bug will often become obvious through the fault isolation  process.  At other times, the designers will need to develop  better simulations of the circuitry to determine why the design  did not behave as expected.  As fabrication processes have  scaled, an increasing number of bugs are caused by designprocess interactions.  These interactions may even drive  changes in the assumptions and models that designers use, requiring teams of design and process engineers to work more  closely together to understand the root causes of bugs arising  from design-process interactions.  These root causes will, in  turn, drive future design-for-manufacturing (DFM) considerations for those processes and product lines.


Once the root cause of the bug is determined, the fifth step is  to fix the bug.  In practice, this step serves to tweak the design  to fix the fault that was found, but without breaking anything  else.  The fix may become obvious as the fault is isolated and  root cause is determined.  However, other cases are not so  clear-cut, and some fixes may break the design in unexpected  ways.  In simple terms, the designers need to propose a fix, simulate it, implement it, and verify that it works.  The  ultimate fix will, of course, be implemented into the mask set  for the device.  Tools for pre-mask fix validation using circuit  edit capabilities, such as with Focused Ion Beam (FIB) equipment, provide a methodology to test a bug fix before it is  committed to the mask set.  This allows a circuit fix to be  verified much faster (and cheaper) than by developing an  experimental mask set.


The final step of the process is to verify the bug fix.  This is  basically a repeat of Step 1 with fixed Silicon.  Initially, a fix  implemented via a FIB circuit edit can be tested against  previously failing tests to confirm that the engineering change  order (ECO) actually fixed the bug.  Then, the whole test suite  may be run on the fixed device to confirm that nothing else  was broken by the ECO (providing high confidence in the  proposed mask fix).  It is not uncommon to see multiple  iterations through Steps 4, 5, and 6 before a final bug fix is  found (and with that, consider optimizing Steps 4 and 5  together to be able to iterate quickly and smoothly).  The  ultimate verification, of course, is with new Silicon using the  new masks that contain the design fix(es).


Tool Sets for Debug


Five possible tool sets are associated with the six Debug steps.  Steps 1 and 6 (fault detection and fix verification) utilize a  common tool set that serves to support volume testing.  These


tools emphasize functional verification, actual performance  verification, test coverage, AC/DC specification, parametric  testing, throughput, and test productivity.  Typical equipment  utilized includes end-user systems, production ATE (automatic test equipment), handlers, and temperature control  units (in turn utilizing hardware (HW) test fixtures to support  volume testing).  Typical software (SW) includes test control  SW, test patterns, and end-user applications.


For Step 2 (fault characterization), the tool set supports  engineering test analysis.  These tools should emphasize  functional analysis, timing analysis, parametric analysis, and  engineering productivity.  Optimal tools are both equipmentand software-oriented around engineering analysis (such as  engineering testers, production ATE with engineering tool  sets, and end-user systems with engineering capabilities  added).  Good test fixtures incorporating temperature control  are often needed here.  SW tools that take advantage of  Design-for-Test (DFD) methods such as Scan are also used to  optimize Step 2.  Test SW tools should be developed that  identify module, block, node, or even gate information from  test results.


The most appropriate tools for Step 3 (fault isolation) are  probing equipment with accompanying test capabilities.  The  purpose of these tool sets is to provide precise measurements  within the die.  These tools should emphasize technical  capability to match the process technology of the product, transistor level analysis, timing measurements, voltage  measurements, and engineering productivity.  Equipment  options include micro-, e-beam, laser, and optical probing  equipment, with test options of engineering testers, engineering-oriented production ATE, end-user systems that  can run test loops, and on-chip self-test capabilities.  For some  bugs, emission microscopes and similar tools can provide  breakthrough results.  CAD Navigation, sample preparation, and temperature control are important equipment capabilities  for this step.


Step 4 (design flaw determination) is mostly design-centric.  The purpose of this tool set is to analyze the design and its  behavior, so the focus of these tools is on: logic, timing, and  parametric analysis of the design; accurate architecture  specifications, schematics, and layouts of the design; and, any  associated tools that aid in problem solving.  The tool set to  generate the product design is typically employed here.


The design tool set is also used in Step 5 (bug fixing) but, for  this step, the tool set for doing circuit edit is added.  The  purpose of the bug fix tool set is to implement proposed  design fixes.  The emphasis of the circuit edit tools is upon  technical capability to match the process technology of the  product, precision cuts, precision metal deposition, quality  sample preparation, high circuit edit yield, and fast circuit edit  throughput.  CAD Navigation adds an often-critical capability. Typical equipment used for the Debug process is summarized  in Figure 3 and Table 1.

Figure 4: Overall purpose-driven, decision-based process for  Failure Analysis (FA)


The first three steps for FA (Detecting a Fault, Characterizing  the Fault, and Internally Isolating the Fault) have the exact  same purposes as in the case of Debug.  The central concept is  that: (Step 1) failures are found and confirmed through a  volume testing method; (Step 2) the fault is characterized as  extensively and as quickly as possible without breaking into  the package; and, (Step 3) the fault is then isolated to be able  to identify exactly where the fault is on the product schematic  and layout.


Table 1: Equipment and Tools by Debug Process Step


Following Fault Isolation, the emphasis in FA diverges from  that for Debug.  Instead of looking for the root cause of a bug, the focus is on finding and identifying the defect that causes  the failure.  Once that defect is identified, the ultimate goal for  FA is to determine root cause and drive corrective actions to  prevent future (re)occurrences of that failure mode.


Comparing the Debug and FA processes in parallel illustrates  these similarities and differences (Table 2).


Table 2: Debug and FA Process Step Similarities/Differences


Overview of Failure Analysis (FA) Process


The overall purpose-driven, decision-based process for  Failure Analysis (FA) bears a strong analogy to the Debug  process in that it is relatively simple and also consists of six  basic high-level steps (Fig. 4).  As in the case of Debug, detecting a fault or failure initiates the process.  In this case, however, once a fault is detected the overall goal is different.  Instead of a bug (which results from a design problem that  leads to a functional or performance problem and is assumed  to be on every device), the goal of FA is to find the root cause  of a failure, which is a defect that makes this particular device (the DUA) fail where others do not.

Fault Characterization and Fault Isolation for  Failure Analysis Process


Although the high-level process steps of Characterizing the  Fault and Internally Isolating the Fault are the same for  Debug and FA, they do differ in lower-level purpose, implementation, and execution.  In Debug, the design is under  scrutiny so everything (the model, schematics, layout, test  patterns, test setups, etc.) is in question.  In FA, the design and  test results are assumed to be correct, and that the particular  DUA is different from known-good devices.


To characterize the fault, a “black-box” approach is again  employed where the DUA is tested in various ways and the  test results analyzed in detail, with the end goal of comparing  exactly what the part is actually doing to what it should be  doing.  Because the design is assumed to be correct, extensive  use of design models (such as the logic model) should be  considered, and have been successfully incorporated into very  productive FA methodologies [5].  Scan-based methodologies  have proven especially useful for this step [6].


There is a tendency for analysts to rush through this step.  As  discussed earlier, it is critical to thoroughly characterize the  fault in order to: (1) get as much information from the DUA  before steps are taken that may destroy the part or alter its  behavior; (2) carefully observe the passing behavior (which  may be as important as the failing behavior in determining  final root cause); and (3) minimize the time required for  subsequent steps.  Many experienced FA practitioners know  the frustration of units changing behavior or even being  completely destroyed in the sample preparation (deconstruction) process.  In some cases, the behavior change  through de-construction is actually a manifestation of the rootcause defect (such as for failures caused by cracking  phenomena or mechanical stresses between the package and  die).  Another perspective is that the ultimate objective of FA  is not to find a defect, or even a defect that produces the  observed failure, but to specifically find the right defect  among the failure’s many possible defects.  Only the right  defect will implicate each of the failing characteristics and  none of the passing behavior.  Therefore, the better the  definition of failing behavior, the greater the analyst’s ability  to logically rule out the incorrect defects and positively  identify the right one.


Similar to Debug, the best way to internally isolate the failure  is often to probe the device to ascertain exactly where the  device function breaks down; i.e., the exact location of that “smoking gun” (although for FA, the “smoking gun” will be a  defect - not a bug).  Again, micro-probers, e-beam probers, laser probers, and optical probers are all useful tools for this  step.  Analysts tend to underestimate the value of doing this  well because this step can be time-consuming and require a lot  of effort, but it is many times critical to successful FA.  One  reason is that local effects of the failure cause are often  inaccessible to outside test resources due to the design and  construction of the device.  By probing circuitry around the


defect, the analyst gains crucial insight into the defect and its  effect on device functionality.


As in the case of Debug, many analysis efforts overly depend  on Step 2 to isolate bugs, and end up with flawed analyses; or, overly depend on probing to find the exact location of the  fault.  Both approaches are sub-optimal and may end up  costing more time and money than necessary.  A better  approach is to (again) optimize Steps 2 and 3 together, quickly  translating test results into good fault isolation results.


Other tools for Fault Characterization and Fault Isolation, not  typically used in Debug, are required in FA.  For example, tools to analyze I/O leakage (such as curve tracers and multimeters) are often required.  This is a common FA problem but  a rare problem in product Debug.  The use of “global” tools  and techniques for Fault Isolation, such as emission  microscopy and TIVA (Thermally Induced Voltage  Alteration), is much more common in FA than in Debug (although for certain Debug problems, these tools have  provided crucial results - an important reason for debuggers (who are typically designers) and FA practitioners to continue  to seek and maintain synergy between these two disciplines).   During Fault Isolation, it is strongly desirable to do as much  as possible to understand the failure and defect before  performing any steps that may destroy functionality of the  part.


Failure Analysis Process Concluding Steps


Once the fault is isolated, Step 4 (defect isolation) is  employed.  The purpose of this step is to precisely locate the  defect that is causing the particular node or transistor to fail.  That defect may become obvious through the fault isolation  process described above.  However, whether a defect is or is  not apparent at this point, the first priority is a non-destructive  visual examination of the failing circuitry.  Ideally, this  provides a visual confirmation of a defect that, in turn, explains the observed behavior - for example, finding a metal  stringer between a node and ground that explains why that  node is stuck at 0.


Even though an analyst has probed and found the exact  transistor that is failing, the cause of this misbehavior may not  be evident.  Even more challenging, the analyst may know  which node is failing, but with that node mapping to many  places on the DUA.  An emission, for example, may be caused  by a defect directly, or it may be a symptom of the defect at a  location away from the emission location.


In such cases, further analysis, further probing, or some level  of destructive analysis (e.g. local micro-probing) will  ultimately be required to determine why the node or transistor  fails.  This is where fault characterization results are valuable.  The analyst needs to ask a number of questions: What  behavior on this circuit will explain all of the test results?  Will a short (to ground, VCC, or another node) explain the  results to this point?  Will an open circuit (for example, an  open via or open contact) explain the results observed?


Table 3: Major Capability Modules associated with the Debug  Process


Where does all of the data (test results, probing results, emission results, etc.) lead?  If the DUA is still functional, further fault characterization may provide critical insight.  If a  defect explaining the electrical behavior has not been visually  confirmed, all avenues for functional analyses should be  exhausted before more destructive techniques (such as crosssectioning) are utilized.


The result of defect isolation is visual confirmation of the “smoking gun” defect; specifically, that defect which causes  local circuit behavior that precisely explains the external test  results.  Visual confirmation can be simple, such as an image  of an actual particle, stringer, or similar defect; or, it may be  obtained from a curve trace result of a VT-shift or some other  indication of an implant, mobile ion, or hot carrier type  problem which is not easily imaged.


Once a defect is observed, it needs to be identified (Step 5 - defect identification).  The purpose of this step is to describe  the defect, how it causes the observed failing behavior, and its  likely source.  This typically employs a materials analysis  process to determine the composition of the defect, and  usually also requires collaboration with engineers in the  fabrication or assembly processes to understand the probable  source of the defect.


Step 6 (root cause determination) follows defect  identification.  The purpose of this step is to determine how  the defect occurred in the device, with an end goal of  preventing future failures.  For example, in the case of an ESD (electrostatic discharge) failure, a source of excessive  electrical charge may need to be found, or the failure may  indicate a design weakness.  Another example may be a  particle defect in a lower metal layer: it must be determined  what in the fabrication process left the defect on the device.


As in all effective organizations, the analyst needs to work as  a team with those in the responsible areas to identify root  cause and drive/promote any necessary corrective actions.


Implications to Funding, Training, and   Higher Education


Once the above processes are established, it makes sense to  develop roadmaps for capability/capacity, equipment, tools, personnel, skills, training and other ancillary requirements; and also to look at ways to optimize the processes according  to critical criteria (such as cost or time-to-money) for a  company, division, or product line.


This simplified high-level process provides a good framework  for building a roadmap of capabilities and equipment against  product needs.  Reorganizing Table 1 into the major capability  modules identified in Table 3 can serve as a tool to establish  such a roadmap for Debug.  As noted in Table 3, there are  only six major modules that accomplish the entire Debug  process.  Table 4 identifies essential elements for each of these  six modules.  To build a given module, these elements need to  be put in place and integrated together.

By evaluating product needs over time for each of the above  major capabilities, a matrix can be assembled to identify  component needs to be funded for a product group, division, or company (depending upon the scope of the needs analysis).  It is important to realize that three of these modules (Production ATE, Validation System, and Design Tool Suite) are necessary for other functions in product development and  manufacturing, so those should already be funded and  available. the Engineering Test, Probing, and Circuit Edit capabilities, plus advising on any Debug/FA needs for the other three  areas.  A sample template for such a roadmap is illustrated in  Fig. 5.
