Through building this Capability Roadmap, a high quality  needs-and-solutions analysis can be accomplished.  This  framework also provides a template for presenting the  solutions to management for funding.  The details of how to  do this are not addressed in this paper, but by summarizing  equipment and tools in terms of high-level process and highlevel capabilities (within the context of the productdevelopment cycle), communication with management is  much easier and more productive.


This same framework and process can be applied to FA.  For  example, Tables 3 and 4 would require modification and  expansion for FA (a topic for future work).


This overall process and capability framework also has  significant implications to training and college/university  education.  First, analysts need to be familiar with the product  development life cycle.  They need to understand the big  picture of where FA fits into that cycle, and how their  contributions can have the most impact on product success.  In  the context of product development, they need to be trained in  the possible sources of failures.


Second, training modules can be developed around each major  process step and the capabilities required for completing that  step (for example, engineering test, probing, and circuit edit).  This training can add extensive value by emphasizing analysis  with (not just use of) the tools, and by establishing a  philosophy of thinking and questioning.  For example, the  focus of a training module with an engineering tester could be  upon the trainee determining everything possible about a  known failure, both failing and passing.


Third, both the product development life cycle and high-level  analytical processes can easily be taught in college/university  courses at the undergraduate level.  This could be a first step  in the incorporation of related analytical skills education into


higher education curricula.  The above model for the product  development life cycle has been incorporated into Engineering  Economics and the senior capstone design course sequence at  Oklahoma Christian University (OC).  The students grasp the  concepts quickly, and the model has provided an excellent  context for teaching other considerations in engineering  design (required by the Accrediting Board for Engineering  and Technology (ABET) since 2000), including economics, environmental, safety, health, sustainability, and  manufacturability.  The Debug process (as discussed in this  paper) has also been taught in the senior capstone design  sequence at OC.  Although the students are not actually  developing IC’s, this process is very applicable to electronic  and electromechanical systems that the students do design.  In  addition, it provides the students with a good framework on  analytical thought processes for designs and products.


This paper has explored high-level process models for Debug  and Failure Analysis (FA) in the context of the product  development life cycle.  These process models adhere to the  principle of “keep it simple” while still fulfilling the “necessary and sufficient” criteria for getting the analysis job  done.  In summary, for Debug: once a failure is confirmed, that fault is characterized.  It is then isolated, its root cause is  determined, a fix is proposed and implemented, and (finally) that fix is verified.  For FA: the fault is confirmed and then  characterized and isolated.  After it is isolated, the defect is  isolated and identified and, finally, the root cause of that  defect is determined.


From another perspective, fault characterization is doing  everything possible before de-construction begins.  Fault  isolation is doing everything possible before de-construction  to the point of rendering the DUA non-functional.  Defect  isolation is localizing the correct defect before it is lost in any  kind of materials analysis work.


This model has generated a framework that has been used in  capability roadmaps, equipment roadmaps, tool development, management summaries, funding approvals, analyst training, and higher education.  However, this model is really just a  beginning.  Future work may include developing a more  comprehensive model and tool set for FA; building a model  for LYA processes along these same concepts; developing a  process for capability roadmaps; exploring methodologies for  process optimization (especially for minimizing analysis  throughput time); developing cost and (more importantly) return-on-investment (ROI) models for Debug/FA; and, building additional materials for training and higher  education.


Thanks are in order for the many individuals (too numerous to  mention) at Intel and its suppliers who helped in formulating  and using variations of this model throughout the years, to  Tracy Myers and Steve Ferrier for their encouragement to  produce this paper, and to Steve Hoffman for his excellent  mentorship on it.

# Improved Electrical Failure Analysis / Fault Isolation Tool Development on Server Motherboard Platforms based on Historic Failure Modes


Improved Electrical Failure Analysis / Fault Isolation Tool Development on Server  Motherboard Platforms based on Historic Failure Modes


Patrick G. Opdahl


Intel Corporation, DuPont, WA, USA


Electrical fault isolation constitutes the first steps in  characterizing and isolating the failure modes and root causes  of a failing motherboard.  Ideally the Failure Analysis Test  tools provide complete coverage of all motherboard buses and  silicon devices.  Time and resource constraints for tool  development prevent complete coverage, however, so the  challenge is to provide the highest level of debug test coverage  in the shortest development schedule.


A simplified Fault Isolation process has been created based on  historical failure analysis data to reduce the development time  and resources to create tools which allow diagnosing failure  root causes on high-end server motherboards.  This strategy  prioritizes the most common types of electrical failure modes  and the types of Electrical Failure Analysis / Fault Isolation (EFA-FI) tools best suited to diagnose these modes.


The benefits of this strategy include shorter EFA-FI  development times, equivalent success rates in failure root  cause, lower costs, and more effective EFA-FI tools that can  be used within the Design Team and at either OEM or  Contract Manufacturing sites.


Server motherboard designs based on multiple 32-bit and 64-bit processors have until recently enjoyed long design  schedules before manufacturing volumes ramped for  production.  Ample time was available to develop whole suites  of diagnostic tools that would access all available buses, components, and functional features throughout the  motherboard platform.


The original objective for diagnostic tool development was  complete, 100% coverage for a FA Engineer to quickly isolate  a failure in any functional area of a Motherboard.  In the past  this was accomplished by generating traffic among all  hardware components to isolate a failure root cause in its  functional area.  Dedicated headcount and hardware resources  were typically allocated for much of the design period and  well into volume production of a product.  Tool development


did not begin until several revisions of silicon and  motherboard hardware had occurred to produce a more mature  product.  Furthermore, the diagnostic tools developed  historically were complex, required advanced architectural  knowledge, and had no portability between 32-bit and 64-bit  Server architectures.


A typical diagnostic tool development schedule lasted 18  months and produced just over 100 unique test procedures.  Development consumed approximately 20% of total failure  analysis resources.  There was little or no portability of  diagnostic tools across 32-bit and 64-bit architectures.   Success rate, defined as the percentage of total failures whose  root cause was clearly determined, benefited from the extent  of this effort, however, and was greater than 95%.


As successful as this approach was, it soon came under  significant Time-to-market (TTM) pressures requiring shorter  design schedules - some less than 3 months.  This schedule  pressure has also applied to the diagnostic tool development  cycle.  Additionally, pressure on the Motherboard design  teams pushed the need for failure analysis support earlier in  the design cycle – to before even first Silicon release or  power-on.  Obviously there was insufficient time to develop  all the original tests needed for failure analysis so many of  these first tools would simply not be available.  A new  strategy was required to provide diagnostic tests in this  shortened schedule.  Other objectives for this new  development strategy included:


- A tool development cycle of less than 3 months to


correspond to the shortened Design cycle.


- A consistent or better success rate of 95% for diagnosing


failure root causes


- Cost savings through reduced use of tool development


resources


- Portability of diagnostic tools across 32-bit and 64-bit Intel


Architectures


The measurement of success for these objectives included the  development cycle length, development costs (dedicated  headcount and equipment), and the percentage of failure  causes that were successfully determined.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa134


A review of historical failure analysis results on Server  motherboards was conducted to assess which of the original  tools provided the greatest value in isolating failures.  The  results were also reviewed to find which failure modes had  posed highest risks for early appearance, frequency of  occurrence, and difficulty to resolve during motherboard  design.  Experience had shown that many original tools were  more frequently successful for isolating failures than others, and the historical record quantified the differences in success.   Any chronological dependency for previous failure modes was  also of interest to help prioritize which tools were likely to be  required first.


Finally, many of the original tests implemented by these tools  had evolved from an immediate need to address a specific  failure and then over time were automatically included in the  test suite.  The need for a new strategy to meet schedule  constraints created the opportunity to replace this largely  tactical approach with a more strategic, purposeful, designed  approach.  To accomplish this all of the most frequently used  diagnostic tools were broken down into their specific tasks – which buses they used to communicate between components, which configuration settings they were dependant on, which of  their tasks were redundant or similar to other tests, etc.  This  review of results from previous years defined the necessary  functionality of each test that was most frequently successful  in isolating each failure mode.


Historical FA Results


Years of analysis results were the most valuable source of  information to help the team create a new strategy to meet the  stated objectives.  A prioritization for all diagnostic tests to be  developed was needed to provide the appropriate tests at the  time they would be most needed.  Two questions needed to be  answered by the historical data to define this priority: ‘What is  the chronological peak (if any) for each of the most significant  failure modes?’ and ‘What are the critical tools needed to  determine root causes for these modes?’  These questions  define which diagnostic tools will be needed earliest in the  design cycle and therefore dictate the priority, timeline, commonality, and tool availability for development.


Electrical Failure analysis results were reviewed for 4  different Server Motherboard types during the previous 5  years.  Root cause, specific diagnostic tests used, and total  number of occurrences of each failure mode were sought after.  This process is outlined in Figure 1.  Four general categories  were also determined for all failure modes– No Power, PreBoot, BIOS/Firmware, and Post-Boot to group similar failure  modes.  Correlation between failure modes and their  successful debug tests were highlighted.  All failure modes  were sorted by their chronological occurrence in the  motherboard design cycle.  A subset of existing diagnostic  tests was found to have a high frequency of success for the  Pre-Boot failure mode.


Figure 1:  The Process for Diagnostic Test Prioritization.


The “No Power” category contains all failure modes where the  motherboard failed to power-on one or more components prior  to the point when the processor (CPU) fetches BIOS code.  Pre-Boot is the category for failures occurring while the CPU  loads BIOS and initializes all motherboard components and  before the Operating System (OS) is booted.  BIOS/Firmware  failures consist of all modes resulting from corruption in any  of the motherboard’s firmware code, – including  programmable logic device (PLD) firmware.  Post-Boot is the  last category, made up of all failure modes occurring during  the Operating System boot process, or under normal operation  of the OS.


Each of the four categories dictates which diagnostic tools are  available for analysis of its failures and which tools are not.  Software-based tools are unavailable to the FA engineer for a “No Power” type failure mode.  Post-Boot failure modes may  make use of Manufacturing functional test tools and  techniques that would not be operable for a Pre-Boot mode.  Figure 2 details the relative number and peak occurrence of  each failure mode during the Design Phase.  Power-on failures  were first to appear, followed by BIOS/Firmware Corruption  and Pre-Boot Failures.  The Pre-Boot Failure Mode category  had the highest number of failures.


The next step was to classify the failure root causes for each of  the four categories of failure mode.  These Root Cause classes  include Component/Materials, Customer Induced Damage


(CID), Manufacturing (MFG), Design, and BIOS.  These  classes were defined over the years to best meet the reporting  and analysis needs of the Analysis Team and its customers, in  that they represent each of the origination points for defects.  Identifying the origin for a failure root cause is the starting  point for corrective actions to be implemented and the primary  purpose in performing failure analysis.  Beyond origination  point there are unique analysis tools and approaches inherent  to each class which direct the fundamental development in this  new strategy.  In the analysis database there were actually  multiple levels of root cause classification for each failure – to  take into account interactions between groups, such as a  failure with a root cause that consisted of a DesignManufacturing interaction.  Only the first-level Root Cause  classes were considered.  Figure 3 shows the breakdown of  each failure mode by first level root cause.

Component/Materials Class (COM) includes all failures  caused by an individual component or defects in the basic  materials such as the Printed Circuit board.  Customer Induced  Damage Class (CID) includes any defect that can be attributed  to the handling, testing, or system assembly processes of an  OEM or end user that damaged the motherboard, causing the  failure.  Manufacturing (MFG) includes all defects caused  during the original production of the motherboard – defective  solder joints on a BGA component, for example.  Design  Failure Class (DES) includes all defects that are caused by the  circuitry design – for example, an undervalued resistor value  or an incorrect transistor switching voltage.  BIOS Class (BIOS) includes any failure that can be attributed to erroneous  code in the BIOS or Firmware.  Finally, Failure Analysis  Indeterminate (FAI) contains all failures where root cause was  not determined or the failure remained unexplained.


The general process for examination of historical analysis  results in this case could be applied to any generic case, wither  a Server Motherboard product or an integrated circuit  component.  First, correlate analysis success rates with


specific diagnostic tools.  Next, restructure diagnostic  development processes to deliver the most successful tools at  their most productive points in the schedule.  Finally, reevaluate the analysis performance of the resulting tools.

The Strategy


A general strategy was formulated based on the peak failure  mode occurrences seen in the data (see Figure 2).  Power-on  failures peaked earliest in the Design Cycle, and typically  were caused by PLD firmware or analog circuitry issues.  The  next sequential peak in Power-on failures and Pre-Boot modes  were usually ascribed to component and BIOS issues.  Most  Post-Boot failures occurred late in the motherboard design  cycle and so could be prioritized after Pre-Boot and Power-on  for tool development.  Post-Boot results also made frequent  use of Server Management resources and functional tests  available in a Operating System environment, which also  become available later in the Motherboard Design Cycle.  These observations from the previous 4 years of analysis  formed the basis of this new diagnostic tool strategy.


Three phases of diagnostic development during the  Motherboard Design Cycle were defined to correspond to the  relative occurrences of these failure mode categories.  Specific  tools and deliverables were defined within each Phase to  address each Failure Mode.  Phase1 development delivers  tools targeting Power-on and BIOS/Firmware Failure modes.  Phase2 provides tools for Pre-Boot Failures.  Phase3 delivers  tools for Post-Boot Failure Modes.  Refer to Figure 4.


Phase 1


Power-on failures were the first types encountered during  Server Motherboard design – during the time a new  motherboard prototype, or an existing motherboard with new  CPU or Chipset silicon components, is powered up.  Software  tools are unavailable to use when a motherboard fails to power


up.  Schematics and hardware documentation then become the  primary resource available to diagnose electrical circuitry  issues.  Historic review also highlighted the benefits provided  by the motherboard’s own designed-in PLD power-on logic  code for isolating a Power-on failure.  Server motherboards  typically have several Programmable Logic Devices (PLDs) which control the component power up sequence, which is the  basis for this process flow diagram.


Figure 4: Development Phases with Respective Failure Modes


Phase 1 development includes creating a Power-on Document  detailing the step-by-step procedure the motherboard uses to  power up each of the components and subsystems on a  motherboard.  The Power-on document was a novel tool in  this new strategy and a significant key learning.   Key circuit  locations for voltage probing are identified to confirm which  power-up steps have succeeded.  The objective is to quickly  determine where in the power up sequence the system has  halted in order to identify sub-circuitry or PLD code that is  defective.  The majority of the “No Power” failure modes have  been diagnosed with this tool in shorter amounts of time than  previously experienced.


Historically, the second leading cause of “No Power” failures  has been Corrupted or Defective Firmware – specifically in  the PLDs.  Vendor provided In-Serial Programmer (ISP) Tools  are used by the technician to quickly determine if the PLD  devices can be properly read and written to by the system, thus  isolating any possible circuitry or component issues.


Phase 2


After a motherboard has powered up successfully the CPU  begins loading BIOS and initializing all components with their  configuration settings for operation.  Phase2 development  aimed to provide tools needed to isolate Pre-Boot and  BIOS/Firmware failure modes.  To isolate these types of  issues the instructions executed by the CPU must be  monitored and manipulated.  The primary tools for this  include both hardware or software equipment such as Logic  Analyzers and a variety of industry JTAG controllers.


Before this new strategy, debug tools were created to exercise  all existing buses and signal lines on a motherboard to isolate  the fault to a specific Component or subsystem.  Based on the  review of historical data several key buses between  components were found which identified a failure in at least  90% of the cases.  These key pathways include the CPU  Front-side Bus and the chipset component Data/Address Bus, for example.


Originally there were 105 specific tests created for the CPU to  execute to exercise all system buses.  A subset of existing  software tests was defined which isolate these key pathways  for component and BIOS issues.  This subset of software tests  became the priority for Phase 2 test development.  Review  showed many of the original software tests were redundant, were infrequently used, or performed tests on motherboard  subsystems which rarely failed.  The new strategy reduced the  test requirements from the original 105 down to 31 unique  tests, all of which focused on the primary pathways  highlighted in the historical record.


Each of these 31 tests was made simple and streamlined to  read and write basic patterns on specific system buses.  Simplification of these tests resulted in reduced development  time and complexity, and greatly-increased portability  between 32-bit and 64-bit Architectures.  In review it appeared  that over time the original 105 tests had repeatedly changed  and become complex and interdependent.  Years of adding  new features or options, attempts to automate debug  processes, and attempts to debug multiple motherboard  configurations with these original tools all contributed to this  complexity.  Each of the new tests were reduced to basic  signal traffic, which easily scales from a 32-bit platform by  using different data values while adding signal and timing  requirements for a 64-bit environment.


The primary techniques for determining and isolating  BIOS/Firmware corruption issues include confirming proper  transactions between the CPU and firmware devices, and  ensuring proper values are loaded into CMOS and  configuration memory space.  Simplified procedures for these  techniques were created based on historical experience.  The  ability to monitor and confirm proper initialization of each  component was found to be paramount during Phase2.


Another effort to simplify Phase2 development was in  partnerships with BIOS Engineering teams.  Historically a  large portion of debug development included efforts to  understand the steps and values BIOS used to initialize the  motherboard.  Support from BIOS engineering eliminated  several of the most complex and time-consuming tests  originally needed for component and memory setup and  initialization.


Reduction and simplification of the original debug test suite  was the principal source of resource reduction, development  time reduction, and portability across Architectures.  Because  of simplification, dedicated development resources were no  longer required to produce tests unique to a specific platform.


Phase 3


Debug technicians who historically were the consumers of  these tests and performed the debug of actual failures have  been able to consistently create these tests themselves during  the Phase2 time period.  This distributed development  resource model eliminated the need for a dedicated  development team.


The third and final phase of diagnostic tool development  targeted all “Post OS-Boot” failure modes.  As shown in  Figure 3, this failure category is mainly composed of CID and  Component failure types.  This category also contains the  highest level of Failure Analysis Indeterminate outcome.  Fortunately, with the OS loaded and in operation on the failing  motherboard many more tests and tools are available to the  debug technician.


The majority of component issues are isolated using the 31  tests developed in Phase1 and 2.  An additional 6 tests were  defined to give further access to additional system buses such  as LPC and Hublink, and to provide access to the Server  Management system on the motherboard.  Server Management  is the hardware and software found on most Server  motherboard platforms which monitors hundreds of sensors  and environmental factors such as fan speed tachometers and  temperature sensors to warn the user and protect against  possible problems.  Server Management also provides  memory and software error logging.  With access to Server  Management information, the FA Engineer has access to the  hundreds of sensors, memory devices, and error reporting logs  to provide insight into the failure which does not require  development by the diagnostic team.


A review of the original tests developed to diagnose Post OSBoot failure modes found a significant amount of redundancy  with standard Server Management functions.  More than 70% of the information provided by these original tests could be  obtained by proper use of data provided by Server  Management.  A simplified tool was created to provide direct  access to Server Management data records through an industry  standard protocol.


The strategy for development in Phase 3 consisted of the onetime creation of a tool to access Server Management that was  usable on both 32-bit and 64-bit platforms.  Next, a training  document to correlate motherboard hardware to specific data  records of a motherboard’s Server Management was created.  Six diagnostic tests for direct access to LPC and Hublink  buses previously mentioned were then created to validate and  expand information from Server Management.  More than  20% of the original 105 tests were eliminated with this  strategy.   Success rates for the tools of this new strategy are  currently 97%, exceeding the original diagnostic success rate  for Post-OS Failure Modes of 95%.


Results for all objectives for this new development cycle  during the design phase of four (4) Server platforms are shown


in Figure 5.  Overall number of indeterminate failures (FAI) is  down slightly during this period from 5% to 3% for a success  rate of 97%.  The total number of software tools developed  has been reduced by more than 60%.  Dedicated resources for  tool development were reduced by 75% with the elimination  of a team tasked solely with such development.

A general process for examination of historical analysis results  was used to revise the diagnostic tool development processes  by correlating analysis success rates with specific diagnostic  tools from historical results.


A new strategy for developing electrical failure diagnostic  tools has been defined to reduce time and resource  requirements.  The first step in this strategy consisted of  documenting the power-on process for the motherboard  platform.  Next, software processes were created for  communication between specific motherboard components  along main pathways to isolate failing signal paths.  Then  software processes were developed to view and verify proper  component configuration by the motherboard BIOS.  Finally, processes were constructed to access Server Management  hardware to make system-wide sensors, memory, and error  information available during analysis.


This new strategy has been implemented on four (4) separate  Server motherboard platforms and successfully met all  original objectives.  Improved techniques resulted in a  reduction of required time by 80% and resources by 70% while providing increased portability across Architectures  without negative impact to the success rate.  Furthermore, elements of this strategy have demonstrated to be useful and  effective at three separate third-party Manufacturing sites for  improvements in their EFA-FI processes.


Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology:


Tools and Education for Intel Component Defect Reduction


Julie S. Doll


Intel Architecture Diagnostics Development


Systems MFG Analysis Center, Intel Corporation


5200 NE Elam Young Parkway, Hillsboro, OR 97124


julie.s.doll@intel.com


To enable efficient, accurate debug of Intel architecture  components to take place within contract manufacturing sites, and to provide alternatives for the removal of Intel  components from, Intel is deploying a diagnostic capability   and attendant educational collateral known as to achieve these  objectives Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology. This  paper will describe details of Intel® Component Diagnostic  Technology, including the diagnostic fixture and user  interface, diagnostic scripts and analytical coverage, data  management and reporting, and on-site and Web-based  educational offerings.


Intel component technology is growing in complexity, with  components of increasing pin counts and integrated  features/function succeeding each other with each new product  generation. In contract manufacturing environments, maintaining throughput is a business imperative, detailed  knowledge of component architecture is limited, and applying  diagnostic tools requires high levels of both time and debug  expertise, often rare commodities in high volume  manufacturing environments. These factors result in the  removal of components as the primary means to correct  failures experienced in tests of assembled motherboards. This  in turn results in a high degree of miscorrelation between  failure symptoms and root cause and significant costs in  materials, labor, and analytical resources annually. In addition, this also impacts the ability of a component supplier to  respond to legitimate defects.


To establish a sustainable information system that enables  Intel to extract actionable performance data from the industry  on Intel components, to drive internal product, process, and  quality change, to enable timely identification of component  defects, and to enhance the overall quality of industry debug  capability, Intel has developed an analytical solution called  Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology. This solution is  initially targeted at Intel chipsets but is scalable to other


system components. Intel® Component Diagnostic  Technology is based on a diagnostic platform widely utilized  within Intel for component development called In-Target  Probe (ITP). ITP encompasses hardware/software capability  for probing Intel architecture components, enabling quick  failure isolation and providing a Go/No Go decision to the  factory debug technician on parts removal. Data on failures  will be captured and automatically uploaded to an information  system for data review and further failure analysis. This  enables the Failure Analysis teams to proactively review  trends and failure paretos, thus making effective and high  confidence choices on investing their failure analysis  resources. To complement  Intel® Component Diagnostic  Technology, on-site and Web-based training will also be  deployed to enhance the debug and architectural skills of  board assembly technicians world wide. It encompasses PC  and Chipset Architecture and Debug Methods and Techniques  and is intended to enhance the ability of debug technicians to  make alternative choices in his/her investigation technique  when faced with removal of a part that  Intel® Component  Diagnostic Technology has been unable to confirm is  defective.


This paper will review existing processes and proposed  modifications, outlining the imperatives driving change in  board assembly component returns and analytical  methodologies in place today, emphasizing the need for  enhanced timeliness of data access and the cost burden  inherent in the prevailing approach..


Additionally, the following functions of Intel® Component  Diagnostic Technology will be explored in detail:


Diagnostic Fixture and User Interface. The diagnostic  capability of  Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology is  incorporated into a secure, mobile fixture that incorporates a  host processor displaying an easy-to-use operator interface. The fixture enables a debug technician to execute diagnostic  checkout on a failed board in minutes, to receive a clear, graphical indication of whether an Intel part is or is not  defective and if so, which part has failed. The diagnostic


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa139


process also saves component data gathered during board  analysis to a local database for transmit back to an Intel master  archive where defects can be quickly quantified and acted  upon.


Diagnostic Scripts and Analytical Coverage. The analytical  engine of the  Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology  diagnostic capability is built upon a set of functions called  scripts. Key objectives of the script portion of Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology are to provide a high  degree of coverage for component logical functions and  interfaces, and support fast execution times, to enable timeconstrained technicians to quickly complete accurate Intel  component assessment. This section describes the hardware  used to connect the host processor of the fixture to the board  under test and describes generally how the scripts perform  fault isolation.


Data Management and Reporting. Data accumulated from  Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology  output is  accumulated in local databases at individual customer sites in   XML format and can be periodically transmitted to Intelresident databases to support effective data reviews. Multi-site  data is consolidated at Intel and an analysis of the data is  performed to assess occurrence of high impact and/or high


frequency defects impacting product quality. This data is acted  upon by component product development and quality  resolution teams, to provide resolution in a timely fashion. This analysis can also be utilized to drive generational  improvements based on identified design opportunities. The  Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology development team  also uses this data to provide indicators of robustness and  integrity of its solution and to establish the basis for future  Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology product  enhancements.


Web-Based and On-Site Education. A key objective of  Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology hardware/software  is to provide debug technicians with alternatives to removing  IA components from boards. In addition to deploying a  diagnostic fixture for this purpose, the Intel® Component  Diagnostic Technology program is also deploying Web-based  and on-site educational collateral for the same purpose. This  section describes the industry-enabling objectives of these  educational materials as well as its scope and content.

Existing Component Returns Process


Component Diagnostic Information Exchange is being  designed for deployment into both Intel-operated and external (contract) manufacturing facilities to provide data on Intel  architecture (IA) components. Key issues which Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology is designed to address  include (a) reducing time required to obtain quantitative data  on legitimate component defects, thus improving  responsiveness to defects  impacting customers, (b) to reduce  rework costs associated with removal of non-defective parts  from assembled boards, (c) to enable assessment of quality


trends across multiple generations of Intel product, and (c) to  reduce miscorrelation levels that can exist between customer  perceptions of Intel quality based on qualitative or “soft” data  and quality assessments based on quantitative analysis or “hard data”.


The board test process which occurs in a typical assembly  environment employing Intel components is illustrated in  Figure 1, with existing steps illustrated in blue, modifications  to the process illustrated in grey. In this scenario, at a point in  which an Intel part is believed to be failing, parts are often  removed from the board with little or no failure analysis due to  the highly time constrained environments in which board  production occur and in some cases, do to limited debug skills  and analytical equipment possessed by those technicians  responsible for volume board output.


An alternate process would result in Intel® Component  Diagnostic Technology being run at the point in board test at   which the debug technician suspects an Intel component  related failure. If Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology   indicates a component failure, the part may be removed from  the board and returned to Intel for further analysis at a local  Quality Service Center, and later to other FA sites depending  upon the nature of the failure. This returns and analysis  process can be time consuming, labor-intensive, and costly. By contrast, at the time a pass/fail decision is made on the  Intel part, Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology stores  failure data on a host system embedded in the diagnostic  fixture. This data can be made available to both Intel and its  customers in real-time, thus making critical data on  component quality available for analysis and action in a  fraction of the time taken by the current process.


Diagnostic Fixture and User Interface


In order for the diagnostic fixture to be effective in the  environments in which it is being deployed, its initial design  has been optimized to reflect mobility, security, and ease of  use (later implementations in which cost is a predominant  consideration may eliminate certain mobility and security  features). The photos in Figure 2 illustrate a prototype of the  initial design. In the upper left is an external view of the case, showing lock mechanism by which internal contents may be


Figure 2. Prototype diagnostic fixture. Upper left illustrates the portable, secure case. Upper right shows the inside of  the fixture. Lower left shows a board being diagnosed. Lower right shows fixture undercarriage power supplies, storage.


kept secure and demonstrating how, by placement on a cart, it  can be moved from one debug station to another as board  analysis needs across a range of manufacturing lines requires.


The photo on the upper right illustrates the fixture when  opened and before a failed board (ie. unit under test) has been  placed in the test area – equipment in upper right includes a  serial number reader and a label generator. Photo at bottom


left shows an operational flat panel display and a unit under  test sitting upon an anti-static pad and cabled to the host  processor, on which resides diagnostic software capable of  performing board component analysis. The photo at bottom  right illustrates the undercarriage of the fixture, which  contains power supplies and room for spare cabling.


The user interface which the debug technician interacts with  through the flat panel display embedded in the diagnostic  fixture is designed to provide simple, straight-forward  messaging, and will indicate to a user both graphically and in  text form whether an Intel component failed a test and should  be replaced.


Diagnostic Scripts and Analytical Coverage


Diagnostic scripts are designed to interrogate component  functional integrity and if a defect is detected, to isolate fault  to a specific board component. Figure 3illustrates the concept  for a sample segment of board architecture in which Intel  components are utilized. Since component integrity is  concentrated on IA parts and is not intended to provide  comprehensive diagnosis of non-Intel parts, analysis begins  with a known good set of peripherals installed on the failed  board. CPU analysis is then conducted, as the CPU is a key IA  component and must be functionally sound in order for  interrogation of other board components to be conducted. Once CPU function is assured, CPU communication with the  MCH is then validated by ensuring integrity of the Front Side  Bus (FSB) that connects the two. Tests which validate the  MCH internal routing and functional integrity are then  completed. Transactions are then driven to the devices  connected to the MCH to ensure the function of the  interconnects. The North Bridge to South Bridge (MCH to  ICH) connection is then checked by validating the DMI bus, and the same series of operations is performed on the ICH as  was performed on the MCH – checkout of the ICH component  internal registers and interconnects followed by the driving of  transactions to externally connected peripherals sufficient to  ensure bus/interconnect functionality. Since the technicians  who will be using the diagnostic are highly time constrained, it  is important that the diagnostic, in addition to being ease to  use, be streamlined and efficient. Execution time is targeted  for between 3 and 5 minutes.


Figure 3. Portion of typical board architecture covered by  Intel ® Component Diagnostic Technology analysis.


Data Management and Reporting


A key output of the Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology  is generation of an actionable data stream  reflecting  functional status of IA components. The fact that this data is  available in real-time vs. as an output of time-consuming, labor-intensive failure analysis is a critical advantage in  quickly addressing  issues that may stem from test escapes or  other latent component defects, and which may impact both  Intel’s manufacturing customers and end-users. Diagnostic  data within Intel will be used to improve the coverage of  Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology, close test escapes, improve component built-in self test capabilities, and enable  MFG sites to better assess and manage their processes. A  sample of what data might look like for a manufacturing  consumer of Intel components for a range of different board  failures is illustrated in Figure 4.

standard of industry debug capability, this objective can also  be achieved through education. For this reason, the  deployment of the Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology  fixture will be complemented by release of Web-based and onsite education. This education covers PC and Intel chipset  architecture and debug methods and techniques and should  help provide debug technicians with alternatives to board  component removal. Additionally, it will reduce the waste of  time and materials that occur through inaccurate board  diagnosis, increase understanding of new board technology, and enhance debug skill.


Web-based education can be provided through one of two  options. The first uses a server to provide content access  through network-connected workstations/PC’s. The second  enables users access  to content through CDROM’s at their  individual workstations/PC’s. Using a Web-based approach  provides many advantages, including enabling a virtually  unlimited number of employees to utilize a consistent set of  materials, providing for self-paced approaches which permit  individuals to concentrate on just the portion of the content  that is meaningful to them, and low cost. Plentiful graphics  help illustrate concepts and ease the assimilation of material  for audiences for whom English is not a primary language. Quizzes interspersed throughout the Web-based material help  to ensure comprehension. A screen shot from Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology Web-based educational  collateral is shown in Figure 5.


On-site education covers many of the same architectural, debug, and technology concepts as Web-based material but  provide opportunities for hands-on laboratories and interaction  with a knowledgeable instructor. On-site education  encompasses the topics cited below.


Major System Components . Components covered include  the processor, Memory Controller Hub, I/O Controller Hub, Firmware Hub, and system memory.


System Busses . System busses covered include the host bus, PCI and PCI Express, SMB, LPC, and AGP busses.


Peripheral Interfaces . Peripheral interfaces covered include  IDE, SATA, SCSI, USB, IEEE 1394, Video, and Audio.


Ancillary Components . Ancillary components covered  include voltage regulation, clock generation, typical discrete  circuits, system  thermal monitoring, and SIO/Glue  functionality.


Miscellaneous . Miscellaneous coverage includes interrupt  structure, reset and power on map, and DMA.


Troubleshooting . Troubleshooting topics include dead board  debug, POST codes, and oscilloscopes and other lab  equipment.


Intel® Component Diagnostic Technology provides board  debug technicians with alternatives to the removal of Intel  components from failed boards through diagnostic capabilities  which assess failed IA components, and through educational  collateral which enhance understanding of board architecture  and debug techniques. Diagnostic capability employs a simple  user interface and efficient scripts to generate quick pass/fail  indicator on IA components, providing a basis for quantitative  data assessments on quality trends. Educational materials  enable consistent, low-cost knowledge transfer encompassing  board level architecture and debug techniques/methodologies  that will enhance success in quickly and accurately isolating  defects impact manufacturing output quality and throughput.

Capacity Management Solutions


John Drummond, Jeff Wolfe, Martin Smith, Jeff Conner, Ken Brawley, Bart Seefeldt, Cary Davis


Texas Instruments, Inc. Dallas Texas USA


# Capacity Management Solutions


j-drummond1@ti.com, j-wolfe@ti.com, m-smith2@ti.com, j-conner1@ti.com, k-brawley@ti.com, b-seefeldt2@ti.com, c-davis1@ti.com


This paper will  cover some of the options available to manage  the failure analysis process when it is capacity constrained.  This paper will provide a method to model a failure analysis  operations capacity to aid in the decision process of where the  constraints are.  Several examples of solutions to some typical  constraints will be presented also.


How do you even know if the term “capacity constrained” applies to your failure analysis operation.?  Do the external  customers have performance goals the operation is not  achieving?  Does your internal management have performance  goals the operation is not achieving?  If the answer to either of  these questions is yes, you might be capacity constrained.


1.0 Communication


A major contributor in solving capacity constraints is  communication.  Communication does not get the job done  faster, but your customer will be better informed when they  can make decisions based on the requested analysis.  Two key  elements of communication are: giving an estimated  completion date and giving updates during analysis.


The customers most likely have well defined cycletime goals.  However, most customers do not like the “black box” approach of submitting a job to failure analysis (FA) and then  receiving an email upon completion, especially if the total  cycle time turns out to be longer than the goal.  It is more  common to see satisfaction from the customer when an  estimated completion date is given when the job is submitted, along with job progression updates during analysis.


As semiconductor device features continue to decrease in size


from merely sub micron to below 100 nanometers it becomes necessary to mill smaller and higher aspect ratio FIB vias with reduced ion beam current.  This significantly reduces the number of secondary electrons and ions available for endpoint detection and imaging.  In addition FIB gas assisted etching introduces a gas delivery nozzle composed of conductive material.  This component is grounded to prevent charge build up during ion beam imaging or milling.  The proximity of the nozzle to the sample surface creates a shielding effect which reduces the secondary electron detection level as well [1].  The ability to enhance secondary electron imaging for end point detection is required for successful FIB circuit edit and failure analysis applications on advanced technologies. This paper reviews the results obtained using FIB Assist, an image and signal enhancement product for the FEI / Micrion platform, for critical FIB endpoint determination.  Examples of  FIB fabricated probe points with 30 x 30 nm FIB vias and circuit edit applications endpointing on metal 1 with high aspect ratio holes are presented.


One of the most challenging aspects of performing FIB failure analysis applications on device features in the sub micron and nanometer range is the low number of secondary electrons and ions available for endpoint detection and imaging.  An alternate end point detection method, monitoring the sample absorbed current (“stage current”), has been reported and found useful on packaged hardware and samples where pads are exposed for adequate grounding of the sample to the system sample holder


[1].


An alternate approach is available: the results we present were obtained utilizing FEI Micrion FIB system platform models 2500 and 9800 / 986FC, all equipped with 50 kV, “5 nm” FIB columns and each retrofitted with “FIB Assist”, a FIB enhancement system from Fibics Incorporated designed for all FEI Micrion platforms.  FIB Assist consists of a passive hardware and software based package that acquires signal intensity data in real time from each beam dwell point, and presents this data in a number of ways.  In addition to live imaging, both frame integrated and averaged imaging of the mill box are available to be viewed simultaneously or individually on


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa151


# A Novel Approach for Enhancing Critical FIB Imaging for Failure Analysis and Circuit Edit Applications


the FIB Assist monitor. Four imaging quadrants are available;each has individual settings to allow the user to customize the display to best meet the needs of a particular application.


Flexible image processing includes scaling, interpolation and palette manipulation (brightness, contrast, gamma, false color,etc.)  This data is combined with region-of-interest signal intensity graphing showing integrated and averaged results of all data acquired, which has proven to be much more sensitive than the standard endpointing graphs available on FIB instruments.


Additionally, the system is able to display mill boxes with expansion (or compression) on one axis; for example, when cross-sectioning using a long, thin polish box it is possible to display the live milling image with up to a twenty fold expansion of the minor axis, which reveals significant detail regarding the cross-sectioned face and assists the operator in the correct placement of the mill box for optimum sectioning for FIB or SEM imaging and FIB TEM specimen preparation.


The ability to record mill box “thumbnail” images at user defined time intervals ranging from every 0.25 to 60 seconds  provides the ability to review the results of the FIB mill while the sample is still in the system or at a later time for comparison with electrical characterization results. Each thumbnail is stored with a notation showing the dose at the point the thumbnail was acquired, and successive thumbnails can be replayed forwards or backwards in a “movie like” fashion.  These thumbnails can be extremely useful, especially while developing or optimizing FIB process parameters for a given application. The FIB Assist monitor allows imaging of the milled area without having to move the FIB system created template of mill and deposition boxes for viewing of the milled area and then re-align them prior to continuing with the FIB milling process, as is the case when limited to imaging on the FIB system monitor.


Theory of Operation


FIB Assist acquires the signal intensity generated by each FIB beam dwell point as a digital signal by passively eavesdropping on the FIB’s digital signal acquisition circuitry and clock.  This is in contrast to many other after-market signal acquisition systems that sample the analog deflection and signal acquisition circuitry using digital-to-analog converters.  As a result, FIB Assist receives exactly the same information that the FIB does,without introducing any potential quantization error.


The FEI Micrion platform FIB systems (and indeed most FIBs)operate in almost all milling modes as a “contiguous pixel generator”, meaning the FIB produces a rectangular stream of row and column data for each raster pass, where dwell points in immediately adjacent rows or columns can be expected to have a “neighbor” relationship with each other.  There are a few exceptions to this, polygon mills and selected area milling being the most common, but in general this “neighbor”relationship holds true and can be taken advantage of in order to improve the image perceived by the user by interpolating between neighboring dwell points in order to enlarge the image(thus creating more pixels in the display than there were dwell points in the mill box) or eliminating peripheral dwell points to reduce spurious edge effects when milling deep vias.


FIB Assist acquires the intensity at each dwell point, for each raster pass, regardless of dwell time and the resultant time per raster.  Under certain conditions such as during gas assisted etching of small boxes in a gas depleted mode it is not uncommon to have times of well below 1 millisecond per raster.


This means that in excess of 1,000 FIB rasters (or mill box frames) occur every second.  While opinions vary on what is the maximum frame rate a human eye can perceive, few computer displays operate at above 85 Hz (85 frames per second (fps)), 24 fps is considered sufficient for motion pictures and even 20 fps appears smooth when each successive frame contains considerable smoothly varying detail, as is often the case during FIB milling.  Thus, at 1000 rasters per second of FIB raster rate it is possible to integrate 50 FIB rasters into a single frame for display and still achieve a display rate of 20 fps.  FIB Assist takes advantage of this fact and allows the user to display integrated and/or averaged images calculated from a userspecified number of frames.  As each dwell point produces an 8-bit intensity value, each dwell point can have intensity values ranging from 0 to 255.  Averaged images preserve this range of data, however integrated images can reach many thousand counts per dwell point, allowing the user to adjust the FIB Assist image to enhance a particular subset of signal intensity that cannot be resolved in the average image or even on the FIB screen.  FIB Assist provides histogram and intensity adjustment tools to optimize the image for the particular task.  As discussed in greater detail below, these tools can also assist in optimizing the FIB contrast (effectively the secondary particle detector gain) and brightness base settings as well as adjusting how FIB Assist displays this data.


In addition to displaying images, be they live, averaged or integrated, FIB Assist also calculates the intensity data from each and every raster pass, displaying a plot of both the average intensity (0-255) and integrated intensity at a default interval of 250 ms from all rasters received during the previous interval.


As will be shown in the following sections, these graphs can be much more sensitive to endpoint than either the images or endpoint graph on the FIB system.


Probe Points


Both FIB induced deposition and FIB milling are used to fabricate probe point structures which allow electrical characterization of transistor cells, as illustrated in Figure 1.


To allow this characterization, the sample is delayered and then mechanically polished to the contact level, just below the first metal level exposing the tungsten contacts that connect to the underlying transistors.  An SEM image acquired at this point,Figure 2, shows buried nodes of an underlying conductor layer are visible through the remaining insulator.


Figure 1.  SEM image of a FIB fabricated probe point structure.  Note that the entire surface was covered by FIB deposited SiO2 prior to fabrication of the probe points,however the SEM image reveals the location of the contacts through this SiO2.


Figure 2.  SEM image of a thinned sample prior to FIB SiO2 with the FIB via target areas identified.  Exposed contacts are bright, whereas buried conductors appear darker in comparison.


A thin film (~2500 Å) of FIB SiO2 is deposited over the area of interest.  Small vias are then milled through the insulating SiO2 film to expose the tungsten contacts.  For 130 nm diameter contacts a  60 x 60 nm mill box is used.  Currently FIB systems provide an image of the intensity of the secondary electron or ion emission within the box being milled.  This is adequate when the mill box is relatively large (for example ~400 nm at a 12 µm field of view) but it is insufficient for smaller boxes as the solid squares in the corners of the mill box graphic may obscure the entire area of the mill, or the mill area as displayed on the FIB screen can be so small as to be unusable.  The mill time for these small vias is often very short (20 to 30 seconds) and even when the field of view is selected so that the mill box on the FIB screen is sufficiently large, the signal to noise in the FIB image is poor.


The methodology formerly used for milling small vias was to use a predetermined dose with a  built-in over mill.  The over mill was necessary to allow for differences in sample thickness due to polishing variations.  This method produces a larger via than necessary, which increases the risk of inadvertent shorting to adjacent vias as well as underlying structures.  This method also creates a more challenging process for clean up of the tungsten overspray.


FIB Assist allows for both a visual and graphical display of the secondary electron emission during a mill.  It is possible to enlarge the secondary electron or ion  image on the FIB Assist monitor and adjust the contrast such that even the slightest contrast change can be detected during milling.  Beam focus,stigmation and image contrast level are key factors in obtaining the optimum secondary electron image.  The image contrast level can be adjusted by referring to a histogram for further optimization, Figures 3 and 4.  The left (“before”) side of Figure 4 shows the FIB Assist histogram of a lower contrast image, with intensities ranging from 0 to 164, with the majority of  pixels having intensities below 100.  The right (“after”) side shows the same area, after optimal adjustment of the FIB brightness and contrast to cover the entire dynamic range from 0 to 254, with a reasonable number of pixels at each and every intensity over this range.  Note that some FEI Micrion platforms do not tend to generate any pixels with a brightness of 255, so in this case a range of 0 to 254 covers the full intensity range from maximum to minimum.


Figure 3. FIB secondary electron images before (left) and after (right) adjustment for optimal brightness and contrast(detector gain) to achieve conditions for clear endpointing during subsequent milling through FIB deposited SiO2.  The field of view of each image is 12 µm.


Figure 4. The FIB Assist histograms associated with the before(left) and after (right) images of Figure 3.


Using tools within FIB Assist, optimal conditions can be set to allow visual endpointing using the enlarged milling images as seen in Figure 5.  In many cases, such as when the mill box is smaller than the diameter of the tungsten contact, the visual cues within even the FIB Assist enlarged mill box are quite subtle and it is necessary to rely on the integrated endpoint graphing capability in order to achieve successful endpointing.  This subject will be covered in the next section.


Figure 5.  Selected images from a FIB Assist thumbnail sequence of a 300 nm mill box (with 12 mill raster averaging per image) showing endpoint on a 180 nm tungsten contact through a FIB deposited SiO2 layer.  The upper left image (#19 in the sequence, at a dose of 1.10 nC / µm2) shows the typical appearance while milling through the FIB SiO2.  The next three images, #20 through #22 in the sequence, show the characteristic brightening that occurs when reaching the bottom of the FIB deposited SiO2.  Image #24, lower left,shows the appearance of the darker native oxide in the top right of this image, while the final three images show the appearance of the contact, whose liner is clearly resolved,although it appears thicker than in reality due to topography,electron yield, interpolation and spot size effects.  Note that in many cases there is not enough space around the contact to allow a box of this size relative to the contact diameter, and instead the mill box used is much smaller than the contact itself, making visual endpointing more difficult, resulting in greater reliance on the endpoint graphs (Figures 6 and 7).


Utilizing FIB Assist for Process Development


FIB Assist was key in evaluating the feasibility of using smaller mill box sizes to create FIB vias for advanced technologies.  For example, a matrix of mill boxes was created using a 50 µm aperture with 45 pA beam current.  Mill box sizes ranged from 80 x 80 nm down to 30 x 30 nm. To assess repeatability a series of three boxes of each size were milled as shown in Figure 6.


The dose required increases as the size of the mill box decreases as indicated in Table 1.


As the image display became less distinct for the smaller mill boxes, reliance on the graphical representation of the integrated and averaged endpoint signals increased.  The FIB Assist intensity graph provided a clear indication of when milling through the FIB SiO2 was completed and connection to the underlying contact was achieved,  Figure 7.  Note that the signal peaks at the interface between the SiO2 and the tungsten contact, and it is necessary to continue milling beyond this peak in order to achieve good electrical conductivity by milling slightly into the tungsten contact itself.


On a different site on the same sample these small FIB vias were re-created and filled with FIB tungsten with a probe pad attached, Figure 8. Electrical characterization verified continuity and the expected diode characteristics for all vias,indicating that endpoint had been accurately detected and that the vias were adequately filled with tungsten.

The upper line shows integrated intensity, which peaks at about 17,000 counts just at the interface between the FIB deposited SiO2 and the tungsten contact.  The lower line shows the average intensity,representing the approximate gray level as seen on the FIB monitor.  The average intensity peaks at the same point, at about 135 counts. Frontside circuit edit tasks often involve extended milling times in order to access deeply buried metal layers using high aspect ratio vias or multiple actions per site such as cutting through several upper metal layers and re-insulating the resultant hole before opening a small via to access the required metal line.


FIB Assist eases these tasks in several ways.  Mill box thumbnails acquired at frequent intervals allow the user to replay a movie of the mill during milling to review what has occurred, stopping at specific frames / doses as required.  The live display of the image is useful to determine if drift is occurring during milling and the integrated or averaged images are sensitive to the appearance of the desired line as well as any other lines that may be inadvertently exposed.  Observing the FIB Assist image(s) aids in determining whether a given line has been fully cut, even at the bottom of a high aspect ratio hole.  This can be particularly useful when dealing with copper interconnect.  Being able to view enlarged FIB Assist images of milling in real time can also be advantageous for charge sensitive samples as the field of view can be left relatively high,say 150 µm, which can reduce charging and ESD events that can occur during image passes at small fields of view on sensitive samples, while still seeing sufficient detail in the milling image to correctly analyze what is occurring.


The FIB Assist integrated count endpoint graph can be particularly useful when milling high aspect ratio holes and attempting to endpoint on metal lines very low in the stack.


Figure 9 shows the integrated count endpoint graph that results from milling two high aspect ratio boxes down to metal 1 using XeF2 gas assisted etching on a packaged and decapsulated 7+1 metal wire bonded part consisting of an upper aluminum layer


over 7 copper layers.  This work was performed on an FEI Micrion 986 FlipChip FIB using a 90 pA beam current with a spot size of ~30 nm.  Two boxes were milled, the first nominally 800 nm x 800 nm (black line, Figure 9) and the second nominally 250 nm x 250 nm (white line, Figure 9).  In order to compare the two boxes, the dose for each box was normalized to the dose required to expose the metal 1, however the actual dose required was 6.5 nC / µm2 for the 800 nm box and 9.2 nC / µm2 for the 250 nm box. The depth from the top surface of the die to metal 1 is approximately 8 µm, yielding a nominal aspect ratio of 10:1 for the 800 nm box and 32:1 for the 250 nm box.


This region of the device gave direct line of sight to the metal 1 layer with no intervening metal in the way.  It is interesting to note the spikes in the plot of the integrated signal from the 800 nm box.  These spikes may be attributed to the presence of a silicon nitride based layer that occurs across the device at depths corresponding to just above and just below where each metal layer would be.  These spikes, annotated in Figure 9, act as “waypoint” markers that are clearly resolved all the way down to metal 1 for the 800 nm hole.  Note also the distinct drop in signal intensity due to a change in the interlevel dielectric glasses used below metal 3.


Most significantly, from the standpoint of successful circuit editing, is the clear and pronounced increase in the endpoint signal when milling reaches metal 1, rising from just over 20,000 integrated counts in the dielectric below metal 2 to in excess of 50,000 counts once into the metal 1 copper layer.  It is also important to observe that the initial sharp increase is due to the silicon nitride followed by the tantalum based liner over the copper line, and it is necessary to continue milling a bit further to cleanly reach the copper if one desires a good connection.


The case for the 32:1 aspect ratio 250 nm hole is not as clear, in that few of the spikes seen in the graph from the 800 nm mill box are clearly resolved, however there is still a very distinct endpoint signal when the metal 1 is reached, in this case showing a sharp increase from ~4,000 counts up to nearly 6,000 counts.  This particular milling operation took in excess of 15 minutes, and little if any evidence of endpointing was available on the FIB software, however the FIB Assist endpoint graph gives the user considerable confidence that the metal line has been exposed.  Without this endpoint assistance,  after 15 minutes of milling, one often begins to question whether the box has in fact milled through the metal line and is now boring into the substrate beneath it, which can lead to stopping the mill prematurely, resulting in no connection.


FIB Assist’s contributions to backside circuit edit tasks combine aspects of frontside circuit edit and probe point work, with heavy reliance on the FIB Assist endpoint graph to determine if a metal line has been exposed, as well as observation of the averaged or integrated image, particularly during cutting to ensure a given line is fully and cleanly severed.


Figure 9.  FIB Assist integrated intensity data for two XeF2 mill boxes, 800 x 800 nm (black line) and 250 x 250 nm(white line).  Both sites had a clear, metal-free line of site down to metal 1.  Note the sharp increase in the signal for both boxes at a normalized dose of ~ 0.9, indicating good endpointing on the metal 1 line.  The depth from the top surface of the die to metal 1 is approximately 8 µm, yielding a nominal aspect ratio of 10:1 for the 800 nm box and 32:1 for the 250 nm box.  Note also that the intensity signal from the larger box clearly shows the nitride based dielectric that is across the entire die at depths above and below the location of each metal layer (see text for further details).


While there is no doubt that the development of better detectors,newer ion columns and enhanced stage stability [2] all aid in overcoming the challenges associated with silicon microsurgery on devices manufactured with sub 90 nm process technology,FIB Assist makes it much easier to verify that the FIB is set up to achieve good endpoint detection, even on a less than state-ofthe-art system.  When following standard best practice of using a well aligned beam and an optimized milling recipe, FIB Assist has been shown to greatly enhance user confidence and success rate across a range of failure analysis and circuit edit applications.  For probe point applications, success was achieved down to the smallest mill box size tested of 30 x 30 nm, and in fact success with even smaller boxes may well be


achievable.  For circuit edit applications, in cases where deep,sub micron, high aspect ratio holes were required we found that relying on the FIB Assist intensity graphs proved to be invaluable for achieving good endpointing.  Automated thumbnail acquisition during milling operations, and the capability to export these thumbnails and their associated intensity graphs, are features that aid in job review both during and after the FIB session.

Process options of FIB circuit edit accessing active area in silicon through chip backside are presented. The full  process is divided in modules. The technological readiness of the different modules is discussed. New results for  the two most critical modules, endpoint detection of the global FIB trench in silicon, and contact resistivity of


FIB deposited metal interconnect on diffusion, are presented. Investigated endpoint detection processes are FIB  image contrast of the wells and of STI (shallow trench isolation). The contact to diffusion is in the range of 2,5 x  10-7 cm2 on highly doped n-Si, about 10x higher on highly doped p-Si, with linear I-V characteristic.


Processing Focused Ion Beam (FIB) based Circuit  Edit (CE) through silicon from chip backside is an  enormous challenge, so a complete new set of  procedures and techniques is being developed. It is  also a great opportunity to connect active devices  and nodes in Silicon directly.


Fig. 1: Overview on Circuit Edit procedure issues  when processing through Si  from chip backside


Process Options


There are several approaches of circuit edit in Si.  They all use trenches with a very thin remaining Si  layer and the actual editing process can begin (see  Fig.1). The basic process modules are:


1)  Global chip thinning to less than 100 µm.


2)  Operating trench to active structure


3)  Endpoint detection to save active devices


4)  Navigation to edit position


5)  Performing edit trenches


6)  If cut then fill with insulator depo(sition)


7a) Conductor depo to contact metal interconnect


7b) Conductor depo to contact doped silicon layer


These basic process modules consist of many steps  for assuring planarity of the trench, etching Cu etc. that are provided by the FIB manufacturer or  developed by the users. The process modules that  are close to routine application are 1,2, 5, 6 and 7a. Modules 3, 4, and 7b are in development and their  process options are subject of this article.


For module 3 the following layers can produce  endpoint information:


3a) Junction well to substrate,


3b) Silicon-STI (Shallow Trench Isolation)


3c) Junction Source/Drain diffusion to well


The choice of the endpoint interaction can also  correlate to the navigation requirements of module  4 as imaging of the used layer also gives lateral  information within the alignment accuracy of the


respective lithography process.


Module 3a requires depth information with no


material contrast available because it happens  entirely within silicon. The required information


can be obtained in two ways:


A) Image contrast based on junction potential, and  B) Beam induced currents.


In this paper, approach A has been pursued.


Endpointing results of the options 3a and 3b are  subject 1 & 2 of this paper. Module 3c is not


included. The third topic of this work is module 7b


on highly doped silicon layers


Endpoint Detection – Well-Substrate Junction


In backside FIB implementations trenches are  milled through the globally thinned substrate to the  active circuitry (see Fig. 1). Once the trench has  been coated with an insulator, ‘micro-trenches’ are  milled through the floor of the larger trench to the  metal layer where the contact or cut is planned.
