# Contacting Silicon with FIB for Backside Circuit Edit


When milling the operating trench, endpoint  determination within silicon is required to stop  before the sensitive active structures are damaged.


A variety of techniques can be used to get endpoint  information within silicon: An optical technique


uses diffraction fringes and provides the ability to  stop within ~10µm of the active circuitry [1].


Monitoring an optical, electron or ion beam  induced current through a pn-junction in the  substrate can also provide endpoints [2]. The  boundary between the substrate and an inversely  doped well or active diffusion region can be  determined using active voltage contrast, if a bias  voltage is applied between the substrate and the  well or diffusion [3]. A similar image contrast for


the n-wells can also be obtained without the need of  biasing or contacting the device apart from  grounding. The details of this trench process are  described in [6]. Trenching was stopped when the  n-wells contrasted in the secondary electron image  at about 4µm remaining silicon. With an additional   insulator coating, the contrast is enhanced (Fig.2). Module 2a is a very comfortable endpoint because  it leaves all the active area in its original shape. It is  also close enough to the interconnect layers for


Fig. 2: Contrast after 19min of SiOx  deposition on


the trench floor using 15keV beam energy and 4nA  beam current. Imaging parameters are 30keV beam  energy and 6nA beam current. The n-wells appear  much brighter than the p-substrate. Field of view  182x172µm2.


editing those levels. However, minimum pitch  features and the very shallow source/drain  diffusions are not easy to contact, because after  4µm trench milling the endpoint has to be met  within ~50nm.


The FA operation can give an estimated completion date on a  submitted job by using a performance model based on Little’s  Theorem1.  Little’s Theorem, sometimes referred to as Little’s  Law, is widely used to model steady state systems capabilities.  Little’s Law attempts to relate Inventory (jobs in the FA lab), Throughput (how many jobs can be completed in a period of  time), and Cycle time (how long it will take to complete a  job).


By relating these three measures, Little’s Law can give an  estimated cycletime for a new arriving job for any system.


Little’s Law in equation form, is the following:


I = λ*T


I: # of jobs in the system (Inventory)


λ:  Arrival rate of jobs (Throughput)


T: Response time (Cycle time)


An example of how this works is as follows:


The customer submits a job and you want to give them an  estimated completion date.  You know that there are 10 jobs  total in the lab and that you can average 5 jobs out per week.  Using the historical output of the lab as the arrival rate is an  acceptable simplification for an assumed steady state system, where jobs in is equal to jobs out.


T = I/ λ or


Cycle Time = Inventory/Throughput


So, (Cycle Time) = (10jobs)/(5 jobs/week)


Therefore, Cycle Time = 2 weeks


You can tell your customer to expect the job to be complete in  two weeks.


Along with forecasting completion, updates during the  analysis process help solve the communication issue.  An  overall model of the FA operation is useful to help predict  completion times, but updates during the process account for  variations to the prediction model.


2.0 Metrics


Today most successful business operations use metrics to  drive management solutions, which provides direction to  achieving their desired goals.  Metrics provide a competitive  advantage when trying to meet your customer’s expectations  and are essential to understanding where you are relative to  these established goals.    Metrics need to be viewed as your “friend” and that this friend provides you a solution to any  identified capacity constraints.


Metrics should establish an overall view as to how effective  your operation is performing relative the “goals” expectation.  Metrics should provide a view to all pertinent information that  allows you to successfully manage the operation.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa144


The first objective in utilizing metrics is to establish the key “goals” needed to measure success.   Secondly you must  identify all key indices needed to accurately measure your  business goals and objectives.  The final phase is to implement  a business process that captures all key indices in a usable  database format from which the data can be extracted.  As a  suggestion, metrics should be reviewed on a frequency  approximately equal to the average cycle time (CT) of the  task.  Therefore if your average failure analysis CT is seven


(7) days, then consider weekly review of metrics for the most  effective response evaluation process.   In this case consider  using a 12-week rolling to establish “averages of indices” over  time.


You always get what you measure, for that reason, operation  metrics should also have diametrically opposed indices such  as “FA cycle time” vs. “Percentage of Units Unresolved”.  If  your chosen metrics to control the operation do not account  for all aspects of  the deliverables you might induce metrics  bias, only getting what you measure. For instance, when cycle  times are forced to conform to specified goals, which are  significantly different from your existing process, there is a  tendency to want to sacrifice opposing indices such as “Percentage of Units Unresolved”.  You cannot do this  because operation success is judged on all metrics.


Management support and buy-in on metrics helps when trying  to justify major expense items such as equipment, floor space  and headcount.  Metrics will be used to make the correct  decisions on how to satisfy the customer and business goals.


2.1 Failure Analysis Metrics


Failure Analysis cycle time metrics should be broken down  into a minimum of three (3) key areas:  FA Queue Cycle  Time, FA Work–in-Progress (WIP) Cycle Time, and Total FA  Cycle Time, which is comprised of the summation of Queue  and WIP cycle time.  The Total FA Cycle Time is what  Little’s Law is modeling for a steady state.


FA Queue Cycle Time, defines the time interval between  when a job is submitted to the FA operation and when that job  is actually started by the Failure Analyst.  Metrics should be  leading indicators by in which you can determine your overall  operation capacity and also determine if your operation is  capacity constrained.  From Little’s Law, if we maximize  throughput, for a fixed queue or inventory we achieve less  cycle time.  The overall objective is to reach the theoretical  limit of zero on all queue metrics.  Queue is not value added  cycle time, nothing is occurring on the job other then waiting  for a Failure Analyst to be assigned.


FA WIP Cycle Time, defines the time interval between when a  job is assigned to a Failure Analyst and when the analysis is   complete.  Metrics should establish indices about job loadings  in the analysis phase and whether or not CT’s are stable over  time.  A useful metric to monitor is the unusual jobs outside of  the average cycle time.  Both individual analyst metrics and


team metrics can be established that provide insights for  training, development and performance activities.


Total FA Cycle Time, defines the time interval between when  a job is submitted to the FA operation and when that job  completes the FA process.   This is the time your customer  experiences when a job is submitted.


2.2 Application of Queue Metrics to Capacity Constraints


If FA Queue Cycle Time is the dominant contributor to the  total FA cycle time it can be interpreted to show the capacity  constraint is one more of personnel resources than equipment  resources.  Knowing how long queue has been the CT issue  and if it is due to one time events helps decide on the best  solutions.


Out sourcing of jobs to contract failure analysis operations is  one way of  solving capacity constraints if they are queue  related.  If the queue is a bubble due to one time events, then  using external FA contractors will be done on an intermittent  basis.  Not all jobs are equal candidates for out source  solutions, but many in the queue could be.  Jobs requiring  intensive interaction with the group submitting the FA request  might not be the best jobs to out source due to the required  communication.  It is important to know the capabilities and  capacities of the companies you choose for FA out sourcing.  Requesting an out source operation to perform an analysis  they do not have the skills or equipment for is not a good  choice.  Overloading the external contract FA operation with  too many jobs is not a solution either.  Trading one queue for  another is not a solution to the overall capacity constraint.  You may need to develop several choices for FA out source  contractors to account for all the variables of your capacity  constraint.


You might also use external contractors if they have a  capability not within the internal FA operation.  Specialized  materials analysis (Auger, Mass Spectroscopy, FTIR, etc.) are  examples of equipment or capabilities that might not be  present in all FA operations.  Rather then purchasing a piece  of equipment that might only be lightly utilized it is a better  decision to out source this need when required.


Using services to supply contract employees is another option  to solve the capacity constraints based on queue.  These  employees have the benefit of being internal to the FA  operation so they can be better trained for the specific types of  devices your company supports.  The communication with the  groups submitting the requests for analysis can be easier to  support allowing for more complex jobs to be performed by  this person.


If the queue CT has been the dominant contributor to cycle  time and all forecasts of future requests are only increasing, then hiring additional full time personnel is an option.  Using  the metrics, the correct number of personnel to achieve the  desired goals can be arrived at.


2.3 Application of WIP Metrics to Capacity Constraints


If the metrics show you that reductions in WIP cycle time are  what is required to solve the overall FA cycle time then a  different set of possible solutions should be employed.


A typical Failure Analyst can only be actively working on a  small number of jobs at a given time.  Sometimes what  appears to be a simple solution to solve the previously  discussed queue cycle time is to assign multiple jobs to each  Failure Analyst.  This method has not solved the overall CT  since now the WIP cycle time will only increase because the  individual Failure Analyst has more jobs assigned than they  can reasonably work on in parallel.  Over assignment can  sometimes make a cycle time issue look like a WIP issue, when in fact it is a queue issue.


Analyzing and solving WIP cycle time is best accomplished  with a technique called bottleneck analysis.


3.0 Bottleneck Analysis


Whenever you have a process that has multiple steps there are  bottlenecks. If your failure analysis operation is continually  being tasked with increased job throughput and shorter cycle  times, then the issue of bottlenecks in your process flow is  even more critical. Improving the efficiency of the FA process  with respect to bottlenecks begins with proper identification of  those bottlenecks.


It is very important to identify bottlenecks with a systematic  process.  A delay that is perceived as a bottleneck needs to be  investigated with a formal process.  Some of these bottlenecks  might include insufficient job submission criteria, broken or  missing equipment, equipment utilization, equipment  availability (like an Automated Test Equipment (ATE) sign-up  schedule), having to tear down and reconstruct the same bench  or test set up, and multi-tasking which makes the Failure  Analyst a shared resource. Proper bottleneck identification  requires a clear definition of the baseline FA flow.


Failure modes vary greatly with most failure analysis requests, and as such, dictate a unique set of process flow steps to  complete the required analysis for determining root cause. However, for the purposes of identifying bottlenecks a  baseline FA flow with step-wise cycle times may be defined  with which to compare actual performance. The step wise  cycle times should be best case in nature which models what  could be termed “machine time”. This would exclude any  queue time that would involve a job waiting on tool  availability. Although the need for specific steps shown in the  following flow as well as the cycle times could be argued, a  representative 19-step FA process flow could look like that of  the following list. Best case step wise cycle times have been  selected to demonstrate the usage of this baseline flow. If steps  are skipped in a particular analysis, that step’s cycle time can  simply be omitted from the summation.


FA Flow used in Bottleneck Analysis


Step 1: Verify job information (1/4 hr)


Step 2: Visual inspection (1/4 hr)


Step 3: Electrically verify failure mode (1/2 hr)


Step 4: 24-hr bake and retest (1 day)


Step 5:  X-ray (1/4 hr)


Step 6: SAM (1/2 hr)


Step 7: TDR (1/2 hr)


Step 8: Confer with submitter/Eng/peers (1/2 hr)


Step 9: Decap (1/2 hr)


Step 10: Visual inspection (1/4 hr)


Step 11: Electrical isolation (1/2 hr)


Step 12: Delayer/deprocess/inspection (2 hrs)


Step 13: Cross-section (2 hrs)


Step 14: Physical defect I.D. (1/2 hr)


Step 15: Confer with submitter/Eng/peers (1/2 hr)


Step 16: Write report (1hr)


Step 17: Report review/approval (1/2 hr)


Step 18: Close out job (1/4 hr)


Step 19: Archive data (1/4)

From just these two examples, we can see that non-productive  time can be due to other issues besides equipment and other  resource bottlenecks. It’s vital to accurately identify the  bottlenecks so that they can be resolved effectively.  The  number of jobs studied in detail to reach your bottleneck  decision should be limited to not become an identified  bottleneck itself.


3.1 Equipment Utilization and Bottlenecks


Analytical equipment can be very costly.  Purchasing things  like Scanning Electron Microscopes, Focused Ion Beams,


Emission Microscopes, Scanning Acoustic Microscopes, etc.


can consume millions of capital dollars.  There is pressure to  show that the purchased equipment is providing an adequate  return on the investment.


Quite often return on investment of the equipment is measured  by how high the utilization is of that specific piece of


equipment.  Equipment being used all the time must be more  valuable than a piece of equipment rarely used, that is a simple  financial method of evaluating the equipment.  A pure


financial evaluation begins to drive the concept that the more  expensive the equipment is, the higher the utilization must be.  These are excellent concepts for production line


methodologies.


Unfortunately performing failure analysis on failing units


doesn’t always fit a production line methodology.  The


challenge of failure analysis is to get the right answer as fast  as possible.  There should be no tradeoffs of “right” versus


“fast”.  The analytical tasks performed will be ones most


likely to yield results based on the supplied clues and previous  results from prior analytical tasks.  That means the


combination of analytical tasks performed will be unique to


the specific failure being analyzed.


Every analytical task has its own average process time and a  distribution of time around the average process time.  For


instance performing x-ray on a failing unit might just need a


single low magnification top down x-ray to show the missing  bond wire.  Other x-ray analysis might need several higher


magnification images at various angles to show wire sweep


issues or malformed solder balls.  All of this variability can be  captured per analytical step and modeled as an average cycle  time and a normal distribution around that average to account  for as much variability as you care to model.


For an arbitrary single analytical task the average process time  can be represented by the variable APTn and the standard


deviation of the normal distribution of that process cycle time  can be represented by σAPTn.  If we are interested in


predicting or modeling the expected total cycle time for a


series of analytical tasks applied to a failing unit just add


together all the average process cycle times.


Mathematically the total analysis cycle time would be


represented as:


APT(total) = APT(1) + APT(2) + APT(3) +…….APT(n)


In terms of failure analysis the total cycle time would be


Total Cycle Time = x-ray cycle time + Electrical Verification  cycle time + Decap cycle time + FIB probe pad cycle time + internal probe cycle time + delayering cycle time+ SEM


inspection cycle time + report writing cycle time.


The effect of each of the standard deviations of the individual  average process times needs to be accounted for in the total


cycle time.  Standard deviations add up as the sum of the


squares of the pieces being equal to the total standard


deviation squared.  Mathematically the total standard


deviation is represented as:


(σAPT(total))2 = (σAPT(1))2 +  (σAPT(2))2 +


(σAPT(3))2….+ (σAPT(n))2


The standard deviation of the sum of all the analytical tasks


applied to a specific unit will be larger than any of the


individual standard deviations of the tasks making up the total.  The largest standard deviation of the pieces making up the


total standard deviation is the dominant factor to consider in


any bottleneck analysis.  This is an important concept to


remember when the utilization of the equipment is factored


into the cycle time equations.  Good financial practices for


manufacturing processes may create bottlenecks for the FA


process.


4.0 Signature Analysis


Using previous analysis as a method to reduce future job  submissions is another valuable method to solve capacity  constraints.  Based on the predicted operation performance by  Little’s Law, having less jobs in process will reduce the  average overall cycle time.


Signature analysis is often spoken of in reference to the tools  developed for prediction of failure mechanisms in failure  analysis. Signature analysis is not a single occurrence  measurement, but rather an ongoing process of modeling to  determine if received requests for analysis fall within a set of  criterion that may be used to respond with a level of  confidence.  This response may be used to cease or reduce  physical or electrical analysis when neither will increase the  confidence of determining additional failure mechanism  information.


A failure signature may be complex or simple.  Direct  measurement of a sample set of sufficient size may be used to  derive the confidence factors that relate to any question we  may ask about the sample.  If we derive these factors for an  electrical overstress failure, we must first define the  mechanism sufficiently.  When this has been done, a signature  of this mechanism is needed to allow for direct representation  within the model. An example signature analysis model is an  on-going process model that defines what is called an X/Y  criterion.  This criterion means that, for a given signature, one  is X% confident that Y% of future failures will have the same  failure mechanism.  It may be used: 1) When there are a large  number of previously analyzed units (>20) with the SAME  failure mode and whose failure mechanisms are known, 2) there is a dominant failure mechanism for a particular fail  mode, and 3) there is predicted to be a sufficient volume of  future failures to justify creating a signature.


An example of X and Y computation comes from2:

X = % confidence


Y = % future failures with the same fail mechanism


x = number of analyses resulting in the primary     failmode


α = x + 1


β = n – x + 1


Γ (x) is the generalized factorial Gamma function, which allows for factorials of complex numbers and negative  numbers.


Ө = true proportion of parts that would result in the  failure mechanism if analyzed.

Another less statistically rigorous method is a simple database  organization of analysis results over a period of time that may  aid in gathering much the same information that would be  found in any signature analysis study. While this may not be  statistically significant, it could prove to furnish enough  insight into the types of failures and groups of failures enough  to be of use when making judgments similar to signature  analyses related to repetitive analyses.  A failure analysis  operation has but to keep up with the failure mode and  mechanism as requests are completed to have a ready source  of information appropriate for sorting.  Once that data is  saved, it may be sorted to arrive at decisions that lead to “hands-off” analyses that are as useful for corrective actions as  any full report.  This is true not only because the analysis task  was undertaken many times previous to this occurrence, but  also because those occurrences lead to a high confidence  factor.


4.1 Shared Risk based Capacity Constraint Solutions


Sometimes it is advantageous to perform less detailed analysis  if additional information is available.  While there is some risk  associated with performing a quick turn Physical Failure  Analysis (PFA) job, the risk/reward must be agreed upon  between the requestor of the analysis and the FA lab.  This  agreement may lead to rapid identification of a problem saving  time and resources.


The documentation and authoring of FA reports consumes a  considerable amount of an Analyst’s time.  Many devices  submitted for FA have obvious physical or electrical damage  which can sometimes be solved by a group of images or other  simple analytical techniques without the need for a formal  report to be documented and published.


Examples of the types of jobs would be external package


damage resulting in shorted or open pins (See figures 7 and 8).  This damage could be a result of the removal process of the


device from a board, or mishandling during subsequent ATE


testing.


Figure 7


Figure 8


The images supplied are usually enough evidence of the cause  of a suspected failure mechanism and time consuming analysis  will lead to no additional actionable items.


What if the group or person submitting the failure analysis  request has their own internal capability of performing  the  analytical tasks?  Why not let this group or person perform the  analysis?  An open operation where the equipment is used by  many organizations is an option to decreasing the capacity  constraints, providing this does not create an equipment  bottleneck.


This paper has shown modeling the capacity of a failure  analysis operation and the proper interpretation of the metrics   can lead to the solution of any capacity constraints.

Endpoint Detection – Contrast STI-Silicon


Another image contrast mechanism that can be used  for trench endpointing in silicon is the FIB image  contrast between Si and SiO2 when the FIB-trench


hits the bottom of STI (Shallow Trench Isolation)


[5]. This is a very sharp material contrast and  perfectly fits navigation and endpointing needs. Fig. 3 illustrates the degree of accuracy an overlay  of a FIB image and layout can achieve, such that  the local trenches to the contacts can be positioned  very precisely. The complexity of this process  originates in the STI depth of usually below 500nm


as is illustrated in Fig.4. When such a contrast  appears, the FIB-trench has already hit the wells. The proper electrical function needs to be well  observed and may depend much on a variety of  parameters like trench bottom flatness, mechanical  stability, electrical integrity of the wells and device  degradation. With careful processing even large

Essentially, a  current is forced through a reference contact into  the silicon and to the FIB test contact.. The voltage  drop within the reference contact, the silicon layer

and the test contact is obtained by voltage probing  needles whereas the current is supplied on separate  needles. The resistance of the reference contact is  expected to be negligible, and the resistance of the  silicon layer typically is obtained (see ref [7],[8])


by varying the distance between the contacts. The  silicon wafer was doped with a 1.5µm deep  phosphorous layer to 1x1020/cm3 surface


concentration. The contact area has been defined by  a regular FIB oxide etch plus platinum deposition  process to 1x1µm2 and 3x3µm2. Common  sense in


metal-semiconductor contact technology claims the  need for silicidation to achieve low ohmic


characteristic [7], [8], For that reason, a proper  subsequent local silicidation process has been  applied. The reference contact was an IC


technology low resistivity contact (< 1 ) of 1mm


length.

The initially introduced process modules of  contacts to silicon in FIB circuit edit are making  good progress towards routine practice. Operational  endpoints in silicon can be performed stopping  before active layers right under the wells or before  the source/drain layers on the STI bottom. Contacts  to diffusion have reasonable low resistance with  straightforward processing on high doping levels. With the help of numerical simulation we are able  to evaluate the experiments quantitatively. Low  resistance contact processes on lower doped silicon  and endpointing on source/drain remain to be  investigated.

IC specification improvement through direct   passive component modification in the FIB


B. Domengès, B. Feron and S. Ledain


# IC specification improvement through direct passive component modification in the FIB


LAMIP, laboratoire de microélectronique ENSICAEN-Philips, 2 rue de la Girafe BP 5120, F-14079 Caen Cedex 5, Bernadette.domenges@philips.com


B. Tiphaigne


STEPMIND OUEST, Parc d'Activités de la Folie Couvrechef (ACTIS 1), 16 rue Bailey, F-14000 Caen Place


It is shown in this study that it is possible to modify under a  controlled way the resistance of a passive component either  through the milling of part of the volume of a polysilicon  resistor or on the contrary through the deposition of  a Pt strap  parallely connected to the involved device polysilicon resistor. In the latter case, each modification step being followed by an  electrical characterization, the evolution of device VCO phase  noise versus equivalent resistor value could be drawn and the  optimum value quantified.


Usual device modifications in FIB are based on cuts and/or  new connections through Pt or W deposition and devices  often include spare passive components available for new  connections during the process of its performance  improvement. The resistance of Pt straps is an important  parameter of device modifications and several studies have  been performed in order to minimize it or control it [e.g. 1-2] But sometimes, FIB passive component modification may be  the only way to validate the improved design. We present in  this paper two examples of FIB passive component  modification : first, it was possible to rise semi-quantitatively  the resistance value of a component by milling in the FIB part  of the volume of a polysilicon resistor ; secondly, an FIB  modification led to a controlled decrease of the resistance  value of a passive component and allowed the study of the  evolution of a VCO noise as a function of the resistance.


Example 1 : raising of the resistance value of a  polysilicon resistor


Our aim was to validate the influence of raising the resistance  value of a resistive component on an IC gain.The simplest  modification would involve new platinum connections, but  these ones should, in that case, stand several mA currents.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa162


Thus, we decided to try to modify the resistance through a  reduction of the passive component volume, i.e. through a  direct milling of part of the polysilicon resistor. This resistor  being rather deep (7µm) and thin (0.3µm), two parameters  should be controlled during the milling : aspect ratio and  depth of the drilled hole in order to obtain enough precision  on the milled volume. These difficulties were overcome using  iodine enhanced etching (3), which ensured an aspect ratio of


3.3° (Fig. 1). Also end point detection curve (direct  measurement of current flowing through the sample during  the milling) allowed to follow the different milled material on  the beam path.

Electrical measurements confirmed the influence of these  modifications on the IC performances. It was also possible to  relate semi-quantitatively the sputtered volume with the IC  gain improvement.


Example 2 : lowering of the resistance value   of a polysilicon resistor


The design problem was to evaluate the influence of a 3 kWresistance on VCO noise at low frequency offset without  affecting the noise value at high frequency offset. The  expected influence can be schematized as shown in figure 2  and the aim of this study was to find out the coordinates of the  intersection point of both curves (high frequency – low  frequency offsets versus resistor value). The architecture was  differential so that two blocks of resistors would be  symmetrically modified to allow a correct measurement of  VCO noise. The involved resistive component was based on


two 6 kW resistors parallely connected on one side by M3  lines of a five metallic level design and on the other side by  M2 lines. The easiest and primary modification consisted in  shunting one of the resistors in order to test the effect on VCO  noise, which appeared to be deteriorated in 2dB. Then a series  of modifications were settled out, based on progressive  decrease of resistance value. The experimental procedure  would be : adding in parallel a Pt strap of controlled resistance  to the existing resistors, ensuring  the possibility to verify the  resulting equivalent resistance by the opening of a window in  the passivation for probing on a close M5 line (Fig. 3) and  finally keeping another VCO block unmodified on a same  device for comparison but with the same opened window on  M5 line ; this would ensure an internal reference of the  measurement procedure and subsequently of the VCO noise  characterization.

Modified device electrical characterization and discussion


Parallely to device modification, electrical characterization  was performed, trying to reach step by step, the optimum  resistance value for VCO noise minimization. Figure 4 gives  VCO noise measurements at low offset for device A, B and C. The VCO1 block is the reference. It should be notified that  VCO noise at high offset was unchanged ensuring that we


always were on the right side of the minimum of the curve  VCO phase-versus resistor value. From modifications on  device A, it clearly appears that the rise of the resistance from  3kW to 6kW degrades the noise and the lowering back to 4.5  kW resistance improves but not enough the noise value. From  sample B to C, the noise improvement doubles with a  lowering of the resistor value from 1.5 kW to 0.43 kW. The  evolution of the VCO phase noise could be drawn versus  resistor value (Fig. 5).


During this study, we showed that by a controlled FIB  modification of a resistive passive component, followed step  by step by the electrical characterization, it was possible to  validate qualitatively the design modification. Furthermore, could we quantify through control of the resistance of the Pt  deposition the optimum value of the equivalent resistance of  this component, which corresponds to the best performance of  the device in terms of VCO phase noise.

FIB Chip Repair:  Improving Success by Controlling


Beam-Induced Damage and Thermal / Mechanical Stress


Steven Herschbein, Chad Rue, Carmelo Scrudato, Edward Hermann


IBM Microelectronics, Hopewell Junction, NY  USA


Focused Ion Beam (FIB) success has become more difficult as


microchip process technology advances, requiring new  techniques for damage control both during the microsurgery  procedure and before the finished product can be electrically  tested.  Ultra thin gate dielectrics, shallower junctions, less ‘white space,’ and new materials surrounding active devices  all create additional challenges for imaging, targeting, controlling instantaneous charge damage, and the removal of  residual implanted charge.  On the macro level, global  thinning of bulk silicon housed in hybrid packages is causing  new problems with thermal management and mechanical  stress.


Techniques and procedures used to control electrostatic  discharge type damage become ever more critical when  working on poorly buffered or isolated device elements, especially from the backside.  Implanted gallium and residual  charge perturb electrical characteristics, and must be dispersed  prior to power-up thru carefully controlled bake steps.  Left in  place, these FIB-induced perturbations are likely to cause poor  functionality or even latchup.  The mechanical rigidity and  thermal dissipation properties of newer, complex package  types must also be restored post-FIB, otherwise cracked  silicon or a thermal overload event might be the outcome.


In this paper, we will attempt to address some of the common  causes of FIB-induced failure on newer silicon and package  technologies, and how they might be overcome.  FIB  techniques and preparatory processes must continue to evolve  in order to deal effectively with the problems of direct beam  damage, residual charge elimination, and sample stress  management.


FIB modification for chip repair and internal signal probing  has become an integral part of the process for bringing  advanced products to market.  As devices become more  complex, with more levels and tighter geometries, conventional frontside FIB methods is yielding to the routine  use of backside access.


# FIB Chip Repair: Improving Success by Controlling Beam-Induced Damage and Thermal / Mechanical Stress


In addition to basic backside ‘cut & patch’ microsurgery, we  are now adding precision elements such as resistors and  capacitors to change the dynamics of circuit nodes.  But  frontside is far from dead – it is used most often in our lab for  direct access to the discrete transistors of individual SRAM  cells for margin and failure characterization.  [1] The latest  versions of our FIB “wagon wheel” pad cage are built in  layers, with up to 12 terminations occupying less than 1  square micron (roughly the size of the 6 transistor cell itself). Much of today’s work, whether it involves backside access & functional repair or precision frontside cell wiring, requires  that we operate a charged particle beam in very close  proximity to active circuit elements.  When doing this there  are two unique charge phenomena that the FIB user needs to  be concerned about.


In the first case, care must be taken not to subject thin gate  oxides and shallow junctions to beam induced voltages  beyond their breakdown limits.  A combination of bleed paths  and appropriate beam scan techniques must be used to protect  these delicate components from sudden, severe damage. [2]


Our second concern centers around charge pockets left below  the surface.  The primary gallium ion beam can penetrate and  implant into the sample.  Some of the generated secondary  electrons cannot escape, plus other tunneling mechanisms may  come into play.  Charge becomes trapped.  It is believed that  these pockets of charge can alter circuit electrical  performance, leading to unintended results – functional  abnormalities at best, severe latch-up and destroyed chips at  worst.  [3,4,5]


On the macro level, global thinning of bulk silicon, particularly when in combination with certain package  configurations, is causing new problems with thermal  management and mechanical stress.  Heat spreaders and  stiffeners are integral with many of the newer high  performance designs.  A plan for rebuilding these package  components must be formulated as part of the sample  preparation process.  Not restoring them after the completion  of FIB repairs can place severe limits on subsequent chip  operation.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa166


Charge Control During FIB Processes


A well understood issue with medium current beams in  frontside applications is surface charge accumulation and the  possibility of a sudden discharge event.  One needs to provide  a suitable path such that positive charge from the primary  gallium (Ga) beam is not coupled into an active circuit  element.  Irreparable damage such as blown gate oxides or  leaking junctions results when the only path available is  through one of these elements and the chip’s own metallurgy  to a grounded pin.  [2]


Considering the close proximity of the beam to circuit  elements (gates & junctions), one would expect samples  subjected to backside FIB work to be equally or even more  susceptible to damage.  And indeed the risk is high, as  powerful beams (20nA is common) are employed in the  removal of bulk silicon up to within a few microns of the  underside of active circuitry.  This value can be even less (a  few tenths of a micron) in the case of isolated substrates.


For many years one of the best available solutions was the use  of the electron flood gun to achieve a net neutral surface  charge state.  But this method, while effective, requires that  imaging be done with secondary ions rather than secondary  electrons.  This is still an acceptable procedure during bulk  trench mills at higher currents, but is generally not needed  because the substrate silicon drains the charge very well.  However, once the coarse trench has been excavated, a switch  must be made to a smaller, more controllable beam to achieve  the precision required by today’s technology.  The problem is  that at beam currents much below 30pA, the secondary ion  yield is relatively low.  Even with the gain turned up, the  reduced particle count reaching the detector is not sufficient to  produce a quality image (poor signal to noise), and is  especially not adequate for precise endpoint determination  with any degree of certainty.  Electron imaging thus again  becomes the only option, and the electron neutralizer must be  turned off.


To a certain extent, what was ‘old’ has become ‘new’ again.  Fibbers have had to rediscover, but with considerable  refinement, grounding methods that were once used for charge  dispersion prior to the widespread adoption of electron flood  gun neutralization.


While it might seem that backside repair, with its high level of  bulk silicon exposure would offer an adequate drain pathway, this is not always the case.  If metal traces are to be deposited, large expanses of the nearby silicon will need to be covered  with oxide to provide isolation.  Emerging technologies with  isolating barrier layers will essentially already have this oxide  in place.  Either will require a temporary path to ground as the  large expanse of floor oxide limits natural shunts in the  immediate vicinity of the repair zone.


DFT based tester method by using custom pattern set


This method involved extensive use of a DFT focused tester  called Inovys.  The part was tested using a set of ATPG  patterns. A single pattern was taken and modified to generate  custom patterns. The part was tested to verify that it failed this  pattern. The failing bit on the pattern is a part of scan chain0. A new pattern set was prepared by replacing all the vectors on  the scan chains with 0’s except scan chain0. It was found that  the pattern set was passing. A different pattern set was  prepared from the original, this time by replacing the vectors  of scanchain1 with 0’s and leaving the vectors for the other  chains the same as the original pattern set. The part still  passes.  This process was repeated by using different pattern  sets each time replacing vectors with 0’s on different scan  chains. The part fails always except when vectors on  scanchain1 were replaced with 0’s. Hence it was concluded  that a particular bit on chain1 when flipped to 0 was causing  the pattern to pass.


Fig 5 shows the binary search conducted to isolate the cause  of fail to a single bit


A binary search was performed by replacing the vectors on the  chian1 with 0’s. A single bit on scan chain1 was found, which  when flipped from 1 to 0 made the part to flip from the fail to  pass state.


The cone of logic feeding to this particular bit in the scan  chain was identified. This entire logic was mapped onto the  database and checked if these nets are neighbor nets to our


original suspect nets. None of these nets were exact neighbors  but were found to lie in the same general area.


A correlation metric was calculated for each of the nets of the  cone of logic with respect to the suspect nets. A high  correlation of more than 90% was found for one of the nets in  the cone of logic leading to the isolated bit. This net was  mapped onto the database and found that it went very close to  the original suspect nets. But still it did not isolate to a small  area.


Global Fail Site Isolation


A third method was attempted to validate the results from any  of the above methods. Global Fail site isolation using  Emission/TIVA/LIVA [Ref 3] techniques was attempted.  The  DUT was powered in DC mode sourcing 170mA of current. A  TIVA hotspot was found overlaying with the original suspect  net region.


Fig 6 shows the TIVA hot spot.


One of the neighbor nets isolated by both the above two  methods was also found lying close to the TIVA spot region. Having information electrical isolation, Physical failure  analysis was attempted mainly inspecting the region isolated  by the above three methods.


A floating node was found on one of the suspect nets as  shown in fig 7 in the area isolated by a combination of the  three methods.


Fig 7 shows an open on one of the suspect nets


Precise fail site isolation has been done on an ATPG fail by  using a combination of different methods. Understanding the  fastscan data log and what it means when a single net is stuck  at both 0 and 1 is an important step. Three different methods  were discussed which led to the successful isolation of the  defect.

D.Martin, G.Haller


ST Microelectronics, Z.I. de Rousset, 13106 Rousset, France

The continually increasing complexity of integrated circuits


has made fault localization progressively more difficult. Despite  significant imp rovements in test and diagnosis  tools, probing  is still required for acquiring new information and for  confirming test results.  For this reason, we have developed an  optimized diagnosis -to-probing flow which significantly  reduces the number of nodes to be probed and which  dramatically cuts the cost of fault localization. With this  approach, probing can be integrated in test and diagnosis   operations to reach nodes which are known to be untestable .


Fault localization is started at the test level. When testing is  insufficient, diagnosis techniques are used to refine and extend  the localization of potential candidates for fault origin(s). Finally, probing at the die level of one or more nodes may be  required to remove remaining uncertainties. Probing can be  very time consuming and requires a high level of knowledge of  the die. This is why it is often used as a last resort.


To limit probing to only a few nodes and to benefit from this  ability to reach otherwise unreachable nodes, we have  developed a diagnosis flow (see Figure 1) [1]. From an initial  Automatic Test Pattern Generation (ATPG) and datalog tester  resulting from EWS (Electrical Wafer Sort), a first diagnosis is  performed to create a list of potential failing nodes. To reduce  this list of suspects, we specifically rerun ATPG to generate  new patterns and to individually test each node of the list. The  result (PASS/FAIL) is correlated with the sensitivity of the  pattern on each net to eliminate certain candidates. If several  candidates remain after the list has been maximally reduced  with tester emulation and result comparisons, internal probing  is used. Probing is used as an internal capability to bring new  information back to the diagnosis flow. It makes it possible to  converge faster with a higher degree of confidence on the  researched fault. The result is compared to the correct value -


# Optimised Probing Flow for High Speed Fault Localization


obtained from simulations and the acquisition of new data is  reused with diagnosis tools to generate a reduced new fault  list. Probing can then be conducted on the final nets to  discriminate equivalent faults in the netlist, such as the input  and output of an inverter, which produce the same tester  datalog.  We will present the application of this diagnosis flow  through a case study to highlight how probing can be coupled  efficiently with ATPG to bring added testing and capabilities to  specific nodes.

A second part of our paper will be focused on probing  technique optimisation. The goal is to take into account the  probing technique, the duration involved and node  accessibility in order to reduce the time and cost of our  diagnosis  flow. To check signals from the front side on metal  layers, frequently used techniques include mechanical and ebeam probing for node logic levels. Both techniques are fast. However, access to buried metal layers is more challenging and  requires some preparation. The choice we have automated  involves either probing a top metal layer which is a few gates  after the node of interest or preparing the device (added time  and cost) and probing the node directly if it is just to confirm  that it is not the root cause of the failure.


Methodology


To optimise design modifications for probing, our strategy  uses fault propagation in order to acquire equivalent signals  on easier probing nodes. To do this, we convert signals to  probes and generate new patterns  to emulate a node and  propagate its value.


The FIB (Focused Ion Beam) is put into the equation to create  probe points on buried metal layers. To optimize FIB work we  define the following approach:


Optimal FIB probe placement calculation


The goal is to predict the duration and difficulty of FIB probe  points. A grade is calculated to assess the success rate and  the cycle time. Questions that must be resolved before starting  are: Is the FIB operation do-able, are the metal lines accessible (front side or backside), where is the optimal location, and what  are the risk, time and cost involved?


Using the layout information, the equipotential line of each  electrical node to be probe is extracted. The equipotential  correspond to the series of polygons (e.g., rectangles of metal  line) connected together between an output of a gate and the  next input.


Figure 2: Proposed flow to define the best node to probe.


The next step is to extract the “accessible part”, i.e., the part of  a metal line which is not covered by above layers. At this  point, if there is “accessible” metal, it means that the FIB probe  point is possible.


To calculate the optimal placement, three parameters are used:  Minimum separation α: The visible part of the buried metal line  is reduced by a factor α due to the cone shaped ion beam and  beam shift.


Minimal line width β: A line is accessible if it size is larger than  its factor β.


Minimal distance between two lines  λ: The proximity  coefficient λ is used to filter out parts of the equipotential that  are too close to other lines.


In addition to these parameters, the FIB time is calculated for  the optimal probe point [3].


When we add this optimized probing to our diagnosis  flow, we  can jump to the generated list of potential failed nodes.  To  measure signals by internal probing we follow our algorithm  whose input is the node to be probed, extracted from the list, and whose output is the right or wrong status of the node. If  the measured net has a different value from the simulation, we  have identified the guilty net; otherwise, we reduce the fault  list.


If the node to be probed is an upper metal level, the cycle time  and the success rate are good. The design modification (by  FIB) required for acquiring new information is quite cheap (in  terms of time vs. success rate cost value). However, a node on  a lower metal level is more difficult to reach because of its  depth. This measurement is expensive because of a long cycle  time and a low success rate in comparison with the first node. In this case, fault propagation is taken into account to measure  the input value of a gate on the output of this gate.

Figure 3: Optimal FIB probe point calculation. Proximity of  nearby metal lines is taken into account to increase success  rate of FIB operation while minimizing cycle time.


This automated diagnosis and probing flow is made up with  four major parts:


The fault propagation: considering the schematic/netlist, we  look for the logical gates involved by the electrical net we will  propagate. We define the outputs relatives to these logical  gates and the constraints to add and others inputs to correctly  propagate the fault.


The optimum layer: a script, which allows extracting the upper  metal level of an electrical net: we enter the name of the net we  want to analyse (during the design stage, this net is in fact  several polygons) and thanks to navigation tools, we can  determined the metal level of each polygon. By treatment, we  define the upper metal level polygons.


The optimum pattern: before the probing stage and for net  emulation, we generate Diagnosis -ATPG patterns. We use  commercial ATPG tools, but we just add in the fault list, the  suspect net we want to probe; one pattern is generated (“0” forced on the net to check a “stuck-at 1” for example). In term  of time, no difference between one pattern generation and an  other one and for the success rate, it is binary: we succeeded (100%) or not (0%) to generate the pattern.


The optimum placement [2]: we define the best place to do the  probe point taking into account the neighbourhood metal lines  of the interesting electrical net, as shown in Figure 3.


Mechanical and e-beam probing vs TRE probing


The approached we have presented in the above paragraph  was first meant for front side IC investigation with mechanical  and e-beam probing. With the increasing complexity of  devices, Time Resolved Photon Emission (TRE) has open new  capabilities. TRE can detect the faint emission coming from  switching transistors, through the silicon backside. The  advantage of TRE is to suppress any FIB work since  transistors are probed instead of metal line.


With TRE, the cycle time can be very long for small  technologies. With TRE acquisition, the device test pattern is  looped in order to increase the chances of detecting photons  from transistor commutations. Cycle time is calculated as a  function of the number of commutation, the test pattern length  and power supply VDD. The success rate is more difficult to  access. The two main factors are VDD and the minimal distance  between two switching transistors λ for optimal probing. More


detail on IC debug with TRE and circuit simulation can be  found in [4].


Experimental results


The experiences have been done with a fully scanned design, a


0.18 micron technology with 6 metal levels.  Two examples will  be detailed to understand the benefit of this methodology.

Diagnostic Fault Simulation for the Failure Analyst


Dan Bodoh, Anthony Blakely, Terry Garyet


Freescale Semiconductor, Austin Texas


Dan.Bodoh@freescale.com, Anthony.Blakely@freescale.com, Terry.Garyet@freescale.com


Scan testing has led to the development of software tools to


diagnose faults.   A fault diagnosis tool uses simulation to  create a list of faults that explain failing test results.  Because  these tools originated in the design-for-test (DFT) realm, most  have abstractions that reflect a designer’s viewpoint.  These  abstractions prevent easy application of diagnosis results in  the physical world of the FA lab.


We developed a fault diagnosis system, DFS/FA, which  bridges the DFT and FA worlds.  It produces easily  understandable results and better diagnoses than commercial  tools.


DFS/FA is not only a diagnosis tool.  It is a collection of tools  that are designed to help the failure analyst perform defect  isolation more quickly.  In the paper, we will describe the  concepts behind many of the DFS/FA features and show how  it has been used to aid failure analysis.


This paper contains five major sections.  In the first section, we describe the motivation for building DFS/FA and how it is  an improvement over off-the-shelf tools.  The second section  describes the DFS/FA building blocks on which the diagnosis  tool depends.  In the third section, we describe the diagnosis  algorithm in detail.   The fourth section overviews some of the  supporting tools that make DFS/FA a complete solution for  failure analysis.  Finally, in the fifth section we show a failure  analysis example where DFS/FA has been applied.


Motivation


We made the decision to build a new diagnosis tool after years  of using commercially available off-the-shelf tools to perform  diagnosis.  We identified several deficiencies in these tools:


1. Most off-the-shelf tools use the stuck-at fault model.  Although the stuck-at fault model may generate patterns  that detect defects more complex than the fault model  itself, its use during diagnosis may not pinpoint the  location of a complex defect [1].  Note that in this paper, a fault is a simulation abstraction and a defect is a real, physical problem on a device.


2. The un-ranked list of diagnostic callouts that most offthe-shelf tools provide is not helpful to the failure analyst, who may decide to destructively pursue one of the many  callouts.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa181


# Diagnostic Fault Simulation for the Failure Analyst


3. No off-the-shelf tool considers the physical layout to  propose realistic faults.


4. The off-the-shelf tools tend to be DFT-centric, because  they are automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) tools  that happen to have a diagnosis feature. The diagnosis  inputs and the output are not represented in a form to  which a failure analyst is accustomed.  The off-the-shelf  tools also do not provide any supporting tools that a  failure analyst needs to perform further defect isolation.


5. In a company with many design teams, any diagnosis tool  must interface with the different ATPG tools  commercially available.  Diagnosis tools built into the  ATPG tool do not satisfy this requirement.


We believe that DFS/FA addresses these five deficiencies, and  has many advantages over off-the-shelf tools:


DFS/FA is fault-model independent


Commercial diagnosis tools use the stuck-at fault model, but  real defects exhibit behavior that is much more complex.  DFS/FA eschews the stuck-at fault model (and, in fact, all  fault models) by improving on the SLAT [2] and iSTAT [3] algorithms.  By not assuming any specific fault model, DFS/FA can pinpoint faulty wires even in the presence of a  defect with a complex behavior.


DFS/FA explains its results


Fault models re-enter the picture after the initial fault-model  independent diagnosis of the failing patterns.  The failing  pattern behavior of each diagnostic callout is analyzed and  explained as a common fault type.   DFS/FA can explain a  callout as a stuck-at fault, a bridging fault, a slow-to-rise fault, a slow-to-fall fault or as an unexplained fault.


DFS/FA analyzes its results for physical proximity


The wires in each callout are analyzed for physical proximity  using the GDSII layout database and netlist that have been  imported into the FA navigation tools.   This allows realistic  bridges and other proximity-based defects to be identified.  Bridges that are physically realistic are ranked above those  that are not.  The coordinates and layers on which the wires  are neighbors are listed in the diagnostic output.


Complete wires are faulted


Most diagnosis tools define a fault as an incorrect value on a  gate input or output.   A real defect on a wire with a large  fanout can cause faults on many gate inputs, confusing singlefault-assuming diagnosis tools.  DFS/FA recognizes this  situation and defines a fault as affecting any of the various  permutations of the fanout of a gate.  Therefore, DFS/FA can  consider defects on multiple-fanout wires as one fault, rather  than as many faults.  This improves diagnosis results and  understandability.


DFS/FA is closely tied to the ATPG tool


DFS/FA directly reads the inputs and outputs of the scan  ATPG tool, using the ATPG netlist as its simulation model.  Importing a new design into DFS/FA is relatively easy for an  FA group, because it leverages the DFT effort to import the  design into the ATPG tool.


DFS/FA is closely tied to the FA navigation tools


DFS/FA derives a mapping between the ATPG netlist and the  FA navigation tool netlist.  The ATPG netlist is often an  abstracted view of the physical netlist used in the FA  navigation toolset.  Presenting diagnosis results in terms of the  ATPG netlist can be confusing for the failure analyst, so  DFS/FA presents its results in terms of the physical netlist.  Mapping the ATPG netlist to the physical netlist also enables  DFS/FA’s proximity-checking feature described above, which  happens in the physical space.


DFS/FA includes a robust data log translator


The data log translator must convert a failing tester cycle and  pin name into a failing scan pattern number and scan cell.  Since a poor data log translation will lead to poor diagnosis  results, our data log translator verifies the expect data in the  data log against the original pattern to prevent transparent  errors.


DFS/FA includes supporting tools


DFS/FA has several support tools that together make it a  complete software-based diagnosis system for failure analysis. These tools are detailed later in the paper.


DFS/FA Building Blocks


DFS/FA is built upon several application program interfaces (APIs).  New tools can be built on the existing APIs to easily  add new functionality to DFS/FA.  Each API is described  below.


FNL API


The FNL API provides functions to create and read gate-level  netlists whose hierarchy has been flattened.  Efficient use of  memory was a primary design consideration, because a flat  netlist can be extremely large.


To achieve efficient memory use, gate and wire names are  stored in a separate dictionary file that is not loaded into  memory.  The netlist proper uses integers, called GWIDs, to  represent gate and wire names.  The name-to-GWID mapping


is only performed when writing diagnosis results.  FNL allows  multiple dictionaries, so several different forms of the gate  and wire names can be stored.  The netlist itself is designed to  be directly memory-mapped into virtual memory to reduce  load time.  The benefit of efficient memory use is clear in one  of the larger designs imported into DFS/FA: a 2.5-million gate  design requires only 94 MB of virtual memory space.


The netlist represented in FNL is derived from the netlist and  libraries used for ATPG, which is typically in structural  Verilog.  FNL can represent all Verilog’s structural primitive  gates, as well as ATPG-specific primitives such as a flip-flop, a d-latch, and memory array constructs.  Non-default Verilog  drive strengths are not implemented, because ATPG tools  ignore Verilog drive strength.  However, gate delays are  implemented even though they are ignored by ATPG tools.


The most commonly used FNL API functions allow  navigation through the netlist.  Other functions translate  GWIDs to names and vice versa, retrieve information about  gate port directions and memory read/write port behavior, and  provide a mechanism for creating a new FNL.


The translator that reads the Verilog ATPG netlist and flattens  the netlist into FNL only supports those Verilog constructs  used by ATPG tools.  For example, behavioral structures such  as always are not understood, except where the behavioral  structures define memories for the ATPG tool.  Only  structural gates and Boolean assign statements are understood.  The Boolean assign expressions are translated to NAND/NOR  equivalents in an attempt to match the expression’s  implementation in silicon.


FaultSim API


The FaultSim API provides functions to perform gate-level  simulation and fault insertion.  The netlist that FaultSim uses  is FNL; the stimulus is provided through FaultSim’s API.


The primary design goals of fast simulation and efficient  memory use required tradeoffs to achieve a good balance.  Simulation speed is primarily achieved through the technique  of parallel simulation [4].   Given one netlist, FaultSim can  simulate 64 machine states simultaneously.  The 64 parallel  simulation slices can be allocated to 64 different patterns, or  64 different faults with one pattern, or any combination in  between.


FaultSim, like Verilog, has four wire states: 1, 0, X and Z.  The state also carries one of four strength values – Verilog’s  drive strengths are implemented, but not its capacitive  strengths.  To efficiently use memory, each wire state in each  parallel simulation slice is represented by two bits: isHigh and  isLow.  If both bits are 1, the wire is X.  If both bits are 0, the  wire is Z.  If only one bit is high, that bit defines the logical  state of the wire.


The signal strength requires two bits per parallel simulation  slice to encode each of the four Verilog strengths.  However, many gates, such as AND and OR, ignore strength on their


inputs, and drive a default strength of 2 on their outputs (FaultSim ignores Verilog’s non-default drive strengths).  Therefore, the two strength bits are only allocated to those  wires that connect to gates, like NMOS, that use the strength  information.  Since most gates in a design are Boolean, this  technique reduces FaultSim’s memory usage considerably.


Good grounding begins with the sample holder.  Full  thickness individual die can be clamped into a sliding vise that ‘bites’ into the edge of bulk silicon.  Wafers should be ‘buffed’ at the three-point mechanical clamping spots to  ensure removal of process films and good silicon contact.  Backside thinned conventional bulk process silicon that is C4  mounted onto ceramic substrates can obtain some connection  thru the direct contact of the substrate-to-application bumps to  the DUT holder.  This connection scheme can be  supplemented by the use of double-sided conductive tape as  an interface to overcome planarity issues.


While relying on package pins for backside silicon grounding  may prove acceptable, some chip processes lacking a good  silicon base connection will require a hard wired supplemental  path.  This can easily be achieved thru the use of carbon tape  or paint, creating a bridge from the silicon, across the ceramic  module, and onto the sample holder (Fig. 1).  Some  forethought about the locations of fiducial and repair trench  mills is required, as paint/tape must not impinge on these  areas.


Figure 1: Supplemental grounding path for backside FIB  repair – conductive tape from silicon, across the package, and  down to the sample holder.


Once the trench floor is reached and the beam is within close  proximity of active circuitry, additional measures are required.  Some repairs may benefit from a ring strap or thin blanket  deposition of metal placed on top of any oxide that will be  worked upon for an extensive period of time.  This local  film/strap is connected to a trace that leads up onto the  exposed backside silicon, or to a plug drilled thru layers to a  proper circuit ground point (Fig. 2).  In this way, much of the  circuit modification work and imaging done in the immediate  area will benefit from some level of beam charge reduction.  The drilled connection or bulk connection lead is severed, and  the film/straps removed as part of the cleanup steps when the  work is completed.


Similar approaches can be employed during “wagon wheel” wiring of isolated memory cell elements from the frontside.  Grounding rings or blanket depositions of conductor films can  be connected to plugs drilled down to the substrate in a region  outside of the cell array, or to a wired power supply trace that  is still intact.


Figure 2: Charge bleed strap (upper left) connects the  perimeter of the ring of pads to a substrate ground until all  other work is completed.


Another way to reduce the incidence of damage is to limit the  instantaneous and cumulative ion dose delivered during  operations near active circuit elements.  The most obvious  approach is to decrease mill & deposition beam currents to the  bare minimum required to achieve the desired operation.  In  addition, a higher reliance on CAD overlay, use of local drift  compensation fiducial marks, active stage and beam  placement compensation, or elaborate box templates can all be  employed to reduce the number of frame ‘grabs’ required.  Anything that reduces the total number of beam exposure  events greatly increases the chance of DUT survival.


Residual Charge & Post-FIB Processes


For a number of years we had observed that some FIB  repaired circuits did not function as ‘crisply’ as we believed  they should.  Analog circuits seem to be particularly  troublesome, sensitive to beam dwell time and proximity  effects.  Early experiments with post-FIB baking sometimes  had a profound effect on the outcome, restoring functionality  or at least tightening the performance distribution.  We were  not alone in our findings, as a number of other FIB users were  discovering and reporting similar results in the same time  period.  [3, 4]


When we began doing backside repairs, baking became much  more of a necessity.  Depending on the fabrication technology  node, circuit function or density, we found that many repaired


chips simply would not operate properly without an extensive  post-FIB bake.


In the beginning, it was rather hard for us to understand why  relatively simple backside repairs were becoming so  problematic.  Target a specific cell in a memory array, and  along with it a dozen surrounding cells within the field of  view would also fail.  Work in a logic block, and often the  whole block would malfunction.  On some occasions, parts  would quickly go into latch-up and thermal runaway.  We  quickly learned to place current clamps on power supplies, and bring everything up very slowly and carefully (Fig. 3).  On one such occasion we were able to shut down quickly and  save the unit from damage.  On a hunch we baked it overnight  and tried testing it again the next morning.  The performance  of the part after annealing was flawless!


Figure 3:  This IR optical photo shows the damage sustained  at a backside FIB repair site when the charge dispersal  anneal was insufficient.


Clearly, some experimentation would be required.  We needed  to better understand what could be controlled in our FIB  process to minimize the problem, and to determine the optimal  conditions for a ‘standard’ post-FIB recovery bake.


Several different known and testable circuit arrangements  were used as evaluation vehicles, but by far the safest (least  likely to go into latch-up) and easiest to interpret was the  SRAM cell array.  Over the course of a year, a number of  SRAM designs were prepared for backside FIB.  The product  groups were mainly interested in verifying logical-to-physical  descramble by directing us to damage specific cells.  We used  the opportunity to learn much more by investigating the  amount and effect of the residual charge incurred during a  number of standard FIB operations.  We looked at wide and  narrow area imaging, material deposition, and site-specific  milling.  Bitmap testing was done to monitor the extent and  pattern of functionality loss, and cell balance recovery after a  series of successive bakes.


Shown in graphical form is composite data from a number of  SRAM arrays, subjected to a series of bakes at three different


temperatures (Fig. 4).  While the highest temperature yielded  the best results, the goal was to keep the excursion as low as  possible.  At this point we were looking for a set condition  that could be used on all submissions to our lab, without  regard to whether they were simple repairs, or fail sites under  investigation.  We did not want to risk initiating ‘bake  recovery’, for instance, on a stress-test module that had been  submitted for help with failure analysis!
