Figure 4:  Composite SRAM cell bake recovery results


Initially, a room ambient atmosphere oven was used for postFIB baking.  It was quickly realized that the tungsten traces  and pads developed considerable oxidation in the process, creating higher resistance lines, and pads that were more  difficult to probe.  Moving to a partially sealed oven with a  nitrogen purge reduced the surface reactions to a manageable  level.


In the end, a bake of 200°C for 8 or more hours in dry N2 was  determined to satisfy most demands, and has become part of  our standard procedure.  This was largely arrived at  empirically.  Someday, we hope to add more ‘science’ to it  and fine-tune the parameters.  We might be able to apply a  different, optimized bake profile depending on the type of  repair or task attempted.


Many questions remain.  What is the failure and recovery  mechanism?  Why is the bake process so effective?  Theories  currently center around the presence of residual electrical  charge.  This is the result of the primary beam and/or  secondary charged particles, and tunneling electrons that  become trapped in the immediate vicinity of transistor  elements. [5] These trapped charges change fundamental  circuit operation close to where they reside.


The 30-50 keV source extraction process of the modern FIB  tool yields a positively charged beam of gallium ions. Gallium  is also a p-type dopant.  In the straight sputter mode (no gas), a small amount of the primary beam is implanted into the  surface.  The mean depth of penetration and the straggle


distribution can be modeled, much as it is done for any  diffusion implantation process.  Using commercially available  semiconductor processing charts for similar sized ions  implanted into oxides or silicon, a reasonable guess can be  made.  More accurate determinations of the depth and path of  the gallium ion can be obtained thru Monte Carlo simulation (SRIM modeling [6], for example).  Assuming uniform  stopping power and no channeling, most of this implanted  gallium probably resides within 30-50 nm of the surface.


FIB gas assisted etch processes change this dynamic, as a  chemical component is now introduced into the equation [7].  It is reasonable to assume that the effective gallium  penetration depth would be reduced as the surface is stripped  away as fast as it is being implanted (competing processes).  During the large trench mill and some subsequent gas driven  operations, the gallium penetration and concentration  probably doesn’t come into play.  But during the final steps of  backside circuit edit, some of the work must be done by  straight sputtering with minimal gas processing in order to  avoid unintended spontaneous etching.  FIB depositions are  also assumed to generate considerable implantation below the  interface. The combination of close proximity and raw beam  exposure directly beneath FET devices, and subsequent charge  trapping, may be the cause of anomalous electrical behavior.      These injected and now trapped charges, if located in critical  spaces in relation to FET devices, can probably influence S-D  conduction through field effects, acting as a Vt component.  Or, they may even provide an alternate conductive path  between devices, leading to a latch-up phenomena.  The net  effect is electrical performance inconsistent with intended  circuit design.


We considered the possibility of direct doping of the channel  as the mechanism, but dismissed it based on the presumed  depth of gallium penetration and dose involved.  Plus, there is  question as to whether this would be as easily bake  recoverable.   Fortunately, as long as the FIB work itself is not  too ‘heavy handed,’ the damage is pretty much reversible with  the bake.  With time and temperature, the gallium ions become  neutrals, and the trapped charge concentration is dispersed.  Normal device performance is again restored.


Packaging and Sample Prep Considerations


Until fairly recently, C4 bonded chip products were typically  mated to multi-layer ceramic modules.  The ceramic substrate  provided mechanical strength as well as an additional path for  thermal management.  The underside of the ceramic contained  the pin or ball arrangement that served as the interface to the  system level card.  A solid or finned cap in contact with the  backside of the die and sealed to the ceramic served as both an  additional heat spreader and mechanical damage shield.


After the lid is removed, the die can be thinned down to the  requisite 75um or so either by a planar polisher or computer


numeric controlled (CNC) milling machine.  The choice of  grinding methods is usually dictated by what, if anything, surrounds the die.  If there are no obstructions, then the planar  autopolisher is the most expeditious approach.  If there are  chip capacitors or other integral structures along the sides at  die height, then a CNC tool may be the only choice (Fig. 5).  Even if this is necessary, the setup parameters for the tool will  be easy to determine, as everything is in full view.


Figure 5:  Ceramic ball grid array (BGA) module.  Lid  removed and chip thinned/polished by CNC miller.


The ceramic-based package offers a number of distinct  advantages.  To begin with, it is strong and rigid.  It does not  generally rely on the presence of a lid for it’s mechanical  strength.  The die is C4 bonded in place with a high degree of  flatness (no bowing).  This is an important factor when it  comes to backside CAD driven blind navigation.  Even after  mechanical die thinning and FIB trenching, the assembly  remains robust and holds up well to general handling.


We generally like to have all modules retested after sample  prep to insure full functionality prior to beginning any FIB  work.  With some due caution about insuring good heat  dissipation, this is entirely possible at almost any step with  ceramic modules.  They can be inserted into a number of  clamp socket arrangements for functional evaluation without  causing silicon damage.  In the case of high power  components, a small stock plate or square of polished silicon  can be placed on top of the thinned die to restore the interface  to the tester’s cold chuck. This becomes a critical issue as  today’s high performance processor chips can dissipate in  excess of 100 watts of power. With minor modification they  can even be card level mounted using the original lid for  protection and thermal dissipation.


A few years ago a new style of composite ball grid array (BGA) package was introduced for flipchip applications.  The  key critical construction detail pertinent to this discussion is  the use of a semi-flexible fiber resin board as a substitute for


the ceramic base.  The die is still C4 mounted on the topside, but surrounded (in most cases) by a perimeter stiffener.  The  cap is attached to both the stiffener and the die.  As a  completed assembly, the unit is quite rigid.  All of the  interfaced materials work together to contribute mechanical  strength and heat removal.  But without the lid, the board can  flex considerably – enough to crack a thinned die during  subsequent handling.


This challenge required a major change in approach.  It was  no longer possible to remove the entire lid as we needed to  maintain as much of the package integrity as possible.  Using  the CNC machine in a plunge router mode, a window just  large enough to clear the FIB’s gas delivery nozzles was cut in  the lid.  The chip visible beneath was thinned and polished  after some tool setup changes (Fig. 6).  It was also no longer  practical to retest the die, even with the partial lid remaining.  The loss of uniform ‘down pressure’ in the central region  repeatedly resulted in cracked chips when they were clamped  into sockets.  And even if it survived mechanically, the heat  load might quickly overwhelm the entire assembly.


Figure 6:  Hybrid BGA module.  Window cut in lid by CNC  miller - larger than the die area, but smaller than the  perimeter stiffener (located between the lid and fiber board  substrate). The chip was also thinned using the CNC miller  after a bit and program change.


FIB repair proceeded pretty much as usual, except that all  work received an overcoat of oxide to help protect it from  future mechanical or chemical damage.  The standard anneal  bake was applied.  The last step was to restore full structural & thermal integrity so that the unit could be tested and  eventually mounted on the system application card. Precision  measurements were made of the milled cavity, and a metal  slug machined to fit the space.  A thin layer of thermal grease  was applied to the back of the die (including into the FIB  trench), and the slug worked into place.  Warmed epoxy was  flowed into the gap around the slug, and fully cured in a low


temperature oven.  The entire slug and lid region was then  polished completely flat so that any future socket or heat sink  applied downforce would be equally distributed (Fig. 7).


Figure 7:  Topside view of a composite BGA package after  rebuild.  Slug in center section replaces the lid material  removed over the chip, restoring mechanical strength and  thermal transfer ability.


This package type is now in widespread use in a number of  different applications, ranging in physical size from ‘medium’ to ‘extra large.’ With two years experience in opening and  reassembly, we have met with very good success.  But the  process is time consuming and complex.  The other downside  with this method is the loss of ability to perform active  probing while electrically cycling, as we no longer have  access to the chip backside surface.


As a side note, this is one package type in which a gas cell  laser silicon micromachining tool might be quite useful.  Assuming that the FR-4 based package assembly could be  shielded from damage by the chlorine gas environment, laser  stair stepping might be a way of retaining more of the  otherwise lost die structural integrity.


In the course of this paper, specific recommendations were  made concerning the control of surface charge, negating the  detrimental effects of injected charge and dealing with unique  chip packaging.


The incidence of beam damage can be reduced through chip  attachment and sample holder modifications, as well as the use  of blanket, strap and plug grounding in the repair zones.  We  have also worked to minimize surface scans and optimize gas  etch and deposition applications accordingly, in an effort to  reduce beam exposure and thus total dose.


We have also experienced and continue to experiment with  changes in device operating characteristics as a result of  implanted gallium ions and/or secondary/tunneled electrons in  the regions adjacent to active areas.  Fortunately, the problems  encountered in recent backside repairs seem to be reversible  by instituting a post-FIB bake.


Package opening and die thinning can compromise a total  methodology designed to protect high wattage chips from  bending stress and severe temperature excursions.  After the  completion of FIB repairs, it is advisable to consider  rebuilding these assemblies to insure survival in tester sockets  and system level use.


In summary, backside FIB chip repair failure rates were  greatly reduced when better charge control was added to the  procedure, a post-FIB bake was introduced, and the thermal / mechanical integrity of the die & package was restored prior  to testing and delivery to the customer.


The authors wish to thank Jeff McMurray for his valuable  discussions and insight in the field of charge trapping and  electric field contribution.

# Precise Fail site Isolation using a combination of Global, Software and Tester based Isolation Techniques


Precise Fail site Isolation using a combination of Global, Software and Tester based Isolation  Techniques


Deepa Gopu, George Ontko, Chin Phan, Kartik Ramanujachar, Scott Wills


Texas Instruments, Stafford, Texas  U.S.A


Alan Hales


Texas Instruments,


Dallas, Texas


U.S.A


Precise fail site isolation plays a very important role today in  the world of semiconductors. Its importance increases more, as the devices are of cutting edge technology with increasing  complexity and decreasing dimensions. Global fail site  isolations techniques (like XIVA, Photo Emission, FMI etc) and tester based techniques (using automatic test equipment, Fastscan etc) alone, are no longer sufficient and may not be  successful. Long net lists and large fail sites isolated by these  methods pose problems for physical failure analysis. Planarity  of these large areas during parallel lap and inspection times  using the SEM is difficult and tedious, thus leading to long  cycle times and low resolution rates. There exists a need for  precise fail site isolation. In many cases, no single technique  can be used to narrow down a fail site significantly. Instead a  combination of different techniques must be used.


In this paper we present a case study, where a combination of  complimentary techniques are used to successfully isolate a  fail area of more than 1300 microns in length to less than 100  microns on a single failing net.


Semiconductor chip fails are very important during  qualification (Qual) stage of a product. Every defect found on  the Qual fails is very precious as this data is directly fed back  to the FAB for corrective actions. ATPG fails are a subset of  the fails found. Hence successful resolution of the ATPG fails  plays a very important role. Time of resolution plays an  equally important role.


Many methods exist and have been discussed in several  papers on isolating ATPG fails [Ref 1]. When no single  method works, a combination of methods is to be used. This  paper discusses a case study where a combination of different  techniques was used to isolate an ATPG fail.


Hence when any single technique does not work in resolution  of a fail, a multitude of methods are to be used for a quick and  successful resolution of as defect.


This paper discusses once such fail where different methods  were used.


Four different techniques were used:


A) ATE (Automatic Test Equipment) to obtain fail vector  information


B) ATPG (Automatic test pattern generation) tool-Fastscan to  obtain failing net information


C) Bridging analysis [using nearest neighbor nets to the  failing net to calculate fail correlation matrix using fast scan] to check for bridge location information


D) DFT (Design for test) based tester (Inovys) to narrow the  fail area further using custom ATPG vectors.


E) TIVA for global fail site information,


Case Study


A .18 micron technology semiconductor chip is chosen for the  case study. The device under test (DUT) was tested using  ATE. The chip failed for ATPG patterns. The fail vector  information was collected and fed to the ATPG tool, Fastcan.


Figure 1 shows the failing nets isolated by Fastscan.


Diagnostics was performed by the tool which came up with a  set of failing nets. These failing nets were mapped onto a  layout database and the length of the nets was found to be  more than 2000 microns on the database. Physical failure  analysis was not attempted as maintaining the planarity of the


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa172


large area was not feasible. Further electrical isolation as  attempted.


Fig 2 shows the nets mapped onto the database.


ATPG Report Analysis


Examining the fastscan report shows one of the nets to be  stuck at both 0 and 1. Hence there is possibility of a bridge to  an adjacent node or a floating node. A net that is bridged to  any adjacent net can be stuck at both 0 and 1 value, depending  on the values of the aggressor net that it is bridged to. One of  the two nets acts as the aggressor and the other acts as a victim  net depending upon the drive strengths of the respective nets. A floating node can appear either as stuck at 0 or 1 at various  times depending upon its neighboring net values. Bridging  analysis was first attempted.


Bridging Analysis


The nets reported by the ATPG tool were mapped onto the  layout database. The neighboring nets to the failing nets were  extracted manually at all levels of metal. This is very time  consuming and tedious. A new method was experimented. The parasitic capacitance information of all the nets in the  design was found using a parasitics extraction tool like  Synopsys Star RCXT. The report contains the parasitics  information for all the nets in the design with respect to the  adjacent nets. A search on this report file for the failing nets  also gives its adjacent nets. This automated procedure helped  us cut down the man hours from 2 weeks to 2 hours after the  initial setup time. Once the neighboring nets have been  identified, the driver nets of these nets are to be identified. For  example consider the circuit in Fig3:


The figure shows the output of a Buffer going to the input of  an AND gate. However this single net has two different  names. The output of the buffer B1 is called N1 and the input  of the AND gate A1 is called N2. Logically both the nets are  same, but have different names on the layout. ATPG tool  requires the driver net name for simulation. . Hence if the


neighboring net is N2, then it is required to get the driver net  name i.e. N1 from the circuit.


Fig 3 shows an example of driver nets.


A do file is created by using the add lists command for all the  driver nets to log the states of these nets for both passing and  failing vectors. The patterns are segregated into passing and  failing group. Fig 3 shows the states of the driver nets for  failing and passing nets got from fastscan simulation.


Fig 4 shows an example of neighbor nets and their simulated  values.


Compare the simulated values of the suspect nets with respect  to the adjacent nets. Create two lists, one for passing vectors  and the other for failing vectors.


On the passing vector list if the suspect net and any of its  neighbor have the same values, increment the pass metric for  that neighbor net by 1.  Similarly increment the fail metric of  neighbor nets if the simulated values do not match values of  suspect nets.  Then compute the sum of fail and pass metric  for each neighbor net and give percentage rankings for each  neighbor net as compared to the total number of vectors on  each pattern.  If any net has 100% correlation on both passing  and failing vector calculations then the chances of a bridge to  that net are very high. Any correlation above 90% is usually  considered high and likely a suspect area, but needs other  methods to confirm the defect location.


There is a lot of ambiguity in computing the correlation metric  when don’t care conditions exist in the pattern set.  An


approximate analysis is done by replacing the don’t cares’s  with 0 and then with 1. If the correlation metric is found  greater than 90% for any net, then the net can be taken into  consideration, but should be confirmed with other methods.


The correlation metric for the case study was around 68%. It  is low; hence other methods were investigated taking this net  into account.

2.3. Step 3: Ranking Multiple Candidates


Multiple candidate faults are ranked by an algorithm that is  adopted from the algorithm proposed in [3]. We review the  scan chain diagnosis algorithm previously proposed in [3] by  using a simple example. In [3] the algorithm was originally  proposed to diagnose intermittent scan chain hold-time faults. In this paper we adopt this algorithm to diagnose any  intermittent scan chain faults. We use an intermittent stuck-at0 fault in the example shown in Figure 3.


Figure 3: Example to illustrate algorithm in [3]


As shown in Figure 3, suppose a faulty chain has 8 scan cells  numbered from 0 to 7 counting from the scan output. The  algorithm proposed in [3] injects one fault at a time on the  faulty scan chain and searches the best matching candidate  based on ranking scores. The above example illustrates how to  calculate scores for the fault candidate at the output of scan  cell 4. Assuming a scan pattern 11011001 is applied to the  faulty chain, in Step 1, the loaded pattern will be modified by  setting “X” to any possibly corrupted bit. Under the  assumption that an intermittent stuck-at-0 fault is at scan cell  4, a loaded scan cell might have incorrect value if it is in the  downstream of scan cell 4 and it is supposed to be loaded with  a logic “1”. For the given example, the loaded scan pattern  will be modified by setting cells 0 and 3 to “X”. In the next  step, 4-value (0,1,X,Z) logic simulation is performed under the  assumption that only the scan chain has faults and logic is  fault free. In Step 3, the captured response will be modified by  setting “X” to any possibly corrupted bit during the unloading  procedure. For the given example, an unloaded scan cell might  have incorrect value if it is upstream of scan cell 4 and it is  captured with a logic “1”. Thus scan cells 4, 5 and 7 are set to “X”.  In the last step, Score A (matching score) and Score B (mismatching score) are calculated for the injected fault  candidate. Score A is defined as the ratio of the number of the  failure bits covered by the simulated “X”s over the number of


1.  Transliteration. Each tool in the design process has  certain characters that it does not allow in gate and wire  names.  Although most tools provide an ‘escape’ mechanism to indicate that a name contains illegal  characters, designers may instead transliterate the illegal  characters to legal characters..


2. Standard Cell Abstraction.  In the physical netlist, standard cells contain transistors.  In the ATPG netlist, standard cells contain Verilog or ATPG primitives such  as AND or DFF gates.  The netlists are functionally  equivalent, but the internal wire names may be  completely different.  For small standard cells such as  NAND gates, the problem is negligible.  But larger  standard cells like flip-flops can have tens of internal  wires.


3. ATPG Tool Abstractions.  The ATPG netlist may be  abstracted to improve the ATPG process.   The scan mode  used by ATPG is a test-only mode, so circuits that are not  active in scan mode, such as PLLs, may be modified or  removed.  Other circuits may be modified to improve test  coverage or to speed up ATPG.  Although functionally  equivalent to the physical netlist that represents the  silicon, there may be different gates and wires that cannot  be correlated.


The DFS/FA mapping tool, MapATPG2Nav, combined with  SchemGen, the Freescale toolset used to import designs into  the FA navigation tool, can address transliteration and  standard cell abstraction.  ATPG-tool-abstracted circuits are  typically not mapped.


MapATPG2Nav uses similarity in three domains to perform  the mapping:


1. hierarchical similarity,


2. gate and wire name string similarity [5-6] and,


3. gate and wire connectivity similarity.


MapATPG2Nav will not be described in detail in this paper.  It creates a physical FNL dictionary that contains the physical  name of each gate and wire in the ATPG netlist.  If the name


cannot be mapped, it receives a unique ‘unmapped’ name in  the physical dictionary.


Scan Chain Load Simulation


As data are being shifted into the scan chain prior to the  capture cycle, the combinational logic downstream of the scan  cell outputs is being exercised with random logic values.  ATPG tools ignore the device state during shifting, because  the results cannot be observed in scan cells until the capture  cycle.


When a failure analyst microprobes a device, however, the  effects of the random data being shifted into the chain prior to  capture is visible on the oscilloscope.  The analyst can make  use of this additional information to isolate the defect.  When  using backside waveform acquisition tools such as laser  voltage probing [7] and time resolved light emission [8], only  transitions can be detected.  In basic scan patterns, transitions  will only occur during the shifting.


Since the ATPG tools are not concerned with the shift data, they do not provide a mechanism to view the simulated  waveforms during the shift.  We have created a companion  tool for DFS/FA, Patsim, that simulates up to 63 shifts prior to  the capture cycle.  The simulated waveforms of each wire in  the failing cones are dumped to a Verilog Change Dump (VCD) file, which that can be read by any VCD viewer.  Analysts can use simulated waveforms to compare against  probed waveforms to aid defect isolation.


The Patsim tool takes advantage of the parallel simulation  feature of Faultsim.  Each shift step and the capture cycle is  simulated in parallel, and the results are stitched together into  continuous waveforms over the entire 63 shifts.


A DFS/FA Example


Two measures of the quality of a diagnosis tool are the  precision and accuracy of its results [9].  A small results list is  precise, but if the list does not contain the real defect it is not  accurate.  This example demonstrates how the consideration  of physical proximity improves the accuracy without  sacrificing precision.


Several devices were submitted to the failure analysis lab to  aid in yield improvement.  All devices failed scan patterns  with a particular signature.  One particular device was chosen  to test the capabilities of DFS/FA.  This device failed 33 of  120 scan patterns in one particular test pattern.


With the ranked DFS/FA results, accuracy can be measured  by the number of top-ranked, equally-scored multiplets.  At  diagnosis Step 3, 40 multiplets were created. All 40 were  equally scored and hence top-ranked after the consideration of  failing patterns.  Step 4, the consideration of passing patterns, reduced the number of top-ranked multiplets to 10.  There  were no complex patterns in this diagnosis, so after Step 5 the  top-ranking count remained at 10.  Finally, as shown in the


appendix, when physical proximity was considered, only one  multiplet remained top-ranked.


DFS/FA explained all the multiplets as two-wire bridges.  Only the top-ranked multiplet after proximity consideration  contained neighboring wires.  The coordinates of line  segments along which the two wires are neighbors are added  to the diagnosis report.  These coordinates specify the fence  line between neighbors.


As shown in Figure 4, optical inspection revealed a defect at  metal 8 between the wires in the top-ranked multiplet.  The  defect is on the highlighted fence line in the appendix.  Further deprocessing destroyed this particular sample.  Other  analysis on the same lot found CMP gouging causing copper  bridges at metal 8.


Figure 4.  Optical micrograph showing a bridge at metal 8  between the two wires in the top-ranked multiplet.  The dark  squares are CMP tiles above the metal layer.


The diagnosis results in the appendix are expressed as  physical gate and wire names.  The ATPG names suffered  from transliteration, which has been corrected by DFS/FA: /XAAA/LFA0_ICBI_ADDR&1<6>


is /XAAA/LFA0_ICBI_ADDR__1[6] in the ATPG netlist.  The  report also contains evidence of ATPG tool abstractions:  the /XAAA/LAAA.LFLO.LFA0.SNOOP_ADDR_LATCH.LAT CHES.ICELL9/???? gate is an ATPG gate that could not be  found in the physical netlist.


Conclusions and Future Work


DFS/FA has demonstrated that an emphasis on usefulness to  failure analysis and quality of diagnosis must be a primary  consideration for diagnosis tools.


Future development will occur in several key areas.


1. The diagnosis tool must be improved to handle those  cases when Step 2 and 3 fail to generate results.


2. Additional information can be extracted from the physical  database.  Dominating bridges and opens could be further  isolated with physical information.


3. On-chip scan vector compression and logic BIST are  becoming popular to reduce test time.  These techniques


reduce the visibility of scan stimulus and response, preventing traditional fault diagnosis.


4. DFS/FA performs poorly on patterns that contain multiple  sequential levels during the capture cycle.  We must fault  through all levels, rather than only the last sequential  level.

Diagnosing DACS (Defects That Affect Scan Chain and System Logic)


Yu Huang     Wu-Tung Cheng     Kun-Han Tsai


Mentor Graphics Corporation, Design-for-Test Department,  8005 S.W. Boeckman Rd., Wilsonville, OR 97070


Greg Crowell     Chris Mcmahon


LSI Logic Corporation, Product Engineering and Development Department,  1621 Barber Lane, Milpitas, CA 95035


In this paper, DACS stands for Defects that Affect Chain and  System, which could be any type of silicon defects caused by  an unintentional interaction between a scan chain signal and  a system logic signal. The device could fail scan chain testing  or show up as a latent failure in the customer’s system. A  novel diagnosis methodology is proposed to locate both ends  of a DACS. The proposed algorithm can be generally applied  to any type of DACS. Experimental results on industrial chips  demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.


1 Introduction


The profitability of IC production is determined by the time  spent on silicon debug, yield learning and yield improvement. Failure analysis plays an extremely important role in these  processes. However, without precise guidance, the failure  analysis instruments are too inefficient to isolate root causes  responsible for the failures in a modern VLSI design. Consequently, algorithmic diagnosis methods at the logic or  transistor level are widely adopted to provide a good starting  point for failure analysis at the physical level.


The field of VLSI diagnostics typically consists of two  independent areas.


(1)


Scan chain defect diagnosis [1][2][3].


System signal defect diagnosis [4][5][6].


It is worth noting that although the problems in these two  areas have been studied for many years, a search of research  papers did not find any previous work that falls into the  intersection area of (1) and (2). In this paper we will fill the  gap by investigating diagnosis of Defects that Affect both scan  Chain and System logic (DACS). A typical example of DACS  is a bridge defect between a scan chain signal and a system  logic signal. Crosstalk between a scan chain signal and a  system logic signal is another good example of DACS which  cannot be ignored as today’s VLSI designs approach  nanometer process technologies. DACS is worth investigating  due to the following reasons.


(1)   Full scan design has become the most pervasive DFT  technique used in the VLSI industry today. Typically scan  chains occupy 10% - 30% silicon areas [1]. Therefore the


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa191


# Diagnosing DACS (Defects That Affect Scan Chain and System Logic)


possibility for a defect that happens between a scan signal and  a system logic signal could be high.


(2)   All previously proposed scan chain diagnosis  algorithms assumed that the defects only exist on scan chains, but system logic is defect-free. Under this assumption, the  failures only come from loading and unloading procedures, but the capture procedure is always assumed correct for scan  patterns. For DACS, failures could happen at any procedure, which may invalidate the previously proposed scan chain  diagnosis methods. On the other hand, all previously proposed  scan-based system logic diagnosis algorithms assumed that the  defects only exist on system logic but scan chains are defectfree. Under this assumption, the failures only come from the  capture procedure, but the loading and unloading procedures  are assumed correct for scan patterns. Once again, for DACS, these assumptions may not hold and the diagnosis results may  be misleading.


(3)   Under some special conditions, the previously  proposed algorithms can correctly diagnose one end of a  DACS, but it is impossible to locate both ends of a DACS. For  example, if the system logic end of a DACS is always  dominating, the previously proposed scan chain diagnosis  algorithms may correctly locate the defective scan chain signal  only. However, for a defect that involves multiple signals, it is  desirable to diagnose all affected signals. If we only locate one  end of a DACS at logic level, it may not be easy to identify  corresponding defects at physical level if the located signal is  very long and spans a large silicon area. In contrast, if we can  locate both ends of a DACS at the logic level, it is likely that  the defect is present in the area where the two signals are close  to each other physically. This additional information is quite  valuable in guiding the failure analyst in localizing the defect.   The objectives of this work are:


(1)   To propose a general algorithm to diagnose DACS.


(2)   To correctly locate both ends of a DACS.


(3)   To achieve good diagnosis resolution, i.e. the size of  reported candidates is small enough to provide meaningful  guidance for failure analysis.


The paper is organized in the following manner. In Section 2, a DACS diagnosis algorithm is proposed. This section  includes three subsections and the proposed algorithm consists  of three steps, with one step described in each subsection.


Experimental results on three industrial test cases with DACS  are presented in Section 3, followed by the conclusion section.


2 Proposed Algorithm for Diagnosing DACS


The proposed algorithm consists of three steps. Step 1 is to  identify a DACS and to model it. Step 2 is to find candidate  faults based on scan chain flush patterns. For some cases, we  may find only one candidate fault composed of one scan chain  signal and a class of equivalent system signals. If so, we are  done with the diagnosis. If we find multiple candidate faults  we have to apply Step 3 to rank these candidates based on  scan patterns.


The proposed algorithm is applicable to diagnosing any type  of DACS under two assumptions:


(1)  We assume that only one DACS is in a circuit. Multiple DACS diagnosis will be discussed in future work by  extending the proposed algorithm in this paper.


(2)  We assume the system signal of the targeted DACS is  not constantly tied to a logic “0” or “1” (e.g. Ground, Power, or their equivalent). Otherwise the DACS can be modeled  with a stuck-at-0 or stuck-at-1 fault at the scan chain signal. In  this scenario, it is easy to locate the DACS in the scan chain, but the candidate set may be too large at the system logic end  of the targeted DACS because all system signals with constant “0” or ”1” are candidates.


2.1. Step 1: DACS Fault Models


In previous work [1][2][3], chain flush patterns are used to  identify faulty scan chains and their fault types. In this paper  we use chain flush patterns to identify and model DACS as  well. As an example given in Table 1, suppose a scan chain is  loaded with a chain flush pattern 001100110011, where the  leftmost bit is loaded into the scan cell connected to scan chain  input and the rightmost bit is loaded into the scan cell  connected to scan chain output. Column 2 gives the unloaded  faulty values for each type of permanent fault. Column 3 gives  examples of the unloaded faulty values for each type of  intermittent fault.  Note that the “X”s depend on the previous  or the next chain flush pattern.


As we can see from Table 1, the scan chain fault models can  be classified into two categories based on the results of chain  flush patterns. One category contains various permanent scan  chain faults and the other category includes various  intermittent scan chain faults. Based on our observation from  defective industrial chips, DACS are most likely to behave as  intermittent scan chain faults. For example, an intermittent  stuck-at fault is often caused by a short defect between a scan  chain signal and a system signal. The fault is triggered at the  scan signal when the shorted signals have opposite logic  values and the system signal is dominant over the scan signal. Since this triggering condition happens intermittently, we see  an intermittent stuck-at fault. In contrast, a permanent stuck-at  fault shows up when the scan chain is open or it is shorted  with ground / power lines.

As another example, an intermittent fast-to-rise fault is likely  to be caused by crosstalk between a scan chain signal and a  system signal. Crosstalk might speedup (or slow down) a  signal transition if the coupled lines have the same (or  opposite) transitions. When hold-time margin is small and the  crosstalk speeds ups a “0”->”1” transition on a signal between  two scan cells, a fast-to-rise (a.k.a. hold-time) fault is triggered


[2]. Again, since this triggering condition happens  intermittently, we see an intermittent fast-to-rise scan chain  fault. In contrast, a permanent fast-to-rise fault usually shows  up when the hold-time violation between two scan cells is  always there with or without crosstalk. Therefore in this paper  we assume all intermittent scan chain faults are caused by  DACS. As explained in assumption (2), it is difficult to  diagnose a DACS at the system logic end if it is constantly  tied to “0” or “1”. Hence in this paper we will apply the  proposed algorithm to diagnose all intermittent scan chain  faults except for intermittent stuck-at-0 and stuck-at-1, i.e. all  fault models in the shaded areas in Table 1.


As shown in Table 1, the unloaded patterns always follow  some fixed rules for a specific fault model, except for an  intermittent stuck-at-0/1. For example, a fast-to-rise fault only  happens when the good values of a corrupted bit and its left  side neighbor construct a “0” to “1” transition. Another  example, a slow fault only happens when the good values of a  corrupted bit and its right side neighbor are different. Therefore by analyzing the unloaded chain flush patterns we  can find out whether they follow any of these known rules. If  we find all unloaded chain flush patterns follow a certain rule, we know the fault type of this chain. Otherwise, it is likely  that this faulty chain has an intermittent stuck-at-0/1 fault  caused by a short DACS. Therefore we propose using a  model, denoted as (FC short FS), to represent a short DACS, which means a scan chain fault FC is caused by a short with a  system signal where a fault FS is located. Similarly, we  propose using a model, denoted as (FC crosstalk 0->1 fast FS), to represent a crosstalk DACS, where a scan chain fast-to-rise  fault FC is due to speedup in a “0”->“1” transition caused by a  crosstalk from a system signal where a fault FS is located. The  objective of Step 1 of the proposed algorithm is to find an  appropriate fault model for DACS, such as short, crosstalk 0->1 fast, etc.


It is worth noting that sometimes a DACS might behave like a  permanent scan chain fault under some flush patterns. For  example, if the logic value at the system signal of a short  DACS did not have a chance to switch from “0” to “1” under  the given patterns, the short DACS would never show any  intermittent stuck-at-1 behavior in the scan chain. As another  example, if 0->1 transition never happens at the system logic  end of a crosstalk DACS, it might never show any intermittent  fast-to-rise behavior at the scan chain. Misjudged fault types  could result in the use of an incorrect fault model in the


proposed diagnosis algorithm. We may reduce the probability  of this fault type misjudgment by running ATPG to produce  chain flush patterns that have higher chance to trigger an  intermittent fault. However, in this paper our focus is  diagnosis instead of ATPG. In the test cases we used, we run  regular chain flush patterns such as 0000..., 1111..., 1100... and some random patterns such as 1110010... Based on our  observation, it seems that random patterns are better than the  regular patterns at triggering intermittent scan chain faults.

The objective of Step 2 of the proposed algorithm is to find  the two ends of the targeted DACS, i.e., the locations of FC  and FS for the fault model identified in Step 1. A short DACS


example in Figure 1 is used to illustrate Step 2 of the proposed  diagnosis algorithm based on flush patterns. Suppose a faulty  chain has 4 scan cells numbered from 0 to 3. Assuming one of


Unknown: Any multiplet that can’t be explained receives the  unknown explanation.


If a multiplet receives two or more explanations (for example, it is possible to explain a multiplet as stuck-at-0 and slow-torise), then the multiplet, including its score, is duplicated so  each multiplet has only one explanation.   The scores of all  multiplets are then adjusted so the sum is normalized back to


1.0, as required by Dempster-Shafer.  Analysis of passing  patterns, Step 4, will then differentiate the scores of the  duplicated multiplets.


Diagnosis Step 4: Consideration of Passing Patterns


The iSTAT paper describes that passing patterns must be  taken into consideration to prevent loss of resolution  compared to other algorithms.  Similar to iSTAT, DFS/FA  assigns each multiplet a belief value in the range (1.0, 0.0) based on the percentage of wires in the multiplet that predict a  pass.  DFS/FA departs from iSTAT in that it considers the  multiplet’s explanation.


The same good machine simulation described in Step 2 is  performed on each passing pattern, and the same data are  collected.  These data are used to decide if a multiplet is  activated.  A multiplet is activated if its fault type explanation  is activated.  For example, a stuck-at-1 fault is activated only  if the wire contains a good machine value of 0 at the time of  capture.  Similarly, a bridge is activated only if at least one  wire as an opposing value to the other wires at the capture  time.


If a multiplet is not activated, no faulting is performed: the  multiplet is given a passing pattern belief of 1.0, indicating  that this multiplet predicts a pass and is consistent with the  tested passing pattern.


If a multiplet is activated, then DFS/FA follows iSTAT.  Each  wire in the multiplet is faulted individually. Rather than  faulting permutations of the gates driven by the wire, all nonzero score gates inputs in the PINSET entry for the wire are  faulted.  For multiplets not explained as bridges, the belief is  the ratio of multiplet wires that predict a pass to the size of the  multiplet.  For multiplets explained as bridges, any wire  causing a fail creates a belief of zero for that multiplet.


As is described in the iSTAT paper, the computed belief  values for each multiplet are combined via Dempster-Shafer  with the original score from Step 3 to compute a new score.  The same high degree of doubt, 0.5, is used in DFS/FA.


Because there can be thousands of failing patterns, DFS/FA  will terminate Step 4 when the number of top-ranked  multiplets stabilizes.  Step 4 also takes advantage of the  parallel simulation capabilities of FaultSim.  One fault is  simulated across 64 failing patterns simultaneously.


Diagnosis Step 5: Consideration of Complex Patterns


Complex patterns are those failing patterns that did not  generate any entries in MATCHLIST.  In other words, complex failing patterns require multiple simultaneous faults.  The analysis of complex patterns follows iSTAT closely, and  is similar to Step 4.  Multiplet activation is not a consideration  during complex patterns.  As in Step 4, all non-zero-scored  gates in the pinset for a wire are faulted simultaneously.  The  complex pattern belief is scored like iSTAT and will not be  repeated here.  Each multiplet’s complex beliefs is combined  with the existing multiplet score via Dempster-Shafer to  compute a new score.


Diagnosis Step 6: Consideration of Physical Proximity


The iSTAT paper suggests that the physical proximity, based  on the layout, of the wires in a multiplet would a very useful


additional scoring mechanism.  However, the iSTAT paper  does not implement physical proximity scoring.  DFS/FA can  optionally adjust the multiplet scores based on physical  proximity.


Physical proximity is considered in two steps.  The first step  slightly improves the score of multiple-wire multiplets in  which the wires are neighbors.  The second step significantly  decreases the score of multiplets explained as bridges that are  physically impossible.


The first step considers each multiplet containing two or more  wires. DFS/FA calculates a belief in the range (1.0, 0.0) indicating the physical proximity of the wires.  Multiplets of  size 1 are assigned a physical belief of 1.0.  These beliefs are  combined with the original multiplet scores via the DempsterShafer algorithm to compute new multiplet scores.   The  Dempster-Shafer doubt value is relatively high (0.75), because  proximity itself does not indicate a defect and should not  significantly raise a multiplet’s score.  Instead, proximity  serves to differentiate similarly-scored multiplets.


The second step only considers multiplets explained as  bridges.  All other multiplets receive a belief of 1.  A bridge  multiplet receives a belief of 0 if its wires are not neighbors  and 1 otherwise.  The doubt value is very low, because  bridged wires must be neighbors.


DFS/FA uses the Physical API to access proximity  information in a physical database independent method.  Two  types of databases have been used to access proximity  information: a parasitic capacitance database and the  GDSII/netlist database imported into the failure analysis  navigation toolset.


Often, wire and gate names in the ATPG netlist that DFS/FA  uses for diagnosis are different than those in the physical  netlist that the Physical API references.   An FNL dictionary  that provides the translation is required.  The creation of this  physical dictionary is described later.  This dictionary may not  be perfect – some ATPG netlist gates and wires may not have  translations.


Given a multiplet containing more than one wire, each wire is  looked up in the physical dictionary.  If at least two wires  contain a valid translation, then the process continues.  Otherwise, the multiplet is awarded a physical belief of 0.5 in  physical Step 1 indicating that the wires may have some  unknown proximity.


If enough wires have physical name translation, the Physical  API is asked to return a Boolean value indicating if the wires  are neighbors.  For data sources such as parasitic capacitance  databases, the Boolean value indicates if there is a capacitance  between the wires.  For data sources such as cross-mapped  GDSII/netlist information, the distances between polygons for  each wire on each layer are computed, and compared against a  limit to determine if the wires are neighbors.  GDSII/netlist  databases are also queried for the list of layers and locations  on which the wires are neighbors for reporting to the user.


If the result of the proximity lookup is true, the multiplet is  awarded a physical belief of 1.0.  If it is false, the multiplet is  awarded a physical belief of 0.  As discussed above, these  beliefs are combined with the previous multiplet scores to  generate new scores.


The Diagnosis User Interface


DFS/FA provides a command-line user interface intended to  be as simple as possible for the failure analyst. The most  common usage is simply ‘dfs deviceName datalogFile’.


For each device, DFS/FA allows multiple datalog formats to  be supported.  The datalog type is determined by using regular  expressions specified in the configuration of deviceName, the  datalog type is determined, and the DL2FF program (described below) is launched with the proper arguments to  convert datalogFile to a standard-format fail file.  The fail file  contains the failing tester pattern name, the failing scan  pattern numbers and failing scan cells.


Each device may have multiple mask revisions and/or scan  domains.  If test engineering embeds the revision and scan  domain information into the name of the scan patterns, DFS/FA can use that information to simplify the diagnosis.  Regular expressions provided in the configuration files for  deviceName specify how to extract the revision and scan  domain names from the failing tester pattern name.  Given the  revision and scan domain information, the user interface can  select the correct FNL and chain information for diagnosis.


Upon invocation of the diagnosis tool, the failing tester  pattern, if not already converted to DFSPAT format, is  converted from its native ATPG format, and a good machine  simulation is performed in order to ensure that the conversion  was performed correctly.


Finally, the six steps of diagnosis are performed using the  FNL, chain information, failing pattern and fail file, and the  results are stored in a file for the failure analyst to use.


DFS/FA Supporting Tools


DFS/FA is more than a diagnosis tool.  It includes several  supporting tools that together are a complete solution for  software-based failure analysis defect isolation.


Robustly Converting the Datalog with DL2FF


A critical process in the diagnosis flow is the conversion of  the


datalog into a fail file containing the failing tester pattern  name, the failing scan patter numbers, and the failing scan  cells and/or primary outputs.


To avoid transparent errors that would result in a bad  diagnosis, DFS/FA requires the datalog to contain the expect  data for the failing vectors, along with the fail data. The  expect data are compared with the original ATPG test pattern  to ensure that the correct vector is selected. If the datalog


expect data does not match the ATPG expect data, then  nearby vectors are searched for the correct expect data, until  the specified search limit is reached, or a match is found.  This  prevents the wrong scan cell from being specified in the fail  file used in diagnosis, and allows for the correct conversion of  datalogs whose cycle number is slightly off from the ATPG  pattern.


Mapping ATPG Gate and Wire Names to the Physical  Netlist


Failure analysis navigation tools use the GDSII mask data and  the physical, transistor-level netlist.  ATPG tools use an  abstracted gate level netlist.  For this reason, the diagnosis  results from off-the-shelf ATPG tools have been hard to apply  in the FA lab.  Also, this is probably why no off-the-shelf  tools use the GDSII mask data to find realistic faults.


Three differences between the physical netlist and the ATPG  netlist account for the difficulties in correlation between them:

the scan cells has a short defect with a system logic signal (not  shown in Figure 1). Two chain flush patterns 0000 and 1111  are consecutively shifted in and out the faulty chain and the  observed unloaded values are 0100 and 1010. According to  Step 1 of the algorithm introduced in the last subsection we  know that it is an intermittent stuck-at-0/1 fault on this chain, which indicates a short DACS. Thus we use the fault model (FC short FS), where FC could be one of F0 –F3 and FS could  be any system signal fault. In this step we search all faults of (FC short FS) that are possible candidates for the targeted  DACS.


The shifting procedure is illustrated per shift cycle at each row  in Figure 1.  Assuming the initial values on the scan chain are  all “X”s, 12 cycles are required to finish the 2-Pattern chain  flush test. The column under Fi (0≤i≤3) illustrates the scan cell  values at each shift cycle if the scan chain end of the DACS is  at the output of cell i. 1/0 (0/1) means the good value is 1 (0), but due to the DACS it is corrupted to 0 (1). For example, assuming F3 is the real fault at the scan chain, we know that  the observed failures would be induced at cycles 3, 5 and 7. If  the real fault is F2, we know that the observed failures would  be induced at cycle 4, 6 and 8 and so on. The shaded cells  indicate where a failure happens given a faulty scan cell. As  we know the two ends of a DACS must have opposite values  when a failure happens. For the given example, if a logic  signal A has “100” at cycles 3, 5 and 7, it will construct a  candidate fault together with F3, i.e. (F3 short FA) is a  candidate fault that produces the observed failures. Similarly, if logic signals B and C both have “100” in cycles 4, 6 and 8, they will construct two candidate faults together with F2, i.e. (F2 short FB) and (F2 short FC) are candidate faults that  produces the observed failures. If the simulation shows no  system signals have logic values “100” at cycles 5, 7, 9, it  means F1 is NOT the scan chain end of the targeted DACS. Therefore “100” is used as a signature to find candidate faults  based on simulation results at a selected set of cycles for each  possible fault on the scan chain.


The general short DACS diagnosis algorithm is described in a  flow chart in Figure 2.


The proposed algorithm injects one fault at a time on the  faulty scan chain and finds any system signals that are  possibly shorted with the scan cell where the fault is injected. It only performs simulations at failing cycles. This is because  the shorted system signal is only guaranteed to have the value  that is opposite to the value of the candidate scan cell during  the failing cycles. For the passing cycles, the shorted system  signal might have the same logic value or opposite value (but  not strong enough to corrupt the candidate scan cell) of the  other end of the DACS. Therefore if we observe N failing  cycles during chain flush test, we have a N-bit signature to  use. However, to improve efficiency, we use 32-bits (or 64-bits, depends on the machine used) as one sub-signature in  each run, which can speed up the algorithm by dropping noncandidates in the middle. For an injected fault Fi, it has a  candidate list Ci, which includes the system signals that are  possibly shorted with the scan cell i. Ci is initialized with all


system signals that are not tied to logic “1” or “0”. Given Fi  and the currently considered 32 (or 64) failing cycles, it is  easy to calculate 32 (or 64) snapshots of the loaded patterns at  these 32 (or 64) cycles where failure should occur if Fi really  is a fault. These snapshots are simulated by using a traditional  parallel pattern simulation method, which uses a word of 32 (or 64) bits to store the simulation results for 32 (or 64) patterns. Then the 32-bit (or 64-bit) simulated result of each  system signal in Ci is compared with the 32-bit (or 64-bit) signature. If it is a mismatch, the system signal is not a  candidate and hence is dropped from Ci. If Ci is empty, it  means Fi is not a candidate fault on the faulty scan chain and  we will inject the next candidate until all candidate scan cells  are tried. If Ci is not empty, we will get the next 32-bit  signature and repeat the previous procedures until all failing  cycles and signatures are used up.


Figure 2: Proposed chain diagnosis algorithm


Finally, if we end up with only one equivalent class of  candidate faults, we are done. Two candidate faults are said  equivalent if the candidate faults on scan chain are the same  and the candidate faults at system logic are equivalent. For  example, (Fi short FA) and (Fi short FB) are called equivalent  if FA and FB are equivalent. If we have multiple equivalent  classes of candidate faults, we will use Step 3 to do score  ranking with scan patterns.


For a crosstalk DACS, the above proposed algorithm can be  applied as well. The only difference is that we have to use the  appropriate crosstalk fault model to calculate an appropriate  signature. For example, if in Step 1 we know the DACS is  modeled by using (FC crosstalk fast FS) then each bit of the  calculated signature indicates a type of transition. For  example, “0” is used to indicate a “0”->”1” transition and “1” is used to indicate a “1”->”0” transition. Each bit of the  signature is determined by one failing cycle and one cycle  immediately before it. To compare the transitions of a system  signal with the signature, 2-pattern simulation is used for each  bit, where the 2 patterns are 2 immediately adjacent snapshots  during shifting. Since we know that the fast fault is caused by  same transitions between two coupled signals, the simulation


FaultSim is an event-driven simulator [4].  The stimulus is  provided through the API with fsim_force() on device pins or  fsim_induce() on internal wires.  Faults are introduced with  the API call fsim_fault().  This call faults a selected gate input  in a selected simulation slice.  Faulting either means to invert  or X the gate input before evaluation, throughout the entire  simulation time that the fault is active.


PatApply API


The PatApply API reads scan patterns and applies selected  scan patterns as FaultSim stimulus under the control of the  calling program.  As each vector is applied, the calling  program receives a callback allowing it to modify the behavior  of PatApply or FaultSim, or inspect simulation results.


PatApply reads scan patterns that have been converted to the  DFSPAT format.  The DFSPAT format retains the structure of  the scan pattern, and PatApply passes the structural  information in its callbacks.  A DFSPAT file can contain  many scan and scan chain patterns.  A single pattern has the  following structural sections:


Test Setup places the device into scan mode,


Load gets the scan chains ready for loading data,


Shift shifts the scan data by one element, and contains the  actual scan-in data for each chain,


PostLoad handles any tasks necessary after shifting,


ForcePI forces the primary inputs to specified values,


MeasurePO measures the primary outputs,


Capture captures the data launched from the scan-in chains  and places it at the output of the scan cell,


Unload gets the scan chains ready for unloading captured  data, and


Shift again shifts the scan data by one element, containing the  scan-out data for each chain.


Because this structure is a required element of DFSPAT, the  source pattern format must contain enough information from  which the structure can be derived.  In particular, flat WGL  files are not sufficient.  STIL, parallel WGL and other  structural formats can easily be converted to DFSPAT.


The Test Setup function is common across all patterns in a  DFSPAT.  To speed up simulation, PatApply saves the  simulation state to disk after Test Setup has been applied so it  is only simulated once.


Rather than simulating the entire scan chain load, which  would require significant time, PatApply performs a parallel  load of the scan chains.  The value destined for each scan cell  is placed on that scan cell’s input, and one Shift function is  applied to load the value into the scan cell.  PatApply can also  place the value one cell away and perform two shifts.  This


feature is used during diagnosis to look for transitions  between the beginning of the final shift and the capture cycle.


Physical API


The Physical API provides a gasket between the diagnosis  tool and physical representations of the chip.  Two physical  interfaces have been developed for DFS/FA: an interface to a  parasitic capacitance database, and an interface to the failure  analysis navigation software.


The Physical API provides functions to relate netlist wires to  their locations on the die.  The API is general enough to allow  for different data representations.  For example, when using a  parasitic capacitance database, the Physical API can answer  the question, “are these two wires neighbors?”  When using  the navigation database, the Physical API can answer the  question, “what are the polygons locations and layers that this  wire is routed in?”


The wire names in the database used by the Physical API may  differ from the wire names in the ATPG netlist.  An FNL  dictionary must be available to the Physical API that can  perform the translation.  The creation of this physical  dictionary is described later.


The Diagnosis Algorithm


The heart of DFS/FA, the diagnosis tool itself, builds upon the  APIs presented above. The DFS/FA diagnosis algorithm is  based on a modified version of the iSTAT algorithm [3]. The  iSTAT algorithm itself is an improvement of SLAT [2], which  introduced the concept of multiplets, the diagnostic output of  all three algorithms. DFS/FA and iSTAT provide a ranked list  of multiplets, while SLAT’s multiplet list is unranked. In  DFS/FA a multiplet is defined as a set of one or more wires  that, when considered together, completely explain the failing  test results.  The top-ranking multiplet contains the wires that  DFS/FA believes are most closely related to the defect that  caused the test fails.


Diagnosis proceeds through six steps.  The first three steps  create the multiplet list.  Subsequent steps change the  multiplet scoring, and hence ranking, as new data are  considered.


Diagnosis Step 1: Identify Failing Cones


A failing cone is the combinational logic that feeds a failing  scan cell.  The inputs to the failing cone are scan cells  containing scan-in data, and the output is one failing scan cell.  Failing cones can contain either clock wires or data wires.  Clock wires are cones behind the clock inputs of the state  elements (flip-flops and latches) in the scan cell.  Data wires  are any wires behind the data inputs of the scan cell state  elements.


Step 1 first extracts the wires in each failing cone, FAILINGCONE(f), for each unique failing scan cell or  primary output, f,  over all the failing patterns.  The cone  terminates at scan cells or the device’s input pads. Each wire


in FAILINGCONE(f) is tagged as a data or clock wire.  Recombinant logic is identified; the wire at the output of the  gate at which recombination occurs is tagged as such in  FAILINGCONE(f) and the divergent-recombinant wire pair is  stored in RECOMBINANTS.


Non-intersecting failing cones can be diagnosed separately to  partially avoid the costs of multiple-fault diagnosis.  Diagnosis  Step 1 investigates the failing cones to identify one or more  supercones. As shown in Figure 1, a supercone is a set of  cones in which each cone in the set intersects at least one  other cone in the set. Any cone not in the supercone must not  intersect any cone in the supercone.  A particular failing cone  can exist in only one supercone. Step one collects the failing  cones for each supercone into the set SUPERCONES.


Figure 1.  Failing scan cells are marked 'F' and source scan  cells are marked 'S'.  Cones A, B and C make up one  supercone.  Cone D is a second supercone.


Step 1 then looks at each failing pattern independently.  If at  least one failing pattern exists that fails for SUPERCONESi  and no other supercone, that supercone is eliminated from  SUPERCONES.  If, at the end of this process, SUPERCONES is empty, diagnosis continues onto Step 2.  Even though multiple supercones may exist amongst the  failures, this process has guaranteed that Step 2 will generate  some results. Step 5 should be able to extract data from those  patterns that fail multiple supercones, which are impossible to  diagnose with a single-fault assumption.


If SUPERCONES is not empty, Step 1 partitions the failing  scan cells and patterns into individual supercones and re-starts  diagnosis for each individual supercone.  The analyst must  combine the individual diagnosis results by inspection.


Diagnosis Step 2: Fault Model Independent Diagnosis and  Failing Pattern Data Collection


Step 2 is repeated for each failing pattern.  Like iSTAT, each  failing pattern is diagnosed independently. The results are  combined after the Step 2 diagnosis, in Step 3.


Prior to diagnosis, good machine simulation is performed on  the failing pattern – in other words, the simulation proceeds  without any faulting.  During the Shift function, Step 2 uses  PatApply’s 2-shift feature.  At the beginning of the last shift, Step 2 collects the values from every wire in every  FAILINGCONEi.  These logical values are stored in  PRELAUNCHVALUES, and used later to identify transition  faults in basic stuck-at scan patterns.


During the ForcePI, MeasurePO and Capture functions of the  good machine simulation of the failing pattern, several data  are collected as each vector is applied (the vector is indexed as ‘i’):


1. the entire simulation state in CAPTURESTATEi,


2. each failing scan cell state element that is clocked the  applied vector is saved in ACTIVESTATEELEMi, and


3. each failing primary output that is measured in the  applied vector is saved in ACTIVEPOi.


After good machine simulation, the wires from all cones in  FAILINGCONE that fail in the failing pattern being  diagnosed are intersected into INTERSECTION.  The  intersection   boundary is then mapped as demonstrated in  Figure 2.  Any gate that has at least one input wire in  INTERSECTION and its output not in INTERSECTION is  added to BOUNDARYGATES.  Any gate in  BOUNDARYGATES whose output is in at least one of this  pattern’s failing cones is tagged as affectsCone.  Any wire in  INTERSECTION that drives a gate in BOUNDARYGATE  whose output is in all this pattern’s failing cones is tagged as a  rootWire.


Figure 2.  The Passing scan cell is marked 'P'.  The bolded  wires are the intersection of the two failing cones.  Gates 'a' and 'b' are boundary gates.  Gate 'a' is tagged as affectsCone. The sets INTERSECTION and BOUNDARYGATES specify  which wires to fault.  Next, DFS/FA decides when to fault  those wires.  The failing scan cells and primary outputs may  not capture data all at the same time in the pattern, especially  in at-speed or sequential scan patterns.  ACTIVESTATEELEM and ACTIVEPO are consulted to  determine the latest CAPTURESTATE for the faulted wire.  Faulting on the wire begins at that capture state and continues  through to the last CAPTURESTATE.


Up to this point, the concept of a fault has not been defined.  In DFS/FA, a fault is defined as a change of a wire’s value, only on a subset of the gate inputs that the wire drives.   The  change can either be an inversion of the wire’s good machine  value, or an X.  This concept of a fault is different than most  other fault simulation tools, which consider a fault to exist  only on a single gate input or output.  The DFS/FA fault  definition allows for defects that affect a subset of a wire’s  fanout to be represented with one fault.   These types of  defects are commonly found during failure analysis and not  easily diagnosed with other diagnosis tools.


A single wire may be faulted multiple times, each with  different permutations of faulted gate inputs.  Doing all  permutations on a large fanout wire would be computationally  expensive, so the permutations are reduced.  Gate inputs from


gates in BOUNDARYGATES whose output is not in any  failing cone are never faulted.  If the number of remaining  gate inputs is greater than an arbitrary number, or if the wire is  not listed as divergent in RECOMBINANTS, then all  remaining gate inputs are simultaneously faulted.  Otherwise, all permutations of the remaining gate inputs are faulted.


DFS/FA follows iSTAT in its evaluation of a fault.  A fault  must match the datalog perfectly for the failing pattern under  consideration.  It must cause all failing scan cells and failing  primary outputs to fail, and must not cause any passing scan  cells or primary outputs to fail.  If it passes the evaluation, then the wire and the list of gate inputs are added to  MATCHLIST.


To reduce the number of faults that must be introduced, DFS/FA works backwards from the dominant faults [4].  Fault  simulation starts at the rootWires, working backwards through  the logic in a breadth-first search, and not straying outside of  INTERSECTION.  If a faulted wire does not get included in  the MATCHLIST, then the search terminates on that branch  unless that wire appears in RECOMBINANTS.  If it is in  RECOMBINANTS, then the faulting continues from the  divergent wire.


The good machine and fault simulation take advantage of  FaultSim’s parallel simulation.  Up to 64 failing patterns are  simultaneously simulated during good machine simulation.  For each failing pattern, up to 64 faults are tested  simultaneously during fault simulation.  To take full  advantage of the parallel simulation, some speculative fault  simulation is performed since Step 2 works its way backwards  from the rootWire.


This Step 2 process is similarly followed for the clock wires in  all cones in FAILINGCONE.  Clock cone analysis may be  omitted to speed up diagnosis.


Diagnosis Step 3: Multiplet Creation, Scoring, and  Explanation


The fundamental unit of a diagnostic output is the multiplet.  Every failing pattern that has at least one entry in  MATCHLIST must contain at least one wire in each multiplet. In other words, a multiplet covers every failing pattern that  has been successfully diagnosed.  The failing patterns that  don’t have any entries in MATCHLIST are considered  complex patterns, and like iSTAT, are considered later (in  Step 5).  If no failing patterns have results in MATCHLIST, then diagnosis terminates with no results.  This is one  weakness of DFS/FA which will be addressed in the future.


The multiplet, as described here, is different than the SLAT  and iSTAT multiplet.  The members of a SLAT or iSTAT  multiplet are stuck-at gate pin faults.  Figure 3 illustrates the  difference between Step 2 results in iSTAT and DFS/FA.  The  iSTAT algorithm creates two multiplets:


1: x s@1, x s@0


2: y s@1, x s@0


DFS/FA creates only one multiplet, consisting of the entire  wire: ‘A’.  As in this example, a particular failing pattern may  have several entries in MATCHLIST for a single wire, indicating different permutations of the fanout that caused a  matching fail signature.  However, all those entries only  contribute one possible wire to the multiplet


Figure 3.  This example demonstrates how iSTAT and  DFS/FA faulting and multiplet creation differ.  The iSTAT  algorithm faults gate input 'x' and 'y' independently, but never  simultaneously.  DFS/FA faults each individually and then  together.  The iSTAT result is a list of the gate inputs (x and y) that fail in each pattern.  The DFS/FA MATCHLIST is the list  of wires (A) that fail, with the gate inputs attached.


Because the DFS/FA multiplets do not contain information  about which gate inputs on the multiplet’s wires were faulted, Step 3 constructs an additional data structure, PINSET.  One  PINSET element exists for each unique wire in MATCHLIST.  Each PINSET element lists the gates driven by that wire.  Each gate is given a score: the ratio of the number of times  that gate appears in MATCHLIST faulted with the wire to the  number of times the wire appears in MATCHLIST.  The  PINSET score gives an indication of where a defect may exist  on a wire with large fanout.  The PINSET in this example  includes one element: A (x=1.0, y=0.5).


DFS/FA also differs from its predecessors on its choices of  which combinations of faulted wires can be called a multiplet.  All three algorithms reject adding redundant faults to a  multiplet -- to be added, a fault must cover some patterns not  already covered by the growing multiplet.  SLAT rejects all  but the minimum-sized multiplets.  iSTAT allows for  multiplets greater than minimum-sized, but is not clear what  rule is applied to reject wire combinations as multiplets.  DFS/FA enforces the rule that a multiplet cannot contain a  smaller multiplet as part of itself.  DFS/FA also sets an  arbitrary limit on multiplet size.  Both these rules help the  failure analyst, because it’s better to a have partial explanation  of the defect rather than many competing explanations.


DFS/FA follows the iSTAT algorithm to score multiplets, which introduced the use of the Dempster-Shafer algorithm.  The iSTAT paper provides a good explanation of DempsterShafer, which will not be repeated here.


The iSTAT paper introduced plausibility metrics to add  meaning to multiplets.  For each of several common fault  models (stuck-at fault, node fault, gate fault, bridging fault, path fault), iSTAT scores the plausibility that an individual  multiplet matches that fault model.  The plausibility metrics  use only the multiplet and possibly the netlist as input.


DFS/FA improves upon iSTAT’s plausibility metrics in  several ways.  First, the DFS/FA explanation of a multiplet  has been simplified.  Rather than using DFT-centric fault  models, DFS/FA tries to stay closer to the familiarity of  failure analysts to physical defects.   Second, DFS/FA collects  data during good machine simulation of the failing patterns to  aid explanation.  Third, DFS/FA takes the explanation into  account when analyzing passing patterns.  A multiplet is  explained by its behavior during the failing patterns, and that  explanation is enforced during the scoring of passing patterns. DFS/FA explains the multiplets with one or more of the  following fault types: stuck-at-1, stuck-at-0, bridge, slow-torise, slow-to-fall, slow-to-rise-and-fall, and unknown.  The  saved good machine simulation information in  ACTIVESTATELEM, ACTIVEPO, PRELAUNCHVALUES  and CAPTURESTATE is used to compute the explanation.


Stuck-At-1 or Stuck-At-0:  If all wires in the multiplet have the  same good machine value at the capture time through all  failing patterns, then the multiplet is explained as being stuck  at the opposite value.


Bridge: If the multiplet contains 2 or more wires and at least  one wire contains an opposite value as the other wires at the  capture time through all failing patterns, the multiplet is  explained as a bridging fault.


Slow-To-Rise or Slow-To-Fall: If all wires in the multiplet  undergo the same type transition (rise or fall) between the  PRELAUNCHVALUES and the capture time, and through all  the failing patterns, then the multiplet is explained as slow-torise or slow-to-fall.  Since PRELAUNCHVALUES are  collected prior to the last shift, even basic scan patterns may  exhibit a slow-to-rise or slow-to-fall fault if the wire  transitions on the last shift.  In the DFT domain, this is not  traditionally considered a transition fault in a basic scan  pattern because it does not occur at speed.  However, defects  that cause these faults are seen in the failure analysis domain. Slow-To-Rise-And-Fall: If all wires in the multiplet undergo a  transition, rising in some patterns rising and falling in others  falling, then the multiplet is explained as a slow-to-rise-andfall fault.


total failure bits in this pattern. Score B is defined as the ratio  of the number of good bits covered by simulated “X”s over the  number of total good bits in this pattern. The procedure  iteratively runs for each candidate cell on the faulty chain and  reports the cell (or a group cells) that has maximum Score A  and minimum Score B as the final candidate fault site.


This method has one problem if it is applied to DACS  diagnosis ranking. In step 2 of [3], due to DACS, the system  logic could have a fault as well. Without knowing the fault site  in the system logic, the simulation results may be invalid and  consequently invalidate the score calculation and ranking.


In this paper, Step 3 of the proposed algorithm will mask all  possible system logic faults in the capture procedure. Fortunately, for each candidate scan chain fault Fi, we have  already calculated a set of candidates (Ci) of system logic  signals in Step 2. To calculate scores for Fi, all the system  signals remained in Ci are set to X during capturing procedure. This way, the effect of faulty system logic is masked and the  original ranking method can be applied.


3 Experimental Results


The proposed algorithm is implemented into a commercial  EDA tool. It is applied to three industrial VLSI circuits of the  same design. Each test case has one short DACS, which is  introduced via a Focused Ion Beam (FIB) machine. The  defective chips are tested with both chain flush patterns and  scan patterns. The failing data is collected from tester and read  in by the diagnosis tool. The tool reports all candidate fault  sites. Some information of the test cases is shown in Table 2.

Case II has a bridge between the output of scan cell 98 and a  buffer connected to the output of scan cell 639 of the same  chain. As shown in Figure 6, Step 2 of the algorithm reports  338 candidate faults including [0, 541], [1, 542] …[98, 639], … [337, 878]. The numbers in the brackets are numbers of the  candidate scan cells. An interesting observation is that each  candidate fault consists of two scan cells that are 541 cells  apart on the faulty chain. Using flush patterns alone cannot  locate where the failure really happened. In this case scan  patterns have to be used in Step 3. The diagnosis results based  on scan patterns report that failure at scan cell 98 has the  highest score. Combined with the previous results from Step 2, we known the DACS is at (98, 639).


Case III also needs step 2 and step 3 of the proposed  algorithm. In step 2, 18 candidate faults were reported. In step  3, 4 of out these 18 scan cells have higher ranking scores than  the others. An interesting observation is that the 4 candidate  scan cells are consecutive on the faulty chain. They cannot be  distinguished by the ranking scores (They have the same Score  A and the variances of Score B are within 0.1%). The real  DACS is within the reported candidates.


The proposed algorithm was run on a Linux machine with 2.4  GHz CPU and 512MB memory. Up to 10K failure cycles were  collected using ATE. Case I and III required about 8 hours of  processing time each. Case II required about 40 hours, which  is caused by the large number of candidate faults reported in  Step 2. The performance of case II could be improved in  future by some intelligent learning since the reported  candidates follow an obvious pattern.


4 Conclusions


DACS is defects that affect both scan chain signals and system  signals. For the first time, diagnosing DACS was investigated. A general diagnosis algorithm was proposed, which includes  three steps. In Step 1, we proposed using various intermittent  scan chain faults to model the faulty behavior of DACS. In  Step 2, chain flush patterns are applied. We use per shift cycle  based simulation and 32-bit (or 64-bit) signature matching  algorithm to identify a set of candidate system signals. If  multiple candidate faults are obtained in Step 2, we rank the  candidates with a scan pattern based algorithm, which is  adopted from previous work [3]. The algorithm was applied to  industrial designs with short DACS introduced via FIB. The  diagnosis results match the injected defects on chip with good  resolution. Although in this paper we only use short DACS  and crosstalk DACS as examples, the proposed method can be  applied to all kinds of DACS.
