# Timing Analysis of a Microprocessor PLL using High Quantum Efficiency Superconducting Single Photon Detector (SSPD)


Timing Analysis of a Microprocessor PLL using High Quantum Efficiency  Superconducting Single Photon Detector (SSPD)


Peilin Song, Franco Stellari,


IBM T.J. Watson Research Center, Yorktown Heights, NY, USA


James P. Eckhardt, Timothy McNamara, and Ching-Lung Tong


IBM Systems and Technology Group, Poughkeepsie, NY, USA


This paper describes the analysis of a Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) internal phase detection circuit built in IBM’s 0.13 µm  Silicon On Insulator (SOI) CMOS technology by using the  Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis (PICA) [1,2] tool  equipped with the high quantum efficiency Superconducting  Single-Photon Detector (SSPD) [3,4]. Signals corresponding  to the internal nodes of the PLL are for the first time measured  and compared to circuit simulations in order to characterize  the behavior of the different components of the circuit.


In order to achieve high speed and performance, modern  processor chips require the distribution of a reliable, lowskew, high-frequency clock signal [5]. A key feature of the  clock system is the use of a PLL to synchronize all  communication within the system. The PLL-based design  facilitates distribution of a relatively low-frequency reference  oscillator to each of the components in the system. Each  component contains a PLL, which then multiplies that  frequency to the higher frequency that it requires while  maintaining proper phase alignment for a synchronous design. The ability of a PLL to multiply the reference oscillator  frequency is critical, since the systems may have a number of  components running at different frequencies. Another  advantage of this design concept is that it permits the use of  programmable ratios that can be adjusted to take into account  variations in the signal propagation [6].


However, since the PLL is used in a synchronous system, it is  very critical to keep the clock skew between the various  system components very low. In particular, the phase shift of  each clock that arrives at each PLL must be independent from  the on-chip clock distribution delay. This requirement must be  maintained in all the possible operating conditions of the chip  in term of temperature, voltages, etc.


In this paper, we show that the PICA technique [1,2] can be  used to debug a PLL problem by extracting signals strictly  correlated with the PLL operation. The Superconducting  Single-Photon Detector (SSPD) [3,4] is effectively used to


collect the faint near-infrared (NIR) luminescence from the  circuit, thanks to its extended sensitivity towards longer  emission wavelengths. We will show that SSPD provides a  significant reduction in acquisition time for the collection of  optical waveforms, thus maintaining the usability of the PICA  technique for present and future low voltage technologies.


PICA measurements proved that the phase shift in the  PLL-generated internal clock signal was due to excessively  leaky capacitors. This problem was later confirmed by  Physical Failure Analysis (PFA).


Phase Locked Loop (PLL)


In general, Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) circuits provide a clock  frequency that is higher than the external reference signal but  with a well controlled phase relationship.


Fig. 1 shows a block diagram of a PLL. The phase detector  generates pulses with widths equal to the phase difference  between its two inputs (the reference clock with frequency fref  and feedback signal). The charge pump (see the details in  Fig. 2) receives these pulses and converts their width into  charge that gets stored on a capacitor to set a bias voltage:

where Q is the charge injected on the filter capacitance C, Ibias  is the bias current of the charge pump, and Ton is the width of  the charging (TINC) or discharging (TDEC) pulse. In this design, the value of Ibias can be changed as much as 35% by setting  some tune bits in the test pattern.


The amount of charge on the differential capacitors is  increased or decreased by the charge pump until the correct  bias voltage is reached. Once the PLL is “locked”, the  difference between the pulse width of signal “INC pulse” of  inverter INC and the pulse width of signal “DEC pulse” of  inverter DEC represents the steady phase shift/error of  reference clock and feedback clock. This difference decides  the voltage drop across nodes “filt” and “filtn”, which  subsequently determines the amount of current that goes to the  current controlled oscillator (ICO). In fact, the voltage-tocurrent (V-to-I) converter transforms the bias voltage across  the capacitances into a current that is injected into the ICO, IICO determining the oscillator frequency. When the PLL  circuit is “locked”, the feedback divider, on the feedback path  of the loop, determines the relationship between the chip clock  frequency and the reference clock frequency:

(4) where M is the divisor factor. The forward divider generates a  lower on-chip frequency that may be used to trigger the PICA  system during optical measurements.


A primary indicator of PLL performance is jitter. The PLL  aligns its clock signal with the external reference and the clock  signal of other chips in the system. Consequently, accumulated phase shift/error (i.e. the phase difference  between the PLL output and the reference clock) is important. The PLL studied in this paper showed an “early mode” timing  failure. An extensive electrical test of the chip demonstrated  that the internal clock signal is arriving earlier than expected  by design. The amount of phase error depends on both the  frequency of the reference signal and the supply voltage of the  PLL. In general, the timing of signals “INC pulse” and “DEC  pulse” (see Fig. 2) is very critical in order to achieve a desired  clock frequency. Ideally, these two signals are lined up very  well to guarantee a stable clock output frequency. However,


either due to the design limitation or process variations, excessive phase error on these two signals could cause the  PLL to be either too slow or too fast. For this particular chip, an excessive phase error was detected.


Fig. 3 shows a zoom-in of the microprocessor chip image  taken with a Laser Scanning Microscope (LSM). Two PLLs  are placed near the center of the dual-core chip, surrounded by  a field of filter capacitances. The block diagram of the PLL  circuits is shown in Fig. 1. By default the PLL generates an  output frequency that is 8 times the one of the incoming  reference clock. However, the PLL can also be programmed to  different multiplication factors by scanning latch bits. Similarly, other tune bits can be set to change the strength of  the charge pumps.


Test setup and detectors


Fig. 4 shows the electrical and optical setup used during the  test of the microprocessor PLL. The circuit under test is  packaged using a Temporary Chip Attach (TCA) socket  mounted on a test board that provides supply voltage and  ground, as well as access to the I/O pins that are required to  run the test. In order to collect hot-carrier NIR emission, the  TCA package must be opened, the silicon substrate thinned  down to about 100 µm and polished for backside analysis. An  IMS tester, scanning in the test pattern, is used to initialize the  chip state and operation; an HP8133A pulse generator is used  to provide the reference clock to the chip. The trigger signal  for the PICA technique [2] is also derived from the external  pulse generator instead of using the PLL divided output in  order to reduce possible additional sources of jitter during the  optical measurements. The board is mounted upside-down  over the LSM as shown in Fig. 4. The microscope can image  the circuit for navigation, as well as collect the emission and  focus it onto the S-25 PMT or into the optical fiber that is  connected to the Superconducting Single-Photon Detector (SSPD), housed in a cryostat. The individual transistors can be  distinguished by closing mechanical blades inserted in the  optical path of the microscope that stop the light coming from  neighboring structures in the same field of view.


The time-dependent optical measurements presented in this  paper are acquired using the commercial version of the SSPD  described in [4]. The SSPD is very sensitive to the nearVDDA

infrared light emitted from transistors of new technology  under their normal operating conditions, while the  conventional PICA system based on the S-25 Photo-Multiplier  Tube (PMT) [7] becomes ineffective for the same application. In fact, the continuous trend of the modern semiconductor  industry towards smaller devices and lower supply voltages


[8] is causing significant changes in the intensity and spectrum  shift of the light emitted by present generation ICs: the total  detectable light decreases exponentially with the electric field  in the transistor, and linearly with the lateral dimension of the  FET. In particular, the progressive shift of the spectral  distribution of the emitted light towards longer wavelengths


[9] makes the use of the conventional PICA technique based  on the use of the S-25 PMT [7] more challenging, due to its  lack of sensitivity in the NIR region of the spectrum.


The SSPD detector is fabricated with a 10 nm thick stripe line  of NbN bent in a serpentine shape (meander) covering a  10 µm × 10 µm area. The meander shape has a lower dark  count rate (due to the area factor) and a higher critical current  to maintain the superconductive state. The latter guarantees  also a larger electrical signal detected from the front-end  electronics and therefore a better time resolution. The best  detection efficiency of the SSPD can be achieved at a bias  current that results in a 1,000 cps dark count rate. However, the dark count rate can be reduced more than one order of  magnitude by decreasing the bias current of the detector with a  very small loss of detection efficiency (~10% variation from  the top performance of about 4-5%) [3,4].


At temperature below the critical temperature TC of a  superconductive material, the absorption of a photon with  energy


ω ∆  creates, through electron-electron and  electron-Debye-phonon interactions, a local non-equilibrium  perturbation (see Fig. 5(a)). A large number of excited  hot-electrons (>300 in the case of NbN excited with 790 nm  wavelength light) is generated along with an increase of the


average electron temperature above TC [10]. This initial  thermalization phase results in the formation of a resistive  hot-spot (i.e., a local non-superconducting region of the  superconducting material) that tends to grow is size as  hot-electrons diffuse out of its center (Fig. 5(b)). At the same  time, the supercurrent is expelled from the hot-spot volume  and is concentrated in the ‘‘sidewalks’’ between the hot-spot  and the edges of the 200 nm-wide film (Fig. 5(c)). If the bias  current is sufficient to exceed the critical current in the  sidewalks, a non-superconducting barrier is formed across the  entire width of the device (Fig. 5(d)), giving rise to a voltage  signal that can be detected at the terminals of the device [10]. The hot-spot formation process competes, of course, with the  cooling process, as electrons diffusing out of the hot-spot lose  their energy through electron-phonon scattering. Thus, after a  time depending on both the diffusion rate and the relaxation  time, the hot-spot heals itself, leading to the restoration of the  superconducting path along the strip line [10].


Analysis of the PLL operation


The Picosecond Imaging Circuit Analysis (PICA) technique


[2], based on the collection of near infrared light (NIR) emitted by hot-carriers in the transistor channel, has been  demonstrated to be an invaluable method for detecting timingrelated faults in backside packaged ULSI circuits [2]. Many  innovative applications of the PICA technique have been  developed in the past years, based on the detection of Light  Emission due to Off-State Leakage Current (LEOSLC) [11,12], oxide tunneling current and carrier recombination


[13], thus leading to completely new application areas and  even more contributions to quick turn around times for circuit  debugging and defect isolation. In this paper, we use the PICA  technique with the SSPD to extract the signals inside a PLL  built in 0.13 µm SOI CMOS technology.

Time-integrated images of the emission taken with a silicon  back-illuminated NIR CCD can be overlaid to the LSM  images of the circuit to help in localizing the emission sources  as shown in Fig. 6. These images simplify the navigation  effort during time-dependent acquisitions with the SSPD that  allows only single-point measurements [14], compared to the  parallel acquisition of multiple points of the S-25 PMT used in  the conventional PICA technique [1].


Fig. 7 shows some optical waveforms taken with the SSPD  from the inputs of the PLL phase detector (see block diagram  in Fig. 1). An excessive delay is observed, thus confirming the “early mode” timing failure, initially discovered by extensive  electrical testing of the chip. The feedback signal is arriving  too late and the excessive phase error is causing the different  chips in the system to loose synchronization. The  measurements show also that the phase shift depends on the  analog supply voltage of the PLL and the frequency of the  incoming reference signal.


Once confirmed that the problem was repeatable and  observable with PICA, a series of acquisitions was taken along  the most critical signal path of the PLL loop. However, anomalous delays/skews were not detected in the elements of  the PLL, leaving only the charge pump and the filter capacitor  to be analyzed.


Charge pump circuit characterization


In order to monitor the operation of the charge pump circuit, the INC and DEC pulses generated by the phase detector (see  the block diagram in Fig. 2) are characterized as a function of  the frequency of the incoming reference clock. The pulse  delay and duration is much easier to measure for PICA than  the analog current of the pump itself. In general a direct  measurement of the these pulses is possible during the first  stages of development of the PLL circuit when it is  implemented in test chips and more signals are available to be  monitor. However, in more integrated situation in which the  PLL is surrounded by logic circuitry, the only way to monitor  the INC and DEC pulses is with PICA.


Fig. 8 shows the PICA time-dependent optical waveforms  from the inverters INC and DEC (see Fig. 2), while the PLL is


exercised by different frequencies of the reference clock  ranging from (a) 500 MHz to (d) 2 GHz. Note that the  extended detection efficiency of the SSPD detector allows the  observation of weaker p-FET switching transitions. Therefore, by positioning the collection area of the detector in between  the n-FET and the p-FET of the INC and DEC inverter, one  can acquire both switching transitions with only one  acquisition. For this reason, the first two peaks in each chart of  Fig. 8 represent the rising edges of INC pulse and DEC pulse, while the third and fourth peaks represent the falling edges. The measured time delay between the p-FET and the n-FET  switching transition of each inverter represents the duration of  the activation pulse for the current sources charging or  discharging the filter capacitors of the PLL.


In this case, the falling edges switch at the same time for both  INC and DEC signals. The phase shift shown in the top part of  Fig. 8 demonstrates that the PLL is faster than the required  frequency. However, PICA measurements show a time shift  between the rising edges of the INC and DEC pulses while the  PLL is locked to a steady reference clock. This phase error  indicates that a different amount of charge is needed to  maintain a steady differential voltage across the two filter  capacitors, which fixes the frequency of the internal oscillator. Moreover, PICA measurements highlight that such phase error  is also varying depending on the frequency of the incoming  reference clock. At high frequency (Fig. 8(d)), a phase  inversion of the two signals is also visible.


PLL tune bits point to leaky capacitors


The observation of different durations for the INC and DEC  pulses of the charge pump, along with their relative variations  with the frequency of the incoming reference clock suggests a  possible problem with high leakage in the filter capacitors  related to process variation. In fact, capacitor leakage has a  strong (exponential) dependence on the applied voltage: the

higher the voltage across the capacitor, the larger the leakage. Consequently, at different operating points (i.e., different  frequencies of the reference and ICO) there is a differential  voltage betweeen the two filter capacitors (i.e., Vfilt ≠ Vfiltn) in  order to maintain the PLL locked. However, this difference  causes a different amount of leakage of each capacitor (i.e., the capacitor with higher voltage has also a much larger  leakage current). Consequently, changing frequency will  change the static offset that is needed to compensate for the  differential leakage current through the filter capacitors.


In order to double check the previous assumption, other  optical waveforms are acquired from the same inverters. However, in this case some tuning bits of the PLL are used in  order to increase by ~35% the current that the charge pump is  able to provide to the filter capacitors. Fig. 9 shows the  corresponding PICA measurements in the same condition  previously discussed. From a direct comparison with the  acquisitions in Fig. 8, one can notice that the phase shift  between the rising edge of the INC and DEC pulses is reduced  as expected. With a higher current capability of the charge


pump, the difference in the pulse duration needed to  compensate for the different leakage through the capacitors is  also reduced. Fig. 9(d) shows also that the signal inversion is  still present for high output frequency.


Table 1 summarizes all the measurements performed at  different oscillation frequencies with and without the tune bits  turned on. The delay extracted from the optical waveforms  confirms the estimation based on circuit simulations: a ~35% reduction in the phase error is observed.


Based on the PICA measurements for different PLL operating  conditions, it was determined that the excessive leakage in the  thick-oxide differential capacitors caused the big phase shift  for this chip. This problem was later confirmed by Physical  Failure Analysis (PFA). Special-designed thicker-oxide  capacitors were used to reduce the leakage current for correct  circuit operation [15].

The test chip was processed in a 90 nm process technology  with a nominal supply voltage of 1.0V. To ensure frontside  observability no tiles or interconnect was placed above the  transistors. The impact of tiles is addressed in a separate part  of the test chip and is not covered in this paper.


Photon emission microscopy


PEM measurements were performed with two systems. System one is a slow-scan CCD camera (Roper Scientific,

Figure 4: Relation between Isub and Vgs of a single N-MOST  for Vds of 1.0 to 1.8 V in steps of 0.2 V for matured silicon.


From literature it is well known that the substrate current is a  good indicator of the photon emission intensity. Figure 4  shows the Isub versus Vgs curves of a single N-MOST made  in 90 nm for several supply voltages. Typically substrate  currents of more than 1 nA indicate sufficient emission for  detection with a CCD camera system. The curves start with an  initial increase due to the increase in Ids as a function of gate  voltage. Hence, the total number of available electrons  increases as function of Vgs. However, a larger gate voltage  means a reduction in Vds - Vgs and therefore a reduction in  the fraction of hot electrons. As a result Isub drops back to  almost zero for Vgs close to Vds. The maximum in the Isub  is  obtained at Vgs between 0.25 and 0.3 Vdd and indicates that  the two effects compensate each other (or in other words the  increase in the absolute number of electrons is compensated  by the reduction in the fraction of ‘hot’ electrons).


PEM with CCD


From Figure 1 it becomes clear that PEM with a CCD system  is not easy in very deep sub-micron technologies and that from  a sensitivity point of view an MCT system is preferred. However, a CCD system has as advantage that, owing to the  shorter wavelength employed, its position resolution is better  than what can be obtained with an MCT system. Therefore it  is interesting to determine what we still can achieve with a  CCD system. To this end we activated a low ohmic short of  about 300 Ω. We confirmed its activation with logic and Iddq  testing. PEM from either front or backside did not reveal an  emission spot at the nominal supply voltage of 1 V. Based on  our analysis in Figure 1 this was expected. Nevertheless it  does not mean that a CCD system is not usable anymore. One  option to enhance the emission is to increase the supply  voltage. Figure 4 shows that the photon emission rate can be  increased several orders of magnitude if Vds is increased. Typically, CMOS technologies can survive supply voltages of  about twice the nominal supply voltage. Of course some  degeneration can occur as well as that the overall lifetime is  limited (typically weeks). So this method should be applied  with care during regular failure analysis since it increases the  risk of destroying the sample or modifying the root cause. In  our case samples is not an issue. Moreover, we applied  voltages up to 1.9 V without damaging any sample. This  indicates that the risk is not very large.


One of the purposes of this test circuit is to investigate the  capabilities of PEM in 90 nm technologies. The circuit was  manufactured in early versions of this technology. Especially  for the first batch the N-MOS transistor characteristics were  not up to specification (the drive strength is okay but the  threshold voltage is affected). This becomes also clear from  Figure 5 that shows the Isub versus Vgs behaviour. The  generally expected behaviour is present, however, all curves  are shifted to the left. As a result it does not show the strong  decrease in Isub for Vgs close to 0 V as was observed in  Figure 4 (which is based on more recent silicon of Q2 2003). This anomalous behaviour of the early silicon enhances the  light emission for off-state N-MOSTs. This has as advantage  that it allows us to highlight some aspects that are less obvious  in mature silicon.


Vds = 1.2 V Vds = 1.6 V


Figure 5: Relation between Isub and Vgs of a single NMOST for Vds of 1.2 to 1.6 V in steps of 0.2 V for early  silicon.


Figure 6 shows the photon emission of the circuit for a supply  voltage of 1.6 V when no shorts are activated. Although none  of the shorts is active we still get photon emission from the  complete circuit. Closer investigation showed that all NMOSTs in the off-state emit light. This is the expected  behaviour based on Figure 5.  For a Vgs of 0V already  substantial Isub currents are flowing. For conventional PEM  one would consider this as an annoyance since it obscures the  light emission of malfunctioning parts. However, this ‘offstate’ light emission shows also that PEM has capabilities  beyond the localisation of defects. The light of the off-state NMOST reflects the state of the logic and therefore the state of  the circuit. This logic mapping is in general possible as long as  there is sufficient difference in emission fro off- and on-state  transistors. Furthermore, it requires sufficient emission  intensity, which could require the use of elevated supply  voltages.


Figure 6: Backside photon emission photograph of the lefthand side of the circuit (early silicon) when no defects are  activated. All emission spot are N-MOSTs, in ‘off-state’.


Since we are applying supply voltages well above the nominal  supply voltage it is worthwhile to check if the photon emission  still behaves as expected. One simple test is to check whether  the light emission scales properly with supply voltage and  substrate current. Figure 7 shows the light emission and the  substrate current for a Vgs of 0V for the early and matured  silicon. All data are plotted as a function of reciprocal supply  voltages. The curves show the expected behaviour and follow  the same trends. The substrate current (filled squares) and the  photon emission intensity (filled diamonds) of the early silicon  run parallel to each other. The substrate current at Vgs is 0V  for matured silicon is about a factor 100 less than for the early  silicon. This matches our observation that for the matured  silicon supply voltages of 1.6 V are required to get sufficient  intensity for detection. Furthermore, Figure 7 shows that both  the early and matured silicon have similar dependencies on the  supply voltage. Also other checks, involving the Igate and Ids  currents showed normal behaviour. Therefore it seems  reasonable to assume that by overdriving the transistor we  merely boost the photon emission rate.


After this sanity check we can start to analyse the photon  emission behaviour when defects are activated. We will focus  our attention to a sub-section of the circuit. This section is

As expected, the intensity profile for rows  1 and 2 remains unchanged. Furthermore, the intensity profile  of row 4 and 6 is almost unchanged. The only relevant  difference is that the transistor just after the short shows an  enhanced emission owing to the mid-level biasing. This  enhancement is small, typically a factor 2, and invisible with  the scale used in Figure 9. That the enhancement is so small is  not surprising if we look at Figure 5. Based on this figure one  can expect a factor 3 at most (note that in normal silicon this is


a factor 100). The interesting changes occur in rows 3 and 5. First, the light emission spots of the left-hand side of rows 3  and 5 shift one inverter due to the different initialisation. The  300 Ω short between rows 3 and 4 is below the critical  resistance [3] and will cause a stuck-at fault. As a result the  light emission spots on the right-hand side for row 3 are again  in line with row 4. The short between rows 5 and 6 has a 2 kΩ  resistance which does not cause a stuck-at fault but only an  elevated Iddq current. Therefore, the emission spots on the  right-hand side of row 5 are still out of line with the other  spots. Second, the light emission of the N-transistor just before  the short is strongly reduced and creates a `hole'. Third, we see  for both row 3 as well as row 5 a new spot emerging, which is  horizontally out of line with the other spots. These spot stem  from the P-MOSTs. These last two observations are analysed  in the next section.

Defect simulations


Defect simulations are well suited to explain phenomena such  as the reduction in intensity and the emerging of the P-MOST  spots. The bridging ‘defect’ shorts two nodes and affects the  voltages on these nodes. The actual voltages on these nodes  depend on the involved transistors and the resistance of the  short. Together they form a voltage divider. The intermediate  voltage at the nodes is interpreted by the next gate and is  usually well defined as either high or low within one or two  gates. conditions and when the two shorts of Figure 9 are activated. The top diagram shows the expected behaviour for the top  rows where no short is present. All N-MOSTs in off-state emit  light. The bottom two diagrams show the impact of the shorts. The two N-transistors with a reduced intensity (first transistor  in row 3 and 5) are explained by the reduction in Vds. In the  defect-free case Vds is equal to Vdd but with the defect  activated this is reduced to 0.25 and 0.6 Vdd and based on  Figures 4 or 5 we can therefore expect a strong reduction in  intensity.


Intermediate gate voltage levels also explain the emission  spots for the P-MOST. The P-MOST does behave normally in  both the early and matured silicon: little emission is expected  in the on and off-state and an increase in light intensity is  expected for intermediate gate voltages. Analogous for the NMOST in Figure 4 (but inverted) this maximum is at 0.75-0.7  Vdd. For row 5 the first inverter after the short has a gate  voltage of 0.6 Vdd and causes sufficient light emission of the  P-MOST to be detectable. For row 3 this is not the case since


0.25 Vdd gate voltage is not sufficient. However, the next gate  has a gate voltage of 0.9 Vdd which is sufficient for detection. As a result we see that for row 3 the P-MOST in the second  inverter after the short (instead of the first) emits light.


Figure 9 and 10 thus show that we can shift the photon  emission of the P-MOST over one gate. Under the right  conditions it is possible to shift it even further. Figure 11  shows the light emission of rows 7 to 10 which contain  inverters with larger drive strengths. Rows 7 and 8 are used as  reference while between rows 9 and 10 a short is activated. The impact of this short is similar to those in Figure 9 except  that it is now the third P-MOST that emits light. Defect  simulations show that this is indeed expected. This  combination of defect simulations and PEM allows one to  obtain more information about the defect than its position  alone.  Note: we showed this capability on early silicon  because it provides reference spots but that the method is also


in general possible in combination with a CAD navigation  system.


PEM with MCT


The previous paragraph shows that PEM is still feasible with a  CCD camera system but that it already requires elevated  supply voltages to get sufficient light emission. An MCT  camera system should outperform a CCD system as Figure 1  shows. Therefore we also performed frontside emission  measurements with an MCT system. Frontside PEM does not  show a real improvement over a CCD system. The main  bottleneck for frontside use of an MCT system seems to be the  infra-red transmission coefficient of the stack. Although SiO2  itself has a transmission coefficient close to 1 between 1000  and 5000 nm this is not necessarily true for some of the  protection layers or low-k materials used in modern processes. Backside emission is not hampered by the introduction of new  materials and the transmission through (doped) Si was  sufficient in older technologies. Planned backside MCT  measurements are expected to show the benefits of an MCT  system.


row 7 8 9 10


Figure 11: Frontside photon emission photograph of the  circuit with defect activation. Dotted lines are guides to the  eye and the grey boxes represent the shorts.


We designed a circuit with selectable shorts in a 90 nm  technology to investigate the capabilities of PEM with CCD  and MCT camera systems in advanced technologies. The  reduction in supply voltage reduces the number of `hot  electrons' and their electron temperature. As a result CCD  camera systems are not suited anymore to perform PEM while  using nominal supply conditions. Nevertheless, PEM with a  CCD system is still feasible in 90 nm technologies if one uses  elevated supply voltages. For 65 nm technologies it is doubtful  if elevated supply voltages will help and MCT systems  become a requirement. The impact of the selectable shorts is  clearly visible in the photon emission micrographs. We  furthermore showed that PEM is capable of logic mapping and  that in combination with defect simulation and the localisation  of the P-MOST emission spot one can obtain additional  information, e.g. the resistance, of a short.

# Quantifying the work of adhesion between an AFM cantilever tip and MEMS test structures after packaging


Quantifying the work of adhesion between an AFM cantilever tip and MEMS test  structures after packaging


E. J. Thoreson*, and N. A. Burnham,


Worcester Polytechnic Institute, Worcester, MA, USA


J. Martin


Analog Devices, Cambridge, MA, USA


Adhesion is important to the yield and performance of MEMS (Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems) and NEMS (NanoElectro-Mechanical Systems). Measuring the work of  adhesion, with an AFM (Atomic-Force Microscope), allows  one to study surface interactions from an energy perspective  as opposed to an adhesion (force) perspective. The works of  adhesion were measured with different AFM tip radii on  multiple types of samples. Two sample variables were  examined: four die attach conditions (no attachment, silicone, polyimide silicone, and silver glass), and two surface  conditions (native oxide with and without a few angstroms of  vapor-deposited diphenyl siloxane). For a normal silicon  cantilever, the work of adhesion seems to be slightly less for  the treated surfaces than the untreated, except for the silverglass die attach material. There were at least three orders of  magnitude difference in the works of adhesion for the  different AFM tip radii. Presumably, the trend is due to some  combination of material properties, interfacial roughness, and  torque on the AFM cantilever.


As the size of an element decreases, the surface to volume  ratio increases dramatically.  For this reason, surface effects  can dominate the interaction between small devices [1]. Measuring the work of adhesion allows one to study these  surface interactions from an energy perspective as opposed to  an adhesion (force) perspective. The work of adhesion is the  amount of energy per unit area required to separate two  surfaces from contact to infinity [2]. The quantification of the  work of adhesion is important to understanding why two  moving surfaces can become stuck to each other (known as “stiction”) for NEMS (NanoElectoMechancial Systems) and  MEMS (MicroElectroMechanical Systems) structures [3], [4].  Many techniques exist to measure adhesion (the amount of  force required to separate two surfaces) or work of adhesion.  Peeling and detachment, contact angle measurements [5], and  AFM (Atomic-Force Microscopy) [6], [7], are all examples of


methods for measuring the adhesion. Peeling and detachment  studies typically involve an array of cantilever beams of  different lengths. The array of cantilevers is caused to come  into contact with a substrate either by electrostatic actuation or  submersing in liquid (and allowing the liquid to evaporate, which forms a meniscus between the cantilever and substrate). When the stored energy in the cantilever is greater than the  interfacial energy of the surface, the cantilever peels or  detaches from the surface. This occurs at some critical length  and cantilevers that are longer than the critical length remain  stuck to the substrate. The critical length is inversely  proportional to the work of adhesion. Since one needs to have  a prefabricated array of cantilevers, the method is most useful  for determining the effectiveness of the release processes (supercritical drying, sublimation drying, and dry release  etching) during MEMS fabrication. For contact angle  measurements, a liquid drop is placed on the substrate and the  angle that the drop makes with the substrate (contact angle) is  related to the amount of interfacial energy or surface tension, which is proportional to the work of adhesion. The method  requires that one resolve the contact angle between the drop  and the substrate so fairly large droplet sizes need to be used. The AFM, in the very recent past, has become a very good  tool for qualitative analysis. By comparing the work of  adhesion for one type of system (cantilever tip and substrate) to another type, relative changes in the adhesion are observed. However, using the AFM as a quantitative tool has been more  difficult (accurate and precise values for the spring constant  have been difficult to measure for each experiment). Once the  spring constant is well known, then an understanding of the  contact mechanics must be understood. With a calibrated  AFM, absolute forces and works of adhesion (between the  cantilever tip and substrate) can be measured from atomic  sized tip radii out to micron sized tip radii. The AFM closely  simulates the movement of micro- or nanostructures, making  it a useful tool in the analysis of stiction.


The purpose of this paper is to delineate results for the work  of adhesion between a cantilever tip and various types of  samples. In order to do that, the type of contact models will be  listed, a short discussion of which mechanical model is most  applicable will be given, the precision and accuracy of the  AFM will be given, and finally results for the work of


adhesion on various types of samples for different tip sizes  will be shown.


Theory


There are various contact mechanical models to describe the  forces experienced by an AFM cantilever: 1) Hertz [8], assumes there are no surface forces, 2) JKR (Johnson, Kendall, Roberts) [9], assumes that short-ranged surface  forces act only inside the contact area and the contact  geometry is allowed to deform, 3) DMT (Derjaguin, Muller, and Toporov) [10], assumes that long-range surface forces act  only outside the contact area, 4) Maugis [11], 5) BCP (Burnham, Colton, Pollock) [12]. The last two assume that  surface forces act everywhere and the contact geometry is  allowed to deform.


The AFM is capable of measuring the amount of deflection  experienced by a cantilever near to or in contact with a sample  substrate. Therefore, if the deflection and spring constant of a  cantilever are known, one can quantify the forces acting on  the cantilever when it approaches a surface or is retracted  away from it.  The adhesive force (the pull-off force as  measured by the AFM) is the amount of force required to  separate two surfaces. In 1997, Johnson and Greenwood  showed that there is smooth transition (for the relative pull-off  force as a function of an elasticity parameter) from DMT  mechanics to JKR [13]. Prior to that, D. Maugis (1992) also  presented a smooth transition from DMT to JKR [14]. The  elasticity parameter (µ) is a ratio between the elastic  displacement and the effective range of interaction. First  introduced by Tabor [15],

(1.2) where Rtip is the radius of the cantilever tip. Hence the work of  adhesion should be independent of the dimensions of the  surfaces involved. This can be tested by varying the  dimensions of one of the surfaces. The convenient surface to  vary is the cantilever tip radius, because it can be modified by  attaching beads to tipless cantilevers. Studying the response of  the work of adhesion to dimensional changes can give insight  as to the nature of mechanical failure (stiction). For instance, if two surfaces come into contact repeatedly, there is the  potential for one or both of the surfaces to wear causing a


dimensional change in the system. Additionally, shrinking a  MEMS or NEMS device also causes a dimensional change in  the system. If the work of adhesion were to vary, only the  material properties, surface roughness, or torque on the  cantilever could cause the change in the work of adhesion. If a  water layer is present on the surface, then the work of  adhesion would be measured to be greater than 142 mJ/m2. Depending on the angle of repose, it is estimated that the  torque would contribute about 5 % to the total measured work  of adhesion. If the interfacial roughness is large, then work of  adhesion could be affected to a large degree. Since, the true  contact are could be over or underestimated to a large degree. The cantilever-substrate system can be modeled as a springdashpot system with the cantilever as the spring. Therefore,

(1.3) Where k is the spring constant and δz is the compression or  extension (deflection) of the spring. Typically, the deflection  is well known, on the order of a couple of angstroms. However, the reported tolerance for cantilever spring  constants is very broad, often 100 percent or more. In order  for the AFM to be a quantitative tool, the spring constant and  tip radii must be known for each experiment.


We have calibrated spring constants and tip radii for AFM  cantilevers, so that the work of adhesion can be determined to  an accuracy of 14% and a precision of 10% [16], [17], [18]. The precision and accuracy may seem high, but they are at  least a factor of five improvement over current methods. Hence, we will present our results for the calibrated work of  adhesion between an AFM tip and unpatterned silicon die that  were solder-sealed in 5 mm x 5 mm LCC (Leadless Ceramic  Chip Carrier) packages.


Methods


The radius of the cantilever tip and the spring constant of the  cantilever were measured before each experiment. Two  sample variables were examined: four die attach conditions (no attachment, silicone, polyimide silicone, and silver glass), and two surface conditions (native oxide with and without a  few angstroms of vapor-deposited diphenyl siloxane).  This  results in eight different kinds of samples. The lids for each  LCC package were removed and the dies were placed on the  AFM stage. Two different types of tips were used to study the  work of adhesion. The first was a “normal” (SiOx) AFM tip (assumed spherical). The second were beads (SiO2 spheres) attached to tipless cantilevers. A large size bead (~60 µm) has ~ 5 nm surface roughness, as verified by imaging the bead  with a normal AFM tip. A two-micron square topography  image of the surface was acquired and the RMS surface  roughness was determined. The samples’ surfaces were  known to be relatively flat, so limits were set for the RMS  surface roughness. For normal AFM tips (SiOx), the RMS  surface roughness was set to be between 0.1 and 1.0 nm. For  beads attached to tipless AFM cantilevers (SiO2), the RMS  surface roughness was set to be between 0.1 nm and 5.0 nm. If


the surface roughnesses did not fall in these ranges, the  sample substrates were reimaged after a more careful  adjustment of the scan parameters. Then, sixteen approach and  retraction force curves were obtained across a two-micron  square section of the die and the amount of adhesive force was  determined from those curves.  The average and standard  deviation of the deflection for the sixteen points were  determined.  The number of standard deviations away from  the average value was found for each point. Those that were  greater than two standard deviations were rejected. However, no more than three data points out of sixteen were rejected. Otherwise, the set of pull-off force measurements was  repeated.


All work of adhesion measurements (see Figures 1-4) were  made at a relative humidity of 24.5 ± 1.5 % and temperature  of 22.5 ± 1.9 °C.  Assuming the system was in the DMT  contact mechanics regime, the works of adhesion at all points  were calculated from the measured adhesive force (pull-off  force) and radius of the cantilever tip, Eqn. (1.2).


Figures 1 – 4 show the measured works of adhesion as a  function of increasing tip radius. Conventional wisdom  dictates that the work of adhesion should be constant as the  radius is increased. However, it is evident from the graphs that  this is not true. There are at least two orders of magnitude  difference in the work of adhesion as the radius increases.


From Figure 1 it is seen that for all, except the silver-glass die  attach material, the work of adhesion seems to be slightly less  for the treated surfaces than the untreated. This is most  pronounced in Figure 4. For the normal AFM tip (Figure 1), material transfer may have caused the treated surface of the  silver-glass mounted sample to have a higher work of  adhesion (the untreated sample had been measured with this  tip). For the two-micron tip (Figure 2), it was not clear that  there was any difference between the untreated and treated  samples. Our laboratory is able to attach beads sized 12  micron and larger to tipless AFM cantilevers. The two-micron  beads were attached for us by Nova Scan Technologies. Their  process is proprietary and may have affected the measured  work of adhesion. We attach the beads using UV glue. A drop  of UV glue smaller than the diameter of the bead is placed on  the cantilever, the bead is placed into the glue, and then the  bead-glue system is irradiated with UV light. This results in  the beads being fixed to the cantilever, such that the cantilever  will break before the glue yields.  It is unlikely that this  process has any effect on the work of adhesion for tip sizes  greater than 12 microns.  However, care must be taken for the  UV glue droplet sizes to remain small. Otherwise, capillary  action can cause the bead to be coated with UV glue.


Figure 1:  Works of adhesion between a silicon cantilever and  various types of die-attachments and treatments. Treated  samples are coated with a few angstroms of diphenyl siloxane  and the untreated ones are not coated. The error bars  represent two standard deviations from the average and the  systematic error should be less than 14%.


Figure 2:  Works of adhesion between an SiO2 sphere (2 µm) and various types of die-attachments and treatments.


Figure  3:  Works of adhesion between an SiO2 sphere (6 µm) and various types of die-attachments and treatments.


Figure 4:  Works of adhesion between an SiO2 sphere (60 µm) and various types of die-attachments and treatments.


Figures 1-4 indicate that the work of adhesion decreases as the  radius of the tip increases. The reason for this trend is not  clear. Presumably, it is due to some combination of material  properties, interfacial roughness, and cantilever torque.  However, any single cause seems not to effectively explain  the behavior. All experiments were performed in ambient  conditions (room temperature and at ~1 atm), so adsorbed  moisture was present on the surfaces. The dew point in the lab  was such that condensation was unlikely. The surfaces treated  with hydrophobic diphenyl siloxane would have less moisture. Another issue for ambient conditions, is surface contaminants (any films or particulates that are not of the type that are  intended to be measured, i.e. hydrocarbons). Should either  moisture or contamination come between the tip and the  sample substrate, the measured work of adhesion would  change. The formation of a contamination layer arises because  the sample substrates are assumed to have a higher surface  energy. The addition of particles lowers that surface energy. In the case of a thin meniscus forming, the cantilever would  need to break free of the surface tension, thereby increasing  the work of adhesion. Since water monolayers are thin, they  would have a more pronounced effect at smaller tip sizes. Formation of a contamination layer or monolayer of water, for  the case of treated surfaces, is minimized, since the diphenyl  siloxane lowers the surface energy and is hydrophobic. An  equivalent method to reduce the contribution of a monolayer  of water would be to submerse the system in a liquid, but this  does not effectively simulate the operating conditions of  MEMS devices.


There are many more issues to consider. However, one of the  largest contributors is the surface roughness. The topography  image, from which RMS roughness is gleaned, is a dilation (Minkowski addition) between the sample surface and the  AFM tip. The way in which the tip intermeshes with the  surface can have a profound effect on the work of adhesion.


The work of adhesion was measured on the eight different  samples with four different cantilever tip radii (60 µm, 6 µm,


2 µm, and < 1 µm). Data for the 60 µm radius cantilever tip  indicate that the treated surfaces had a lower work of adhesion  as compared to their untreated counterparts, the untreated  silicone and silver glass die-attachments had the highest work  of adhesion, and the surface-tip interface might have been  dominated by material transfer. Smaller sized tips produced  similar results with the exception of the two-micron tip. Future work will include analyzing the work of adhesion as a  function of radius on the eight different samples, coating the  cantilever tips with diphenyl siloxane, and, then, remeasuring  the work of adhesion.

Analysis of 0.13 um CMOS Technology Using Time Resolved Light Emission


Peter Ouimet, Jason Goertz, Olivier Rinaudo, Lousinda Long, Simon Yeung


Freescale Semiconductor, Austin, Texas, USA


This paper describes case histories of 0.13 um bulk CMOS  technology analyses using Time Resolved Light Emission (TRLEM). Using this technique, scan chain, timing, and logic  failures are shown to be quickly and decisively  identified  thereby meeting the need for rapid feedback on 1st silicon  failures and process excursions.


Failure analysis of deep sub-micron System On A Chip (SOC) bulk and SOI technologies has become increasingly complex  for several reasons. Traditional FIB pad probing is made  difficult due to up to eight levels of metal. Another large  factor in SOC failure analysis is that design teams are often  scattered around the world and unavailable to assist the  analysts due to resource constraints. Scan based designs  coupled with Automatic Test Program Generation (ATPG) and Diagnostic Fault Simulation (DFS) utilities can usually  identify high probability candidate nodes. It is still necessary, however, to probe nodes to confirm a timing problem or defect  site, and TRLEM provides an efficient means.


Time resolved light emission uses a light microscope with an  IR light source for imaging from the backside of the die. The  die must be thinned [2] to approximately 100 um so that  adequate signal can be acquired. Some type of thermal relief is  necessary in some cases. If the device is packaged in a BGA  type package, it needs to be re-packaged in a backside  compatible package [3]. Acquisition times are measured in  minutes for loop lengths on the order of 40 us. It must be  noted here that it is unnecessary to overdrive the supply


voltage above nominal to achieve acquisition times of 10’s of  minutes. The tool that is used for probing in this paper is the  Optonics Emiscope. A very detailed description of this  technique can be found in [1]. The pulses observed on a  TRLEM waveform represent the integral of time resolved  photons emitted when a CMOS transistor switches during the  tester looping. The tester is looped over test vectors to achieve  an adequate signal to noise


# Analysis of 0.13 um CMOS Technology Using Time Resolved Light Emission


ratio against the background noise. The probability of  detecting a photon is higher during the high to low transition  of a CMOS output (falling edge) than during the low to high   transition (rising edge), resulting in taller pulses for high to


low transitions. By using this property, data transitions can be  measured throughout the chain and logic, and the individual  instance where the data appears abnormal can be quickly and  accurately identified.


The simplest type of failure in a scan based design is a chain  failure, where the scan chain is broken, and no information  can be inferred from the scan data. These types of failures are  usually present when defectivity is the predominant factor in  yield loss, and are more straightforward to analyze than ATPG  scan failures.  Typically, the scan chains lengths are kept  below 1000 scan chain latches and a binary search is done to  identify the failing latch.  This can be done very efficiently  with TRLEM and the isolation process can be done in one  day.


Timing failures are also often encountered during design  verification efforts, and present problems for traditional FIB  pad probing. The number of metal layers often precludes  probing of the desired node. Also, traditional FIB pad  capacitive loading can obscure the timing problem when the  desired node is accessible. These problems are overcome with  TRLEM because there is no electrical load induced by the  probing.


Case Study 1: Test Control Mode Failure


This paper primarily deals with scan chain based analysis. But  in one analysis, a SOC first silicon yield loss was caused by  devices that would not go into scan mode out of reset. In this  case, it was especially important that the analysis be efficient  because neither scan ATPG nor scan chain analysis were  available to determine the root cause. The arbitration among  many chip modules needed to be probed to determine if the  root cause was a design problem or was related to defectivity.


On one failing device, an incorrect signal that put the device in  test control, or scan mode was traced back with TRLEM  probing. Figure 1 shows the waveforms from the design  simulation.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa203


Figure 1: Simulation waveforms showing proper entry into  test control, or scan mode.


The six pulses at the bottom of Figure 1 are two waveforms  that indicate that the device is going into scan mode properly. The system clock is the waveform at top. Figure 2 shows the  TRLEM signals probed on a passing and failing unit. The  pulses represent time resolved photons emitted on the falling  edges for the signals shown in Figure 1. The scale is 500  ns/div. The peaks are actually gaussian with a full width half  maximum of approximately 200 ps. This number is driven by  tester and detector jitter. Rising edges are not detected here  due to the relative inefficiency of PFET devices in emitting  photons. In later analyses, also presented, improvements to  detector quantum efficiency allowed detection of rising edges.


Figure 2: TRLEM waveforms comparing a passing (middle/green) and failing (bottom/red) unit. Scale is  500ns/div..


The clock is shown as the top waveform in Figure 2. The  green signal is the output of a feedback circuit with a single  input to start the generation of the six output pulses shown in  Figure 1. This input was probed and was correct. The red  waveform shows the output of the feedback circuit on the  failing unit.


The absence of the six pulses in the circuit output could only  be caused by the feedback loop being open. Physical  deprocessing revealed a voided via in the feedback net.


Analysis on six other units with the same failure mode also


revealed defects and several NDF’s (no defect found). The  overall analysis isolated the root cause to defects and absolved  the design. The cycle time for this analysis result would have  been much greater if other methods would have been used.


Case Study 2: Timing Race Condition


During the transfer of a mobile phone baseband controller  design from one fab to another, a problem was encountered  with the device jumping to an invalid DSP memory location.    Experimentation determined that the DSP core was fetching  the wrong ROM address during the standard code sequencing, resulting in the DSP becoming “lost”.  The timing  measurements in this analysis would have been very difficult  to obtain using conventional topside probing methodologies.  The loading from the probes would have skewed the timing  measurements and the signal lines would have been difficult to  access.  Backside probing using the TRLEM system  eliminated both of these concerns.


An evaluation board was used to duplicate the failure mode.  Code was written to first load the lower half of the PRAM (Program RAM) memory (addresses $6400 - $7FFF) with a  JSR $9B9B instruction (jump to a subroutine located at  address $9B9B).  The upper half of the PRAM memory (addresses $8000 - $FFFF) was then loaded with unique  illegal opcodes.  Finally, an RTS (Return) instruction was  written to location $9B9B within the PRAM.  If the code was  executed properly, the devices would begin executing the JSR  instructions and then return to the next address in PRAM, i.e., a JSR from $9B9B from address $6400 should return from the  subroutine to address $6402.  The JSR/RTS sequences were  checked for all of the locations in the lower half of the PRAM.  Depending on the severity of the failure, the device being  tested would fail for a certain number of the JSR/RTS  sequences.  When a failure occurred, the device would return  to an incorrect address within the upper range of the PRAM.  By reviewing the data that was fetched from the incorrect  return address (one of the illegal opcodes), the incorrect  address value could be determined.  In most cases, the  incorrect address was off by only one bit, A15.  For example, if the JSR was executed from location $6402, the RTS  instruction would incorrectly return to location $E404.


TRLEM probing was used to acquire signals from the  backside of the die.  This allowed access to multiple signals in  a short amount of time versus topside probing which would  require probe pads to be placed on each signal node.  The  probing was begun in the DSP core address generation  circuitry for the address bus signals.  The address signals  within the DSP core were found to match the simulation.


The probing effort was then focused on the address decode  circuitry within the PRAM module.  Figure 3 contains a  schematic of the PRAM address buffer latch circuit.  The  krd_b signal acts as the clock for the latch.  The ain signal is  the data input to the latch.  It represents one of the 16 address  bits being latched by the PRAM.  The q signal represents the  latched address bit within the PRAM.  If the krd_b signal  transitions high before the address input switches, the latch  will not capture the state change on the address line for that  clock cycle.  When the transition is not captured, the incorrect  return address is fetched during the RTS operation. This  results in a system malfunction because an illegal instruction  is fetched from the incorrect address.


krd_b


Figure 3: Schematic of the PRAM address buffer latch circuit.  The krd_b signal acts as the clock to the latch.


Figures 4 and 5 contain the TRLEM waveforms acquired for a  failing (A15) and passing (A7) address bit (drawn  representations of the waveforms are also included to make  the transitions on the signals more understandable).  The  TRLEM waveforms are similar to those shown in Figure 2 at a  finer time resolution. The A15 waveforms show that the krd_b  signal is transitioning at approximately the same time as the  A15 signal input to the latch circuit.  Because these two edges  occur simultaneously, the latch fails to register the high to low  transition on the A15 line within the memory decode.  This  high to low transition represents the switching from address $9B9B to $6402.  For the failing condition, this transition does  not occur and the data at address $E402 is fetched.  The A7  waveforms show that the krd_b signal goes high  approximately 750ps before the A7 signal from the DSP  transitions low.  This allows the latch to register the high to  low transition on the A7 line and this is reflected by the  transition on the latch output.  The waveforms have been  magnified to illustrate the timing relationships between the  signals.  The timing measurements were determined by taking  the full-width half-maximum (FWHM) points on the acquired  waveforms.  The issue was fixed by inserting additional delay  into the krd_b signal to assure that all of the address bits  would transition before the krd_b signal went high.

Case Study 3: Scan Chain Failure


The TRLEM technique has been proven to be a very efficient  technique in identifying defectivity issues responsible for yield  losses in wafer fabs. The following three cases are a perfect  demonstration of its accuracy and efficiency.


A 0.13 um bulk CMOS SOC was experiencing a double digit  fall-out in scan chain probe yields. After assembling the  reported failing die in a flip-chip package and subsequently  back thinning their substrate, the TRLEM technique could be  used.


The scan chains are exercised by shifting a succession of


“11001100” patterns from the scan chain input through a  succession of scan enabled latches to the scan output. The  tester reads the data transmitted at the scan output and  compares it with the expected data. By conducting a binary  search along latches of a failing scan chain, the individual  instance where the scan data path appears broken or abnormal  can be quickly and accurately identified.


TRLEM was used in such a manner in the case described here. While the correct high to low and low to high transitions could  be detected at the output of early instances of the chain, they  were no longer detected as expected at the output of scan latch “dft_cmlm_reg”. See Figures 6 and 7. Latch “dft_cmlm_reg” was consequently identified as the failing instance of the  chain.

Case Study 4: Scan Chain Failure


In another instance, a SOC built on a 0.13 um CMOS bulk


process was also experiencing a double-digit yield fallout for  scan chain testing.


TRLEM analysis identified a faulty latch on the first part  under investigation. In this case, an abnormal TRLEM signal  was detected at the output of latch labeled 318 as displayed on  Figure 9. This type of waveform typically indicates that one of  the transistors controlling the output is not turning completely

TRLEM probing of the  subsequent latch in the chain, latch 317, indicated there were  no scan data transitioning at its output. Based on these results, it was concluded that latch 318 was the likely instance where  the failing scan chain was broken.

In order to confirm the TRLEM finding, top-side mechanical  microprobing of the faulty latch was carried out. It revealed  that latch 318 metal 2 output was in fact shorted to an adjacent  metal 2 line as described on Figures 10 a,b.

TRLEM analysis of additional failing units quickly identified  other faulty latches and based on the initial finding, via1 pairs  with minimum spacing became the main suspects. Subsequent  inspection of these via1 pairs confirmed the initial failure


mechanism as the “killer” defect for this wafer lot. Figure 12  gives another example of such via1 bridging resulting in a  scan chain failure.


The corrective action taken to solve this issue was a mask  change to physically off-set via1’s forming a pair of minimum  spacing.

Case Study 5: Scan Chain Failure


In this section, two scan chain analyses demonstrate the  efficiency of using TRLEM to address significant yield loss in  first silicon products. A few setup issues, which were  experienced during the probing process, are also described.


In the two devices analyzed, abnormal TRLEM waveforms  were detected within the failing latches. An attempt was made  to locate these small local emission sites using conventional  backside LEM, but only half of the sites were detectable. Furthermore, even the emission sites that were detected did  not all correspond to the defective location.  Hence, although  traditional light emission microscopy might be able to detect  these small local photon emissions, probing using the TRLEM  microscope is also necessary in most of the situations. The  location of the emission can be narrowed down to a 2 um x 1  um area. Hence, once the failing latch was isolated through a  binary search, local emission sites were detected by marching  the detector field of view through the whole latch. This  narrowed the inspection area further and increased the success  rate in locating a physical defect. Figures 13 and 14 show the  TRLEM signals captured on these two scan chain failures. In  Figure 13, the light emission occurred only when the output of  the failing latch (Latch 143 output) was at a low logic level. Furthermore, the light emission was found only at the output  of the defective latch. In Figure 14, the light emission was  isolated near the input of the faulty latch.


Figure 13: Shows the local light emission site found during  the TRLEM probing. The photons only emitted when the


output of the latch was at a low logic level.


Figure 14: Shows another example of the local light emission  site found during the TRLEM probing. In this faulty latch,


photons were emitted continuously.


After deprocessing, polysilicon bridges were found at the light  emission sites in both scan chain failures. This type of poly  bridge is sensitive to the layout, so the defect  will randomly appear in the same type of cell layout  implemented all over the die. For these cases, the layout  sensitivity causing the bridge happened to be inside the scan


latches. This explained the excessive scan chain failures  observed in first silicon for these products. Figures 15 and 16  show the SEM photos of the defects found in these different  devices. Using the analysis results, the fab quickly addressed  the layout sensitive photolithography issue.


Figure 15:  Shows a SEM image of a polysilicon bridge found  inside a faulty scan latch.


Figure 16: Shows a SEM image of a polysilicon bridge found  in the second scan chain analysis.


When using the TRLEM system to analyze these scan chain  failures, two problems were encountered. In one of the  devices, the normal Idd drawn was over 1.5A and since there  was no copper at the back of the die to serve as a heat sink (the  backside of the die was exposed and thinned during sample  preparation), the failing device was severely overheated. In  addition, the excessive heat generated a significant amount of  thermal noise and over time damaged the device.  To solve  this problem, compressed air was blown directly onto the die  when probing. The second problem encountered during the  analysis was caused by a device not failing consistently when  looping over the scan-in code.  In this particular case, the  failure was always verified by running the pattern once.


However, in doing a loop, incorrect data was found passing  through the chain and it was collected by the TRLEM system  each time the pattern was executed. Because the failing  circuitry was not exercised the same way each time the loop  was executed, incorrect data was collected and the TRLEM  signals were difficult to interpret. In this case, the problem  was resolved by modifying the operating voltage and  frequency of the device such that the chain always failed.


The length of the scan chains of the two devices was 816 and  316 latches. The average time required to localize the failing  latch in the broken chain was approximately 2 hours.


Feedback for 1st silicon issues and process excursions is often  urgently needed. In this paper,  five case studies have been  presented where feedback was made available in a very timely  and efficient manner. The efficiency of these analyses allowed  for multiple samples to be analyzed to be certain that the real  killer defect was isolated, and that the defect found was not  random defectivity.


Future work will include scan logic failures using the  information from ATPG and DFS tools to isolate defects in  the chip logic which are propagated out through the scan  chain.

Photon Emission Microscopy in 90 nm CMOS Technologies


Bram Kruseman, Martijn Goossens, and Victor Zieren


Philips Research Laboratories,


WAY41, Prof. Holstlaan 4, 5656 AA Eindhoven, The Netherlands


The capabilities of photon emission microscopy with CCD


and MCT camera systems for the 90 nm CMOS technology  node were investigated. This was done with a dedicated test  circuit with selectable shorts with resistance between 0 to 40  kΩ. Our investigations showed that conventional PEM with  CCD systems is not possible anymore due to the reduction in  photon emission intensity in the visible range. However, photon emission can be enhanced by using elevated supply  voltages. For these overdrive conditions PEM with a CCD  system is still feasible. We furthermore show that PEM is in  principle capable of determining the state of a circuit and that  PEM in combination with defect simulations can determine  defect characteristics. In this manner, for example, the  resistance of a short can be estimated by localising the PMOST emission spot.


Photon emission microscopy (PEM) is one of the main failure  analysis techniques. The direct link between an affected  transistor and a light emission spot makes it very useful for the  localisation of defects. The technique was threatened in the  90's when the amount of metal layers and the introduction of  tiles hampered the observability from the frontside. This threat  was removed by the introduction of backside PEM. Moreover, the technique has been extended by time-resolved PEM which  allows to investigate the dynamic behaviour of circuits [1,2]. A remaining issue for PEM is the reduction of the supply  voltage in advanced technologies. This reduction in supply  voltage decreases the number of `hot electrons', which are  responsible for impact ionisation (the conventional source for  light emission). Furthermore, the spectrum will shift to longer  wavelengths due to a reduction in electron temperature. Figure  1 shows how this affects the light emission expressed as  photo-electrons generated in CCD and HgCdTe (MCT) camera systems for different technologies.


This graph was constructed as follows. First, the substrate  current (peak) per transistor width W was calculated for  NMOSTs in six technology nodes (nA/µm). Next, from  spectral PEM analysis (400-900 nm range) for NMOSTs in


0.18 µm and earlier nodes, we know that a proportionality of  about 10-7 W/A exists between photon output  power and   Isub.

The calculations are based on the  nominal supply voltage and a Vgs, which gives maximum  emission. Vertical dotted lines indicate the range applicable  to a commercial MCT PEM system with a  cryogenic filter.


Extrapolation into the NIR leads to a (conservative) estimate  of 6200 photons/s generated by 1 nA of Isub. Based on  Maxwell-Boltzman statistics, this number was used to  calculate the photon distribution function (photons/eV/s/µm). In this photon distribution function we inserted an effective  electron temperature based on an empirical relation to the bias  conditions as established with previous spectral PEM


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa210


analyses. Finally, when we assume that all emitted photons  arrive at one camera pixel (which is true for at least one  dimension of the emission stripe), the camera’s quantum  efficiency (electrons/photon) is included and we arrive at  Figure 1.


Integration of the curve (yielding INTW in e-/s/µm) and  accounting for the transistor width W, camera pixel size (Wpix) and optics (mainly objective lens (M and NA)) yields the total  number of photoelectrons (S) after an integration time texp:


S=texp. INTW . NA2. min(W, Wpix/M)


S should be sufficiently larger than the camera’s detection  limit (mainly dark current noise) to allow detection. If one  compares two successive technology nodes then we observe a  strong reduction in the number of generated electrons of more  than an order of magnitude. This is directly related to the  reduction in the number of hot electrons (and emitted  photons). Additionally we see that the slope of the curve  becomes steeper. This is related to the lower electron  temperature.


Figure 1 indicates that the amount of photons in the visible  range is strongly reduced. Also the typical transistor width  becomes smaller and as a result the expected emission rate is  becoming too small to be detectable. The reduction in  capabilities of CCD based camera systems is the main reason  that led to the introduction of MCT systems, which are  sensitive in the infra-red spectrum. However, Figure 1 shows  that also the capabilities of an MCT system are affected and  that it will run out of steam in the future. It is therefore upfront  unclear what one can expect of PEM (either with a CCD or  MCT camera system) in a new technology. To be able to  address this we designed a circuit with selectable shorts. The


chip was processed in a 90 nm technology. Some of the more  interesting observations, viz. the potential for logic mapping  and photon emission of P-MOS transistors, are covered in this  paper.


Figure 2: Circuit under test.


Experimental setup


Circuit under test


The circuit under test is a small test circuit of 5k standard cell  gates (see Figure 2) without any dynamic logic. The main  purpose of this circuit is to evaluate failure analysis and test  methods. This is achieved by incorporating shorts in the  design. Figure 3 shows the typical structure employed. This  structure consists of two inverter chains controlled and  observed by flip-flops. The two chains are connected to each  other by a ‘short’. If both flip-flops contain the same values  the defect is inactive, if they contain opposite values the defect  is active. The impact of a short strongly depends on the  resistance of the short in combination with the driver strength  of the involved transistors. Therefore resistances of 0 (hard  short) up to 40 kΩ were incorporated in combination with two  driver strengths of the inverters. The impact of these designed ‘shorts' is comparable to real shorts. Some combinations will  cause stuck-at fault behaviour while others are only  observable with Iddq testing. Furthermore, we can activate  and deactivate the impact of the defect. This makes it easy to  separate general technology characteristics from defect  characteristics. These capabilities make the test circuit well  suited to evaluate the capabilities of PEM in 90 nm  technologies.
