Reliability of polycrystalline MEMS : prediction of the debugging-time


O. Millet *


DELFMEMS


IEMN, Cité scientifique, Avenue Poincaré, B.P. 69, 59652 Villeneuve d'Ascq Cedex, France


* Corresponding author: Tel. (+33) 3 20 19 79 79, Fax (+33) 3 20 19 78 84,


olivier.millet@delfmems.com


P. Bertrand, B. Legrand, L. Buchaillot


# Reliability of polycrystalline MEMS : prediction of the debugging-time


2 IEMN, Silicon Microsystems Group, Institut d'Electronique, de Micro-Electronique et de Nanotechnologie, ISEN Dpt. IEMN, UMR CNRS 8520, Cité scientifique, Avenue Poincaré, B.P. 69, 59652 Villeneuve d'Ascq Cedex, FRANCE


D. Collard


CIRMM / IIS-CNRS, Institute of Industrial Sciences. The University of Tokyo


The debugging-time for polycrystalline MEMS structural  layers is the aim of this paper. A description of the fatigue  phenomenon for elementary structure in the case of  microactuators is presented. It is obtained by combining  elementary in situ test benches of varying dimensions and  cyclic actuation; in the same way, the debugging-time is  determined according to the design and the structural  material. Test benches have been developed allowing  performance of bending fatigue tests of polycrystalline  structural layers, describing the fatigue phenomenon and  obtaining a constant debugging-time for a same  polycrystalline layer, whatever the excitation frequency and  the beams length.


One of the final goals of the reliability study is to get a  predictive modeling, indicating the evolution of the dynamic  system behavior when subjected to high-cyclic actuation. It  is important to note that cyclic stresses induce material  degradation via the generation and motion of dislocations. The fatigue phenomenon has been studied for single-crystal  materials: the first work on the cyclic fatigue of Si MEMS  structures was done by Connally and Brown, showing that  cyclic damage processes can appear in this type of structures


[1]. Van Arsdell and Brown et al. have established that  polysilicon undergoes fatigue damage under ambient  environment [2]. Afterwards, Muhlstein et al. have  presented successive and significant works suggesting the  influence of the native SiO2 layer thickness on the Si  structures [3]. Sandia Lab. has worked on the lifetime of  multi-levels polysilicon microengines and on the influence  of the environment (vibration, humidity, etc.) on the failure  probability [4]. Millet et al. has studied the fatigue  phenomenon for polycrystalline materials [5].


This work aims at showing the debugging-time existence  and determining it for polycrystalline layers by observing  the fatigue phenomenon for elementary structure in the case  of microactuators. Based on M-Test [6], test benches have  been actuated allowing performing bending fatigue tests of  polycrystalline structural layers, showing the existence of a


debugging-time and obtaining a predictive modeling for the  debugging-time determination.


This paper presents recent experimental evidences of  debugging-time. Firstly, the used in situ benches are  described. Secondly, FEM analysis of the structures will be  presented in order to determine the stress induced during  actuation, followed by the fabrication process presentation. After the characterization methods and the experimental  results of the fatigue tests are presented. Afterwards, the  determination of the predictive modeling is explained. Finally, the built predictive modeling is experimentally  validated.


Principle


In the case of the surface micromachining, the use of  electrostatic forces involves the preponderance of bending  over other mechanical solicitations due to the capacitive  coupling. So, to quantify the fatigue phenomenon in  dynamic mode, it appears interesting to analyze the  evolution of properties (stiffness, etc.) of mechanical  structures, which are submitted to a bending stress due to  upward and downward movements, vs. the number of  operations. M-Test benches are suitable as in situ test  benches for fatigue test for several reasons [6]. First, bending tests induce large displacements but require small  force as M-Test structures already studied. Secondly, microelectromechanical systems are often the combination  of elementary parts (beams, membranes) as M-Test  structures. Finally, test procedures of this type of devices  have already been setup, like pull-in voltage measurement. One specific structure is studied here consisting of clampedclamped beams with a buried electrode placed underneath  the mechanical layer. The principle of the designed benches  is that under electrostatic forces action, the free plate  achieves out-of-plane displacements. During fatigue tests, the structure is then submitted to a cyclic actuation and is  characterized every n cycles. The ‘movable plate’/’fixed  electrode’ gap is 2 µm. The structure is 50 µm in width (w), its length (L) ranges from 200 µm to 500 µm by step of  50 µm and its thickness (t) is (2 µm, polysilicon) or (0.6 µm, gold).


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa221


Fabrication


The fabrication process of the test benches is based on  surface micromachining and requires two levels (buried  electrode, structural layer). The structural materials of the  devices are either gold or polysilicon doped by diffusion.


Polysilicon process


A 0.35 µm oxidation is performed followed by the first Low  Pressure Chemical Vapor Deposition (LPCVD) n-doped  polysilicon layer (Fig. 1b). After electrode patterning (Fig. 1c), the polysilicon was oxidized (Fig. 1d) and covered by a  LPCVD low stress SixNy layer (Fig. 1e). A 2 µm Low  Temperature Oxide (LTO) (Fig. 1f) was deposited followed  by the Reaction Ion Etching (RIE) of contacts (Fig. 1g). A  2 µm LPCVD polysilicon layer was deposited (Fig. 1g). This layer is doped by diffusing dopants in the polysicon via  the use of a PhosphoSilicate Glass layer (removed in  Hydrofluoric acid –HF- after diffusion). The structural  pattern was defined by SF6, CF4 and O2 RIE (Fig. 1h). Next  the structure was annealed at 1000°c for 60 min to relax  residual stress. Finally, the structure has been released using  HF (see Fig.1i, 2).


Figure 1: Thin film surface micromachining of polysilicon  structures with one structural layer.


Gold process


A 0.35 µm Plasma Enhanced Chemical Vapor Deposition (PECVD) oxide is deposited followed by the evaporation of  Titanium (0,1 µm) and Gold (0,25 µm). After electrode  patterning, the metallic bilayer is covered by a PECVD  Si3N4 layer at 200°C. A 2 µm PMGI photoresist was  deposited followed by the etching of bushing and contact. Aluminum mask (0,1 µm) was used during etching. A  0,6 µm gold was sputtered. The structural pattern was  defined by chemical etching. Finally, the structure has been  released using O2 RIE and EBRPG etching.


Testing


Modeling


CoventorWareTM has been used to analyze the systems; via  Finite Element Method (FEM), the natural frequencies of


the structures have been found. Moreover, simulations have  allowed the determination of the actuation voltages and the  level of applied stress during actuation of the structure (Figure 2).


Figure 2: a) Meshed structure consisted in (10 µm, 30 µm, 1 µm) brick elements on CoventorwareTM. (b) Picture of the  simulated structure in pull-in configuration, with the  concentration of high stresses in the vicinity of the clamped  ends.


Measurements


Optical and interferometer images of polysilicon structures  are shown in Figure (3); it can be observed that the movable  structural parts have a negligible stress gradient (that is, no  buckling or bending of the microbridges). Finally, a  Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) picture reveals nanoscale structure with an average grain size of about 0.1-0.2 µm (see Fig. 3).


Figure 3: (a, b) SEM picture of the nanoscale Si, Au grains


(c) Visual observation of no-stressed polysilicon clampedclamped beams observed with interferometer. (d) 3D view  of the in situ test gold benches.


Next, cyclic electrostatic actuation has been performed in air  environment; electromechanical determination -pull-in  voltage measurement- has been used to characterize the  stiffness of the tested beams (Figure 4). A buried electrode is  underneath the microbridge and a direct visual observation  via optical microscopy techniques allows the detection of the  pull-in, aided by the buried electrode/microbeam capacitance  observation. A slowly voltage ramp is applied between the  two electrodes until the pull-in detection. Moreover, electrical resistance variations of the tested structures have  been measured during cyclic actuation phase.


Figure 4: Pull-in voltage measurement combined to  electrical resistance determination


The test procedure for the analysis of the evolution of the  stiffness vs. the number of operations is: the test benches are  initially characterized and are next actuated in the air using  an alternative current signal. The actuation voltage  corresponds to the last measured pull-in voltage and the  excitation frequency is synchronized to the first natural  frequency estimated via FEM analysis. Afterwards, every  n cycles, the in situ benches are characterized, allowing the  observation of the evolution of the stiffness vs. the number  of functioning cycles (Figure 5). Concerning electrical  resistance measurements, a low current is applied to result in  a very low Joule heating in order to avoid plastic  deformation of the polysilicon.


From the experimental results, it can be shown that the  fatigue phenomenon can be divided in five different phases (Figure 5, 6) due to several successive failure mechanisms: dislocations in the grain joints, microcracks apparition, compression of grains, dislocation in the grains and a  stability phase (Figure 6) [7]. At that point, a change from  operations number scale to time scale has been realized by  normalizing to the resonant frequency of the beams (Figure 5); the time scale is then the time of actuation at the  resonance frequency. This modification has allowed  observing that stiffness evolutions of all tested beams were  stable after a constant time that we define as the debuggingtime (Figure 5).


Figure 5: Conversion from operations number scale to time  scale in the case of the evolution of the stiffness of  polysilicon clamped-clamped beams


Figure 6: Evolution of the stiffness and of the electrical  resistance vs. the number of operations, in the case of a  beam submitted to cyclic actuation and characterized with  an electro-mechanical technique (pull-in measurement).


An average of all points’ x-coordinates (representing the  beginning of the stability phase) has been performed to get  an estimate of the debugging-time, based on experimental  results obtained with (200, 250, 350, 400, 450) µm length  beams (Figure 6). The estimated debugging-time of the  tested structural layer is then 6100 seconds in the case of  polysilicon layers (actuation during 6100 seconds at  resonance frequency) (Figure 5), and 5400 seconds for gold  structures.


Based on the division of the ‘stability point’ x-coordinates (Figure 3) by the resonant frequency of a clamped-clamped


beam, the debugging-time of a specific polycrystalline  structural material determining the beginning of the stiffness  stability phase can be established. This prediction has been  validated with experimental results (i.e. obtained with (300, 500) µm length beams) not included in the first estimation  of the debugging-time (Figure 7), the error is 17% (Figure  7). These results show that the debugging-time can be  predictable, the total error being less than 12 %. Finally, the  built modeling allows predicting when the stability of the  beam stiffness occurs; concerning the stiffness value, the  modeling only gives qualitative data (decrease during  stability is 5-10%).


Figure 7: Comparison between the predictive debuggingtime and the experimental results concerning the evolution  of the stiffness vs. the number of operations.


Finally, the modeling has been validated with structures that  were not excited at the resonant frequency, allowing  confirmation that the fatigue phenomenon does not depend  on the time and on excitation frequency. Thus, no tracking  of the resonance frequency was required during cyclic  actuation of the structures.


This study presents behavior of polysilicon/gold elementary  microbeams, which are submitted to elementary movements (bending). Test benches have been used to analyze the  fatigue phenomenon. It appears that this phenomenon can be  divided in four different phases and a stability phase. It has  been shown that the debugging-time of the structures can be  predicted and is linked to the structural material. This  modeling allows predicting the debugging- time of clampedclamped beam; it will have to be taken into account to  improve the design and reliability of RF switches or  electromechanical radiofrequency filters.

Failure Analysis of Electrothermal Actuators Subjected to  Electrical Overstress (EOS) and Electrostatic Discharge (ESD)


Jeremy A. Walraven, Richard Plass, Michael S. Baker, and Michael J. Shaw


Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM  USA  jawalra@sandia.gov


Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) that sense, think,


and act are enabling technologies currently employed in many  industrial applications.  To operate these devices, a stimulus is  required to produce motion.  In MEMS, this stimulus may be  thermal actuation using current to produce joule heating, or  electrostatic actuation using voltages to create electric fields.  To qualify MEMS technology, these devices must undergo  repeated characterization and testing and at both the die and  system level.  Electrical overstress (EOS) and electrostatic  discharge (ESD) are two important tests used to assess the  robustness of a device to steady state and sharp voltage and  current transients.  Identifying the failure mechanism and  understanding the root causes for failure is paramount to the  overall improvement and success of any MEMS based system.  In this paper we will focus on the effects of EOS and ESD  events on surface micromachined polysilicon based  electrothermal actuators fabricated using the SUMMiT V process.


EOS and ESD events have been shown to severely damage  ICs, semiconductors, photonic devices, and MEMS [1-3].  The  damaging effects and loss of product due to EOS and ESD  have led to a host of device handling procedures that are now  industry standards.  Assessing the damage caused by EOS and  ESD in MEMS is relatively simple.  In MEMS technology, the location and degree of damage will be easier to identify  than their IC counterparts.  The degree of damage will be


# Failure Analysis of Electrothermal Actuators Subjected to Electrical Overstress (EOS) and Electrostatic Discharge (ESD)


based on device design, fabrication layers and materials, and  method of stimulation.  Since MEMS components are  designed to perform a variety of tasks such as route optical  signals, detect chemical changes, etc., the stimulated area of  the device (or components in close proximity) will be affected  by an EOS or ESD event.  Methods for stimulating or  producing motion in MEMS include electrostatic actuation, opto-thermal actuation, and electro-thermal actuation.  The  devices used in this experiment were powered using electrothermal actuation.


Electrothermal Actuator Design and Operation


Electrothermal actuators (or bent beam thermal actuators) are  devices designed to operate using current to create Joule  heating in the applied area.  Joule heating leads to thermal  expansion of the polysilicon resulting in device displacement  either in the x, y, or z direction.  For the devices used in this  experiment, thermal expansion produces a displacement in the  plane of the wafer.


The devices used in this experiment are fabricated in a  shallow V-type symmetry and provide tens of microns of  displacement as well as hundreds of micro-newtons of force  output.  Typical V-type thermal actuators consist of legs, a  central shuttle, anchors with contacts, and a shuttle guide as  shown in Fig. 1.  In this experiment, the polysilicon legs are ~ 300 µm long with widths ranging from 3.0 – 4.5 µm and  fabricated at offset angles ranging from 0.7 to 2.3o.  The offset  angles are designed to provide a direction of throw, and also  determine the geometric amplification factor for the output  displacement.  The legs are designed to be thicker (normal to  the substrate) than they are wide to prevent out-of-plane

To understand the force output and amount of displacement, it  is necessary to know the amount the legs expand.  If the  temperature profile along the heated leg is known, the thermal  expansion of each leg design can be calculated using:

Where α is the temperature dependant coefficient of thermal  expansion for polysilicon, T(x) is the temperature of the beam  at position x, and Tsubstrate is the temperature of the substrate


[4].  Knowing the expansion, one can derive the force exerted  by the component using finite-element techniques.


The leg design of these actuators is fabricated in the shape of  an I-beam comprising of various layers of polysilicon shown  in Fig. 2.  The I-beam design allows for actuators to be  fabricated that are more resistant to out-of-plane deflection  while still increasing the cross-sectional area and beam width.  Larger cross-sectional areas and wider legs result in higher  force output.  The versatility in design is one of the strengths  of the electrothermal actuator over its electrostatic  counterpart.  This device can be tailored to deliver a specific  force output based on leg width, thickness, length, and offset  angle [5].  Control of stimulus parameters such as current, voltage, and pulse time also contributes to tailoring the force  output and displacement.


The electrothermal actuators used in this experiment are  operated using 8-12 V with 10 – 20 mA based on device  design.  Since electrothermal actuators operate based on Joule  heating, controlled duration voltage/current pulses can be used  to heat the legs (controllably) to produce the desired force and  displacement.  The duration of the pulse and values of current  and voltage depend on how quickly a device is intended to  reach the temperature for thermal actuation.  For rapid pulses, higher voltages and currents are needed to heat the structure  more quickly to increase the actuation speed and produce a  given force and displacement output.  The same temperature  can be achieved using steady-state voltages with lower voltage  and current settings if actuation speed is not a concern.


EOS/ESD Test Procedures


EOS Procedure


EOS tests were performed by sequentially increasing the  voltage and current applied to the actuator under static (DC) conditions.  Each voltage/current state was held for ~ 1 min.  The actuator was brought back to a zero voltage state and  analyzed after each stress test [6].  In this setup, an  electrothermal actuator is stressed at one volt for one minute.  After analysis, if the device has no observed damage or  degradation, the voltage is increased (in one volt increments) and analyzed again until failure or changes in device geometry  or surface texture is observed.  Changes in surface texture are  noted and the test proceeds.  The objective of this experiment  was to allow the electrothermal actuators to reach thermal  equilibrium with power applied and assess the effects of a  device left in a continuous powered state.


ESD Procedure


ESD tests were performed using the human body model (HBM) and machine model (MM) ESD transient models.  These tests are designed to simulate an electrostatic discharge  through human contact and machine short circuits.  For the  HBM, the model is based on contact with the device having  the discharge occur through the tip of the finger.  For the MM, the model is based on a discharge from a low resistance  component to the device under test.  In both instances, the  maximum pulse is delivered within the first 5 – 25 ns (5 – 10  ns for MM and 15 – 25 ns for HBM).  Examples of the HBM  and MM equivalent circuit diagrams are shown in Fig. 3a and  b.  In the HBM ESD model, the discharge is forced through a  1500Ω resistor with an exponential drop in voltage, whereas  the MM pulse is a direct short with minimal resistance and  significant ringing as shown in Fig. 4a and b.


The HBM and MM waveform required by this test standard is  similar to that of MIL-STD-883D Method 3015.7, but the  characteristic ESD stress test methods are refined to assure  optimal HBM and MM ESD event simulation fidelity.  These  ESD tests followed the MIL-SDT specifications for single  pulse events.  After each test, the device was electrically and  optically analyzed for structural and electrical integrity.  Failures were defined as devices with damaged or nonfunctional components.  HBM tests were performed using an

IMCS Model 2500 ESD tester.  An HP 4155 Parametric  Analyzer was used to electrically analyze the device after each  ESD pulse.   MM ESD tests were performed at a qualified  service company using a Thermo KeyTek ZapMasters  instrument.


A MEMS EOS/ESD failure is defined as the inability of a  device to operate to designed specifications.  Since  electrothermal actuators operate using specific voltage/current  waveforms to drive displacement and force, the voltage and  current required to induce failure will vary based upon device  design and device dimensions.  Failure mechanisms ranging  from electrical shorting to particle contamination will render a  device inoperable.  Results from the EOS, HBM, and MM  tests are discussed below


EOS


Several electrothermal actuators have been stressed under  EOS conditons.  EOS failures in ambient laboratory  conditions occurred as the result of excessive heating leading  to significant damage and deformation along the polysilicon  legs.  Evidence has shown significant changes in surface  texture and device geometry of the electrothermal actuator  after an EOS test as shown in Fig. 5a and b.  This is an  extreme example of thermal degradation resulting in failure  and not typical of normal operation.  In this example, a device  is held at 14 V pulling approximately 21 mA (300 mW) through the device until it failed (during the one minute  holding period).  These results, compared to the functional as  fabricated electrothermal actuators in Fig. 1 and 2c, show  distinct differences between geometries and surface  topographies.  The dominant failure mechanism resulting from  sequential EOS stresses is oxidation along the polysilicon leg, roughening and degradation of the surface of the leg,

Fig. 3a and b.  HBM and MM circuit models. [7]


Fig. 5a and b.  EOS damage to a poly123 electrothermal actuator tested in ambient laboratory condition at 14 V pulling ~ 300 mW.  Note the molten polysilicon.

deformation of the leg (from its as fabricated geometry) and  finally melting.


Thermal modeling of an electrothermal actuator of the same  design as those used in these experiments was performed.  In  an electrothermal actuator, heat is generated from current  passing through the polysilicon legs.  Heat is lost through  conduction into the substrate, radiation, free convection, and  heat conduction through the air [6].  At these dimensions, radiation and convection are negligible, and conduction along  the legs and through the air into the substrate are of great  importance.  The properties of interest for thermal modeling  include thermal conductivity of the poly and air environment, electrical resistivity, and coefficient of thermal expansion.  To  assess the effects of heating, a finite-difference thermal code  was developed using Matlab to solve for the temperature  profile along the length of a single heated leg, and integrate  the thermal strain along the leg.  When a device is operated in  ambient laboratory conditions, the dominant mechanism for  heat loss is conduction from the heated legs through the  surrounding air and into the substrate [6].  The predictive  model for a poly 123 device configured with 3 µm wide legs  that are 300 µm long at 5.03 V should pull 10.19 mA and  generate ~ 250oC in ambient laboratory conditions.  The  results shown from thermal image analysis in Fig. 6 reveal a  lower temperature (212.6oC) than that predicted by the model.  We believe the experimental results are less accurate due to  the difficulty associated with obtaining a thermal image based  on device geometry, tool resolution ((10 µm spot size) based  on device geometry (2 – 4 µm)) and heat dissipation through  the air and substrate.  Accurate heat measurements of 3 µm  wide legs using an instrument with 10 µm resolution will lead  to blurred or lost temperature resolution, but do provide a  qualitative idea of temperatures generated as well as potential  local hotspots during operation.


Twelve poly123 devices w/ 300 µm long legs were tested  under these conditions.  Overall, EOS failures in ambient  laboratory condition occurred between 12 and 15 V w/ power  levels ranging from 260 – 300 mW.  Significant plastic  deformation in the legs was observed prior to catastrophic  failure (melting of the polysilicon legs).  Changes in surface  morphology and texture were observed indicating grain  movement and/or growth, and a change in polysilicon leg  geometry.  All of these damage mechanisms are harmful to the  device.  Deformation of the legs (without melting) will result  in unintentional displacements.


ESD


Electrostatic discharge tests were performed on electrothermal  actuators using the human body model (HBM) and machine  model (MM) ESD waveforms.  The results of these ESD test  revealed a surprising failure mechanism.  Instead of melting or  thermal degradation as we have seen in the EOS tests, electrothermal actuators failed as a result of fracture at high  stress locations.  As shown in the as-fabricated sample in Fig. 1, the high stress concentration sites will be located on the  connections between the poly legs and shuttle, and poly legs  and anchor.  As shown in Fig. 7a and b, a thermal actuator  suffered two fractures on two legs at the same anchor region  of the actuation pad after a 1900 V single pulse HBM ESD  transient.  Closer examination of the fracture site of the


Fig. 6.  Thermal image of a poly123 electrothermal actuator driven at 5.01 V pulling 10.589 mA to achieve 219.6oC.  These  results differ from the parameters predicted in the model to achieve 250oC.


Fig. 7a and b.  a) Fractured polysilicon legs along the anchor of a 1900 V HBM ESD transient .  b) Close examination of the fracture surface of the bottom leg does NOT show signs of thermal degradation attributing to failure.


bottom leg (Fig. 7b) reveals no sign of thermal degradation  that could have attributed to its failure.  This result indicates a  high degree of force was exerted from the device to induce  fracture.


Fracture induced failures were not limited to the anchor  region.  Several thermal actuators revealed failures at the other  stress concentration sites.  As shown in Fig. 8a and b, similar  fracture observed along the shuttle area is not attributed to  thermal degradation of the device.  Again, severe force was  required to damage the device or force it to actuate beyond its  designed tolerance.


The same failure mechanism was found in MM ESD tested  components where damage was observed at both the anchor  and shuttle regions.  Fig. 9a and b show damage similar to that  found in the HBM ESD test along the anchor region.  Fig. 10a  and b show MM ESD induced damage along the shuttle area.  In many cases, the electrothermal actuators failed as a result of  fracture along high stress concentration areas.


In very few instances, melted polysilicon was observed after  an ESD induced failure.  In these few instances, the DUT was  damaged during wire bonding causing polysilicon particulates


and contamination in close proximity to the device.  When the  ESD pulse was initiated, a short was created between the


particle and the device that resulted in a melting failure.  These results are shown in Fig. 11.  Note the melted regions  and spot damages where the ESD event took place.  Since  these components were damaged during wire bonding, the  ESD test results will not provide an accurate account of their  robustness and are not included in the data set.  However, the  results do stress the importance of damage free wire bonding  for MEMS manufacturing, packaging, testing, and assembly.


The failures induced by ESD testing are shown in Fig. 12.  The voltages varied considerably from device to device.  In  the HBM alone, devices failed at 1000 V, while several were  tested up to 6500 V with no failure (6500 V was the maximum  test voltage).  In the MM, many devices failed at lower  voltages while one device did not fail up to 6500 V.  More  components are being tested to verify these results.


The results discussed above show the dominant mode of  failure is associated with current rather than voltage compared  to their electrostatic counterparts [2].  The current delivered to  the device is what impacts the functionality and is what


induces the damage.  This result is expected given the nature


Fig. 9a and b.  Fractured polysilicon leg along the anchor.


Close examination of the fracture surface does NOT show signs of thermal degradation.


Fig. 8a and b.  HBM ESD failed electrothermal actuator.  a)This device failed at 1900 V by a severe fracture through the polysilicon actuator leg at the shuttle (arrow).  A close-up of  the fracture surface (b) does not reveal any thermal effects attributing to failure.


of how electrothermal actuators operate using current  compared to voltage.


The damage observed during EOS testing is consistent with  thermal degradation and melting leading to catastrophic  failure.  As the polysilicon legs heat up, deformation will  occur changing not only the physical shape and dimensions of  the device, but it will also effect the operation of the actuator.  By altering the leg shape and design it may become more  susceptible to out-of-plane motion.  The conductive heating  mechanism allows this device to be operated in short pulses to  reach the desired temperature, but sustained power (such as an  EOS test) without compliance settings will heat the  polysilicon legs and result in permanent deformation, then  melting.  The plastic deformation observed in the devices  prevents proper device actuation.  The dominant failure  mechanism in this test is overheating resulting in damage to  the polysilicon.


Results of ESD testing did not show the expected thermal  degradation failure as was observed in EOS tested samples.  In both ESD tests, the devices failed via fracture at high stress  regions.  The unexpected fracture failure mechanism indicates  that substantial forces are generated in an electro-thermal  actuator using HBM and MM ESD pulses.  It is well  understood that during normal operation, the pulse used to


heat the actuator is controlled, thus controlling the force  output and displacement.  In an ESD event, a high voltage, high current pulse is deposited into the device resulting in an  unknown force output for a brief period of time.  Performing  transient modeling to predict the force output is extremely  difficult.  A steady state force displacement model was  generated based on a worst case condition such as uniform  heating of a polysilicon leg up to 1200 oC (melting point).  In  the model, the polysilicon was allowed to freely expand to its  maximum displacement.  The results do not show enough  force (or stress) would be generated by (or in) the actuator to  induce fracture.


Constraining the actuator (preventing displacement during  heating) could result in fracture at high stress concentration  areas.  The peak for either the HBM or MM pulses occurs  very quickly, more quickly than the mechanical natural  frequency of the device.  Under these conditions, the  electrothermal actuator may not be able to respond quick  enough to move and result in higher stress in the sample.  A  combination of these two models (high temperature, and  sample constraints) may result in more insight into  determining the root cause of fracture.

The fracture failure mechanism was found to be independent  of the ESD test performed.  However results do show a higher  degree of ESD susceptibility (lower voltage to failure) for  MM ESD transients.  We believe this result is due to the  higher current and ringing effect typically found with MM  ESD testing.  The wide distribution in failures may be  attributed to small differences in leg widths.  The tolerance for  width fabrication is +/- 0.1 µm where the impact of a thinner  leg will result in lower ESD test conditions to induce failure.   ESD induced failure modes may be particularly harmful to  electro-thermal actuators with attached loads.  As previously  mentioned constraining a device to prevent motion (such as an  attached load, or a device pushing on another component), additional stresses can build up and result in premature failure  due to fracture.  Overall, the ESD robustness of electrothermal  actuators has been significantly higher than the ESD  robustness for most other MEMS components.  Failure has  occurred at levels greater than 1000 V, considerably higher  than results found from electrostatic actuators [6].


Future Work


Analysis should be performed to determine the effects of  various offset angles and polysilicon leg thicknesses of  devices with I-beam geometries to EOS and ESD robustness.  ESD testing of loaded components will provide empirical  evidence to validate the model.

Detecting the 10 Angstroms that Changes MEMS Performance


Erika Schutte, Jack Martin


Analog Devices, Inc.  Cambridge, MA  USA  Erika.Schutte@analog.com


An ellipsometry based measurement protocol was developed


to evaluate changes to MEMS sensor surfaces which may  occur during packaging using unpatterned test samples. This  package-level technique has been used to measure the 0-20  Angstrom thin films that can form or deposit on die during the  packaging process for a variety of packaging processing  conditions. Correlations with device performance shows this  to be a useful tool for packaged MEMS device and process  characterization.


Reliability and performance of low-g accelerometers are  closely linked to sensor surface characteristics and the market  for low-g products is rapidly expanding. Surface film changes  after packaging of only a few angstroms have resulted in  altered performance and wear life in inertial MEMS, but  standard characterization techniques cannot measure  nanometer films on packaged die. Post-package measurement  is useful because it allows product performance to be  correlated to the Back End and Front End processes that form  or affect these films to pinpoint where process refinement  needs to occur to maximize device performance.


Performance changes were observed in low-g MEMS  products when packaging manufacturing conditions were  changed. The likely culprits were the die attach, curing  process, or package plating. If die attach or plating  components were vaporized and then redeposited on the die, these residues should be detectable as an increase in surface  film thickness.


Ellipsometry was one of the methods chosen (in addition to  TOF-SIMS and AFM) to evaluate these potential residues  because it is sensitive to sub-Angstrom changes in film  thickness1. Additionally, it is largely insensitive to index of  refraction (Fig. 1) for the thicknesses of interest, expected to  be less than 50A, so compositional variation would not  confound the thickness data, or would do so only minimally. (Select samples prepared for this ellipsometry study were sent  for further characterization with TOF-SIMS and AFM for a  parallel evaluation.) Experiments were run to validate the

Experimental Setup


A manual Rudolph AutoEl-IV ellipsometer with fixed  wavelength of 6328Å and a 70° angle of incidence was the  instrument chosen for measurements. This setup matches that  of the volume of ellipsometric studies done before variable  angle spectroscopic ellipsometers became practical, so the  models used for fitting ∆ & Ψ to thickness are well developed  and reliable. But the ellipsometer is optimized for wafer, not  die, measurements.


To meet the need for surface characterization of packaged test  dice, we installed microspot optics on a manual ellipsometer  to reduce the measurement spot size to be smaller than the die, and developed a sample preparation and test protocol to  measure die surface films on test samples after packaging. Care had to be taken with sample height and alignment  because they affect components of the thickness equation and  packaging added height to the samples. The challenges for this


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa232


study were to optimize the equipment and sample preparation  and to ensure valid, repeatable data.


Possible Sources and Resolution of Experimental Error


Calibration/Repeatability:  Standard calibration2 of this tool  is done daily before use and checked against a NIST traceable  standard of approximately 1000A. While this assists with day  to day matching of data, it wasn’t known how possible  variation of this tool at 1000A would correlate with  measurements an order of magnitude thinner. Also, microspot  optics slightly increase the variability of the measurement. To  address this, a wafer with film thickness of about 80A was  generated and measured as part of the calibration process. Variation for both the standard and 80A sample while using  microspot optics were found to be less than 2Å over the  period of the study. (Repeatability is better with normal optics  due to the larger spot size.) Therefore film thickness changes  greater than 2Å can be considered significant and measurable. A constant value of n=1.460 was used for all measurements. Atmosphere:  To minimize possible effects of atmospheric  interference, samples were removed from their packaging  immediately prior to measurement in a cleanroom  environment.


Packages:  The samples examined in this study were  hermetically sealed in 5mm x 5mm leadless chip carrier (LCC) packages. The die had to be removed from packaging  because the sides of the package occluded the optical path and  even with the sides removed, the package backing added  sufficient thickness to the sample that the angle of reflectance  was changed. The removal was complicated by the constraint  that the surface needed to remain undamaged. The solution  was to thin the package base to about 20 microns. This  allowed the package sides to be easily broken off, and in most  cases, for the die to be removed from the package base  entirely so the die thickness would match the initial wafer  thickness.  Initial samples were measured with optical  interferometry to confirm that this process did not add  particles to or scratch the samples.


Experimental Plan


1) Measure initial thickness of unpatterned single crystal  silicon wafers with one of two surfaces:  native oxide or  diphenyl siloxane chemically bonded to native oxide.


2) Dice wafers into test samples (backside dicing3 protected  surface from contamination).


3) Use Die Attach to affix samples to packages.


4) Run samples through heated Organic Burn Out (OBO) or  Cure process.


5) Seal lids onto the packages.


6) Backgrind packages.


7) Remove samples from package immediately prior to  measurement.


8) Measure samples:


a) At least two samples of each variant were measured  for each data point.


b) Each measured sample was measured at least twice, then rotated 90° and measured at least twice more in  case anisotropy was present either in the film  reflectance or the sample alignment due to backside  residues.


c) All measurements for each variant were averaged  together. Data values in subsequent charts show the  average with an error bar showing +/- 1 standard  deviation from the average.


9) Evaluate change in surface film thickness by subtracting  the initial thickness from the thickness measured after  packaging.


Experimental Data and Results


Experiment 1:  Effects of die attach on diphenyl siloxane  and oxide surfaces.4


Test samples were prepared with 4 die attach variants (Table  1):  silicone, silver glass, polyimide-siloxane thermoplastic  copolymer, and no die attach (NDA). Each was put through its  associated OBO/Cure step, with the NDA sample receiving no  treatment. All were then sealed at 350C in Nitrogen.


For the diphenyl siloxane samples (Fig. 2), the silicone die  attach showed a 10Å increase in thickness, whereas the  remaining 3 samples showed increases of 3Å or less. To put  this in perspective, subsequent tests showed that wafer box  outgassing can account for up to 2Å of deposition, and the  measurement error may be as much as 2Å. Changes to MEMS  accelerometer product performance during testing had been  observed when this silicone die attach was tried. Film  deposition was a primary suspect; this experiment confirmed  the root cause.

Experiment 2:  Are the results repeatable if Experiment 1  is redone with a new set of wafers and packaged at a  different time?


This experiment (Table 2) was to validate the results of  Experiment 1 by attempting to repeat both the packaging  induced changes and the measurements. It is a repeat of  Experiment 1 using diphenyl siloxane coated samples with  minor changes:  the silver glass die attach was cured in  nitrogen (N2) instead of clean dry air (CDA) and two  additional OBO variants were run for the copolymer die attach (reported in Expt. 3).


The results (Fig. 4) show good matching between the first and  second data sets for silicone and silver glass, well within the  expected measurement variation of 2Å. This shows that the  effects of packaging and the measurement thereof are  repeatable. However, significant variation was seen with the  copolymer (6Å) and no die attach (4.6Å) samples. The  variation in the NDA sample could be a result of the  packaging process; there is no clear protocol for atmosphere  containment and handling for this preparation and it could  have changed from one set to the next. The copolymer result  is discussed in Expt. 3.

Experiment 3:  Effects of copolymer OBO/cure.


Performance changes were also observed in functional  packaged parts when the copolymer OBO process was moved  from a belt furnace to a box furnace and run in a closed  container (not vented) inside the furnace, but did not show the  same change when run in an open (vented) container. Test  samples, both diphenyl siloxane coated and native oxide, were  assembled for each variant (Table 3) to check for correlation  of film thickness change to product test results. The  expectation was that the closed container samples did not have  full solvent removal and the higher partial pressure of  outgassed materials in the container caused redeposition.


Differences were observed between processing variants (Fig. 5) which indicate that one variant may have a performance  issue, but the 9Å increase does not match the process  observed to have changed. Additionally, since the belt furnace  variant does not match the initial belt furnace data while the  box furnace samples do match the initial belt furnace data, it is  possible that the samples were mixed up during processing. Additional testing would be needed to clarify this, but the “box oven, closed” process has been removed from  manufacturing.

Experiment 4:  Effects of lid type variants used with silver  glass die attach.


This experiment (Table 4) checked for effects from sealing  plated lids in the presence of oxygen (CDA) or without  oxygen (N2), and from the use of a combination lid in the  presence of oxygen (CDA). Plated lids processed with silver  glass die attach have an increased relative humidity after seal. A theory was proposed that increased relative humidity could  impact product performance, possibly by causing film growth. The following questions were asked:  Does this humidity  show up in deposited film thickness? Does the combination  lid, designed to reduce humidity, affect film thickness? Does  the presence of oxygen in the plating atmosphere (N2 vs. CDA) affect the film surface thickness? Should we pursue this  line of inquiry further?


No changes were observed between the variants for diphenyl  siloxane coated surfaces (Fig. 6). More, the thinner film  thickness increase for the oxide sample (Ox-PA) with the  standard OBO plated lid does not support the theory that  increased humidity induces surface changes. This study  cannot answer whether or not increased humidity affects  product performance due to non-permanent changes to the  sensor surface because they samples are open to ambient  atmosphere at the time of measurement. The consistency of  these samples along with the lack of film growth on diphenyl  siloxane led us to drop this line of inquiry.

Adaptation of the Planar TEM Sample


Preparation Method for Auger Depth Profiling


A procedure for specific area planar sample preparation for  TEM has been described by Subramanian et al. [3]. The planar  TEM sample preparation uses a combination of backside and  cross-sectional grinding followed by a focused ion beam (FIB) milling to remove the material from top side and backside to  achieve a thin planar slice for TEM analysis. The FIB method  for removing semiconductor material layers provides excellent  control over the amount of material that is removed and the  depth at which the removal of material is stopped. This  method for thinning semiconductor material layers was found  to be ideal as a sample preparation method for Auger depth  profile analysis. It produces very controlled and repeatable  results. Layer thickness < 100nm are easily obtained.


To illustrate the planar sample preparation method for Auger  depth profile analysis, Figure 4 shows the location of a Metal  3 to Metal 1 via stack. Figure 5 shows a cross section TEM  photo of this via stack. For demonstration purposes, this  sample will be prepared for Auger depth profiling on the Via2


– Metal 2 interface.


Figure 4: Optical microscope image showing the location of a  via stack. A tungsten micro-probe pad to metal 1 had been   placed just ahead of the via stack for electrical analysis.


The device is first removed from the package. A glass cover  slip is attached to the top surface of the device with jeweler’s  wax to protect the surface. The via stack location is marked  with a laser marker (Figure 6). The sample is then mounted on  a chuck to be placed on a polishing wheel. The edge of the  sample is polished down on one side until the polished edge is  within ~20 micrometers of the via stack of interest (Figure 7). The device is taken off the chuck and the glass cover slip is


removed. The sample is cleaned and mounted on a FIB holder. The sample is oriented so that the surface of the polished edge  of the sample can be aligned perpendicular to the focused ion  beam.


Figure 5: Cross section photo showing the via stack. The  sample preparation method for Auger analysis will be  demonstrated on the Via 2 – Metal 2 interface.


Figure 6: Optical microscope image showing the laser marked  location of the via stack. Arrows shows direction from which  the edge of the device will be polished down to within a few  microns of the via stack.


Figure 7: Optical microscope image showing the laser marked  location of the via stack after the edge of the sample has been  polished down to within a few microns of the via stack.


In the author’s laboratory, the sample is loaded into a dual  column FEI 820 FIB and oriented so that the device circuitry  can be imaged using the e-beam (Figure 8). The surface  containing the device circuitry is tilted 38 degrees with  reference to the e-beam. At this orientation the surface  containing the device circuitry is parallel to the ion-beam and  the surface of the polished edge is perpendicular to the ion  beam (Figure 9). A protective layer of tungsten is deposited on  the device cross sectioned edge as is shown in Figure 10 and  Figure 11. The amorphous tungsten layer ensures uniform  milling of various device components and minimizes artifacts  created by FIB milling.


Figure 8: E-beam image of the sample with surface tilted 38  degrees with reference to e-beam. The polished edge is at the  top.


Figure 9: Ion-beam image of the polished edge of the sample. The top surface containing the device circuitry is parallel to  the ion-beam. The dark line at the front edge is the actual  semiconductor device. The rest is silicon substrate.


The sequential cross sectioning function for the ion-beam is  then set up for the sample at the failing via stack location (Figure 11). Once started, the ion beam sequentially cross  sections into the sample beginning at the device surface. As  the ion beam mills away the material layers of the  semiconductor device, the ion beam’s progress is monitored  using the e-beam imaging. The ion-beam deflects slightly  outward as it hits the top edge of the sample (Figure 12). This  causes a sloping or beveling effect. The material layers closest  to the top edge of the sample are milled away slightly sooner  then the material layers farther away from the top edge. This  beveling effect of the sequential FIB milling process is used to  the analyst’s advantage when removing the material layers and  determining when to stop the sequential milling process.


Figure 10: High magnification ion-beam image looking down  on the polished edge of the device. A FIB box is set up to  deposit tungsten on the top polished edge to protect the area  of interest from being milled away while viewing with the ionbeam. The amorphous tungsten layer also gives a more  uniform result when the sample is milled with the ion beam.


Figure 11: A close-up Ion-beam image showing the sequential  cross section function of the FIB after tungsten has been  deposited on the polished edge of the device.  This FIB  function mills away material layers front to back from the  device surface towards the substrate.


Figure 12: Schematic of the FIB sequential cross section  function showing the ion beam deflection as the beam mills  away the semiconductor material layers. This deflection  causes the ion beam to mill away slightly more material at the  top edge then it does farther down on the sample resulting in a  slight slope or beveled edge effect.


The milling process is carefully monitored with the e-beam (Figures 13a – f). As the ion beam mills, the passivation is  removed exposing the top layer of metallization which is  Metal 3. Again, it can be seen that as the material layers are  being removed, the layers closest to the top edged of the  sample are removed first followed by the material layers  farther down from the top edge. In Figure 13b, the Metal 3


lines near the top edge have disappeared exposing the Via 2  plugs. Because the material interface of interest is at the  bottom of the Via 2 plugs, the rate at which the material is  being sequentially milled away is now slowed by reducing the  magnitude of ion beam current.


As the bottom of the Via 2 plugs are reached, the via plugs at  the top edge of the sample disappear first exposing Metal 2 (Figure 13c). The milling is slowly continued until the via  plugs located to the left and right of our via stack disappear (Figure 13e).  A very thin layer of the Via 2 plug on the via  stack still remains (Figure 13f). The milling rate at this


Figure 13a: The first of a series of E-beam images showing  the progression of the FIB sequential cross sectioning from  the device surface into the device. The passivation layer has  been milled away and the Metal 3 lines have been exposed. Because the ion-beam deflects towards the front as it mills  away the material layers, the layers closest to top edged are  removed first giving a beveled effect.


Figure 13b: E-beam image showing the Metal 3 at the top of  the sample has been milled away exposing the top of Via 2  plugs. At the targeted Via stack location, Metal 3 remains over  the top of Via 2 plug in the stack.


Figure 13c: E-beam image showing the Metal 3 line over top  at the via stack location is almost milled away. The Via 2  plugs at the device edge have disappeared and the Via 2 plug  at the via stack location are beginning to appear.


Figure 13d: E-beam image showing the Metal 3 line over top  of the via stack has been completely milled away and the Via 2  plug of the via stack under the Metal3 line is fully exposed.


location of the via stack was slightly slower due to the  tungsten FIB probe pad to Metal 1 that was placed down for a  previous micro-probe analysis. At this point, the milling is  stopped. The remaining via plug of interest should be < 100nm  in thickness and Auger depth profiling can begin.


Auger Depth Profiling Analysis


Auger depth profiling was performed on the Via 2 plug – Metal 2 interface of the via stack. Figure 14 shows a close-up  cross section TEM image for reference. Figure 15 shows the  Auger depth profiling results for this sample preparation  method. The tungsten of the Via 2 plug is detected first by the  Auger tool. As the sample is milled, the thickness of the  remaining Via 2 plug is measured by where the tungsten and  barrier metal signals cross. The results show that the sample  preparation method left ~40nm of the tungsten Via 2 plug over


the metal interface. This result is well below the desired  100nm maximum layer thickness for the top material layer for  Auger analysis.


Figure 13e: E-beam image showing the Via 2 plugs to the  right and left of the via stack have been mill away exposing  Metal 2. Because the tungsten FIB probe pad to Metal 1 was  above the via stack, the ion-beam mill rate through this area  was slightly slower leaving a very thin layer of the Via 2 plug  of the via stack. This was the desired results.


Figure 13f: Higher magnification view of the previous e-beam  image showing the Via 2 plugs to the left and right of the via  stack have been milled away. A very thin layer of the Via 2  plug of the via stack is still remaining due to the protection  provided by the overlying tungsten material.


Figure 14: Cross-section TEM image of the Via 2 – Metal 2  interface. The material layers are tungsten (W), barrier metal (TiN), and aluminum (Al).


Figure 15: Auger depth profile analysis results on the Via 2 – Metal 2 interface shown in Figure 14. The results show that  the sample preparation method left ~40nm of the tungsten  Via  2 plug which is well below the desired 100nm maximum layer  thickness for the top material layer for Auger analysis.


This paper presented a sample preparation method adapted  from a planar TEM sample preparation method so that Auger  depth profiling could be used as a practical tool for identifying  very thin layers of foreign materials at interfaces buried deep  within semiconductor devices. The physical effects of ion  beam milling such as the deflection of the ion beam as hits the  sample and the slightly different material milling rates are


used to the analyst’s advantage to provide the control  necessary to prepare the sample for Auger depth profiling. Most importantly, the high degree of control provided by the  sample preparation method gives the analyst the ability to  easily thin down material layers to less than a 100nm of a  target layer thereby significantly reducing sample preparation  time as well as analysis time on the Auger tool.

# Identification and Characterization of Ultra-thin (<100 nm) Flakes Using a Combination of Face-lapping, High Energy (10 kV) SEM Imaging, and TEM


Identification and Characterization of Ultra-thin (<100 nm) Flakes Using a  Combination of Face-lapping, High Energy (10 kV) SEM Imaging, and TEM


D. Mitro, S. Subramanian, S. (Wai Lung) Yeung, T. Chrastecky, B. Hagedorn, and E. Widener


Ultra-thin (<100 nm) flakes shorting metal lines are difficult to


detect and often cause the device to fail after reliability stress  or at the customer site. In most cases, the common technique  of inspecting the device in an optical microscope followed by


conventional low energy (<3.0 kV) scanning electron


microscopy (SEM) is often not able to detect this type of


defect. In rare cases, where the defect is successfully exposed  by the traditional procedure, it is very challenging to perform


additional transmission electron microscopy (TEM)


characterization of the defect without introducing arifacts


during sample preparation of the exposed flake. A new  procedure to identify these defects using a combination of  face-lapping and high energy (>10 kV) SEM imaging is


described in this paper. In this method, the failing device is  carefully face-lapped and inspected frequently using a high  energy (>10 kV) scanning electron beam.  The high energy  electron beam penetrates through the oxide layer and detects  features embedded below the oxide. This technique greatly  incresases the chances of detecting the flake, as the method is  capable of detecting the defect at a larger range of oxide  thickness as opposed to the traditional method. Additionally, TEM results were improved when the ultra-thin flakes were


detected below the surface with the high energy SEM  technique. Several examples of ultra-thin flakes found using  the high energy SEM vs. low energy SEM will be presented.


As the semiconductor industry continues shrinking the critical  dimensions of integrated circuit technologoy, smaller foreign  particles become a greater factor for yield. In sub-micron  technology thin flakes smaller than 100 nm often cause latent  defects which fail after reliability stressing or at the customer  site. As technology continues to shrink to critical dimensions  smaller than 0.13µm, ultra-thin flake defects will play a larger


role in yield loss and latent defectivity. Therefore analysis  techniques must be improved to detect and characterize ever  smaller killer particles to diagnose and give direction to yield  improvement efforts in the more advanced technologies.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa255


Traditional techniques worked well to find killer defects in


older technologies with critical dimensions greater than


0.5µm. However the success rate of finding latent defects in  newer technologies (critical dimensions less than 0.5µm) began decreasing in the failure analysis laboratory.  It became  apparent that the deprocessing technique needed to be  improved when no physical anomaly was found on several  failing devices in which electrical analysis isolated the fail to a  single node. Historically the success rate of finding the  physical defect on a device with the fail electrically isolated to  a single node was nearly 100%. Therefore, a new technique  needed to be developed to improve the detection and  characterization of latent defects on the shrinking  technologies. The new method of combining face lapping, high energy SEM, and TEM has greatly increased the  laboratory’s success rate of finding and characterizing ultrathin flakes.


Detection of Ultra-Thin Flakes


Traditional Low Energy SEM Method


Analysis of a latent defect begins with verifying the failure in  the laboratory setting followed by non-destructive detection  techniques such as liquid crystal or light emission analysis.  Additional electrical isolation and characterization through  microprobing may then follow. There had been a high rate of  success of finding a defect on older technology when the fail  had been isolated electrically to a specific location. However  on newer sub-micron technologies it was found that even with  precise isolation of the fail, often no defect was physically  detected.  The traditional method for deprocessing a device to  find a latent defect is a top down method that involves of the  repetition of 2 steps. First, material on the surface of the  sample is removed with face lapping or chemical  deprocessing. Face lapping involves polishing the surface of  the sample using 0.05 um alumina grinding media embedded  in a polishing cloth. Chemical deprocessing involves  selectively etching the various layers of material off one at a  time. About half way through each layer the area of interest is  then inspected on a confocal optical microscope followed by a  low energy (<3.0 kV) SEM inspection.


There are several disadvantages of using the traditional  method to find a small defect such as an ultra-thin flake. First  of all the ultra-thin flakes have proved to be transparent to  optical microscopes.  Additionally, the low energy SEM


images the surface of a sample and therefore can only detect  the flake when it exposed to the surface [1]. Because of the  thin nature of the flakes, there is a narrow detection span to  target during deprocessing.  Furthermore, the depth location of  the flake within the sample is unknown at the onset of the  deprocessing. Therefore, it is likely to remove too much  material during deprocessing and accidentally polish or etch  through the flake before inspection. If the flake is successfully  exposed during deprocessing, there is still the risk that the  flake may fall out of the sample or become damaged during  deprocessing or handling. TEM characterization of a surface  exposed flake may not be conclusive as surface exposure of  the particle can lead to sample contamination with TEM  preparation artifacts [2].


High Energy SEM Method


A new method was developed to increase the chances of  finding the defect while it is still embedded below the surface  of the sample.  Increasing the voltage on the SEM to 10 kV or  higher allows the SEM to image features a short depth (on the  order of 0.5 µm) below the surface of the sample. This allows  for a wider detection span as the target depth range of  detecting an ultra-thin flake is increased by an order of  magnitude. This improves the chances of detecting the flake  embedded below the surface which in turn significantly  decreases the chances of the particle being damaged or  contaminated during deprocessing or handling. TEM  characterization of a defect embedded below the surface  improves the integrity and feasibility of the TEM analysis.


Case Studies


Case Study 1


In case study 1 the fail was isolated electrically to a single bit  within the SRAM array. The traditional and new methods  were compared during the physical analysis. The fail was top  down deprocessed using the face lapping technique. The  suspect region was inspected in the SEM at both 2.5 kV and  10 kV periodically during the face lapping.  When the device  had been deprocessed down to the metal 1 layer no anomaly  was detected using 2.5 kV. However the 10 kV SEM was able  to image a particle that shorted a metal 1 bit line to an adjacent  storage node.  Figures 1 and 2 display a comparison of the  device imaged on the SEM with 2.5 kV vs. 10kV.


In this case the 10 kV method successfully detected the  particle while it was still embedded below the surface.  The


2.5 kV method may have also found the particle if the next  iteration of polishing exposed the copper particle to the  surface.  However, the next iteration of face lapping could also  have entirely polished through the anomalous particle.


Fortunately, the particle was detected in the 10 kV image and  EDS analysis was performed to further characterize the defect. The EDS data determined that the foreign particle was  composed of copper.


Figure 1: A 2.5 kV SEM image of the Case Study 1 failing bit


cell at metal 1 is displayed.  Surface features such as metal 1,


via 1, and residue can be seen.  No signs of an anomaly are


found.


Figure 2: The same failing bit cell shown in Figure 1 is


displayed here imaged on the SEM at 10 kV.  Surface features


such as via 1 and residue are no longer seen.  Instead features


a short distance below the surface are seen such as metal 1,


contacts, and an anomalous particle.


Case Study 2


The device analyzed in Case Study 2 had a functional failure. Microprobe analysis isolated the fail to a single node. The part  was face lapped down to the top of metal 1 and inspected in


the SEM at 10 kV.  A particle shorting a source contact to a  metal 1 gate was revealed below the surface as shown in  Figure 3.  Figure 4 shows a comparison image of a good node  near by.


Figure 3: A 10 kV SEM image of the failing node polished


down to the top of metal 1 is found to contain an anomalous


particle.


Figure 4: A 20 kV SEM image of an adjacent good node is


displayed for comparison.


The anomaly was then cross-sectioned and prepared for TEM  analysis. The TEM image clearly shows the path of the metal  short between the source contact and the bottom of an adjacent  metal 1 gate line. (Fig. 5) The TEM image also indicates the  particle was located about 200 nm below the surface and was  only 80 nm thick. (Fig. 6)  In this case the geometry of the  flake gave the 2.5 kV SEM technique only a 100 nm detection  span, whereas the 10 kV SEM proved to have atleast a 400 nm  detection span.


Figure 5: A low magnification TEM image of the anomaly  reveals a copper flake shorting a source contact and a metal 1  gate.


Figure 6: A higher magnification TEM image of the flake  indicates it is located about 200 nm below the surface.


Case Study 3


In Case Study 3 a multiple column Flash failure was analyzed. Microprobe analysis isolated the fail to a small region within  the program buffer circuitry. The device was face lapped and  inspected optically and in the SEM at each layer. The optical  inspection at metal 1 did not reveal an anomaly. (Fig. 7)  However the 10 kV SEM inspection proved to find a defect  below the surface. (Fig. 8)


A TEM cross-section of the anomaly was then prepared and  revealed the presence of an ultra-thin copper flake that shorted  the barrier metal between two adjacent metal 1 lines. (Fig. 9)  The TEM image shows that the flake is located 75 nm below


the surface and is less than 3 nm thick.  The ultra-thin  dimensions of the flake proved to be optically transparent.


Figure 7: An optical image of the failing program buffer


polished to metal 1 is shown. The location of the optically


transparent defect later found on the SEM is indicated.


Figure 8: A 10 kV SEM image of the anomaly found at metal 1


in Case Study 3 is displayed.


Figure 9: A 10 kV SEM image of the anomaly found at metal 1  in Case Study 3 is displayed.


Case Study 4


A single bit RAM failure was isolated to a single failing bit


through microprobing in Case Study 4. The device was face  lapped and inspected at both 2.5 kV and 10 kV in the SEM at  each layer. At metal 1 an anomaly was observed at 2.5 kV, however nearby surface residue introduces some uncertainty  in distinguishing the between a true defect and random surface  artifacts. (Fig. 10) The 10 kV SEM can determine whether a  suspected anomaly is a true defect or simply residue because  the surface residue will not have any depth into the device and  therefore will not be imaged at 10 kV. A 10 kV SEM image of


the suspected anomaly is shown in Figure 11 and shows that  the suspected anomaly is a true defect embedded in the  sample.


Figure 10: A 2.5 kV SEM image of the anomaly found at metal  1 in Case Study 4 is indicated by the white arrow. The TEM  cross-section direction and location is indicated in black.


Figure 11:  A 10 kV SEM image of the anomaly found in Case  Study 4 is shown. The 10 kV SEM distinguishes the anomaly  from the surface residue seen in Figure 10.


A TEM cross-section of the anomaly classified the defect as a  stainless steel flake shorting a metal 1 VDD bus line to a metal  1 segment on the failing bit. (Fig. 12) The TEM shows that the  particle was located just below the surface of the sample when  it was detected in the SEM. This example shows that both the


2.5 kV and 10 kV SEM techniques are capable of revealing  anomalous particles in which a portion of the particle is  exposed at the surface. However, the resulting TEM crosssection of a surface exposed particle does not contain as much  information about the defect as a TEM of a particle embedded  deeper below the surface as in Case Studies 2 and 3. The  cross-section of the entire particle is captured in the TEM  when the flake is found below the surface. It is possible that  part of the particle shown in Figure 10 was polished away, however enough of the particle remained to show the path of  the short.


Figure 12: The TEM cross-section of the stainless steel flake  found in Case Study 4 is displayed.


Case Study 5


Case Study 5 is another example in which the 2.5 kV SEM  was able to detect the particle as well as the 10 kV SEM. In  this case a single bit SRAM fail was analyzed and again  electrically isolated to a physical location. The 2.5 kV and 10  kV SEM images of the failing node polished down to metal 1  are shown in Figures 13 and 14 respectively.  The anomalous  particle is clearly seen in both images and indicates a short  between the metal 1 bit line and metal 1 VDD contact. A TEM  cross-section of the particle was prepared and is displayed in  Figure 15. The TEM illustrates that the defect was exposed to  the surface when detected in both the high energy and low  energy SEM. As a result part of the particle appears to have  been polished away. Again the analysis was ultimately  successful in finding the root cause of the fail.


Figure 13: A 2.5 kV SEM image of the anomaly found at metal  1 in Case Study 5 is displayed.


Figure 14: A 10 kV SEM image of the anomaly found at metal  1 in Case Study 5 is displayed.


Figure 15: The TEM cross-section of the defect found at metal  1 in Case Study 5 is displayed.


Ultra-thin flakes are often the cause of latent defect as seen in  the 5 case studies presented.  The high energy SEM technique  has a higher detection span below the surface of the sample  and therefore provides the analyst with more opportunities to  detect the defect. The high energy SEM can increase the  detection span of ultra-thin flakes up to an order of magnitude  over the low energy SEM. Therefore the thinner the defect, the  more important it is to use a high energy SEM inspection.


Additionally, the high energy SEM technique can identify the


defect while it is still embedded in the sample, allowing for


improved TEM results. Although the high energy SEM


method improves the success rate for detecting ultra-thin  flakes, the method is not fool proof.  Even though the


technique is capable of detecting the defect at a larger range of  deprocessing depths, the location of the defect is unknown  until detected and therefore relies on the analyst’s ability to  blindly deprocess down to the target detection range.  If the  defect has been exposed by the deprocessing, the low energy  SEM can image the defect just as well as the high energy  SEM.  Successful analysis also depends in a large part on  isolating the defect electrically to a small physical area prior to  deprocessing.


The recommendation based on the results of this study is that  it is best to inspect a sample during deprocessing with both the  low energy and high energy SEM to gain the most information  about a potential defect. It is also best to try to detect the  defect while it is still embedded under the surface for

Figure 3: (a) Pareto of ultimate shear strength values at 10-4   strain rate and (b) 10-3 strain rate for all solder alloys tested.


Comparison between the data sets indicates that the test  temperature has an effect on the response of the solder. At  high temperatures the strength decreased rapidly. In the case  of the Sn-3.5Ag solder in Fig. 3 (a), as the temperature is  increased from 24 °C to 95 °C the ultimate shear strength  decreased by 41% from 26.7 MPa to 15.8 MPa. This trend is  also seen in the Sn-10In-3Ag solder where the ultimate shear  strength decreased by 22% as the temperature was increased  from 24 °C to 95 °C.


In crystalline solids, plastic deformation corresponds to the  net movement of dislocations in response to an applied stress. At room temperature, only a certain fraction of the  dislocations have sufficient energy to overcome dislocation  barriers such as impurities, grain boundaries and other  dislocations that impede the motion of dislocations. The  ability of the solder alloy to deform is severely restricted and  renders a stronger and harder alloy. As the temperature is  raised, the fraction of dislocations present that have the energy  to surmount the dislocation barriers increases. The increased  mobility of these dislocations results in a smaller stress  required to initiate plastic deformation. Thus, at higher  temperatures the solder alloys tend to be weaker and have  lower shear strengths


Comparison of the ultimate tensile strengths between the  samples tested at 10-4 s-1 and 10-3 s-1 strain rates clearly shows  that the stress-strain behavior is dependent not only on the  temperature and type of solder used but also on the strain rate. For example, for the strain rate of 10-4 s-1, the ultimate shear  strength of eutectic Sn-37Pb was reduced by 67% as the  testing temperature was raised from room temperature to  60oC.  For the strain rate of 10-3 s-1 the ultimate shear strength  was reduced by 48.6%.  Strain hardening effects on eutectic  Sn-37Pb solders were shown to increase the ultimate shear  strength by 97% at room temperature and by more than 200% at 60oC.


This behavior can be explained on the basis of dislocation – dislocation strain field interactions. At higher strain rates, the  amount of plastic deformation experienced by the solder alloy  increases. Since the formation of dislocations is directly  correlated with an increase in plastic deformation, the  dislocation density is higher at 10-3 s-1 strain rate compared to  10-4 s-1 strain rate. Consequently, the dislocations are  positioned closer together. Due to the close proximity of the  dislocations, the dislocation motion is hindered by the  presence of other dislocations. Therefore, the shear stress  required to deform the solder material increases when the  strain rate is increased.


Preliminary visual inspection of the fracture surfaces shows  that the Sn-0.7Cu solders have a more fibrous and dull  appearance compared to a more granular appearance observed  for the Sn-3.5Ag solders. SEM images of the fracture surfaces  further reveals the extent of plastic deformation for Sn-0.7Cu  solders as seen in Fig. 4 (a) compared to the Sn-3.5Ag solder  shown in Fig. 4 (b). The gross plastic deformation


experienced by Sn-0.7Cu and pure Sn solders indicates that  these solders experienced a more ductile failure compared to  the Sn-3.5Ag and Sn-10In-3Ag solders.


Figure 4: Fracture surface images of solder joints sheared at  room temperature and strain rate of 10-3 s-1for (a) Sn-0.7Cu  and (b) Sn-3.5Ag


Elongations at break values reflect the limits of shear strain  before rupture. The maximum elongation at break is  summarized in Fig. 5 (a) and (b) below. In this study, the total  elongation at fracture decreased when the test temperature was  increased. The data also showed that elongation at fracture  increased when the samples were sheared at higher strain  rates. The behavior seen in our data is atypical from those  found in literature where, in general, ductility increases as the  test temperature is increased or when the strain rate is  decreased. This behavior can be attributed to several reasons. Most of the basic data on mechanical properties of materials  are obtained from tension tests and on bulk materials. In our  test, lap shear specimens were used to investigate the strength  of the solder joints. When the solder joints are created during  the reflow process, the base metal (copper) is dissolved into  the solder matrix. The introduction of Cu into the solder  matrix will affect grain boundary sliding and the overall


ductility of the material. In addition, reflow process create  intermetallic compounds such as Cu6Sn5 that also affect the  strength and ductility of the joints. Structural changes such as  precipitation formation in the bulk solder alloy during the  reflow process also occur to alter this general behavior.

The summary shows the eutectic Sn-3.5Ag solder to be the  strongest under all testing conditions. This is attributed to the  formation of small scallop type Cu6Sn5 intermetallics along the  solder / copper interface as well as the formation of Ag3Sn  intermetallic compound precipitates within the primary β-Sn  matrix as shown in Fig. 6.


Figure 6: Microstructure for Sn-3.5Ag solder joint


According to the work of Ma et al.[1], Ag doping in the Sn  solder depresses Cu-Sn IMC formation. Thermodynamic  analysis carried out in their work shows the effect of Ag  addition on the Gibbs energy of Cu-Sn binary system at 125 °C. In the Cu-Sn binary system, Cu6Sn5 will spontaneously  form since the Gibbs free energy is approximated to be -5.4  kJ/mol. When 0.03 moles of Ag is added, the Gibbs free  energy increases to -4.9 kJ/mol. In other words, the driving  force for the formation of Cu6Sn5 IMC is reduced with Ag  addition. Although no thermodynamic calculations were  performed that are specific to this work, i.e no calculations  were done on non-aged samples, a similar reduction in Gibbs  free energy can be considered as a reason for the slower solid  state growth rate of Cu-Sn IMC in Ag doped Pb-free solders.  Apart from the thinner IMC reaction layer, Ag3Sn precipitates  formed during cooling in the bulk solder also imparts strength  to the Sn-3.5Ag solder. This result coincided with the  experimental work performed by other researchers [2-4]. Even  though the presence of the Ag3Sn precipitates does not  degrade strength it does however tend to affect the ductility  and ultimately the fracture behavior of the solder due to its  inherent brittleness.


In summary, experiments were performed on pure Sn, Sn10In- 3Ag, and the eutectic compositions of Sn-Pb, Sn-Cu and  Sn-Ag solders to investigate the effects of strain rate and  temperature on the strength and ductility of the joints. In  general, all solders exhibited the effects of strain hardening  which ultimately increased the strength. When the test  temperature was increased this reduced the strength  significantly. Alloys containing Ag were shown to have  higher ductility at higher strain rates at 60 °C and 95 °C. For a  constant strain rate the ductility decreased with increasing  temperatures.
