# Semiconductor Inter-Material Analysis using a FIB Sample Preparation Method and Auger Depth Profiling


Semiconductor Inter-Material Analysis using a FIB Sample Preparation Method  and Auger Depth Profiling


Randal Mulder, Swaminathan Subramanian, Tony Chrastecky,  Paul Laberge and Cliff Howard


Freescale Semiconductor, Inc., Austin, TX


The physical analysis of failing semiconductor devices by  means of specific area cross section transmission electron  microscopy (TEM) often reveals a micro-layer of foreign  material between semiconductor layers as the failure  mechanism [1]. These thin layers of foreign matter are usually  found at the interface between via plugs/contacts and metal  lines resulting in open circuits (Figure 1). Other places thin  layers of foreign material can be found are at metal-oxide  interface or at the poly-substrate interface resulting in shorts. Often, the layer may be composed of elements that are  abundant in semiconductors (i.e. silicon, oxygen) or low  atomic weight (i.e. oxygen, nitrogen, carbon) elements making  the identification of the material by means energy dispersive  spectroscopy (EDS) very difficult. Also, EDS analysis to  identify these very thin material layers can be ineffective  because the cross sectional volume presented by the layer to  the e-beam is often too small to obtain conclusive results.


Figure 1: TEM image showing a layer of foreign material  between the bottom of Metal 3 and the top of the Via 2 plug. EDS analysis on this layer was inconclusive.


Auger depth profiling [2] can be used as an alternative method  to cross-section EDS analysis for the identification of very  thin layers of foreign material in semiconductor devices (Figure 2). Auger depth profiling analysis is usually performed  perpendicular (top down) to the material layers. This means  that the area of the material layers that is exposed to the  electron beam is larger as the semiconductor materials layers  are being milled away by the tool. Because more material area  is exposed to the e-beam, identifying very thin layers of  foreign material can be easier with Auger analysis. Another  aspect of Auger depth profiling that makes it attractive is that  the e-beam is exposed to one material layer at a time as the  tool mills through the material layers. Therefore, the signal for  that material dominates and the signals for the other materials  normally found in semiconductor devices are reduced to  background noise.


Figure 2: Schematic of the basic principle of Auger analysis. A high energy electron beam is bombarded onto an unknown  material sample. Auger electrons are emitted from the surface  at discrete energies dependent on the material being analyzed.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa248


Via 2


Plug


Metal 3


Metal 2


Auger Depth Profiling Limitations


The most effective way to use Auger depth profiling as failure  analysis tool is to mill through a thin top layer of known  semiconductor material as a reference followed by a thin layer  of unknown foreign material. In most cases, the thickness of  the unknown foreign layer can be less than few nanometers.  To avoid milling through the foreign layer, the milling rate for  Auger depth profiling has to be low (<1nm per Auger data  point in the depth profile). This means that the top layer of  known material can not be very thick (<100nm) or the total  time required for acquiring an Auger depth profile would  make the use of Auger as a failure analysis tool impractical.


The most common methods for removing and thinning  semiconductor material layers are chemical etching and  mechanical polishing. Both of these deprocessing methods  have high risk because the margin for error is very low when  thinning layers to less then 100nm. Remove too much material  and the layer of foreign material is lost. Remove too little  material and the layer above the foreign material is too thick  making analysis very difficult.


Figures 3a-c demonstrates the problem using chemical etching  or polishing as a sample preparation method for thinning  semiconductor material layers for Auger depth profiling  analysis. A failing semiconductor device was submitted for  failure analysis. Micro-probe results indicated that a resistive  Via 2 plug connecting metal layers 2 and 3 to be the fault  location. The device was submitted for cross section TEM  analysis. The TEM results showed a thin layer at the Via 2 – Metal 3 interface (Figure 3a). EDS analysis on the defect  could not determine conclusively the elemental composition of  the resistive layer.


A second device that had the same failure mode signature was  submitted for analysis. Fault isolation of this device was also  traced to the same Via 2 plug. The sample was mechanically  polished to the bottom of Metal 3 and as close to the Via 2 – Metal 3 interface as possible. Considerable time and care was  used during the polishing process to prevent over-polishing. The device was then submitted for Auger depth profiling  analysis of this interface. The results are shown in Figures 3b  and 3c. The Auger depth profiles show that the thin layer of  resistive material causing the failure was composed of silicon  dioxide.

# THE EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE AND STRAIN RATE ON SELECTED LEAD-FREE SOLDER ALLOYS


THE EFFECT OF TEMPERATURE AND STRAIN RATE ON SELECTED LEADFREE SOLDER ALLOYS


Jayamalar Vijayen and James G. Maveety


Intel Corporation, Santa Clara, California, USA


Emily L. Allen


San José State University, San José, California, USA


The temperature and strain rate effects on the shear properties  of selected Pb-free solders were investigated. The experiments  were performed using single lap shear specimens. All testing  was performed using a standard tensile test metrology. The  following results were found: 1) Sn-3.5 wt.% Ag  outperformed all the other solders in terms of its mechanical  strength at all test conditions due to the formation of Ag3Sn  precipitates in the bulk solder and Cu6Sn5 intermetallic  formation along the interface. However, ductility was  sacrificed as this solder strain hardens. 2) The strength and  ductility of the solder joint is strongly dependent on the test  temperature and strain rate. Data in this work reflects a  decrease in strength and ductility when the test temperature is  increased. This phenomenon can be attributed to the increase  in energy as temperature is increased to overcome dislocation  barriers such as impurities and grain boundaries that impede  the motion of dislocation. When strain rate is increased, the  amount of plastic deformation experienced by the solder  increases and more dislocations are formed. Due to the  increase in proximity and number of the dislocations, the net  result is that motion of the dislocations are hindered thus  requiring more stress to deform the material.


Lead free solders such as Sn-Ag, Sn-Cu and Sn-In-Ag have  been identified as potential replacements for conventional  eutectic Sn-Pb. A substantial amount of research has been  published discussing the mechanical properties of lead-tin  solders. However, the mechanical properties of lead-free  solders compared to eutectic Sn-37Pb eutectic solder at  elevated temperatures is still an open question.


The primary objective of this investigation was to determine  the shear properties of selected lead-free solders at elevated  temperature. Shear tests were carried out in this work because  stresses occurring in solder joints are predominantly in shear  resulting from coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) mismatch conditions. Solder interconnects in electronic  packages encounter temperature cycling resulting from both  environmental changes and in-circuit functional changes.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa244


The solders that were studied in this work are:  100 wt.% Sn, Sn-3.5 wt.% Ag, Sn-0.7 wt.% Cu, and Sn-10 wt.% In -3 wt.% Ag. Eutectic Sn-37 wt.% Pb was used as the baseline to  compare the shear properties of the aforementioned solders.   The shear properties were investigated at three different  temperatures; room temperature (RT ~ 24 °C), 60 °C, and 95 °C.  This range is consistent with the range of temperatures  experienced by electronic packages.  As the temperature of a  solder alloy is raised, the distance between the atoms in the  lattice increase.  The atoms are said to be thermally activated. The thermal activation increases the mobility of atoms and  vacancies and increases the mobility of dislocations within the  solder.  These induce slip-system changes and the creation of  new slip systems and deformation at grain boundaries.  As the  temperature approaches the melting point of the solder alloy, it loses strength while its ductility and elongation usually  increase.


The effects of strain hardening were also investigated by  testing at two different strain rates; 10-3 s-1 and 10-4 s-1.   In  electronic packages, solder joints can experience strain rates  over the range of 10-5 to 104 s-1. However, on average solder  joints experience strain rates on the order of 10-3 s-1. The strain  rate is dependent on temperature fluctuations, material  properties and geometry.  The two strain rates of 10-4 and 10-3  s-1 provided a large enough range to investigate the effects of  strain hardening while still producing ductile failures.


Experimental Methodology


The experiments were performed using a single lap shear  specimen configuration as shown in Fig 1 (a).  Both halves of  the lap shear specimen are constructed from copper and  contain nine raised-land pads measuring 1.22 mm × 2.24 mm.  The solder foils used had a nominal thickness of 0.157 mm.  The solders were cut precisely to the pad dimension using a  punch.  The two copper plates were assembled together with  the aid of two through-thickness alignment holes, and shims  were used to control the final solder joint thickness.


All testing was performed using a standard tensile test  metrology system.  The specimen was loaded into the tensile  tester and the thermal chamber was heated to the temperature  of interest until equilibrium was reached.  The loaddisplacement data was collected using a data acquisition  system and then post-processed to obtain shear-stress and  shear-strain data.  On average 2000 data points were collected  per test.  The load data was converted to average shear stress  using the definition


τ


where F is the load as measured by the load cell and A is the  total area of the nine pads. The displacement data was  converted to shear strain using the approximation

Figure 1: (a) Copper lap shear specimen layout and  geometry. (b) Schematic of solder joint subjected to shear  showing geometry, load and defining shear strain.


Five solder alloys were tested at three temperatures and two  strain rates in order to investigate the impact of temperature  and strain hardening on ductility and strength.


Some representative stress-strain curves for solder joints  fractured at room temperature and at 10-3 s-1 strain rate are  shown in Fig. 2. From the shape of the stress-strain curves, the  ductility of the solder alloy can be determined. Both pure Sn  and Sn-0.7Cu solder alloys fractured after large plastic strains. In contrast, Sn-3.5Ag and Sn-10In-3Ag solder alloys fractured  at lower plastic strains even though these solders have higher  shear strength. This is expected since ductility is sacrificed for  alloys that are strain hardened and become stronger.

The two pareto plots shown in Fig. 3 (a) and Fig. 3 (b) summarize the ultimate shear strength of the five solders for  the three testing temperatures and two strain rates. Within  each data set there is some scatter. This is not unusual in  experiments involving solders and is mostly attributed to the  difficulty in manufacturing identical specimens.  All the leadfree solders tested in this investigation exhibited higher  ultimate shear strengths than the eutectic Sn-37Pb solder. This  could be desirable for package geometries requiring additional  strength. Also, the requirement of the electronic industry is  that the joints should be able to support stresses up to 12 MPa

# Materials Characterization of Lead Free Compositions for Minimum Temperature SMT Processes at the SLI-Second Level Interconnect Solder Joint


Materials Characterization of Lead Free Compositions for Minimum Temperature  SMT Processes at the SLI-Second Level Interconnect Solder Joint


Norman J. Armendariz and Prawin Paulraj


Intel Corporation, Hillsboro, OR, USA


The European Union is banning the use of Pb in electronic


products starting July 1st, 2006.  Printed circuit board


assemblies or “motherboards” require that planned CPU


sockets and BGA chipsets use lead-free solder ball


compositions at the second level interconnections (SLI) to


attach to a printed circuit board (PCB) and survive various


assembly and reliability test conditions for end-use


deployment.


Intel is pro-actively preparing for this anticipated Pb ban, by  evaluating a new lead free (LF) solder alloy in the ternary TinSilver-Copper (Sn4.0Ag0.5Cu) system and developing higher  temperature board assembly processes.  This will be pursued  with a focus on achieving the lowest process temperature  required to avoid deleterious higher temperature effects and  still achieve a metallurgically compatible solder joint.


One primary factor is the elevated peak reflow temperature


required for surface mount technology (SMT) LF assembly,


which is approximately 250 oC compared to present eutectic


tin/lead (Sn37Pb) reflow temperatures of around 220 oC.  In


addition, extended SMT time-above-liquidus (TAL) and


subsequent cooling rates are also a concern not only for the


critical BGA chipsets and CPU BGA sockets but to other


components similarly attached to the same PCB substrate.


PCBs used were conventional FR-4 substrates with organic  solder preservative on the copper pads and mechanical daisychanged FCBGA components with direct immersion gold  surface finish on their copper pads.


However, a materials analysis method and approach is also  required to characterize and evaluate the effect of low peak  temperature LF SMT processing on the PBA SLI to identify  the absolute limits or “cliffs” and  determine if the minimum  processing temperature and TAL could be further lowered.


The SLI system is characterized using various microanalytical techniques, such as, conventional optical


microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, energy dispersive  spectroscopy and microhardness testing.


In addition, the SLI is further characterized using macroanalytical techniques such as dye penetrant testing (DPT) with  controlled tensile testing for mechanical strength in addition to  disbond and crack area mapping to complete the analysis.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa261


Second Level Interconnect


The SLI is essentially defined as the region between the


component substrate and PCB substrate at which metallic


constituents and intermetallic compounds interact, but also  include the package and PCB substrate materials.  Both


substrates are typically organic resins reinforced with silica  fibers and layered with Cu planes patterned for signal, power  and ground connections on both sides of the solder joint


resulting in the final PBA-printed board assembly, Figure 1.


Figure 1  Printed board assembly cross-sectional schematic  and the location of the SLI-second level connection region   between the component BGA package and PCB substrate.


Minimum Low Peak Temperature Experiment


Traditionally, the minimum reflow temperature has been 15-20 oC above the melting point of the solder. In the case of  eutectic solder, the alloy melts at 183 oC and the minimum  reflow temperature is approximately 200 oC.


This same 15-20 oC buffer for LF solders with an alloy melt of  217 oC would put the minimum required temperature around  237 oC. The maximum allowed component temperature, as  specified by the J-STD 020B specification, is 245-250 oC as  measured on the package body.  This amounts to a process  window of around 10-13 oC considered too narrow for  practical purposes in terms of current PBA reflow temperature  control process capability.


The properties of the LF alloy referred to in this paper are


summarized in Table 1.

Solder Joint Height Analysis


Solder joint height or pad-to-pad stand-off analysis revealed  that PBAs processed using the low temperature groups 1 and 3  with peak reflow temperatures of 220 and 224 oC, respectively, exhibited taller solder joints. The solder joint heights and shapes of the relative higher lowtemperature groups 2 and 4 with peak reflow temperatures of  224 and 228 oC, respectively, approached that of the control or  plan of record (POR) solder joints.

Microstructural Analysis


SEM and energy dispersive spectroscopy were performed on  the cross-sectioned samples for groups 1, 4 and control group  at the solder ball center, package-side and near PCB-side  intermetallic compound (IMC) regions,  Figures 5- 9.


Figure 5: Group 1 Peak Temp 220oC, TAL 30s. SEM crosssectional view of SLI (L) showing the microstructure at  component side (C) and PCB side (R).


Figure 6: Group 4 Peak Temp 225oC, TAL 40s. SEM crosssectional view of SLI (L) showing the microstructure at  component side (C) and PCB side (R).

Figure 8: A closer view of center region of group 4 samples  shows a  mixture of nodular and elongated Ag3Sn particles in  a metastable Sn-Ag-Cu eutectic ternary (L). The control group  exhibited predominantly nodular Ag3Sn particles in a eutectic  Sn-Ag-Cu ternary matrix(R).


Figure 9: A closer view near PCB side of group 4 samples (L) and control group (R) exhibited similar intermetallic  compositions and morphologies although the intermetallic  layer of group 4 was slightly thinner.


Groups 1 and 3 showed areas where the solder ball and solder  paste constituents did not mix very well as revealed by the  mottled or gradient appearance of the microstructure, Figure 3. In areas where mixing did occur, the microstructure analysis  between each of groups differed primarily in the structure of  the eutectic ternary especially in the shape of the Ag3Sn  particles.  The lower peak temperature samples showed  increasingly more elongated Ag3Sn particles within what  appears to be a metastable eutectic Sn-Ag-Cu ternary as  compared to the control group which exhibited primarily  Ag3Sn nodular or spherical particles within a more defined  eutectic Sn-Ag-Cu ternary.


The package side IMC did not seem to significantly change in  terms of thickness or morphology and seemed slightly thicker  than the PCB IMC for all groups.  However, a very slight  increase in PCB IMC thickness was observed with increasing  peak temperatures.


Microhardness Testing


Microhardness measures a materials resistance relative to a  significantly harder material or indenter with a given geometry  by applying a load for a given amount of time, then measuring  the area of the indentation created.  A Vickers hardness  indenter with a square-based pyramidal diamond geometry  and a face angle of 136° was the standard selected.


Microhardness of the bulk solder is used to characterize the  metallurgical condition of the solder joint.  Microhardness is  able to discern subtle changes in the microstructural properties  from thermal process effects such as reflow temperatures, bake and thermal cycling. These properties are often not  readily interpretable by geometrical or chemical  microstructural analysis.  Microhardness can be used to  measure the consistency of the process, as well as, correlate to  the ductility or deformability performance under various stress  and reliability conditions.

The difference in the hardness observed may be related to the  microstructure density and morphology of the Ag3Sn particles  formed within the metastable Sn-Ag-Cu matrix.  A more  homogeneous or finer precipitate structure forms using faster  cooling rates from higher peak temperatures.  This will result  in a denser and thus harder bulk microstructure.


Dye Penetrant w/ Controlled Tensile Pull Testing


Conventional metallographic cross-sectioning has been the  preferred method to characterize the SLI, but has been limited  to selected single rows or planes, whereas, dye penetrant  infiltrates the disbonded interfaces of the entire component  SLI solder joint array, which are then exposed after  component removed.


Moreover, when used in conjunction with an instrumented  mechanical test system, the force required to remove the  component from the PCB provides additional information as  to the overall strength of the SLI system as it relates to the  SMT low temperature reflow peak temperature and TAL  process conditions.


DPT performed in a controlled tensile manner with the sample  encased in epoxy is the preferred method.  This will ensure a  consistent removal of the component and provide the option to  measure component SLI mechanical strength.


Using this method, an equivalent set of BGA components  were mechanically pulled from the PCB as part of the dye  penetrant testing to measure the force required to remove the  component.  At the same time, the interface disbond type, location and frequency can be determined, as well as  inspection for any discontinuities or fractures and their  severity (dye stain area) after various SMT processes.


The interface location where the component disbonds also  provides valuable information as to the weakest or most  susceptible interface that predominates within a given SLI  system in order to better focus the upstream process  development, Figures 13 and 14.


Figure 13: Cross-sectional schematic of the SLI system  defining the key interface disbond categories numbered Types  1-4 designated where a disbond interface occurs.


Figure 14: shows the controlled mechanical test fixture that  measures the force and deflection (L) required to remove a  epoxy encapsulated component from the PCB (R).


No dye stain was observed for any of the groups after DPT.  However, the resulting DPT patterns showed a predominantly  Type 4 disbond location (between the PCB pad and PCB  substrate) for the lowest peak temperature groups 1 and 3.


Groups 2, 4 and C exhibited an increased mixture of Type 1 (between the package pad and package material) and Type 3 (between the solder ball and PCB pad) disbond locations, Figure 15.


The maximum tensile pull force required to remove the  component form the PCB increased with an increased percent  of Type 4 disbond locations, Figure 16.  In addition, the  maximum tensile pull force showed an increase with  decreasing processing peak temperatures as well as TAL, Figure 17.


The decrease observed in the maximum pull force with  increasing peak temperature and TAL may be the result of the  increased thickness of the PCB IMC and/or softening of the  PCB substrate material.  These effects may serve to transfer  the weakest interface from a Type 4 to the relatively weaker  Type 1 and Type 3 interfaces.

The presence of relatively hard Ag3Sn particles forming along  grain boundaries and eutectic Sn-Ag-Cu ternary within the  solder ball microstructure appears to explain the increase in  microhardness observed with increasing peak temperature and  TAL.  This may correspond to a higher cooling rate formation  mechanism.


Although the maximum pull force was higher and the micro  hardness was lower, the lowest peak temperature and TAL  groups 1 and 3 resulted in non-collapsed solder balls with  relatively high stand-offs and irregular SLI solder joints as  compared to groups 2 and 4.


Therefore the absolute minimum “cliff” peak temperature of  approximately 224 oC and a absolute minimum “cliff” TAL of  approximately 35 seconds appear to be the low limits for leadfree SAC405.


Group 4 and the control group closely resembled each other in  terms of stand-off, disbond type, microhardness and  mechanical pull force.  The bulk microstructure was slightly  different, but would not be expected to be detrimental to the  SLI.  More importantly, the thinner IMC did not seem to be  different in terms of morphology and composition.  In fact, a  slightly thinner IMC may be more desirable.


Therefore, the minimum SMT “process” peak temperature can  be lowered from 230 to 228oC with no deleterious  metallurgical effects expected at the SLI, but TAL remains at  40 seconds to reside within the SMT reflow process capability  of the equipment.


The materials analysis demonstrated that the micro and macroanalytical techniques that were developed and employed  correlated to the processing conditions and provided  actionable data to optimize the LF SMT reflow process.


In other words, microhardness testing was able to discern  subtle changes in the mechanical properties of the solder ball  metallurgy and controlled component testing obtained along  with DPT correlated to the different SMT thermal process  conditions, as well as, to the disbond interface locations, and  provided further insight into lead-free material interactions at  the SLI for SMT assembly.

# Measurement of Solder Joint Strength and its Dependence on Thermal Aging in Freestanding and Board-Mounted Packages Using a Laser Spallation Technique


Measurement of Solder Joint Strength and its Dependence on Thermal Aging in  Freestanding and Board-Mounted Packages Using a Laser Spallation Technique


Vijay Gupta, Jun Tian


University of California Los Angeles, California, USA  vgupta@ucla.edu


Cheryl Hartfield, Kejun Zeng, Cheng Chiu, and Roger Stierman


Texas Instruments, Dallas, Texas, USA


The continuing evolution of semiconductor packages to finer  solder ball pitches, shrinking solder ball volume, and new  solder materials, mandates the availability of methods to  accurately assess solder joint reliability both at the component  and at the board level. Many tests in use for this purpose  cannot provide direct measurements of solder joint interfacial  strength. This paper reports on the investigation of laser  spallation for interfacial strength assessments and  understanding of failure mechanisms on chip scale package (CSP) solder joints.


Ball grid array (BGA) packaging of integrated circuits is an  important technology that utilizes solder balls as the  interconnect to the board, instead of the leads used by  peripheral array surface mount package types. The use of  solder balls allows higher pin counts, and offers other  advantages such as robust processing, enabled by their higher  pitch, better lead rigidity, and self-alignment characteristics  during the reflow process.  It is the technology of choice for  chip-scale packages (CSPs).


It is well known that the formation of intermetallic compounds (IMC) helps maintain a good bonding between the solder and  the underlying package substrate and printed circuit board (PCB) metallic pads. However, under high temperature  environments, IMC growth can become excessive. This results  in brittle interfaces and deteriorates the mechanical integrity  of the solder joint. This problem is also compounded by  further changes in the morphology of the IMCs and formation  of interfacial voids during thermal aging. Thus, in-situ  measurement and maximization of the solder joint adhesion, and predicting its degradation by directly relating the joint  strengths to the evolution and stability of the IMCs under high  temperature processing and service conditions, becomes very  important to understand from the standpoint of reliability.


The aim of the work leading to this paper was to explore the  application of laser spallation testing [1,2] for evaluation of


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa267


solder joint strength in both freestanding and board-mounted   CSPs, and whether it could replace or complement drop  testing. Additionally, through SEM/EDX/FIB–based analyses, correlations between solder joint microstructure and laser  spallation results were sought by measuring joint strengths in  packages formed by three different types of solder materials  and pad chemistries and stressed by baking for specific  temperatures and times.


Besides generation of optimized joint chemistry, the above  test matrix allowed an assessment of the effect of board  chemistry on the solder joint strength. Preliminary results  discussed here show that an optimized solution in freestanding  packages may no longer be so when mounted on the board. Thus, industry standards for board chemistry may be required.  Before presenting the specific laser spallation setup utilized  for testing the BGA packages, a brief description of the basic  laser spallation experiment is provided for those who may not  be aware of it. Also because of the page limitation, only  selected data is presented in this communication although the  conclusions are based on results obtained on the entire test  matrix.


The Basic Laser Spallation Test


In this experiment, a 2.5 nanosecond long Nd:YAG laser  pulse is made to impinge over a 3 mm-dia area on a 0.5 µm  thick aluminum film that is sandwiched between the back  surface of a substrate disc (12-25 mm diameter and 1-mm  thick) and a 10 to 20 µm thick layer of SiO2. The meltinginduced expansion of aluminum under confinement generates  a compressive stress pulse (with 1 ns rise time) directed  towards the test coating deposited on the substrate's front  surface – or, in this specific case, directed towards the solder  balls mounted on the package substrate. The compression  stress wave reflects into a tensile wave from the coating's free  surface (or solder ball interface) and leads to its spallation (complete removal) at a sufficiently high amplitude. The  incident laser fluence is controlled by changing the energy of  the laser beam while keeping the illuminated area constant. Also, if spallation does not occur, the laser beam is focused


onto a new spot in order to avoid fatigue effects. The interface  tensile stress is obtained by measuring the transient  displacement history of the coating's (or package substrate’s) free surface by using an optical interferometer and using it in  a wave mechanics simulation that requires the density and  elastic properties of the coating (solder) as an input. Interface  strengths in a variety of systems, including those between  metal, ceramic, and polymeric coatings and engineering  substrates, have been measured. Details of this test method  can be found in a series of publications [3-6].


Testing of Freestanding Chip-Scale Packages


Description of Samples


The samples tested in this work included freestanding fine  pitch CSPs (component-level), and the same packages  mounted to PCBs having Cu/OSP pads (board-level). The test  matrix included packages with both eutectic SnPb and Pb-free  solders, stressed by baking for specific temperatures and  times. The package substrate chemistry was also varied and  included bare Cu and electrolytic Ni-coated Cu pads using  thin (Ni.1) or thick (Ni.2) amounts of Ni.


Specifically, two groups of samples were tested using the laser  spallation apparatus. The “matrix-1” samples summarized in  Table I included both component- and board-level BGA  packages baked at 150oC for 0, 48 and 100 hours. The tested  samples were designated as Cu-E1, Ni.1-E1, Cu-F and Ni.1-F. The designations E1 and F refer to the eutectic and Pb-free  solders, respectively, whereas Cu and Ni.1 refer to the bare  copper and thin electrolytic Ni-covered copper pads, respectively.


Table I. Summary of “matrix-1” samples. The number in the  bracket denotes the number of packages that were tested in  that category.


The “matrix-2” samples summarized in Table II included  seven types of solder/substrate combinations. The samples  were baked at 100 oC, 125 oC, 150oC and 170 oC, for 3, 10, 20, 40 and 80 days. “E1” denotes eutectic solder and is identical  to that in Table I. “E2” is another type of eutectic SnPb solder


with slightly different composition. “F” is a Pb-free solder  identical to that in Table I. The pad chemistry is directly  designated by its chemical symbol such as Cu or Ni with  prescribed thickness (-.1 for thin Ni, -.2 for thick Ni). The last  two digits in the designation such as in Cu-E1, Cu-E2, Cu-F, Ni.2-E1, Ni.2-E2, Ni.2-F refer to the designation for one of  the three solders (E1, E2, or F), whereas the first two refer to  the pad chemistry.

Modified Laser Spallation Procedure for Testing  Freestanding BGA Packages


The basic spallation set-up was adapted to test the componentlevel packages. This was essentially the same as that  employed previously for testing flip-chip packages [1,2]. The  laser pulse was focused on the back surface of the mold  compound, which as in the basic setup, was covered by a


0.5µm-thick sputtered Al film followed by a 50-100 µm-thick  layer of waterglass.


The compressive stress wave generated by melting-induced  expansion of the Al under confinement turned tensile upon  reflection from the free surfaces of both the solder balls and  the polyimide layer. The returning tensile stress wave  generated two failure modes, which are illustrated in Fig. 1.


In most cases, as the laser fluence was controllably increased, the first visible damage was in the form of a bulge whose size  was roughly equal to the diameter of the laser heating spot. This bulge was a direct result of the subsurface delamination  of the polyimide layer. The solder/substrate interface however  remained intact during this failure. As the laser energy was  further increased, individual solder balls were found to spall  like “bullets.” The above sequence of failure was reversed in

cases where the solder joint was significantly weakened by  thermal aging. Note that since the solder ball interface is the  outermost interface of the sample, the tensile wave generated  at the package surface passes first through the solder ball, and  then into the substrate. So, if a given laser energy caused both (polyimide) and (solder ball) failures in the same shot, the  solder ball failure was generated first, and as the tensile wave  moved back from the solder ball side to the mold compound  side of the package, the polyimide failure was generated next.


Figure 1. Two failure modes observed in the freestanding CSP  packages. One type is a bulge caused by subsurface  delamination of the polyimide layer. The other failure mode is  direct spallation of the solder balls from the substrate.


To find the critical laser energy corresponding to the solder  ball spallation, eight shots were taken on the back surface of  the mold compound. The energy was increased gradually until  the spallation of one or more solder balls was observed. This  energy was then recorded as the critical energy for this  specific sample. If there were more than one sample of the  same type, then the lowest critical energy among the samples  was picked as the critical energy for that type of sample.


Only qualitative joint strength data measured in terms of  critical laser energies are reported here. A more detailed  analysis involving measurement of the stress waves in  packages using interferometry, and stress field quantification  using a wave mechanics simulation, are deferred to a later  date. Since the data presented here is directly proportional to  the actual joint strength, it can be used for optimizing the pad  and solder chemistries. The testing procedures for the  freestanding and board-mounted samples, as reported here, can be utilized for reliability and quality control testing.


Results for Component Level Packages (Matrix 1  Samples)


The critical laser energies for the component-level packages  for all samples listed in Table I were determined. The results  are plotted in Fig. 2 versus the aging time. It should be noted  that the critical energies for the Ni.1-F samples were  determined by a different criterion. For these samples, about  10 shots were made at each level of laser energy. If 5 shots  generated solder joint failure, then this energy was chosen as  the critical laser energy. Thus, this criterion to determine the  threshold laser energy generates higher critical energies.


Several points are noteworthy from Fig. 2. First and foremost, it shows that the laser spallation test is able to sense the  interfacial degradation in the solder joint due to thermal aging. It can be seen that the critical laser energies for the Cu-E1, Ni.1-E1 and Cu-F samples drop to about 40 to 50% of their  initial pre-bake value within the first 48 hours when baked at  150oC. The joint strength then undergoes minor changes, either an increase or a decrease. It is interesting that the  critical laser energy for the Ni.1-F sample remained  insensitive to thermal aging. Thus, with respect to mechanical  strength, the Pb-free/thin Ni joint exhibits good short-term  thermal stability at 150oC.

Overall, all pads and solder chemistries are stable during short  aging times, and except for the Ni.1-E1 sample, all showed a  degradation in the solder joint strength as the aging time was  increased. This is all consistent with the diffusion-related  kinetic changes in the joint microstructure. Even though the  as-fabricated joint strength is not the best, the joint in Ni.1-E1  sample is the most reliable.


The effects of temperature, and pad and solder chemistries  were studied by replotting the data in Figs. 3-5. Space  limitation prohibits presentation of such plots here. Snap shots  at fixed number of days of aging clearly indicated the strong  effect of aging temperature on the strength of the solder joints. Only at 80 days of aging, the strength appeared insensitive to  the temperature level. This is consistent with the  microstructural changes such as formation of critical size  interfacial cracks or a uniform IMC layer at such a long  duration of aging.


Testing of Board-Mounted Packages


Sample Description


To evaluate the effect of board chemistry on the strength as  well as the failure mode of the solder joint, the board-mounted  Cu-E1, Ni.1-E1, Cu-F, and Ni.1-F samples were stressed  under the same conditions as the component-level packages  and tested by the laser spallation-based methodology. Three  sample sets were studied, which included packages baked at  150°C for 0, 48 and 100 hours. A 0.5µm thick Al was  sputtered on the back surface of the PCB, and covered with a  10-20 µm thick layer of waterglass.


Modified Laser Spallation Procedure


The same strategy used for testing the component-level  packages did not work for the board-mounted samples. Figure  6 illustrates the problem related to wave propagation in a  typical board-mounted package.


Figure 6: Wave propagation in a board-mounted sample.


The incoming compressive stress wave from the PCB side is  largely reflected back due to the very low impedance of the  plane containing the solder balls on account of high volume  fraction of air pockets. Therefore, only a small portion of the  wave is transmitted into the package and consequently very  little tensile stress can be generated upon reflection from the  free surface of the mold compound to test the solder/substrate  interfaces.


Based on the above investigation, a special strategy was  developed to test the board-mounted BGA packages. Figure 7  shows the schematic of the test setup. The sample was held  vertically while viscous oil was poured into the gap between  the package and the PCB board such that it filled the air gaps  around the solder balls. The oil works as the wave  transmission medium and effectively increases the acoustic  impedance of the plane containing the solder balls. This  allowed substantial amplitude of the laser-generated  compressive stress wave in the PCB to enter the BGA  package, and return as a tensile wave after reflecting from its  free surface.


The returning tensile wave was of sufficient amplitude to  exceed the solder/board joint strength. Complete packages  could be pulled apart. However, due to very limited number of  samples, each mounted package was cut into 3.5mm×3.5mm


four sides separating the islands were made all the way down  to the package/board interface. Thus each island was isolated  from its neighbor. The stress wave was generated by  impinging the laser pulse onto the PCB directly behind one of  the islands. Precise alignment was accomplished by using the  He-Ne laser beam, whose axis was pre-aligned with that of the  main YAG laser. At critical laser fluence, the entire islands  could be spalled off.

group, four samples generated four threshold energies, and the  lowest one was recorded as the critical energy for the group.


Figure 8 shows a plot of the critical laser energy versus the  thermal aging time. The results for the board-level samples are  consistent with the component-level samples in two aspects. First, they show a similar trend in the variation of the critical  laser energies. Specifically, the solder joint strength in boardlevel Cu-E1, Ni.1-E1 and Cu-F samples degrade about 30-55% during the first 48 hours. The critical laser energy then  undergoes minor changes. The board-level Ni.1-F samples  also showed no joint degradation.

This indicates that the Ni.1-F samples exhibit good short-term  thermal stability at both the component and board level  testing. Second, the relationship between different types of  samples is consistent. That is, the stronger component-level  packages remained stronger even after being attached (reflowed) to the PCB.  Note, however, whereas the  component level tests showed all samples except Ni.1-F  having similar 100 hr strengths, the board level tests showed  the Cu-F was markedly degraded from all others.


Repeatability of the Laser Spallation Results


The reproducibility in the measured critical laser energy for  component and board level samples processed under identical  conditions was evaluated. Samples baked for 0 and 100 hrs  showed less variation compared with those processed at 48  hours. For example, the largest variation in pre-baked  component level samples was observed to be 13% for the CuF sample set, while it was 27% for 48 hrs-baked Cu-E1  samples, and 20% for Cu-F samples baked for 100 hrs. Despite the variations in the measured laser energies, the loci  of failures were essentially the same.


For board-mounted samples, the largest variation in pre-baked  samples was found to be 14% in the Cu-F sample set, while  the 48 hr baked samples belonging to the Cu-E1 group  showed a 19% variation. The 100 hr baked Ni.1-E1 samples  showed a variation of 15%.  Again, as for the component level


samples, the failure locus was identical for all samples in the  same set despite variations in the recorded laser energies.


Overall the 48 hr-baked samples, whether board mounted or  not, showed a larger variation probably because IMC  formation was in the transient stage. Also, compared with  component level samples, the corresponding board-mounted  samples showed considerably less variability.


Failure Analyses


The 125oC component-level tested packages where chosen to  correlate the laser spallation results with the microstructure of  the solder joint region. SEM/EDX analyses to determine IMC  type were performed using a JEOL JSM 840A scanning  electron microscope. A thin layer of platinum was deposited  on the failed package surfaces to ensure good conductivity. Focused ion beam (FIB) cross-sectional analysis was also  performed on four samples, using an FEI DualBeam 820 FIB  to make a 30µm×10µm×5µm cut on the pad surface exposed  by spallation of the solder ball. Both electron and ion beams  were used for the observation of the interfacial  microstructures. Because of space constraints only a summary  of results is provided without presenting all of the  micrographical information.


Summary of Failure Loci


Subtleties aside, the failure loci and the associated strengths of  the solder joints studied in this work were governed by the  IMC morphology and its evolution during thermal aging. The  failure was broadly within the IMC layers and the fracture  surface shifted from near the solder/IMC interface to the  IMC/Cu or the IMC/Ni interface as the aging time was  increased. The variations in the recorded laser energies are  due to the intrinsic strength variation of the IMCs and also due  to the formation of Kirkendall voids at the IMC/Cu interface [7,8]. Summary of failure loci for various samples is provided  below.


Solders on Bare Cu Substrates (Cu-F, Cu-E1), 125oC


During solid-state aging, the strength of the solder joints  involving bare Cu substrates decreases continuously. Correspondingly, continuous changes over time were seen  regarding the nature of the interfacial failure of the spallated  joint. Figure 9 shows optical photos of the pad surface  remaining after the ball was spalled off the Cu-E1 sample after  various days of aging. It can be noted there are no bulk solder  failures. All samples failed exclusively at the solder joint  interface. EDX was applied to confirm the exact nature of the  interfacial failure. At 0 days, the solder joint failed between  the solder and Cu6Sn5 interface. By 20 days of aging, the  failure has moved to 100% of the Cu3Sn/Cu interface. Note  the darker, changed appearance of the 80 day sample due to  the formation of Cu oxide. Likely, Cu oxide formed in those  regions where the voids had coalesced into cracks, allowing  oxygen to gain access to the exposed Cu and react during the  125oC temperature application.


Results are similar for the Cu-F sample. The 0 hr samples  failed at the solder/Cu6Sn5 interface, while the failure  gradually shifted to the Cu3Sn/Cu interface. Migration of Cu  into the solder to form IMC also leaves behind Kirkendall  voids at the IMC/Cu interface. With thermal aging, the voids  grow and coalesce to form disk-like cracks. Once such a  critical crack size is formed, the joint stabilizes to its lowest  strength value. This is evidenced in the sequence of crosssectional micrographs in Fig. 10, which show the evolution of  Kirkendall voids at the Cu3Sn/Cu interface at 3, 10 and 40  days of aging in a Cu-F intact sample. Note the void-free  interface in the 0-day aged sample in which the failure was  found to be at the solder/Cu6Sn5 interface. This is consistent  with the recorded critical laser energies for these samples, which show a large initial decrease with the aging time and  then remaining almost constant thereafter.

Solders on Au/Ni/Cu Substrates (Ni.1, Ni.2), 125oC


Ni.2-E1: For the Ni.2-E1 samples, the critical laser energy  decreases gradually and continuously throughout the 80 days  of 125oC aging. The failure locus is gradually transferred from  the upper solder/IMC interface towards the lower solder/Ni  interface.


Unlike the solder on bare Cu substrates, the migration of Cu  into the solder was stopped by the thick Ni layer. Therefore, no voids were observed at the Ni/Cu interface during aging.  Ni.2-F, Ni.1-E1: For the Ni.2-F samples, the critical laser  energy dropped rapidly from 3 to 10 days of aging. The  failure locus was within the IMC close to the lower interface. The locus did not change even though the critical laser energy  showed a variation. Similar to the Ni.2-F samples, the Ni.1-E1  samples also showed variation in the critical laser energy but a  constant failure mode. This is most likely due to the changes  in the intrinsic strength of the Ni-Cu-Sn compounds with its  evolving chemistry due to continuous arrival of the Cu atoms.  It is evident with the Ni.1-E1 sample that voids were  generated at the Cu/Ni interface, most likely during initial  reflow. The Ni dissolved intermittently into the solder to form  pinholes through which Cu diffused into the solder. The  density of these voids was too low to control the failure locus. Instead, the failure was controlled by the intrinsic strength of  the IMCs away from the Ni/Cu interface. This is evidenced in  the cross-sectional image shown in Fig. 11 where the fracture  is not through the voided region.

Comparison of the Failure Loci in Component and BoardLevel Samples, 150oC


The analyses indicated that the Cu-F samples exhibited similar  failure patterns for both the board-mounted and componentlevel samples. At 0 hours, both types of samples failed at the  solder/Cu6Sn5 interface. At 48 hours and 100 hours of aging, both of them failed at the Cu/Cu3Sn interface. Both samples  required only half the laser energy to spallate the ball at 100  hrs compared to the amount of laser energy required to cause  failure at 0 hours. Because of the significantly differing geometries, it is not  possible to compare the critical laser energies for the


component and board level samples directly, even to make  any qualitative strength comparisons. Thus, to understand the  effect of the board chemistry on the interfacial strength, quantification of the stress waves inside these samples using  interferometry and stress wave simulation, as done in the basic  spallation method, is needed. This is presently in progress.


Comparison to Other Solder Joint Test Methods


Ball-shear and ball-pull tests are presently used in the industry  to characterize the strength of solder joints in component level  samples. Figure 14 shows the ball shear, ball pull, and laser  spallation (LS) failure data for joints constructed by Ni-plated  Cu pads and a eutectic solder. The samples were aged at  125oC.


After recording the initial loss in the shear strength of the  joint, the ball shear test was unable to comprehend the  continuous degradation of the joint due to the evolution of the  intermetallic layers and voids. The failure locus was 100% through the bulk solder, which explains the constant shear  strength value recorded by the ball-shear test. This is in  contrast to the laser spallation test data, which was consistent  with the continuously degrading interfacial microstructure.


As shown in Fig. 14, the ball-pull test was able to follow the  monotonic degradation of the joint due to thermal aging, but  significant joint strength degradation is not picked up as  readily as can be done with laser spallation. For example, the  joint strength as measured by ball pull is almost constant  between 3 and 40 days of baking, and a clear drop in joint  strength is not revealed until after 40 days of aging. On the  other hand, laser spallation showed clear joint strength  degradation through each logpoint of baking.


The less sensitive nature of the ball pull results may be  explained in part by a complicated failure locus, which almost  always was a combination of IMC, solder, and interfacial  fractures. This is largely due to the inhomogeneous stress field  generated across the solder joint, which results in the  nucleation of microcracks in the weakest and the highest  stressed regions of the joint and their subsequent coalescence  by cohesive failure of the intervening material. The failure  loci in the laser spallation tests were predominantly through  the interface. This is because a uniform stress field is  generated across the entire solder joint section in the laser  spallation experiment. Efforts to correlate the actual values  obtained from the ball-pull and laser spallation tests are  complicated by strain rate effects. The actual data will  correlate in cases of severely degraded joints where the strain  rate effects, which indirectly affect inelastic deformations in  the joint, will be small due to very low joint strengths. Regardless, both tests are able to record the degrading effect  of aging and in this respect they can both be used to rank the  samples.


Drop testing is an industry-accepted test that is used to assess  the strength of solder joints in a board-mounted configuration. A direct comparison with the laser spallation data is not


feasible because the tests employ different loading  mechanisms. In the drop test, the joint is subjected to dynamic  bending-induced local tensile and shear stresses, whereas laser  spallation induces a predominantly uniform tension across the  entire joint section. Because drop test joint stresses are  induced due to board bending, the relative location of the joint  with respect to the support legs for the board becomes  important to distinguish in the drop test. In contrast, laser  spalltion is a localized test where each joint is subjected to a  uniform tensile stress, provided it falls within the central 3  mm-diameter area of the stressed region.


Figure 14. A comparison of the data obtained by Ball-Shear, Ball-Pull, and Laser Spallation experiments on samples made  from Ni-coated Cu pads and a eutectic solder (E1), aged at  125oC.


Despite the differences in the loading mechanism, a  qualitative comparison between the two tests is still possible. Data for the Cu-F joint in Fig. 15 shows that the laser  spallation and drop data correlate. Both show a monotonic  decrease in the joint performance due to thermal aging at  125ºC.


However, preliminary work with other samples (not shown) indicates that in some cases, the two tests show diverging  trend; one shows an initial rise due to aging before stabilizing  to a steady state, while the other shows a monotonic decrease. Cross-sectional microstructural data on these samples is  presently being evaluated to determine which one of these  tests provides a realistic measure of joint degradation, and to  understand the divergent results between the two test methods.

enabled measurements of interfacial joint strength to be  obtained when only a single package was available for testing.  In addition, laser spallation can be applied to test boardmounted CSPs using the newly developed test approach  described in this paper. This allows assessment of the  influence of the board chemistry to solder joint interfacial  strength. Ball pull and shear tests can not be applied to board  level packages. Although “package pull” tests can be done for  solder joint BLR testing, fracture in bulk solder is often  generated. In contrast, as seen with component-level tests, the  laser spallation board-level tests were 100% successful in  generating failures at the solder ball interface. Laser spallation  is a complement rather than a replacement for other types of  BLR testing, such as drop tests. For example, the  understanding of solder joint strength provided by laser  spallation allows an assessment of whether drop test results  are dominated by interfacial or bulk solder phenomena.


Earlier work showed that solder ball testing of thick packages (such as microprocessors) required lengthy destructive sample  preparation prior to application of laser spallation. [1] Chip  scale packages, on the other hand, are easily tested in their  native form and require only the standard aluminum and  watch glass coatings that are required for many laser  spallation samples. This facilitates the rapid generation of  data, which is important to meet process development  timelines. One can rapidly and easily assess which solder type  produces the strongest interface for a given pad chemistry, and  vice versa.

A Methodology for Characterizing System-Level ESD Sensitivity


Marie-Pascale Chagny, John A. Naoum


Dell Inc., Austin, Texas, USA


Over the years, failures induced by an electrostatic discharge


(ESD) have become a major concern for semiconductor  manufacturers and electronic equipment makers. The ESD  events that cause destructive failures have been studied  extensively [1, 2]. However, not all ESD events cause  permanent damage. Some events lead to recoverable failures  that disrupt system functionality only temporarily (e.g. reboot, lockup, and loss of data). These recoverable failures are not as  well understood as the ones causing permanent damage and  tend to be ignored in the ESD literature [3, 4]. This paper  analyzes and characterizes how these recoverable failures  affect computer systems.


An experimental methodology is developed to characterize the  sensitivity of motherboards to ESD by simulating the systemlevel ESD events induced by computer users. The manuscript  presents a case study where this methodology was used to  evaluate the robustness of desktop computers to ESD. The  method helped isolate several weak nets contributing to the  failures and identified a design improvement. The result was  that the robustness of the systems improved by a factor of 2.


Electrostatic discharges are created by sparks generated during  the contact of the human body and a device at a different  potential. The sparks usually take place in dry environments. They are the result of the ionization of the air gap separating  the two objects. The discharges generate high voltage  transients that can either damage a component or induce an  electric field which only affects the system’s functionality. The latter is less understood and more difficult to analyze  because of its lack of repeatability. The impact of such a  discharge depends on the state of the system (which changes  with time), the strength of the field, and the climatic  environment (e.g. air temperature, humidity) in which the  system operates. If the system’s functionality is affected, the  symptoms of the discharge can be very different: lockups, reboots, shutdowns, or data losses. Their only common point  is that the hardware is still totally operational after recovering  from the ESD fault. These recoverable ESD failures are  intermittent and are more likely to be misdiagnosed as  software problems or non-verified failures.


This paper is based on the case study of desktop computers. The failures were random, but repeated. Further analysis  showed that they were more likely to happen during the usage  of a floppy disk. The diskettes were charged, generating an


# A Methodology for Characterizing System-Level ESD Sensitivity


ESD event when inserted into the drive. The event caused the  computer to fail.


The paper starts with a brief overview of ESD and its impact  on state-of-the-art computer systems. It proposes an  experimental methodology to characterize the sensitivity of  motherboards to ESD failures. The methodology includes a  robustness criteria based on lab measurements and tests. Then, the paper describes how to locate the source of the ESD  sensitivity. The analysis includes noise injection at the  motherboard level and discharges induced by an ESD gun at  the net level. All the methods described include measurements  taken on systems using 130-nm technology chips. The paper  concludes with a discussion of the different design strategies  that can be used to decrease the system-level sensitivity to  recoverable ESD failures.


Failure Mechanism


The systems were experiencing random shutdowns or lockups  when a diskette was inserted. The failure was caused by the  electrical field generated when the charged floppy flap came  in contact with the grounded drive, as shown in Figure 1.


Figure 1: Failure Mechanism.


The phenomenon can be analyzed as follows. When the floppy  flap gets close enough to the grounded drive, the charge  rapidly transfers onto the drive, creating an arc. The resulting  current brings the charged floppy flap to a ground potential. This discharge generates an electric field inside the system.


DOI: 10.1361/cp2004istfa277


The electric field then couples with nets. The degree to which  the nets are affected depends on the strength of the electric  field. If the field is sufficiently large, it can generate enough  noise onto the signals to pull them below or above their logic  threshold. The end result is a failure visible to the user.


The electrical fields resulting from ESD events are  increasingly likely to cause system failures. The reason is that  state-of-the-art computer systems operate at lower voltages  and react faster to transient events. In the past, the amplitude  of most signals was 5 V and ICs were slower to respond to  glitches. Today, ICs react faster and are therefore more  sensitive to high-frequency noise. Typically, discharges occur  in a very short duration (10 ns to 100 ns). At the same time, signal amplitudes are smaller. Experimentally, low amplitude  signals are observed to be more sensitivity to noise, as shown  in Figure 2. Indeed, processor signals (1.3V) submitted to  noise are more likely to fail than PCI signals (3.3V). All these  technology changes make the overall system less tolerant to  disturbances.


Figure 2: Signals Sensitivity.


Motherboard Sensitivity Characterization


This section describes an experimental methodology to  characterize the sensitivity of motherboards to ESD. The  method simulates the system-level ESD events that can be  induced by any computer user.


When inserting a floppy disk, the systems experienced various  failure modes including random lockups, shutdowns, or  reboots. Those events were very intermittent. They heavily  depended on the external environment (e.g. temperature, humidity, floor type, and user behavior). Therefore, they were  very difficult to reproduce in an ordinary lab environment.


Two test techniques are developed to reliably reproduce the  failure. The first one is to discharge the ESD gun on the metal  floppy flap and insert a diskette in the drive, in a controlled  environment. The second test technique is to discharge an  ESD gun on a diskette covered with copper tape that is placed  inside the floppy drive.


Floppy Flap Test (Air Discharge Method)


This test method mimics most accurately the failures that  could be experienced by any computer user. An ESD gun is  discharged on the metal floppy flap, as shown in Figure 3. The  magnitude of the discharge is chosen to model the amount of  charge that would be induced on the floppy flap, when a user  walks on a carpet with the diskette in his or her pocket.


Figure 3: Floppy Flap Test.


This method requires a controlled environment. The  temperature and humidity must be constant to ensure the  repeatability of the test. The reason is that the generation of an  ESD arc can be hard to predict. In addition, the breakdown  voltage of an air gap is greatly influenced by atmospheric  conditions such as temperature and humidity. This  dependency has been studied extensively in the ESD literature [5, 6] and is shown in Figures 4, 5 and 6. All the figures are  taken from [5].


Figure 4 (© 1992 IEEE): Effect of Humidity on Breakdown of  a Rod-Plane Gap of 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm and 25 cm [5].


Figure 5 (© 1992 IEEE): Effect of Humidity on Breakdown of  a Rod-Plane Gap of 5 cm, 10 cm, 15 cm and 25 cm [5].


Figure 6 (© 1992 IEEE): Breakdown Characteristics of RodPlane Gap at Different Humidity Level [5].
